metadata.title: Data Center Site Selection and Navigating Power Procurement
metadata.author: Southern Economic Development Council
metadata.shortDescription:
Thor Equities, via its wholly owned platform Form8tion Data Centers, is a global data center developer. Executives from Form8tion will be speaking on the current state of the data center market, including large end-user site selection criteria and navigating the power landscape. Thor has executed multiple data center transactions with end users both in the US and EU and will be drawing on their decades of experience in the sector.  Participants will gain insight into what opportunities may be possible in their jurisdictions for data center development and what the challenges will be in securing power for those sites.

Speakers: 
Raj Vohra: (rvohra@thorequities.com), Head of Form8tion, Americas

Raj leads Thor’s Data Center program across the Americas, with 20+ years of leadership experience at Google and Deloitte. At Google, he drove data center acquisitions across the Americas, led global economic development initiatives, and shaped key organizational strategies. At Deloitte, he advised Fortune 500 clients on global location strategy. He holds a BA from Denison University and a JD from Notre Dame.

Faraz Ahmad: (fahmad@thorequities.com) Head of Energy and Infrastructure, Form8tion

Faraz leads Thor Equities’ Energy Strategy and Data Center Infrastructure, bringing 18+ years of global experience in energy, sustainability, and infrastructure. He previously led Amazon’s Net Zero Grid program and held senior roles at NextEra Energy, GE, Baker Hughes, and BCG. Faraz holds engineering degrees from the University of Cambridge, completed an exchange at MIT Sloan, and is a Fellow of the Energy Institute.

metadata.title: The Truth About AI Data Center Land (Most Sites Don’t Qualify)
metadata.author: Franklin Andrew Cruz
metadata.shortDescription:
99% of landowners think they have a site for an AI data center.
Most don’t.
I’m going through the process right now on a 130-acre site that could assemble to 288 acres, and these are the minimum requirements we’re confirming before even talking to operators.
First: Power
AI data centers typically require 1 megawatt of power per acre.
Most operators want 100+ acres, which means they need 100 MW or more available from the utility.
You must confirm with your electric company that they can actually supply that capacity.
Second: Natural Gas
AI data centers usually have 80–100 backup generators.
Those generators need a permanent natural gas or methane supply to operate during outages.
Third: Water
Large data centers require a significant water source for cooling systems.
Fourth: Location & Infrastructure
You still need the basics:
• Major power access
• Highway access
• Supportive zoning and municipalities
If you don’t have 100+ acres, 100 MW power availability, natural gas access, and water, your land probably isn’t a real candidate.
That’s the truth behind AI data center development.
Not the hype.

metadata.author: The Power Engineer
metadata.shortDescription:
Imagine a city of a million people moving in next door overnight — every home, hospital and factory plugging in through a single connection. That is what one AI data centre looks like to the power grid today.

This video explains AI data centre load and grid impact: why one frontier campus can draw one to two gigawatts, how AI server racks got ten times hungrier than the racks they replaced, what the IEA's numbers say about data centre electricity doubling by 2030, and the three problems that follow — timing, the connection queue, and cost. Plus the one skill power engineers should build now, because the bottleneck is no longer the chip. It is the plug.

metadata.title: Why AI Data Centers Are Building Their Own Power Plants
metadata.author: Behind the Ordinary
metadata.shortDescription:
Why AI data centers are building their own power plants comes down to a gap the chips cannot close. A new campus can be energized in months, while the grid interconnection queue, new transmission, transformers, and turbines can stretch toward 2031. This video explains why AI electricity demand is a density and rhythm problem, why the grid was never built for loads this large this fast, and why companies are turning to on-site gas generation, batteries, and long-term nuclear deals while they wait. It also follows who builds the power, who pays, and what happens to carbon, water, electricity bills, and the towns asked to host it. The grid is still the destination. The plants are the bridge.

Behind the Ordinary explores the hidden systems and surprising mechanisms behind the AI boom.

metadata.title: Planning for clean Energy - Assessing battery energy storage system (BESS) applications
metadata.author: Regen
metadata.shortDescription:
This video includes a 15-minute presentation based on Regen's guidance for local planning authorities in England on assessing Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) applications, which can be found here: https://www.regen.co.uk/insights/new-guidance-for-assessing-clean-energy-projects-supports-planners-in-delivering-the-transition

It also features two presentations from BESS developers, who discuss the process of identifying project sites, examples of projects where planning-related challenges were experienced and overcome, and opportunities for developers and planners to improve the planning process.

Key topics include:
- Fire risk and safety
- Site design and changing technology
- Operational noise

27:45 Harmony Energy - Frances Nicholson, development director

metadata.title: BESS 101 for developers: sizing, chemistry, revenue stacking
metadata.author: STG Nations Energy
metadata.shortDescription:
Everyone's adding batteries — but most developers can't answer the three questions that decide whether one makes money. This BESS 101 walks through them the way an independent engineer would: sizing (power vs energy — MW vs MWh — and sizing the ratio for the revenue), chemistry (why LFP beats NMC for most stationary grid storage), and revenue stacking (arbitrage, ancillary services, capacity — value that lives in the model, not the datasheet). Plus the three risks solar doesn't have: degradation & augmentation, thermal-runaway safety, and grid connection — and why an independent engineer, not the supplier or EPC, should check it all before you commit capital.
Book a consultation: stg-nations.com/contact / Website: stg-nations.com
Active in: Romania · Bulgaria · Germany · Spain · France · Belgium

developers, wind developers, funds,
utilities. A battery has become the
default answer to almost every energy
question.
But here's the uncomfortable part. Most

answer the three questions that actually
decide whether it makes money.
Not whether it works, whether it pays.
In the next few minutes, we'll walk
through those three questions the way an
engineer on your side would. So a
battery stops being a black box and
becomes a decision you can actually
make.
The first question is size, and it's
where most confusion starts.
People describe a battery with one
number, like 100 megawatt hours, as if
that says everything.
It doesn't, because a battery has two
sizes, not one.
Power, measured in megawatts, is how
fast it can charge or discharge. Energy,
measured in megawatt hours, is how long
it can keep going.
A 50 megawatt battery with 100 megawatt
hours runs for 2 hours.
Take the same energy, but half the
power, and it runs for four.
Same headline number, completely
different machine.
Which shape you need depends entirely on
what you're paid for.
Fast, short bursts of power are one
business. Long, steady hours of energy
are another.
Size the ratio for the revenue. Not for
the number that looks impressive on a
slide.
The second question is chemistry, and
here the market has already voted. For
years, the debate was LFP versus NMC.
NMC, nickel manganese cobalt, is more
energy dense.
It packs more into less space and less
weight.
That density was decisive for phones and
electric cars, where every kilogram
matters.
But a grid battery doesn't move. It sits
on the ground, where space is cheap.
So, the trade-offs flip.
LFP, lithium ion phosphate, is more
thermally stable, much safer against
thermal runaway, and lasts more charge
cycles.
For most stationary grid storage, LFP
wins on safety, on lifetime, and on
total cost. Which is exactly why the
industry has largely moved to it.
NMC still appears where footprint is
genuinely constrained.
But for a typical utility-scale project
in Europe, LFP is the honest default.
The mistake is letting a supplier's
inventory choose your chemistry for you.
The third question is the one that
separates a battery that works from a
battery that pays.
How it earns.
A solar farm has essentially one income
stream.
It sells the energy it produces.
A battery is different. It can earn from
several markets at once, and that
layering is where the real value lives.
It can buy energy when power is cheap
and sell it when power is expensive.
That's arbitrage.
It can get paid simply for being
available to stabilize grid frequency in
an instant.
Those are ancillary services.
It can be paid to exist as backup
capacity the grid can call on.
A well-run battery stacks these
revenues, moving between them as market
conditions change.
And here's the catch. None of that value
is on the data sheet. It lives entirely
in the model.
In the assumptions about prices, about
how often each market pays,
about how hard you can cycle the battery
without wearing it out.
Two identical batteries with two
different revenue models are two
completely different investments.
The hardware is the easy part. The money
is in the modeling. Now, the risks
because a battery has a few that solar
simply doesn't. The first is
degradation.
Lithium cells fade with every cycle. So,
the 100 megawatt hours you install is
not what you keep. If your revenue
depends on delivering a fixed capacity,
you either oversize on day one or
augment later with fresh cells. And who
pays for that fade has to be decided in
the contract, not discovered in year
five.
The second is safety.
A large battery stores an enormous
amount of energy in a small space. And
thermal runaway, a fire that feeds
itself, is the failure mode that keeps
lenders and insurers awake.
Fire suppression, thermal management,
cell spacing, and honest testing aren't
optional extras.
They're what makes the asset financeable
at all.
And the third, quietly, is the same one
that haunts every energy project, the
grid connection.
A battery that can't get the power in
and out on the terms it assumed is just
an expensive room full of chemistry.
So, who checks all of this before you
commit? Not the supplier selling you the
cells, they have a product to move. Not
the EPC building it, they have a
schedule to hit.
This is exactly the gap an independent
engineer fills.
Someone who sizes the battery for your
revenue, not the supplier's stock. Who
chooses the chemistry for your site, not

Who stress tests the revenue model

Someone with nothing to sell, but
judgment. That's what we do.
At STG Nations Energy, we help
developers and investors get battery
storage right. Sizing, chemistry,
revenue modeling, safety, and grid
connection.
Independently, with zero commissions

of the table.
A battery is one of the most powerful
assets in modern energy, but only if

If you're planning a storage project and
want it checked before you commit
capital,
book a consultation on our website,
stgnations.com.

metadata.title: Cummins Power Generation Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) launch unveil
metadata.author: Cummins
metadata.shortDescription:
Cummins Power Generation is proud to expand its sustainable solutions portfolio by launching a zero-emissions Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) product line. 

Cummins Power Generation BESS solutions are available in two architectural designs: a 10ft container (211 to 422kWh) and a 20ft high cube container (633kWh to 2.28MWh). Product distinctions include: 

- Fully containerized product with AC output 
- Expertly designed for maximum performance and safety 
- Proven lithium ferrophosphate (LFP) batteries for high cycle life 
- Optimal liquid cooling thermal management designed to maximize battery life and reliability 
- Comprehensive three-tier fire safety system 
- Plug-and-play solution 
- Designed to meet (or exceed) all major international 50 Hz requirements

The three main use cases for the product are off-grid (remote communities, mining sites, and remote industrial uses), energy management (EV charging infrastructure, commercial properties, and universities) and resiliency (data centers, healthcare facilities, water/wastewater treatment plants).

Learn more about Cummins BESS: https://www.cummins.com/generators/battery-energy-storage-systems

segments.text: Welcome to this explainer. Today, we're
going to completely demystify a
monumental $50 billion global industry
that is quite literally rewriting the
rules of the modern power grid. We're
talking about battery energy storage
systems, or BESS. If you've ever found
yourself wondering how on Earth we're
actually going to transition to clean
energy without the entire grid
collapsing, well, you are definitely in
the right place.
So, let's dive right into this by
anchoring ourselves to a really common
everyday problem. I want you to picture
what happens at exactly 6:00 p.m. The
sun has just gone down, which means
millions of solar panels across the
country have gone completely dark. But,
at that exact same moment, everybody's
getting home from work. Every air
conditioner, every oven, every
television is just getting turned on.
So, what actually happens to our
electricity when the sun sets, but the
demand for power skyrockets? Well, power
engineers actually have a name for this
glaring mismatch. They call it the duck
curve. And if you look at it, the curve
actually forms the silhouette of a duck.
That big belly right in the middle, that
represents this massive flood of solar
power hitting the grid in the middle of
the day when, honestly, nobody's really
home to use it. And that steep neck
reaching all the way up, that is the
sudden dramatic rush for energy in the
evening. To really wrap your head around
why this is such a huge crisis, imagine
a crazy busy restaurant kitchen that has
absolutely zero refrigerators. I mean,
having a massive delivery of fresh
ingredients at noon means absolutely
nothing if you can't store them for that
sudden rush of hungry customers at
dinner time, right? Without storage,
electricity has to be consumed the
precise second it's generated. And
because we don't have that storage
acting as a buffer everywhere yet, the
grid is literally forced to throw clean
power away. The scale of this waste is
just staggering. Just to put it into
perspective, in 2023 alone, the state of
California wasted 2.6 million megawatt
hours of clean solar energy just by
curtailing it. They essentially had to
call up solar farms and tell them to
turn off simply because there was
nowhere for that power to go.
So, how do we fix this? That brings us
to section one. Enter BESS, the hero. In
the absolute simplest terms, a BESS, or
battery energy storage system, is just a
giant rechargeable battery bank
connected directly to the electricity
grid. Think of it kind of like a massive
municipal water tank, or even a giant
smartphone power bank, but scaled up for
the entire electrical grid. It safely
soaks up all that abundant direct
current, or DC energy, during the day,
and then translates it into alternating
current, or AC power, releasing it back
to the grid exactly when we need it
most. Now, obviously, batteries aren't a
new invention, but doing this at a grid
scale, that is a modern marvel. We can
actually trace the evolution of this
technology right here on this timeline.
It starts way back with Gaston Plante's
heavy lead-acid battery in 1859. Then,
we see a massive leap in 1991, when
lightweight rechargeable lithium-ion
technology was commercialized. But, the
real magic, the real game-changer,
happens in the 2010s. That's what kicked
off this unprecedented gigawatt-scale
storage boom that is currently taking
over empty fields all around the world.
All right, let's get a little more
granular in section two, anatomy of
power, zooming in.
Building one of these grid-scale
facilities is, honestly, just like
stacking LEGO blocks, done in four
distinct steps. It all starts at the
base level with a single, small
lithium-ion battery cell. Engineers
group a bunch of those individual cells
together into a larger module. Next,
they take those modules and stack them
vertically into these tall, server-like
structures called battery racks. And
finally, rows and rows of these racks
are safely housed inside a massive,
climate-controlled shipping container.
But, the really crucial point inside
those base cells is the chemistry.
Operators have to carefully weigh this
constant trade-off narrative between
cost, safety, and lifespan. The big
three chemistries you'll hear about are
LFP, or lithium iron phosphate, NMC,
which is nickel manganese cobalt, and
the newer emerging sodium-ion tech. And
each one of these has completely
different strengths. For the grid,
though, there is a very clear winner
right now. You see, because a stationary
grid field out in the middle of nowhere
has plenty of space, engineers actively
choose the exceptionally safe, albeit
slightly bulky, LFP chemistry. It
absolutely dominates the market, making
up over 80% of new utility-scale
projects. It easily beats out the highly
dense, but way more expensive, NMC
batteries. Those are the ones you
typically find packed inside a compact
electric sports car, where saving space
is absolutely critical. Now, to manage
all this complex chemistry safely, those
physical batteries are paired with a
suite of digital brains. The battery
management system, or BMS, is kind of
like a strict teacher, just constantly
watching over the individual cells to
make sure they don't overheat.
Meanwhile, the energy management system,
or EMS, acts more like the school
principal, making high-level strategic
decisions on exactly when to buy and
sell power to the grid. Toss in the PCS
to translate that DC to AC power, and a
robust HVAC system to keep the
temperature perfectly controlled, and
boom, you have a fully functioning
plant.
Let's step back and look at the big
picture now in section three, the
impact, zooming out. What is truly
awe-inspiring about these sprawling
systems is their speed. A modern BES can
detect grid fluctuations, say a sudden
unexpected drop in wind power, and
respond by converting stored DC to AC
power and pushing it out to the grid in
under 20 milliseconds. Just to put that
into perspective for a second, that is
literally faster than a human blink. It
provides instant, seamless stability. To
maintain that incredible speed and
reliability over a decade or more,
engineers meticulously monitor three key
metrics. First is state of charge, or
SOC. That's simply your fuel gauge, how
full the battery is right at this
moment. Next is state of health, or SOH,
which measures long-term degradation.
It's a lot like how your old smartphone
just doesn't hold a charge like it used
to, right? And finally, depth of
discharge, or DOD, which tracks exactly
how much of the battery's capacity was
used up in a single cycle. And that
brings us to the absolute golden rule in
energy storage. Every battery cycle is a
trade-off between how much you use it
today and how long it lasts tomorrow.
Think of depth of discharge like
running. If you go out and sprint a full
marathon every single day, you are going
to wear your body down way faster than
if you just took a light daily jog. In
the exact same way, shallow, careful
battery discharges drastically extend
the overall life of a BSS plant. Okay.

metadata.title: The Economics of Grid-Scale Batteries Explained
metadata.author: Modo Energy
metadata.shortDescription:
Dive into batteries, renewables and US power markets on the Modo Energy Terminal, and talk to Ko, our AI analyst: https://modoenergy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=content-marketing&utm_content=will-bess

From the outside, a grid-scale battery is pretty boring. It's usually white and looks like a shipping container. So why is everyone building them?

In this Modo Energy explainer, we look inside grid-scale battery energy storage (BESS): what it is, why it gets built, and how it makes money.

What is a grid-scale battery?
Inside the container are racks of batteries like the ones in your phone, typically using the same lithium-ion chemistry. The difference is scale and duration. Some batteries, like iron-air batteries, can last for days.

Why are grid-scale batteries built?
Mainly for two reasons: grid reliability, because they can turn on or off quickly when the grid is stressed, and financial returns, because they can charge and discharge when prices spike high or low.

Why do renewables make batteries more valuable?
Intermittent renewable generation makes prices less predictable. Batteries help smooth that out without building expensive, fossil-fuel-heavy natural gas plants.

How do grid-scale batteries make money?
There are three main ways. Energy arbitrage, charging when prices are low and discharging when they are high. Capacity, being paid to stay available in case the grid needs them. And ancillary services, charging and discharging to help manage voltage and steady-state operations.

Why does location matter so much?
Markets, prices and need all vary by region, so where a battery is sited is incredibly important to its returns.

Why can batteries be built faster than gas plants?
Batteries are prefabricated and brought to site, so once you have the land they can be connected and start operating far sooner, often years earlier than a natural gas plant.

Battery storage has gone from an afterthought to what everyone is looking towards. In New York (NYISO), the entire interconnection is either renewables or energy storage.

Let's discuss the property qualifications for data center development. Our Product Analyst, Mehrbano, discusses the 6 different qualifications for property owners to look for when assessing land. 

- Buildable Acreage: How much of your property is suitable for a data center to be built?
- Available Offtake Capacity: Are you near a substation?
- Fiber Optic Lines: Are you near fiber optic lines for easy connection?
- Water Proximity: Do you have water located on or nearby your property for cooling the data center?
- Redundancy Source: Do you have any backup power sources nearby?
- Renewable Energy: Are there any renewable energy sources like solar or wind farms near your property?

Using our tool, LandApp, will help you conduct property due diligence for identifying buildable acreage, electrical infrastructure, water proximity, and potential risks that could exist on the property. Want to learn more about LandApp? https://bit.ly/4bq0ngi

metadata.shortDescription:
Data centers sit at the crossroads of real estate, energy, and technology—and they’re exploding in demand thanks to AI and our always-online lives. In this episode of The Alternative Investing Advantage, host Alex Perny talks with Mike Embry of Embry Companies about how investors and developers can capitalize on the data center boom in the Southeast.

Mike explains how power, fiber, water, sewer, and politics all shape where data centers get built, what it costs to entitle land, and why a single site can generate 3x the profit of a residential project. They also dive into gray-water cooling, natural gas turbines, redundancy, zoning battles, and why having a “Plan B” (industrial, multifamily, or commercial) is critical on every deal.

segments.text: Industry Voice: How powered land is
changing data center site selection.
This Industry Voice comes from Daniel
Faris and Rachel Conrad of Foley &
Lardner LLP, who work across data
centers, digital infrastructure,
technology, and energy.
In the modern-day gold rush to identify
and procure the best sites to support
the AI infrastructure boom, the most
valuable data center asset is not land.
It's land with power or grid
interconnect already attached. Recent
research shows that obtaining power is
the key obstacle to successful data
center development that developers face
during site selection, cited by roughly
2/3 of respondents who were surveyed for
the Foley 2026 Data Center Report. Power
as the gating factor. Most data centers
are connected to the grid as a steady
and dependable source of power.
However, the immense amount of
electricity required by data centers
running HPC loads supporting AI training
or inference systems has quickly placed
strain on current grid infrastructure.
US data centers consumed roughly 176
terawatt hours of electricity in 2023,
about 4.4% of the nation's total, after
more than doubling their draw since
2017. The Department of Energy's
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
projects, in its 2024 US Data Center
Energy Usage Report, that figure could
reach 325 to 582 hours by 2028,
or as much as 12% of all US electricity,
translating to a power demand of 74 to
132 gigawatts. While developers are
pushing to quickly construct and deliver
data centers to answer the skyrocketing
demand for compute power,
the buildout of the grid necessary to
match that expansion cannot keep up.
Because of this, developers must be more
judicious in the site selection process
to confirm that grid capacity is
available, or alternatively, to seek out
multiple alternative energy sources such
as microgrids, gas turbines, fuel cells,
or renewables,
which can come online more quickly, and
in some cases, can provide cheaper
electricity. As power has become the
gating factor for development timelines,
developers are increasingly inverting
the traditional site selection process.
Historically, location decisions
prioritized proximity to network
infrastructure, favorable tax regimes,
climate conditions, and land cost with
utility service treated as a necessary
but largely solvable step that followed
land acquisition.
Today, that sequence is often reversed.
Developers are starting with available
megawatts and working backward to
determine whether a site can support the
balance of technical, regulatory, and
commercial requirements for a data
center campus. This shift has given rise
to the growing premium placed on powered
land.
Sites that already benefit from existing
substations, meaningful load capacity,
or advanced positioning in a utility's
interconnection queue.
In many markets, these attributes matter
more than raw acreage or even real
estate pricing.
A smaller or less than perfect parcel
with confirmed power can be
substantially more valuable than a
larger, greener site that faces
uncertainty around timing or feasibility
of grid upgrades.
Early interconnection as a competitive
advantage.
Power availability is now a front and
strategic consideration.
Developers that secure early
interconnection agreements gain a
significant competitive advantage, not
only by shortening development
timelines, but also by improving project
finance certainty.
Being further along in the
interconnection queue can mean the
difference between moving forward with
construction or shelving a project for
years.
Utilities, for their part, are
increasingly inundated with
interconnection requests from data
center developers whose projected loads
dwarf historical demand. As a result,
queue delays have become common and
utilities are scrutinizing applications
more closely, often requiring detailed
project information and financial
commitments earlier in the process.
This heightened scrutiny has reinforced
a first-mover dynamic.
Developers that move quickly to lock up
power rights can effectively control
future growth in a given region.
That urgency has pushed many developers
to pursue land options or purchase
agreements that are expressly
conditioned on securing power rather
than closing on land and hoping for the
best.
Power-centric site control structures,
including long-term options, phased
closings, or joint development
arrangements with landowners or
utilities,
are becoming increasingly common as a
way to manage risk while maintaining
flexibility. Collocated generation and
behind-the-meter solutions.
Where grid power is constrained or
timelines are uncertain, developers are
increasingly turning to collocated
generation as a bridge or long-term
solution. Onsite or adjacent power
generation, whether gas-fired turbines,
renewable facilities paired with
storage, or hybrid energy systems,
allows developers to bring capacity
online faster while reducing dependence
on large-scale grid upgrades.
These behind-the-meter
solutions can offer additional benefits
beyond speed.
Collocated generation may provide cost
stability, redundancy, and resilience,
particularly in regions with congestion
or vulnerability to extreme weather
events. For AI-driven facilities
operating high-density workloads,
reliability and uptime are paramount,
making self-generation an attractive
option even where grid power is
technically available.
At the same time, collocated power
raises a host of legal, regulatory, and
commercial considerations. Developers
must navigate permitting regimes,
environmental compliance, fuel supply
contracts, and long-term power
management strategies, all while
ensuring that any on-site generation
aligns with sustainability commitments
and customer expectations.
As these structures become more
prevalent, early coordination between
real estate, energy, and regulatory
teams is increasingly essential.
Geographic expansion beyond traditional
data center hubs. The scramble for power
is also accelerating geographic
diversification.
Established data center markets often
face the most acute grid constraints due
to saturation and limited expansion
capacity. In response, developers are
looking beyond traditional hubs to
secondary and emerging markets where
utilities may have greater flexibility
to serve large loads.
These new markets frequently offer a
combination of available land, receptive
local governments, and underutilized
transmission or generation assets.
For some municipalities, large-scale
data center development represents an
opportunity to attract investment and
expand the tax base, provided that
infrastructure impacts can be managed
responsibly. This dynamic has opened
doors in regions that historically saw
little hyperscale development, but can
now support it with the right planning.
However, moving into less proven markets
also carries risk. Developers must
assess not only power availability, but
also long-term regulatory stability,
community support, workforce access, and
network connectivity.
While power may be easier to secure
initially, projects can face delays if
local permitting frameworks are
unprepared for the scale and complexity
of modern data centers. As power-driven
site selection expands the map,
thoughtful engagement with state and
local stakeholders becomes even more
critical. Looking ahead, power as the
primary constraint.
As AI adoption accelerates and compute
demands continue to rise, the pressure
on the grid shows no signs of easing.
While long-term grid modernization and
expansion are underway, those efforts
will take years to materialize at scale.
In the interim, power availability will
remain the dominant constraint shaping
where, how, and how fast data centers
are built. For developers, this reality
underscores the importance of
integrating power strategy into the
earliest stages of site selection and
project planning. Securing land without
power is increasingly a speculative
exercise. By contrast, controlling
powered land or having a clear, credible
path to power can unlock development
opportunities even in otherwise
challenging markets.
In this new paradigm, successful data
center development hinges on seeing
sites not just as parcels of land, but
as nodes in an evolving energy
ecosystem. As the industry adapts, power
will continue to redefine value, drive
innovation, and redraw the data center
map.

metadata.title: PJM Interconnection Explained: How Data Centers Connect to the Power Grid
metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
AI data centers are overwhelming the PJM grid — 
and the rules for how they connect just changed. 
This video breaks down PJM's 2025 CIFP Stage 4 
rules, the 3 connection paths, the new EIT 
fast-lane, and what every data center developer 
needs to know before filing.

Read the full breakdown: https://keentelengineering.com/pjm-large-load-interconnection

📌 CHAPTERS
0:00 The Grid Wasn't Built for This
1:18 Network Load vs. Islanded Co-Location
2:06 Three Paths — One Decision
3:04 Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT)
4:02 Signed ≠ Counted
4:52 Three Projects — Three Lessons
4:48 What Happens and When
6:48 Answers to the Big Questions

#PJM #PowerGrid #LargeLoadInterconnection #DataCenter #GridReliability

segments.text: Welcome to Keen Tell Engineering. This
presentation covers PJM's 2025 CIFP
Stage 4 rules, the most significant
update to large load interconnection
policy in years. If you're planning a
data center in PJM territory, these
rules govern how you connect, how fast
you can get there, and what it's going
to cost you. PJM is forecasting 75,000
MW of new peak demand by the mid-2040s.
There are three workable integration
paths, a new expedited track targeting
10 months from application to agreement,
and a hard cap of 10 EIT projects per
year. Let's walk through what changed
and what to do about it. PJM's peak load
forecast is climbing by 75,000 MW over
the next 20 years, from around 155,000
to 230,000 MW. AI data centers are
almost entirely responsible for that
growth. To put that in context, this
follows more than 15 years of
essentially flat demand growth. The grid
was sized, planned, and operated for a
world where load barely moved. That
world ended. Data centers currently
represent only about 3% of PJM's demand
response capacity, meaning the
infrastructure needed to serve them at
scale has barely begun to be built. That
gap between what the grid was designed
for and what it's now being asked to do
is the entire reason PJM rewrote these
rules. PJM has a clear preference, and
it's worth understanding before anything
else. Full network load integration is
what PJM wants. When you're a network
load, you're counted in the load
forecast and in the reliability pricing
mechanism. You're curtailed only in a
genuine grid emergency, the same
protection residential customers get.
You have access to the EIT fast lane,
and the operational complexity is
significantly lower. The alternative,
islanded co-location under options four
and five, comes with real drawbacks.
You're invisible to PJM planning and the
reliability pricing mechanism. You need
complex relay schemes to manage the
isolation. Your curtailment protection
is weaker, and the regulatory posture
remains uncertain. PJM hasn't closed the
door on islanding, but it has made clear
which side of that door it wants you on.
Once you've decided to integrate as a
network load, you have three paths, and
the right one depends on your timeline,
your risk tolerance, and what generation
you can commit to. Path one is bring
your own generation, the fastest and
most reliable route. You pair your load
with committed generation on a UCAP
basis, and you're curtailed only in a
genuine emergency. Residential-like
treatment. Path two is demand response,
lower cost and more flexible. You earn
better curtailment terms by agreeing to
reduce load during grid stress events.
Data centers represent only about 3% of
PJM's DR capacity today, so there's
significant room to grow into this path.
Path three is non-capacity backed load,
a transitional bridge. It's only
available when PJM supply falls short of
the reliability requirement, and it
integrates at reduced cost with no
capacity charges. The key strategic
point, these paths are not mutually
exclusive. Use path three to get
energized sooner, then migrate to path
one as your generation comes online. The
expedited interconnection track, EIT, is
the most significant process change in
these rules. It's a new fast lane
designed specifically for shovel-ready
generation paired with large load, and
it launches mid-2026.
The headline number is 10 months from
application to interconnection
agreement, a fraction of the years-long
timelines that have become the norm. But
the requirements to qualify are strict.
Your generation must exceed 250 MW of
unforced capacity. That's UCAP, not
nameplate. You'll pay a non-refundable
readiness deposit of $10,000 to $20,000
per MW at application, and there is zero
flexibility after filing. No changes to
site, fuel type, or MW size once your
application is submitted. The trade is
explicit, speed and certainty in
exchange for real capital commitment and
a fully locked design. If you're not
ready to commit completely, the EIT is
not the right track. This is one of the
most important slides in this entire
presentation, and it's one of the most
commonly misunderstood rules. A signed
contract with your utility does not
automatically mean PJM counts your
megawatts in its load forecast. PJM
applies forecast discounting based on
when your project is scheduled to come
online. Projects in the earliest
in-service years are discounted 100%.
They don't count at all until milestones
are met. Projects in the middle years
face roughly a 40% reduction. Later
years see about a 33% reduction. What
you can do to push back on those
defaults, submit your contractual
milestones, provide project-specific
ramp data that reflects your actual load
profile, supply utilization evidence to
demonstrate real operational intent, and
make full duplication disclosure if
you're requesting capacity at multiple
points.
Conservative defaults are PJM's starting
position, but they are yours to override
with the right evidence. Three case
studies, each one illustrating a
different way these rules play out in
practice. Case A is bring your own
generation. The key lesson, UCAP match
governs, not nameplate capacity. You
need to account for forced outage
derating when sizing your generation
commitment. And once you're in the EIT,
inflexibility is the price of the speed
you're getting. Case B is pipeline meets
forecast discounting. The key lesson
here is the one from the previous slide.
A signed contract is not counted
megawatt. PJM's conservative defaults
will apply until you override them with
project-specific evidence. Don't assume
your utility contract translates
directly into forecast credit. Case C is
transitional bridge before supply
arrives. The key lesson, paths are
sequencing tools, not a one-time binary
choice. If your generation isn't ready
yet, path three gets you energized while
you work toward path one. Strategy is
about sequencing, not just selecting.
Here's the full regulatory timeline, so
you know exactly what's in force, what's
coming, and when to act. Right now,
today, duplicate request disclosure
requirements are in force, milestone
inclusion criteria apply, and PJM is
using 3-year ramp and 70% utilization
defaults for all load forecasting. In
June 2026, auction reforms take effect.
The PRD dynamic rate is removed, demand
response dispatch order gets re-aligned,
and a data center specific ELC class is
proposed. Mid-2026 is the big one. The
EIT fast lane opens.
NDA transparency rules take effect, and
state commission review processes begin.
In 2027, forecast reform kicks in with
enhanced methodology, third-party
cross-checking, and milestone waiting
built into the model. And from 2029
onward, longer-term reforms follow, a
limited duration demand response
product, post-CIFP enhancements, and RPM
backstop reforms. The window between now
and mid-2026 is your preparation time.
Use it. Four questions that come up in
almost every conversation about these
rules.
First, does your generation need to be
co-located with your load under path
one? No. What matters is meeting load on
a UCAP basis and committing to the
reliability pricing mechanism, whether
by ownership or PPA.
Physical proximity can help
operationally, but it is not a
regulatory requirement. Second, what is
UCAP and why does PJM use it instead of
nameplate?
Unforced capacity D-rates a generator
based on its forced outage history. In
practice, this means you'll generally
need more nameplate capacity than your
peak load to clear the match. Plan for
that gap. Third, when would you face
curtailment under non-capacity backed
load? You accept pre-emergency
curtailment before firm load procedures
begin. Residential customers retain
priority in extreme conditions. Your
load is interruptible before that
threshold. And fourth, can you combine
paths instead of choosing just one? Yes,
they are explicitly not mutually
exclusive. The most common strategy is
using path three as a bridge to get
energized sooner than migrating to path
one as your generation comes online.
Five actions in priority order.
One, plan to be a network load, not an
island. The regulatory and operational
advantages are clear and PJM's
preference is unambiguous.
Two, decide early which path fits your
timeline. The paths have very different
capital requirements and flexibility
profiles. The longer you wait to choose,
the fewer options you have.
Three, treat your forecast submission as
a deliverable, not a formality. The data
you submit, milestones, ramp profiles,
utilization evidence directly determines
how PJM counts your megawatts.
Four, watch the dockets and the
deposits. EIT has a hard cap of 10
projects per year. When that window
opens mid-2026, positions fill fast and
the deposits are non-refundable. Five,
think sequencing, not just selecting.
The paths are tools to be combined
across time, not a one-time menu. If you
need support with POI interconnection
engineering, power system studies, load
forecast submissions, transmission
planning, or NERC compliance, reach out
to Keentel Engineering at 813-389-7871
or keentelengineering.com.

Conservative defaults are PJM's starting position, but they are yours to override with the right evidence. Three case studies, each one illustrating a different way these rules play out in practice. Case A is bring your own generation. The key lesson, UCAP match governs, not nameplate capacity. You need to account for forced outage derating when sizing your generation commitment. And once you're in the EIT, inflexibility is the price of the speed you're getting. Case B is pipeline meets forecast discounting. The key lesson here is the one from the previous slide. A signed contract is not counted megawatt. PJM's conservative defaults will apply until you override them with project-specific evidence. Don't assume your utility contract translates directly into forecast credit. Case C is transitional bridge before supply arrives. The key lesson, paths are sequencing tools, not a one-time binary choice. If your generation isn't ready yet, path three gets you energized while you work toward path one. Strategy is about sequencing, not just selecting. Here's the full regulatory timeline, so you know exactly what's in force, what's coming, and when to act. Right now, today, duplicate request disclosure requirements are in force, milestone inclusion criteria apply, and PJM is using 3-year ramp and 70% utilization defaults for all load forecasting. In June 2026, auction reforms take effect. The PRD dynamic rate is removed, demand response dispatch order gets re-aligned, and a data center specific ELC class is proposed. Mid-2026 is the big one. The EIT fast lane opens. NDA transparency rules take effect, and state commission review processes begin. In 2027, forecast reform kicks in with enhanced methodology, third-party cross-checking, and milestone waiting built into the model. And from 2029 onward, longer-term reforms follow, a limited duration demand response product, post-CIFP enhancements, and RPM backstop reforms. The window between now and mid-2026 is your preparation time. Use it. Four questions that come up in almost every conversation about these rules. First, does your generation need to be co-located with your load under path one? No. What matters is meeting load on a UCAP basis and committing to the reliability pricing mechanism, whether by ownership or PPA. Physical proximity can help operationally, but it is not a regulatory requirement. Second, what is UCAP and why does PJM use it instead of nameplate? Unforced capacity D-rates a generator based on its forced outage history. In practice, this means you'll generally need more nameplate capacity than your peak load to clear the match. Plan for that gap. Third, when would you face curtailment under non-capacity backed load? You accept pre-emergency curtailment before firm load procedures begin. Residential customers retain priority in extreme conditions. Your load is interruptible before that threshold. And fourth, can you combine paths instead of choosing just one? Yes, they are explicitly not mutually exclusive. The most common strategy is using path three as a bridge to get energized sooner than migrating to path one as your generation comes online. Five actions in priority order. One, plan to be a network load, not an island. The regulatory and operational advantages are clear and PJM's preference is unambiguous. Two, decide early which path fits your timeline. The paths have very different capital requirements and flexibility profiles. The longer you wait to choose, the fewer options you have. Three, treat your forecast submission as a deliverable, not a formality. The data you submit, milestones, ramp profiles, utilization evidence directly determines how PJM counts your megawatts. Four, watch the dockets and the deposits. EIT has a hard cap of 10 projects per year. When that window opens mid-2026, positions fill fast and the deposits are non-refundable. Five, think sequencing, not just selecting. The paths are tools to be combined across time, not a one-time menu. If you need support with POI interconnection engineering, power system studies, load forecast submissions, transmission planning, or NERC compliance, reach out to Keentel Engineering at 813-389-7871 or keentelengineering.com.

metadata.title: Ending the "Stupid Land" Queue: ERCOT's New Rules for Massive Power Loads
metadata.author: WhyPKD
metadata.shortDescription:
The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) is currently facing an overwhelming 438,000 megawatts of large load requests seeking interconnection to the Texas grid by 2032
. Driven largely by a rapid influx of applications for massive new data centers, these staggering numbers live in "stupid land"—representing a volume of speculative projects that lack the global supply chain support to ever fully materialize
.
In this video, we break down ERCOT's new "Batch Zero" strategy, a coordinated planning process designed to rescue grid planners from a paralyzing backlog
. Under the old system, utilities evaluated each massive project individually, leading to morphing study outcomes and endless sequential evaluations as new applications poured in
. Now, ERCOT is hoovering up projects over 75 megawatts and assigning them to a group to evaluate their combined system impact
.
We explain how this new approach will force out weaker, "phantom" loads by imposing strict requirements for project maturity and financial strength
. To join Batch Zero, developers must submit proof of site control and regulatory approvals, post a $50,000 per megawatt deposit, and cover 100% of the direct infrastructure upgrade costs (CIAC) to ensure everyday ratepayers are protected
.
With major deadlines kicking off in July and extending through 2027, Batch Zero aims to bring rationality to the interconnection queue
. Finally, we discuss how ERCOT's transition to a cluster-study approach could provide a vital roadmap for other grid operators worldwide, who are currently flying blind while facing unprecedented urgency to connect massive new loads
.
Key Topics Covered in this Video:
The massive 438,000 MW backlog of data center and large load requests
.
Why the old individual utility study process was failing
.
How ERCOT's new Batch Zero process groups projects over 75 MW
.
Strict financial requirements, including a $50k/MW fee and ratepayer protections
.
The project timeline for developers, from the July 10th submission deadline to final 2027 interconnection agreements
.

metadata.title: Batch Zero 9-Month Clock Starts: ERCOT Large Load Interconnection Workshop 3 — Feb 26, 2026
metadata.author: James Dickey
metadata.shortDescription:
WHAT YOU'LL HEAR
• ERCOT's Batch Zero process is structured as a 6-month initial study + 3-month refinement study, totaling 9–10 months on a 6-month cadence
• MW allocations to large loads are locked after the initial batch study commitment window — allocations do not change during the refinement phase, only the transmission upgrade plan can be adjusted
• Loads that cannot be reliably served in 2028–2032 will be automatically allocated full MWs in 2033, relying on existing transmission planning for solutions
• PUC rulemakings 58-480 (load forecast) and 58-481 (interconnection requirements) are tightly linked — loads must meet 58-481 criteria to appear in ERCOT's planning forecast
• Option 1 for Batch Zero criteria replicates draft 58-481 language in the planning guide now, enabling an earlier start; Option 2 waits for the final rule, delaying Batch Zero until fall 2026
• Loads energizing by end of 2027 must demonstrate development activity — inclusion in the May 2026 QSA, or attestation of begun site prep plus purchase of customer-owned high-voltage transformers and circuit breakers — to qualify as baseload
• A June 1 six-month look-back snapshot will identify capacity that can be reallocated if a load is not consuming what was modeled
• Financial security for the interconnection agreement is set at the end of the 6-month study and is not intended to change based on refinement study outcomes
• PUC's new large load rule 25.37 sets new criteria for loads 75 MW or greater in the 2026 RTP compliance plan — inclusion in the 2025 RTP does not automatically qualify a load for 2026
• Rishi (PUC Project 58-441 commenter) presented a Controllable Load Resource (CLR) concept paper arguing ERCOT's existing SCED infrastructure already supports large loads using paired resources to neutralize delivery constraints
• A CLR compliance framework modeled on existing auxiliary load attestation forms for integrated BESS — requiring ongoing third-party validation — was proposed
• Stability screening occurs during the batch phase as a screening tool; a full robust stability study is conducted during the refinement period
• PUC commissioners had not yet voted to publish the 58-481 draft in the Texas Register as of the hearing date; the final rule may differ from the current discussion draft
• ERCOT stated the batch process is designed as close iterative collaboration with TSPs throughout both phases — not a black-box study followed by a scramble for upgrades

metadata.shortDescription: Iberdrola Renewables has been a part of PJM since 2007, building and operating 815 megawatts of wind power at five facilities -- enough to power more than 210,270 000 homes. PJM Interconnection, the world's largest competitive wholesale electricity market, is a regional transmission organization operating an electric transmission system serving states in the Mid-Atlantic to the Midwest.

metadata.title: Large Load Interconnection to ERCOT
metadata.author: Data Centers Technical Info
metadata.shortDescription:
In this insightful conversation, I had a great discussion with Eric Meier, Supervisor of Planning Modeling at ERCOT, to discuss one of the most dynamic topics shaping the future of the grid: large load interconnection and the rise of data centers.

We explore:
✅ How ERCOT is handling rapid load growth and maintaining network reliability
✅ The role of planning models and forecasting in interconnection studies
✅ The impact of hyperscale data centers and energy-intensive industries
✅ Current industry efforts and initiatives supporting grid stability
✅ Opportunities for collaboration between stakeholders, developers, and system operators

Whether you’re a grid planner, developer, consultant, or just interested in the future of power systems, this discussion offers valuable insights straight from the heart of ERCOT

metadata.title: Should Data Centers Bring Their Own Power or Wait in Line?
metadata.author: Profound Studies
metadata.shortDescription:
Should data centers bring their own power or wait in line? Texas alone has 474 GW in line, more than five times its record demand, and roughly 90% of it is data centers, according to Gov. Greg Abbott's August 3, 2026 letter. So why can't data centers just plug in?

This explainer maps three bottlenecks: the queue in Texas (ERCOT's audit and delayed first study batch), a power shortfall in the PJM region (a July 2026 auction capped at $325/MW-day and about 6.8 GW short of its reliability target), and grid equipment with waits of 160+ weeks for key transformers, according to Wood Mackenzie. It also covers FERC's October 9, 2026 decision largely rejecting PJM's large-load plan while approving a large-load definition and registry.

Should data centers bring their own power, or wait their turn on the grid? Tell us in the comments, and like and follow Profound Studies for more politics, economy and society explainers.

Video credits: B-roll: Pexels (stock footage, illustrative; Pexels license). Object images: Pexels video frames; coins, clock, gavel and cooling towers from Wikimedia Commons (free licenses). Map: Natural Earth and US Census boundaries (public domain). Regions, request locations and the PJM footprint are schematic illustrations, not official boundaries. Figures are attributed on screen to their sources and dated; some may have changed since.

Educational and informational content only.

segments.text: Texas has more than five times its
record power demand waiting in line.
That is 474 gigawatts, and about 90% of
it is data centers.
So why can't they just plug in? Because
there is not one problem. There are
three. And the first one is hiding in
Texas.
On August 3rd, 2026, Governor Greg
Abbott ordered an audit of every data
center in the state's grid queue. Ercot,
the grid operator, delayed the first
study batch of its new large load
process.
The line keeps growing. In June, Texas
regulators approved a first formal
process for connecting large loads when
the queue stood at more than 438
gigawatts. By August, the governor was
citing 474.
But wait, how can a line be five times
bigger than anything Texas has ever
used? Ercot's own forecast says peak
demand could more than quadruple by
2032. Then it adds a warning, that
forecast may be inflated.
Not every request on that list is a
project that will be built. That is why
Texas wants to count before it connects
anything.
Now go east because here the story
flips. PJM runs the grid across much of
the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest. In its
July auction for 2028, the price hit the
cap, $325 per megawatt day.
And the region still came up about 6.8
gigawatts short of its reliability
target. Only 525 megawatts of new supply
showed up. PJM said a 2 gigawatt jump in
forecast demand came largely from data
centers.
What would the price have been without a
cap? Near $555.
PJM put the cap bill at $16.4 billion
against 29.7 billion uncapped.
So here the problem is different. Texas
has too many requests. PJM may not have
enough power to give anyone.
Fine, suppose you fix both. Can you
build it? According to Wood Mackenzie,
speaking to Reuters in July, the wait
for a generator step-up transformer
passed 160 weeks in the first quarter of
this year. In 2024, it averaged 143.
High voltage circuit breakers went from
77 weeks in 2023 to 125 weeks last year.
One utility said big substation
transformers are now pushing past a
three-year wait.
Utilities are changing how they shop.
One municipal utility, Roseville
Electric, moved from planning equipment
one year ahead to planning three years
ahead.
Wood Mackenzie also expects transformer
prices to rise by about 4 to 10% over
the next year. Equipment is getting
slower and more expensive at the same
time.
And demand will not wait. Wood Mackenzie
expects US data center capacity to climb
from about 24 gigawatts today to 110 by
So who decides who goes first? On
October 9th, FERC, the federal
regulator, largely rejected PJM's plan
for connecting big loads. It would have
let data centers connect sooner without
matching new capacity if they agreed to
be cut off during emergencies.
Why? FERC said parts of it intrude on
state control of retail rates and appear
to discriminate against large loads. It
did approve PJM's definition of a large
load and a registry that records each
facility's location, ramp schedule, and
power supply.
Notice the pattern. Texas is auditing
its list. PJM is building a register.
Everyone is trying to find out which
data centers are real.
The idea behind PJM's rejected plan has
a name, bring your own new capacity.
Data centers that accept cuts in an
emergency could connect sooner. FERC did
not accept the way PJM wrote it.
So the grid is not closed to data
centers. It is crowded, short of supply,
and waiting on equipment, all at the
same time.
Should data centers bring their own
power or wait their turn on the grid?

metadata.title: Post-SGIA Interconnection Studies in ERCOT | From SGIA to Grid Synchronization | Keentel Engineering
metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
What happens after a Standard Generation Interconnection Agreement (SGIA) is signed in ERCOT?

Signing the SGIA is a major milestone—but it is not the finish line. Before a solar, wind, BESS, or hybrid project can synchronize and achieve commercial operation, developers must complete a rigorous post-SGIA engineering process involving as-built modeling, Quarterly Stability Assessment (QSA), Model Quality Testing (MQT), PSCAD EMT studies, reactive capability, ride-through, harmonic analysis, protection coordination, energization studies, and TSP approvals.

In this video, Keentel Engineering explains the complete post-SGIA interconnection roadmap in ERCOT, from the signed agreement through initial energization, synchronization, commissioning, and commercial operation.

What You'll Learn

• Post-SGIA ERCOT interconnection requirements
• Quarterly Stability Assessment (QSA)
• As-built PSS®E, TSAT and PSCAD models
• Model Quality Tests (MQT) and model validation
• ERCOT vs. Transmission Service Provider (TSP) requirements
• NOGRR 245 and IEEE 2800-2022 ride-through requirements
• Reactive capability and 0.95 leading/lagging power factor
• PSCAD EMT studies for inverter-based resources
• Harmonic and power-quality studies under IEEE 519
• Transformer energization and inrush studies
• Short-circuit and protection coordination
• Part 1 energization and backfeed
• Part 2 initial synchronization and hold-point testing
• Part 3 commercial operation and field testing
• Post-commissioning model verification

In reality, the project enters a detailed engineering and approval phase. ERCOT evaluates system-wide stability and model fidelity, while the local TSP evaluates protection, switching, power quality, and equipment-specific requirements. A project must satisfy both sides before moving toward synchronization.

CHAPTERS

00:55 The SGIA "False Summit"
01:45 From GINR to QSA
02:35 ERCOT vs. TSP Engineering Requirements
03:35 As-Built PSS®E, TSAT & PSCAD Models
04:25 Model Quality Testing & Validation
05:15 NOGRR 245, IEEE 2800 & Reactive Capability
06:15 Protection, Harmonics & Transformer Inrush
07:10 Part 1, Part 2 & Part 3 Commissioning
08:10 Six-Stage Post-SGIA Engineering Methodology
09:15 Real-World ERCOT Project Lessons
10:15 QSA Schedule & COD Risk
10:40 Final Engineering Takeaways

segments.text: Today we're diving into one of the most
critical yet frequently underestimated
phases in power project development,
post SGIA interconnection in URT.
Signing your standard generation
interconnection agreement is a massive
milestone. But it is not the finish
line. From the moment that ink dries to
the day you synchronize to the grid,
your project enters a rigorous gauntlet
of advanced engineering, stability
evaluations, and utility approvals. This
playbook breaks down the exact technical
roadmap required to bridge that gap and
bring your plant successfully online. In
URT, developers often face what we call
the false summit. The myth is that once
your SGIA is signed, you're essentially
cleared to energize. The reality is far
harsher.
[sighs and gasps]
Between that signed agreement and your
first breaker close lies an intensive
gauntlet of asbuilt modeling model
checks, quarterly stability assessments,
and transmission service provider
approvals. And here are the stakes.
URT's QSA process operates on an
unforgiving quarterly cycle. If you miss
a prerequisite deadline or fail a model
quality test, your synchronization
window slips by a full quarter,
translating to millions of dollars in
delayed operational revenue. Let's look
at the complete architecture from study
to COOD. Phase one is the foundation,
your initial GINR studies, screening and
full interconnection studies. Once the
SGIA is executed, you enter phase 2, the
engineering gauntlet. Note that if your
SGIA was signed after August 1st, 2024,
it triggers strict compliance with
NOGRR245
and ILE E2800 2022 standards. Here you
must clear the cyclical quarterly
stability assessment. Clearing QSA
unlocks phase 3 synchronization.
This rolls out in three distinct
milestones. Part one, initial
energization and back feed. Part two,
initial synchronization with staged hold
point testing above 20 NVA. And finally,
part three, commercial operation
following reactive and primary frequency
response field tests. The fundamental
challenge post SGIA is navigating what
we call the two masters. Your
engineering package is scrutinized by
two separate authorities with
diametrically opposed technical
mandates. On one side, OT is focused on
the macro grid. Their concern is
regional dynamic stability and
systemwide model fidelity evaluated
using PSSE version 36, TAT, and
electromagnetic transient PSCAD models.
On the other side, your local TSP is
focused on micro equipment protection
and local power quality, safe switching,
breaker coordination, NERK FAC00001
and ILE E519 harmonic thresholds.
Costly project delays happen when a
model satisfies URKT but contradicts the
TSP's local requirements.
The key is synthesizing both
requirements upfront into a single
unified study package. While Urkott OT's
modeling rules apply uniformly across
the footprint, your protection and
energization designs must be
customtailored to the specific TSP named
in your GIR. Texas features a fragmented
utility landscape. Investorowned
utilities like Encore, Centerpoint, and
a Texas transmissiononly cres entities
like ET, Lonear, and WET. and municipals
and co-ops such as LCR, CPS Energy, and
Austin Energy. Each entity has bespoke
engineering variables from line
differential versus distance relay
preferences to local harmonic limits,
energization inrush constraints, and
custom RTU or ICCP telemetry protocols.
One size never fits all intercut. This
master diagnostic matrix outlines every
key deliverable required between SGIA
and commercial operation.
Before entering QSA, ERCOT audits your
asbuilt PSS.E and TAP models to ensure
positive sequence data matches procured
hardware.
Concurrently, detailed PSCAD EMT studies
evaluate weak grid stability, while
model quality tests prove dynamic
alignment between all models.
Simultaneously, both your COT and the
TSP verify your reactive capability to
ensure a 0.95 leading and lagging power
factor at the POI.
Leading up to energization and
synchronization, the focus shifts to no
GRR245 ride-through, ILE E 519 power
quality, transformer inrush switching
studies, and relay coordination with
utility breakers. Diving deeper into OT
modeling, generic assumptions are
completely off the table. OT enforces
strict asbuilt lockdowns. Every model
must reflect the exact inverter make,
model, firmware revision, power plant
controller settings, and factory test
reports for main stepup transformers.
Furthermore, PSCAD EMT models are now
mandatory for all inverter-based
resources, regardless of local grid
strength, utilizing vendor compiled
control code. The ultimate proof is the
model quality test. MQTT applies
identical flat starts, voltage steps,
and weak grid fault scenarios across
PSSSE, TAT, and PSCAD. If the response
curves do not cleanly overlay and align
with factory benchmarks,
OOTT will reject the submittal. Under
NOGRR 245, your plant must demonstrate
robust voltage and frequency ride
through inside the mandatory no trip
boundary prior to part two
synchronization while maintaining full
N5 power factor capability across its
active power range. When internal plant
design falls short, choosing the correct
reactive compensation technology is
essential. Capacitor and reactor banks
are cost- effective for steadystate
needs, but their output collapses during
deep voltage dips. Static VAR
compensators offer dynamic response
within cycles, though they require
careful harmonic filtering. Statcoms
provide fast subcycle constant current
injection, ideal for weak grids. While
synchronous condensers deliver genuine
physical inertia and short circuit
strength where grid stiffness is
critically low. Before your TSP
authorizes part one back feed, three
substation level engineering gates must
be cleared. First, protection
coordination. Because inverter-based
resources contribute fault currents
fundamentally different from synchronous
generators, plant protection settings
must be meticulously coordinated with
utility line relays to prevent nuisance
trips. Second, ILE E 519 power quality.
High order harmonic scans of collection
cables, padmount transformers, and
inverters must detect and mitigate
parallel resonances before equipment is
built. Third, energization studies.
Transient simulations must prove that
transformer core inrush will not cause
severe voltage drops, ferro resonance,
or misoperation on the transmission
network. To derisk this process, we
execute a disciplined six-stage
methodology.
In weeks one and two, we conduct an
exhaustive gap review to audit existing
models, identify tsp requirements, and
lock in a realistic QSA target. Step two
is vendor data lockdown, relentlessly
coordinating with OEM engineering to
secure UR compliant PSCAD and PSSE
models, which represents the single
biggest schedule risk. Step three
executes model builds and MQTT
benchmarking. Step four handles TSP
specific harmonic inrush and protection
studies. Step five manages formal
submitts, deficiency defense, and QSA
tracking. Finally, step six supports
on-site part one through part 3
commissioning, closing with the
mandatory 30-day postcommissioning model
verification. Here is how this
engineering rigor plays out in the
field. In our first mission along the
Gulf Coast, a developer switched
inverter vendors post SGIA, invalidating
all interconnection models just 10 weeks
before the QSA deadline. We procured
updated PSGAD code, rebuilt the PSSE and
T-AT models, re-engineered the capacitor
bank, and held the original QSA window.
In central Texas on a hybrid solar plus
storage site, a harmonic scan uncovered
dangerous parallel resonance with the
utility grid. By re-engineering the
capacitor bank into a tuned harmonic
filter on paper, we saved hundreds of
thousands of dollars in post
construction field modifications.
And in West Texas, severe weak grid
control oscillations on a wind repower
project were resolved by directly
reuning turbine PPC control loops,
successfully clearing ILE E 2800 ride-th
through. Our approach is built on
multifaceted sector experience led by
Sundep Sunny Patel. Keintel combines
background spanning electric utilities,
power generation, NERC audit leadership
and specialized consulting. We operate
seamlessly alongside your existing
engineer of record. Your EO retains the
balance of plant civil and physical
electrical design while keintel takes
full ownership of advanced stability
modeling. PSCAD EMT studies and TSP
compliance. You get a single accountable
engineering partner dedicated to
aligning both reviewers and executing
backward from your target COD. If you
have executed your SGIA or are
approaching final interconnect
negotiations, now is the time to secure
your QSA window. To get started, you can
scan the QR code on screen to schedule a
15minute scoping consultation. All we
need to begin assessing your road map is
your project capacity in megawws, your
interconnecting tsp, your battery
collocation status, and your target
synchronization milestone. You can also
reach our 247 technical desk at 813
or email contact atelengineering.com.

metadata.title: 3,800 MW Data Center Load Event Explained | PJM Grid, Ride-Through & Reliability Lessons
metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
What happens when 3,800 MW of data center load suddenly leaves the power grid? This video explains the major July 2026 data center load event in the PJM footprint and the critical electrical engineering lessons it reveals for large computational loads.

A correctly cleared 230 kV transmission fault in Northern Virginia triggered approximately 2,970 MW of initial data center load transfer to on-site generation. The resulting voltage rise then triggered another approximately 1,099 MW, bringing the total load transfer to roughly 3,800 MW.

The important lesson is that the event was not simply an equipment failure. Individual facilities may have operated according to their configured protection and transfer schemes, while the aggregate response created a system-level reliability event.

One of the biggest takeaways is that ride-through should not simply be determined by vendor defaults. The facility's electrical system should be evaluated against the actual disturbance environment, with protection, transfer logic, UPS controls and generator sequencing coordinated around a defined ride-through envelope.

For new and expanding data centers, this means that large-load interconnection studies, voltage sag analysis, power system studies, protection coordination, ride-through testing and commissioning are becoming increasingly important.
