segments.text: Welcome to this engineering analysis of
the 3800 megawatt shockwave and the
emerging challenge of engineering data
centers for grid ride through. On July
22nd, 2026, a major disturbance occurred
within the PJM interconnection system
following a mechanical failure on a 230
kovolt transmission line in Northern
Virginia.
The important point is that the
transmission protection system operated
correctly. The fault was cleared within
approximately 50 to 80 milliseconds. Yet
almost instantaneously, approximately
3,800 megawatt of computational load
disappeared in an instant.
That difference between facility level
reliability and grid level behavior is
the central engineering issue we will
explore throughout this presentation.
This slide establishes the sequence of
events. Before 8:00 a.m., a mechanical
failure occurred on a 230 kovolt
transmission line in Northern Virginia.
Approximately 50 to 80 milliseconds
later, the transmission fault was
cleared correctly by the protection
system. There were no protection
misoperations identified in the event
sequence shown here. Immediately
following the disturbance, approximately
3,800 megawws of computational load
disconnected from the grid and
transferred to backup generation. The
critical distinction is that the load
did not actually lose power. From the
perspective of the data centers, the
facilities continued operating exactly
as they were designed to operate.
However, from the perspective of the
electrical grid, 3.8 8 gawatt of demand
vanished almost instantaneously.
So this was not simply a conventional
outage. It was a massive and coordinated
load rejection event created by the
response of many individual facilities
to the same grid disturbance. And that
is what makes the event particularly
important for future data center
engineering. An important question is
whether the servers and information
technology equipment themselves were
vulnerable to this disturbance.
According to the analysis presented
here, the answer is no. The voltage sag
associated with the event lasted
approximately 3 to 5 cycles. That
duration fits within the standard
voltage tolerance envelopes typically
associated with information technology
and semiconductor manufacturing
equipment.
Server power supplies are designed to
tolerate substantial disturbances,
including significant voltage reduction
and even a complete loss of input for a
portion of a cycle. Therefore, the IT
equipment itself could have ridden
through the disturbance.
The key takeaway is that the servers
were not necessarily the component
making the decision to disconnect.
Something upstream in the facility
electrical system was making that
decision.
This shifts the engineering focus away
from the IT load and toward the
protection settings, UPS acceptance
logic, transfer controls, and other
electrical and mechanical systems
between the utility connection and the
computing equipment. This slide
introduces the transfer logic chain
inside a typical facility. A data center
does not have a single device
determining whether it will remain
connected to the utility. Instead,
multiple layers of protection and
control interact.
The change shown here includes customer
substation protection, automatic
transfer switches, UPS input acceptance
logic, and generator sequencing
controls.
The fundamental engineering principle is
simple. The facility's effective
ride-through capability is determined by
whichever device in this chain has the
tightest acceptance window and the
shortest effective delay.
For example, customer substation
undervoltage protection may be
configured primarily for equipment
protection rather than for expected
transmission level voltage sacks.
Automatic transfer switches can
introduce additional thresholds and
delays.
UPS input acceptance logic can have an
even tighter window than the IT
equipment itself
and generator sequencing may be
programmed to treat starting the engines
and transferring the load as one
combined action.
The result is a system where the IT
equipment might tolerate the disturbance
but an upstream control device may
decide that the utility source is
unacceptable.
That device then initiates a transfer.
This is why ride through cannot be
evaluated by looking at the server power
supply alone. The entire transfer logic
chain has to be evaluated. Now we come
to one of the most important concepts in
this analysis. The possibility of two
waves of load rejection. The first wave
is associated with undervoltage.
Following the initial 230 kovt fault and
voltage sag, approximately 2,970
megawatt transferred to backup
generation. That represents the first
major response of the computational load
to the disturbance.
But the story does not necessarily end
there. Once several gigaw disappear, the
electrical conditions on the grid
change. The load that had been consuming
power is no longer present. While system
characteristics such as shunt
capacitance continue to influence the
network that can contribute to elevated
system voltage,
the second wave is therefore associated
with over voltage. Approximately another
1,099 megawatt transferred to backup
generation in response to the elevated
voltage created by the first wave.
This creates an important engineering
warning. If future requirements address
only undervoltage ride-through,
engineers may successfully prevent the
first wave while leaving the system
exposed to a second wave triggered by
overvoltage.
Therefore, both undervoltage and
overvoltage ride through need to be
considered from the beginning of the
design. This slide illustrates the
fundamental difference between the macro
grid and the micro facility. On the
facility side, the response may look
completely successful. The IT equipment
remains powered. The backup systems
operate. The facility maintains
availability.
From an individual data center
perspective, that can appear to be a
successful protection strategy.
But on the macro grid side, the same
behavior can produce a very different
result.
A 3800 megawatt reliability event can
cause frequency to rise and create
reactive power surplus because a very
large amount of demand has suddenly
disappeared. This leads to the aggregate
behavior problem. Every individual
facility may have behaved correctly
according to its own internal design
criteria, but if thousands of facilities
are all configured to respond to the
same disturbance in essentially the same
way, their combined behavior can become
a grid level problem. In other words,
optimizing each facility independently
does not necessarily optimize the
electrical system as a whole.
Gridaware data center engineering
therefore has to consider both the
individual facility and the aggregate
population of facilities. This slide
presents what can be called the ride
through paradox. From an operator's
perspective, transferring away from the
utility quickly can appear to be the
safest option. The thinking is
straightforward. If there is a
disturbance, disconnect from the utility
before the disturbance becomes worse.
But that strategy can introduce a
different set of risks. An unnecessary
transfer consumes a generator start,
uses fuel, creates the possibility of an
engine failing to start, creates
emissions related operational
consequences, and can introduce
mechanical inrush when the system
recovers. And all of this may occur even
though the original transmission
disturbance was only a short voltage
sag. That is precisely the type of event
a UPS and associated ride-through
systems are intended to absorb. Riding
through a short disturbance using stored
energy may consume only a few seconds of
battery capacity. So the engineering
question becomes, is it safer to abandon
a healthy utility source during a short
disturbance, or is it safer to remain
connected and allow the UPS and properly
coordinated systems to absorb the event?
The answer presented by this analysis is
that riding through an appropriate short
duration disturbance can provide both
better facility resilience and better
grid behavior. Electrical ride through
is only half of the problem. The other
half is the mechanical plant. Data
centers depend on chilled water pumps,
cooling tower fans, air handling
systems, and other motor-driven
equipment to maintain thermal
conditions. These systems frequently use
variable frequency drives or VFDs.
A facility might successfully ride
through an electrical voltage sag at the
UPS and IT load level while a VFD
elsewhere in the cooling system trips
because its DC bus voltage falls below
its programmed threshold. That creates a
dangerous disconnect between electrical
ride through and thermal ride through.
The IT equipment may still have power,
but the cooling system may no longer be
operating normally. Once the mechanical
plant trips, the facility begins relying
on thermal inertia. If the cooling
systems remain unavailable long enough,
that thermal reserve is gradually
consumed. Eventually, the facility faces
a coordinated mechanical restart.
Large motors restarting simultaneously
can produce substantial inrush current
and reactive power demand. The slide
identifies inrush potentially exceeding
six times full load current and
highlights the resulting MVAR demand
during grid recovery.
So a data center cannot claim true ride
through capability simply because its
electrical systems remain online. The
cooling infrastructure must also be
capable of riding through the
disturbance and restarting in a
controlled sequenced manner. This
problem has an important historical
parallel.
The industry experienced a similar
challenge with inverter-based resources
during the 2010s. In that case,
manufacturers initially selected
settings primarily to protect their
converters. In the data center
environment, vendors can similarly
select settings primarily to protect
facility equipment. The symptom is
different in detail, but the underlying
engineering problem is similar. During
correctly cleared grid disturbances,
large quantities of equipment can
disconnect unnecessarily because their
settings are optimized for local
protection rather than system level
behavior.
The inverter-based resource industry
subsequently moved towards stronger
regulatory and technical requirements.
The lesson is that post-event discovery
can become extremely expensive. Changing
software settings or protection
thresholds during design is relatively
inexpensive.
Discovering after commissioning that
installed equipment cannot meet new
ride-through requirements can require
hardware replacement, equipment
retrofits, mechanical modifications, and
operational changes.
Therefore, the lesson for today's data
center projects is clear. Do not wait
for the regulatory framework to become
fully mature before engineering the
capability. Design the ride-through
envelope. Now, this slide describes the
regulatory trajectory presented in the
report. The timeline begins in July 2026
with FK docket RD26-7-o.
The deck states that FK ordered NERK to
develop mandatory reliability standards
for the integration of computational
loads into the bulk power system by the
end of 2026. The expected work includes
definitions, registration criteria, and
initial risk mitigation standards.
Then in early 2027, additional NERK work
is anticipated, including potentially
more stringent ride-th through
performance requirements.
The important change is not simply the
publication of another technical
requirement.
The larger paradigm shift is that
qualifying data center campuses may
become NERK registered entities and
therefore inherit compliance
obligations, evidence retention
requirements, and audit exposure.
In other words, facility behavior can
become a formal condition of grid
connection
for developers and engineers. This means
that ride through performance should no
longer be treated solely as an internal
reliability decision.
It can become part of the compliance and
interconnection framework itself. This
slide identifies a particularly high
value control change. Decoupling
generator start from transfer.
Under a legacy default strategy, a
disturbance is detected and the system
immediately starts the engines and
transfers the facility away from the
utility. That approach can create an
unnecessary system shock. It can consume
fuel, create emissions records, and
cause a large step change in grid
demand.
The alternative strategy is to separate
preparation from actual transfer. When a
disturbance is detected, the generators
can start as a prudent preparation step.
But the facility does not immediately
transfer away from the utility. Instead,
it waits for the defined ride-through
window to expire. If the grid recovers,
the facility remains on the utility
source. If the grid actually fails or
the ride-through window expires without
recovery, then the transfer can be
executed.
This seemingly simple change can have a
major aggregate effect. Applied across a
large population of data centers, it can
convert a massive simultaneous load
rejection into a much smaller number of
facilities transferring only when a
transfer is genuinely necessary. That is
a key example of how control system
engineering can improve both facility
resilience and grid stability. This
slide translates the lessons into
practical engineering requirements.
First is transfer logic. A default
facility may rely on fast dropout and
vendor defined settings. An optimized
facility instead coordinates device
settings around a defined facility ride
through envelope that includes both
undervoltage and overvoltage conditions.
Second is the mechanical plant. A
default design may allow chillers or
VFDs to trip on DC bus undervoltage. An
optimized design specifies DC bus ride
through capability and controlled
restart sequencing to avoid simultaneous
motor inrush.
Third is the UPS utility interface. A
tight acceptance window can cause the
UPS to transfer unnecessarily.
The optimized approach makes fuller use
of stored energy so the UPS can absorb
short duration 3 to 5 cycle sags.
Finally, there is campus scale.
Identical settings across multiple
facilities can produce simultaneous
transfers. Optimized timing can stagger
responses and convert a large step load
rejection into a more gradual ramp. The
common principle across all four areas
is coordination
protection, UPS controls, mechanical
systems, generators, and campus level
sequencing cannot be designed
independently if the objective is true
grid ride through. This slide focuses on
when ride through capability should be
engineered. The design stage represents
the lowest cost opportunity. At this
stage, engineers can characterize the
disturbance environment through fault
and voltage sag studies. They can
establish ride through envelopes in the
basis of design and they can set
equipment thresholds against those
envelopes. As the project moves through
procurement, commissioning and
operations, the cost of making
fundamental changes increases sharply.
After commissioning, achieving the
required capability may involve
retrofitting VFDs, replacing inflexible
static switches, changing mechanical
restart logic, and exposing operations
to potential compliance or audit
consequences.
The message is therefore very direct.
Ride through is cheapest to engineer
before equipment is purchased and
installed. By the time the facility is
operational, the same requirement can
become a major retrofit program.
The slide also highlights a broader
change in interconnection philosophy.
Interconnection agreements are
increasingly moving from simply
specifying how much capacity a facility
can connect to specifying how that
facility must perform during system
disturbances.
For a project already entering its
design and procurement cycle, waiting
for a final standard can mean waiting
too long. Engineering a ride-th through
capability on paper is not enough.
The key principle on this slide is that
a capability that has never been tested
is still only a specific.
The first step is to verify the actual
loaded settings. Every relevant device
should be checked individually.
During commissioning, vendors and
operators may modify settings to resolve
nuisance alarms or operational issues,
sometimes reverting equipment toward
default values.
The second step is to instrument the
point of service. Power quality
recording at the utility interface
provides evidence of exactly what the
facility experienced, including short
duration and subcycle events. That data
becomes especially important when
demonstrating performance during future
compliance audits.
Third, the disturbance response
scenarios need to be incorporated into
integrated systems testing. The IST
matrix should include an appropriate
shortduration voltage sag that the
facility is expected to ride through
without transferring in addition to
deeper and longer duration outages.
Finally, the facility needs to be
retested whenever significant
modifications occur. Every phase of
campus buildout, equipment replacement,
or system modification can change the
aggregate behavior of the facility.
Therefore, ride through is not a
one-time commissioning test. It is an
ongoing engineering and verification
discipline. This final slide brings the
entire discussion together.
Data center reliability and grid
stability can no longer be treated as
completely separate engineering
disciplines. The era of the invisible
passive data center load is changing.
Large computational facilities can
represent extremely significant
electrical demand and their collective
control behavior can influence the bulk
power system. Therefore, surviving the
upcoming regulatory and engineering
shift requires a broader approach.
Engineers need to evaluate distribution
topology, transfer logic, protection
settings, UPS behavior, mechanical
resilience, and restart sequencing
against the actual physics of the bulk
power system.
The objective is not simply to prevent a
data center from losing power. The
objective is to create a facility that
can remain reliable without
unnecessarily destabilizing the grid.
That requires accountable engineering
across large load interconnection, power
system studies, and data center
electrical design. The central lesson is
simple. A data center should be designed
not only to survive the grid, but to
behave responsibly within the grid.
That is the transition from engineering
the individual facility to engineering
the aggregate.

Data center reliability and grid stability can no longer be treated as completely separate engineering disciplines. The era of the invisible passive data center load is changing. Large computational facilities can represent extremely significant electrical demand and their collective control behavior can influence the bulk power system. Therefore, surviving the upcoming regulatory and engineering shift requires a broader approach. Engineers need to evaluate distribution topology, transfer logic, protection settings, UPS behavior, mechanical resilience, and restart sequencing against the actual physics of the bulk power system. The objective is not simply to prevent a data center from losing power. The objective is to create a facility that can remain reliable without unnecessarily destabilizing the grid. That requires accountable engineering across large load interconnection, power system studies, and data center electrical design. The central lesson is simple. A data center should be designed not only to survive the grid, but to behave responsibly within the grid. That is the transition from engineering the individual facility to engineering the aggregate.

metadata.title: Markets In A Minute: A Brief Overview of PJM Markets
metadata.author: pjminterconnection
metadata.shortDescription:
Watch PJM’s Rebecca Carroll explain the different PJM markets, and how each contributes to a reliable power grid. All of these markets match electricity supply to electricity demand, but the objectives of each market differ in terms of timing and the specific system requirements they are trying to meet.

This video contains closed captioning.

segments.text: PJM's energy markets ensure there is enough power to meet the demand on any given day.
PJM evaluates several components, including weather forecasts, generator availability,
and transmission line outages prior to selecting the least-cost set of resources needed to
meet the expected electricity demand on a daily basis. By taking these additional pieces
of information into account, the energy markets are able to secure the precise amount of power
needed so everyone can run their air conditioner on a hot day.
PJM's capacity market provides longer-term reliability by securing enough power to meet the needs of electricity consumers
three years in the future. The capacity market provides incentives that stimulate investment
in the maintenance of existing generation and development of new sources of capacity
to ensure the future reliability of the power system. By matching energy supply with future
energy demand, the capacity market provides assurance that homeowners will be able to
run their air conditioner on a hot day for several years into the future.
Regulation is one of PJM's ancillary service markets that helps correct for short-term changes
in electricity use that might affect the stability of the power system. It helps match electricity
supply and demand by adjusting generation output to maintain the desired electrical
frequency for the grid to function normally. Regulation service helps ensure that an air
conditioner can run normally when there are fluctuations in energy use. Synchronized and
non-synchronized reserves are additional ancillary service markets, which provide energy when
there is an unexpected need for more power on short notice due to unpredictable events
such as a surge in demand, loss of a generator, or loss of transmission line. The power output
of generating units providing these reserves can be increased quickly to help recover the
balance of energy supply and demand. Similar to regulation, reserves help to recover power
supply when there are interruptions so an air conditioner can run normally. Regardless
of the timing or objective, by matching energy supply with energy demand, all of PJM's markets
work together to ensure that there is adequate generation to maintain the reliability of
the electric system today and in the future.

metadata.title: Every US Power Grid Explained
metadata.author: Infrastructure explained
metadata.shortDescription:
The United States doesn't have one power grid. It has three — and they can't fully talk to each other. Within those three, nine separate operators each control a different piece of your electricity. None of them coordinate in real time.

In this video, we cover every major grid operator in the country: the Eastern Interconnection, the Western Interconnection, ERCOT, PJM, MISO, CAISO, SPP, NYISO, and ISO-NE — what they control, why they exist, and what makes each one uniquely fragile.

We also cover the February 2021 Texas grid collapse: how ERCOT came within four minutes of a complete failure, why 246 people died, and what it exposed about the decision to stay outside federal regulation.

And we end with the question the grid industry doesn't like to talk about: the nine high-voltage transformers whose failure could black out the entire country.

0:26 How the three interconnections work
0:35 Eastern Interconnection
1:04 Western Interconnection

1:54 PJM — the world's largest electricity market

4:56 NYISO — the Manhattan problem
5:28 ISO-NE — New England's vulnerability
6:27 ERCOT deep dive — the 2021 collapse
7:31 The Southeast — why it stayed out
8:08 The vulnerabilities nobody talks about

videos.full_text: Most people think the United States has one power grid. It doesn't. It has three. And they can't fully talk to each other. Within those three, nine separate operators each control a piece of your electricity. None of them coordinate in real time. The whole system is decades old, increasingly fragile, and almost no one knows how it actually works. Today, we're covering every part of it. Eastern Interconnection. The US grid splits into three massive alternating current systems called interconnections. Power flows freely within each one, but only limited connections exist between them. The Eastern Interconnection is the largest. It covers roughly 2/3 of the country. Everything east of the Rockies, plus much of Canada. It connects more than 700,000 miles of transmission lines, and serves about 250 million people. It is the most complex machine on Earth that has to be balanced in real time, every second of every day. Western Interconnection. The Eastern grid hands off here. On the other side of the Rockies, the Western Interconnection takes over. It covers the mountains, deserts, and Pacific coast. Its defining challenge is distance. Power generated at a dam in the Pacific Northwest might travel 1,500 miles before it reaches a house in Arizona, losing efficiency the entire way. ERCOT, Texas. Then, there's Texas. And Texas does things differently. The Texas grid deliberately stays entirely within state borders, which means it avoids federal regulation. For decades, that looked like smart independence. In February 2021, it nearly killed the state. We'll come back to that. PJM. Within each interconnection, the actual day-to-day operations are managed by independent organizations called ISOs and RTOs, regional transmission organizations. The biggest by far is PJM. PJM coordinates electricity across 13 states and Washington, D.C. From Illinois to New Jersey, from Michigan down to parts of North Carolina. It serves 65 million people, making it the largest competitive electricity market on the planet. Every second of every day, PJM is balancing supply and demand across hundreds of power plants, matching generation to load within a fraction of a percent. Its name comes from its origins, Pennsylvania, Jersey, Maryland. It has since grown far beyond those three states, but kept the initials. PJM's biggest challenge right now is the rapid retirement of coal and nuclear plants without enough replacement capacity coming online. MISO Next, MISO, the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, covers the middle of the country from Manitoba down through Louisiana. It sits over the best wind resources in North America. The Great Plains states generate enormous amounts of wind power, sometimes more than the region can use. The problem is moving that power east to where the demand is. The transmission lines to do it don't fully exist yet, and building them takes decades of permitting, negotiation, and construction. CAISO, California CAISO runs the grid for most of California and manages some of the most ambitious renewable energy goals in the country, along with some of its most expensive failures. California has installed so much solar capacity that on spring afternoons it produces far more electricity than it can use. Prices go negative. Grid operators pay neighboring states to take the excess. Then, the sun goes down, and within 2 hours demand spikes by 15,000 MW. That ramp from too much to not enough in less time than it takes to cook dinner is called the duck curve, and it's CAISO's defining problem. In August 2020, CAISO ordered rolling blackouts for the first time since 2001. Not because of a storm, not because of equipment failure, because it simply ran out of power at 6:00 p.m. on a hot evening when solar dropped and demand didn't. SPP, Great Plains. The Southwest Power Pool covers the Great Plains from North Dakota down to Oklahoma. It's not as well known as PJM or CAISO, but it quietly runs the most wind-powered grid in the United States. On good days, SPP generates more than 90% of its electricity from wind. The challenge is that wind doesn't blow on demand. Managing a grid that can swing from 90% wind to 30% within hours requires more backup generation or and more flexibility than almost any grid in the world. MISO, New York. New York State runs its own grid operator, NYISO. Smaller than PJM or MISO, but with a problem no other operator faces at the same scale, New York City. The city consumes an enormous amount of power in an extremely dense area. Most of it can't come from upstate. The transmission lines are constrained. So, the city relies heavily on power plants located on the island itself, running on expensive oil and gas, operating only during peak demand. Below Manhattan, there are hundreds of miles of underground cables running through vaults that date back to the 1880s. ISO-NE, New England. ISO-NE runs the grid for the six New England states. By most measures, it is the most vulnerable major grid in the United States. New England has almost no indigenous fuel supply. It depends heavily on natural gas for electricity, and its pipelines are already running at capacity during winter. On a cold January day, New England's grid operators are competing with home heating systems for the same pipeline gas. When pipelines freeze or get disrupted, the grid falls back on oil shipped in by tanker. ISO-NE has been warning about this structural vulnerability for years. Very little has been done about it. ERCOT deep dive. But ERCOT deserves a much closer look. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas operates without federal oversight. FERC, which regulates every other major grid in the country, has no jurisdiction here. Texas made that choice deliberately. Then came February 2021. Winter Storm Uri sent temperatures across Texas to levels not seen in a century. Natural gas wells froze, wind turbines iced over, power plants that had never been weatherized for extreme cold shut down one after another. At its worst moment, ERCOT was within 4 minutes of a complete grid collapse, a failure that would have taken weeks, possibly months, to recover from. 246 people died. Large vertically integrated utilities like Southern Company and Duke Energy own the generation, the transmission, and the distribution. They don't compete in open markets. Less price competition, slower integration of new energy sources, and a grid that is less interconnected with its neighbors. Vulnerabilities. metadata.title: What Is an Interconnection Queue
metadata.author: Dirt to Data
metadata.shortDescription:
Seeing the grid and having the right to use it turn out to be two completely different things.


Suhail unpacks the Q in GTSQT, explains why queue position can become part of the asset, and walks through the Bring-Your-Own-Power debate, including the FERC-versus-state fight over who gets to connect large loads and who pays for it.


Dirt to Data is hosted by Suhail Tayyeb.

The land still matters, of course, but the point of GTSQT is to force us to stop confusing a power story with a line on a map. A transmission line near your property tells you almost nothing by itself about whether a 100 MW customer can operate there 3 years from now. And that may be the larger lesson of the interconnection queue. The queue is not paperwork sitting between you and your project. It's a systems way of reconciling your private development ambition with a shared piece of infrastructure that millions of other customers also depend on. As AI increases electricity demand, we're going to see more experimentation, co-location, private generation, flexible loads, new transmission service structures, large load tariffs, bring your own generation. Some projects may reduce grid consumption during stressed conditions. Others may develop generation that ultimately benefits the broader system. But none of these models eliminates the central question. Who gets access to the infrastructure, when do they get it, and who pays for what has to be built? Once you understand that, the interconnection queue stops looking like a technical detail. It becomes part of the investment thesis. Because in a market where power is constrained, knowing where you stand in the infrastructure process can determine whether you own a data center opportunity or simply another piece of land waiting for electricity. Thanks for listening to Dirt to Data. If you found this episode useful, subscribe and share it with someone interested in real estate, infrastructure, energy, or artificial intelligence. I'm Souheil Tayeb, and I'll see you in the next episode. >> [music]

metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
How has FERC Order No. 2023 changed generator interconnection in the United States?

In this engineering strategy guide, Keentel Engineering explains the shift from the traditional first-come, first-served serial queue to the first-ready, first-served cluster interconnection study process. The video focuses on the engineering, financial, and commercial factors developers need to evaluate before entering a cluster.

The key lesson is simple: interconnection cost is not determined by project size alone. Point of interconnection, transmission topology, surrounding projects, network constraints, electrical impact, and the quality of the project's power-system models can significantly influence upgrade requirements and project economics.

What You'll Learn

• How FERC Order No. 2023 changed the interconnection queue
• First-ready, first-served cluster studies
• Cluster interconnection cost allocation
• Point-of-interconnection (POI) selection
• DFAX / distribution factor analysis
• Network upgrade exposure
• 115 kV vs. 345 kV interconnection considerations
• ERIS vs. NRIS strategy
• Withdrawal penalties and financial risk
• Power flow and N-1/N-1-1 contingency studies
• Capacity deliverability analysis
• Affected systems and contingent facilities
• Strategies for screening a project before entering a cluster

Why Cluster Interconnection Strategy Matters

Under the previous serial queue model, projects were generally studied sequentially. FERC Order No. 2023 introduced a readiness-based cluster approach in which qualifying projects are evaluated together. 

This provides a more realistic representation of cumulative generation and storage impacts on the transmission system, but it also creates greater financial consequences for projects that enter and later withdraw.

guide on cluster interconnection studies
under FERC order number 2023.

how the interconnection process has
fundamentally changed from the
traditional first-come, first-served
queue to a readiness-based cluster study
process.
The objective is to understand not only
the regulatory changes, but also the
engineering and financial consequences
for generation, storage, and
inverter-based resource developers.
We will look at real cluster study cost
distributions, network upgrade exposure,
voltage level impacts, DFACTS-based cost
allocation, inverter performance
requirements, and practical strategies
developers can use before entering a
cluster study.
The key message throughout this
presentation is simple. Under the new
cluster approach, interconnection cost
is no longer determined simply by
project size. The electrical location of
the project, the surrounding projects,
the network constraints, and the
project's modeled impact can become much
more important.
Let's begin by understanding why the old
interconnection queue became such a
major problem. Before FERC order 2023,
the traditional interconnection process
was largely based on a first-come,
first-served serial queue.
Projects were studied sequentially. A
project near the front of the queue
could trigger a network upgrade, and
projects behind it could then require
additional studies when the system
changed.
This created what can be described as a
cascading restudy problem.
The presentation highlights the enormous
backlog that developed with more than 2
terawatts of generation and storage
trapped in the interconnection process.
The delay was also significant. The
median time from an interconnection
request to operation exceeded 4 years.
One major weakness of the old system was
speculative participation.
Developers could enter the queue without
having demonstrated sufficient
commercial readiness, and withdrawal
could force other projects to be
re-studied.
FERC Order 2023 introduces a
fundamentally different approach.
Instead of simply asking which project
arrived first, the process places much
greater emphasis on readiness.
Projects must demonstrate things such as
financial commitments and site control.
And qualifying projects are then studied
together in clusters.
The objective is to make the process
more predictable, reduce speculative
requests, and allocate shared network
upgrades more systematically.
However, as we will see, cluster studies
also create new engineering and
financial risks. This slide summarizes
the fundamental change from the pre-2023
interconnection process to the FERC
Order 2023 cluster model. Under the
traditional process, the priority metric
was essentially the queue submission
date. The assumption was that projects
ahead of you would proceed, and your
project would be studied individually
based on that queue position.
Under the cluster approach, commercial
readiness and site control become much
more important. Study execution also
changes dramatically. Instead of
sequentially studying projects one at a
time, multiple projects within a defined
cluster are analyzed simultaneously.
This creates a more realistic picture of
how the grid will behave when several
projects inject power at the same time.
The allocation of network upgrade costs
also changes. Rather than simply
assigning costs based on project size,
the analysis can consider each project's
proportional impact on the specific
constraint. This is extremely important.
A 200-MW project does not necessarily
pay more than a 100-MW project simply
because it is twice the size. If the
smaller project has a larger electrical
impact on a particular constraint, its
allocated share of that upgrade can
potentially be higher.
Finally, withdrawal becomes much more
consequential. The presentation
highlights escalating financial
penalties that can reach significant
percentages of estimated network upgrade
costs.
The overall message is that the new
process rewards serious, technically
prepared developers, and makes
speculative participation considerably
more expensive. Now, let's look at a
practical example of what a cluster
study can actually look like.
The example presented here is an ISO New
England transitional cluster involving
23 projects. These projects include
battery storage, solar, and wind
resources.
Together, the projects represented
approximately 4,826.5
MW of study capacity.
The total planning grade capital
requirement was approximately $3.21
billion.
But, the most important point is the
enormous variation between individual
projects.
Allocated costs range from $0 for some
projects to approximately $541 million
for another project.
That means two projects participating in
the same overall cluster can experience
dramatically different financial
outcomes.
The cost per kilowatt also varied from
zero to approximately $2,700 per
kilowatt.
This demonstrates why using a simple
dollars per megawatt estimate during
early development can be extremely
misleading.
Location matters, electrical topology
matters, the project's point of
interconnection matters, and critically,
the other projects in the cluster
matter.
The slide also highlights a major
scheduling problem.
Some network upgrades were estimated to
require as much as 93 months to
construct.
For an 18-month battery project, that
could create a delay of more than 7
years.
So, the interconnection study is not
simply a question of whether a project
can connect. It can determine whether
the project is economically and
commercially viable at all.
This slide breaks down where the
approximately $3.21 billion of upgrade
costs are concentrated.
The largest category is system network
upgrades.
Approximately $2.54
billion, or about 79% of the total, is
associated with system network upgrades.
These can include deep grid
reconductoring, transmission line
rebuilding, and transmission statcom
installations.
Substation network upgrades represent
approximately $581 million,
or around 18%. These may include new
point of interconnection substations,
substation modifications, and line taps.
Interconnection facilities themselves
represent approximately $75.5
million,
or about 2.4%.
Distribution upgrades are much smaller
in comparison at approximately $7.7
million.
The strategic insight here is very
important. A developer may initially
focus on the physical facilities
immediately surrounding the project, but
nearly 80% of the illustrated capital
requirement is associated with shared
infrastructure deeper in the
transmission network.
That infrastructure is influenced not
only by your project, but also by the
electrical behavior of the other
projects participating in the cluster.
Therefore, early-stage interconnection
analysis needs to look beyond the
project fence line.
The real financial risk may be many
electrical miles away from the point of
interconnection. This slide illustrates
why the selected point of
interconnection can have a profound
impact on project economics. The example
compares projects connecting at 115 kV
with projects connecting at 345 kV.
At the 115 kV point of interconnection,
14 projects represented approximately
MW of total capacity.
The average illustrated cost was
approximately $831 per kW with total
cost exposure of about $1.88 billion.
Why is this happening? Lower voltage
transmission networks can become heavily
constrained when multiple projects
inject power into the same area. The
available thermal capacity can be
consumed quickly, forcing extensive
network upgrades.
The slide notes that five of the seven
most expensive projects connected at
this voltage level.
Now compare that with the 345 kV point
of interconnection. Seven projects
represented approximately 2,262
MW, which is almost the same total
capacity.
But the average illustrated cost was
approximately $453
per kW with total exposure of about
$1.02 billion.
The engineering reason is that the
higher voltage network generally
provides greater transmission capacity
and can better absorb clustered
injections.
Of course, a 345 kV connection may
involve higher direct interconnection
costs. But the potential reduction in
shared network upgrade exposure can be
significant.
This is why POI selection should be
treated as an engineering optimization
problem, not simply a land development
decision. This slide focuses on
withdrawal risk under the cluster
process. The example considers a
hypothetical 200 MW project facing
approximately $178 million in average
upgrade allocation.
Different stages of the process create
different levels of capital exposure.
At one stage, approximately 5% of the
network upgrade amount corresponds to
about 8.9 million dollars of risk. At
10%, the exposure increases to
approximately 17.88 million dollars. At
20%, the exposure reaches approximately
35.6 million dollars.
The key point is that the financial
consequences are designed to discourage
speculative projects from entering and
later withdrawing from the cluster. This
changes the developer's decision-making
process.
Under the old queue mentality,
developers could potentially enter the
queue relatively early and determine
feasibility later. Under the new model,
entering a cluster requires
substantially more confidence. Before
entering, a developer should have a
strong understanding of the point of
interconnection, the surrounding
transmission system, likely constraints,
project financing, site control, and the
technical validity of the models used in
the study.
The lesson is straightforward. Do not
enter a cluster simply because an
interconnection opportunity appears
attractive on paper. Enter only after
the project has been subjected to
serious engineering and financial
screening. Now, let's examine what
actually happens inside a cluster study.
The foundation is the CEII, or critical
energy infrastructure information base
case. These models represent future grid
conditions and can include challenging
operating scenarios, including off-peak
load conditions.
The first major analysis area is
steady-state performance. Thermal and
voltage studies evaluate normal and
contingency conditions, including N-1
and N-1 scenarios.
These studies identify overloaded lines,
voltage problems, and other constraints
that may require reconductoring or
complete line reconstruction.
The next area is short-circuit analysis.
This evaluates whether existing breakers
and other equipment can safely interrupt
the fault current.
Large clusters of inverter-based
resources and generation can change
fault levels and equipment duty
requirements.
Then we have stability and
electromagnetic transient or EMT
analysis.
For inverter-based resources, especially
in weak grid environments, PSCAD-based
analysis can become critical. The study
may evaluate inverter control
interactions, ride through performance,
and other dynamic phenomena.
Finally, deliverability analysis
examines whether the capacity from the
project can actually reach the required
load under stressed system conditions.
Therefore, a cluster study is much more
than a simple power flow calculation. It
is a multi-dimensional engineering
assessment involving thermal, voltage,
short circuit, stability, EMT, and
deliverability considerations.
This slide introduces two important
interconnection service concepts, ERIS
and NRIS.
ERIS refers to energy resource
interconnection service.
The basic question is whether the
resource can connect and deliver energy
on an as-available basis while meeting
applicable network capability
requirements.
NRIS or network resource interconnection
service goes further. The question
becomes whether the resource's output is
fully deliverable to the load under
stressed peak conditions.
This distinction can have a major impact
on the amount of network reinforcement
required. NRIS can trigger more
restrictive simultaneous output and
deliverability tests.
Those tests may identify transmission
constraints that require substantial
upgrades.
The slide highlights an important
strategic option, an automatic downgrade
to ERIS.
If capacity testing produces uneconomic
thermal upgrades, a developer may
consider whether ERIS better fits the
project's actual commercial strategy.
For certain battery energy storage
projects, particularly projects designed
primarily around energy arbitrage rather
than firm capacity obligations. This can
be an important economic consideration.
The broader lesson is that developers
should not automatically assume that the
highest level of interconnection service
is always the best option. The
appropriate service should be evaluated
against the project's actual revenue
model and operating strategy. This slide
demonstrates one of the most important
concepts in cluster cost allocation. The
impact of multiple projects on a shared
transmission constraint.
Consider a 115 kV transmission line with
a 240 MVA rating.
Before the cluster, the line is already
carrying approximately 200 MVA.
Three projects are being considered.
Project A is 200 MW, Project B is 150
MW, Project C is 100 MW. Individually,
none of these projects necessarily
creates the final overload condition,
but their electrical impacts are
different. Project A has a DFAX value of
.25, creating approximately 50 MVA of
impact. Project B has a DFAX of .20,
creating approximately 30 MVA of impact.
Project C has a DFAX of .05,
creating approximately 5 MVA of impact.
When the impacts are combined, the
post-contingency flow can reach
approximately 285 MVA. That represents
approximately 118%
of the 240 MVA line rating. The critical
lesson is that project size and
electrical impact are not the same
thing.
A project can be relatively large, but
have a smaller impact on a particular
constraint. Conversely, a smaller
project can have a disproportionately
high impact, depending on its electrical
location and network topology. This is
why DFAX analysis is so important for
early-stage cluster strategy.
The previous slide showed how multiple
projects can jointly create a
transmission constraint. Now, the
question becomes who pays for the
resulting upgrade?
The example uses a $40 million network
upgrade.
A common, but incorrect, approach is to
divide the cost according to project
megawatt size.
Using that approach, the 200 megawatt
project A would pay approximately 44% or
$17.8 million. The
150 megawatt project B would pay
approximately 33% or $13.3 million.
And the 100 megawatt project C would pay
approximately 22% or $8.9 million.
But, the presentation emphasizes that
this is not the appropriate way to
understand proportional impact under the
illustrated order 2023 framework.
Instead, the analysis considers the
project's proportional MVA impact on the
specific constraint.
Project A contributes 50 MVA and
therefore represents approximately 58.8%
of the impact. Its allocation becomes
approximately $23.5 million.
Project B contributes 30 MVA,
representing approximately 35.3%
or approximately $14.1 million.
Project C contributes only 5 MVA,
representing approximately 5.9%
or approximately $2.4 million.
This is a crucial strategic point. Your
project's interconnection cost is
dictated by its impact on the specific
constraint, not simply by its nameplate
capacity.
Therefore, understanding the electrical
system before entering the cluster can
provide a major commercial advantage.
This slide focuses on inverter-based
resources and the importance of accurate
dynamic models. In clustered systems
with many inverter-based resources,
especially in weak grids, inverter
controls can interact with one another.
Traditional positive sequence studies
may not capture every dynamic
interaction. If generic or inaccurate
models produce unstable simulation
results, planners may conclude that
additional physical grid equipment is
required. Potential solutions can
include transmission statcoms,
synchronous condensers, or ACSS related
network upgrades.
These upgrades can be extremely
expensive.
This creates what the presentation calls
the hardware penalty. The developers'
defense is high-quality vendor-specific
modeling. That means using validated
PSCAD models, accurate inverter
controls, and the actual plant
controller settings wherever required.
The objective is to demonstrate through
simulation that the project can operate
stably under the required grid
conditions.
For modern battery, solar, and other
inverter-based projects, model quality
is therefore not simply a technical
documentation issue. It can directly
affect the project's capital
requirements.
A weak or generic model can potentially
create a perceived stability problem. A
validated model can provide the
engineering evidence needed to
demonstrate stable operation and avoid
unnecessary hardware requirements.
This slide brings the major lessons
together.
The first message is that project size
alone no longer tells you what your
interconnection cost will be.
The electrical node and the surrounding
cluster participants can be more
important. Two projects with similar
megawatt ratings can experience
completely different upgrade
requirements depending on where they
connect and what constraints they
influence.
The second message is that entering a
FERC Order 2023 cluster study without
adequate preparation creates significant
financial risk.
Developers should perform preemptive
CEII base case screening wherever access
and applicable requirements permit.
That means understanding the likely
system constraints before the formal
study begins.
The third message concerns withdrawal
penalties.
Because the financial consequences can
escalate substantially, developers need
to be confident in their project before
entering the process.
The overall strategy can therefore be
summarized in three ideas.
First, understand the node.
Second, understand the neighbors in the
cluster.
And third, understand the project's
electrical impact before committing
significant capital.
Under the new environment,
interconnection strategy has become a
core engineering and investment
decision. This slide converts the
technical lessons into an actionable
developer strategy.
Before the study window, the first step
is to obtain access to the applicable
CEII information and utility planning
models.
Next, screen potential points of
interconnection using defacts analysis
against known or anticipated
constraints.
It is also useful to evaluate multiple
project sizes.
A small change in project capacity can
sometimes determine whether a project
crosses an upgrade threshold.
Therefore, developers should not
automatically assume that the maximum
possible project size is the
economically optimal size.
Another critical preparation step is
model validation.
Developers should have accurate PSSE and
PSCAD models ready before the formal
study process begins.
During the study, developers should
actively participate in scoping meetings
and verify modeling assumptions. They
should also track the other projects in
the cluster and assess the likelihood
that those projects will remain in the
process. As interim results become
available, developers should review them
carefully and submit specific
engineering evidence when assumptions or
results appear incorrect. After the
study, capital planning becomes
critical. Developers need to prepare for
applicable execution deposits and
monitor contingent facilities. They also
need to understand that network
construction schedules can extend over
many years. Therefore, project
financing, equipment procurement,
construction sequencing, and commercial
operation dates must all be aligned with
the interconnection schedule. The
developer playbook is essentially screen
early, model accurately, participate
actively, and plan financially for the
resulting network upgrades. The final
slide presents the engineering
capabilities supporting this cluster
strategy.
The concept is described as having four
seats at the table: the utility, the
generator, the regulator, and the
consultant. Each perspective provides a
different part of the overall
interconnection picture.
The presentation highlights experience
in grid operations, NERC compliance,
renewable generation, power system
studies, steady-state analysis, PSCAD,
and substation engineering. The
practical services highlighted include
independent CEII base case screening,
validated EMT and PSCAD modeling,
cluster study shadowing and technical
rebuttal, and owner's engineer
substation design from 4 kV
through 765 kV. The key value is
The key value is bringing these
capabilities together before and during
the cluster study process.
For developers, the objective is not
simply to react to an interconnection
study after the results are delivered.
The objective is to understand the grid
early, identify potential constraints,
validate the project's electrical
models, evaluate alternative points of
interconnection, and prepare for the
financial consequences of network
upgrades.
Under FERC Order 2023, successful
interconnection strategy requires both
regulatory awareness and deep
engineering analysis.
If you are developing generation,
battery storage, renewable energy, or
other inverter-based resources and need
support with cluster strategy, CEII
screening, PSCAD modeling, transmission
studies, or substation design, Kentech
Engineering can support the process from
early development through
interconnection and implementation.
Thank you for watching this presentation
on FERC Order 2023 Cluster
Interconnection Strategy.

This is why POI selection should be treated as an engineering optimization problem, not simply a land development decision. This slide focuses on withdrawal risk under the cluster process. The example considers a hypothetical 200 MW project facing approximately $178 million in average upgrade allocation. Different stages of the process create different levels of capital exposure. At one stage, approximately 5% of the network upgrade amount corresponds to about 8.9 million dollars of risk. At 10%, the exposure increases to approximately 17.88 million dollars. At 20%, the exposure reaches approximately 35.6 million dollars. The key point is that the financial consequences are designed to discourage speculative projects from entering and later withdrawing from the cluster. This changes the developer's decision-making process. Under the old queue mentality, developers could potentially enter the queue relatively early and determine feasibility later. Under the new model, entering a cluster requires substantially more confidence. Before entering, a developer should have a strong understanding of the point of interconnection, the surrounding transmission system, likely constraints, project financing, site control, and the technical validity of the models used in the study. The lesson is straightforward. Do not enter a cluster simply because an interconnection opportunity appears attractive on paper. Enter only after the project has been subjected to serious engineering and financial screening. Now, let's examine what actually happens inside a cluster study. The foundation is the CEII, or critical energy infrastructure information base case. These models represent future grid conditions and can include challenging operating scenarios, including off-peak load conditions. The first major analysis area is steady-state performance. Thermal and voltage studies evaluate normal and contingency conditions, including N-1 and N-1 scenarios. These studies identify overloaded lines, voltage problems, and other constraints that may require reconductoring or complete line reconstruction. The next area is short-circuit analysis. This evaluates whether existing breakers and other equipment can safely interrupt the fault current. Large clusters of inverter-based resources and generation can change fault levels and equipment duty requirements. Then we have stability and electromagnetic transient or EMT analysis. For inverter-based resources, especially in weak grid environments, PSCAD-based analysis can become critical. The study may evaluate inverter control interactions, ride through performance, and other dynamic phenomena. Finally, deliverability analysis examines whether the capacity from the project can actually reach the required load under stressed system conditions. Therefore, a cluster study is much more than a simple power flow calculation. It is a multi-dimensional engineering assessment involving thermal, voltage, short circuit, stability, EMT, and deliverability considerations. This slide introduces two important interconnection service concepts, ERIS and NRIS. ERIS refers to energy resource interconnection service. The basic question is whether the resource can connect and deliver energy on an as-available basis while meeting applicable network capability requirements. NRIS or network resource interconnection service goes further. The question becomes whether the resource's output is fully deliverable to the load under stressed peak conditions. This distinction can have a major impact on the amount of network reinforcement required. NRIS can trigger more restrictive simultaneous output and deliverability tests. Those tests may identify transmission constraints that require substantial upgrades. The slide highlights an important strategic option, an automatic downgrade to ERIS. If capacity testing produces uneconomic thermal upgrades, a developer may consider whether ERIS better fits the project's actual commercial strategy. For certain battery energy storage projects, particularly projects designed primarily around energy arbitrage rather than firm capacity obligations. This can be an important economic consideration. The broader lesson is that developers should not automatically assume that the highest level of interconnection service is always the best option. The appropriate service should be evaluated against the project's actual revenue model and operating strategy. This slide demonstrates one of the most important concepts in cluster cost allocation. The impact of multiple projects on a shared transmission constraint. Consider a 115 kV transmission line with a 240 MVA rating. Before the cluster, the line is already carrying approximately 200 MVA. Three projects are being considered. Project A is 200 MW, Project B is 150 MW, Project C is 100 MW. Individually, none of these projects necessarily creates the final overload condition, but their electrical impacts are different. Project A has a DFAX value of .25, creating approximately 50 MVA of impact. Project B has a DFAX of .20, creating approximately 30 MVA of impact. Project C has a DFAX of .05, creating approximately 5 MVA of impact. When the impacts are combined, the post-contingency flow can reach approximately 285 MVA. That represents approximately 118% of the 240 MVA line rating. The critical lesson is that project size and electrical impact are not the same thing. A project can be relatively large, but have a smaller impact on a particular constraint. Conversely, a smaller project can have a disproportionately high impact, depending on its electrical location and network topology. This is why DFAX analysis is so important for early-stage cluster strategy. The previous slide showed how multiple projects can jointly create a transmission constraint. Now, the question becomes who pays for the resulting upgrade? The example uses a $40 million network upgrade. A common, but incorrect, approach is to divide the cost according to project megawatt size. Using that approach, the 200 megawatt project A would pay approximately 44% or $17.8 million. The 150 megawatt project B would pay approximately 33% or $13.3 million. And the 100 megawatt project C would pay approximately 22% or $8.9 million. But, the presentation emphasizes that this is not the appropriate way to understand proportional impact under the illustrated order 2023 framework. Instead, the analysis considers the project's proportional MVA impact on the specific constraint. Project A contributes 50 MVA and therefore represents approximately 58.8% of the impact. Its allocation becomes approximately $23.5 million. Project B contributes 30 MVA, representing approximately 35.3% or approximately $14.1 million. Project C contributes only 5 MVA, representing approximately 5.9% or approximately $2.4 million. This is a crucial strategic point. Your project's interconnection cost is dictated by its impact on the specific constraint, not simply by its nameplate capacity. Therefore, understanding the electrical system before entering the cluster can provide a major commercial advantage. This slide focuses on inverter-based resources and the importance of accurate dynamic models. In clustered systems with many inverter-based resources, especially in weak grids, inverter controls can interact with one another. Traditional positive sequence studies may not capture every dynamic interaction. If generic or inaccurate models produce unstable simulation results, planners may conclude that additional physical grid equipment is required. Potential solutions can include transmission statcoms, synchronous condensers, or ACSS related network upgrades. These upgrades can be extremely expensive. This creates what the presentation calls the hardware penalty. The developers' defense is high-quality vendor-specific modeling. That means using validated PSCAD models, accurate inverter controls, and the actual plant controller settings wherever required. The objective is to demonstrate through simulation that the project can operate stably under the required grid conditions. For modern battery, solar, and other inverter-based projects, model quality is therefore not simply a technical documentation issue. It can directly affect the project's capital requirements. A weak or generic model can potentially create a perceived stability problem. A validated model can provide the engineering evidence needed to demonstrate stable operation and avoid unnecessary hardware requirements. This slide brings the major lessons together. The first message is that project size alone no longer tells you what your interconnection cost will be. The electrical node and the surrounding cluster participants can be more important. Two projects with similar megawatt ratings can experience completely different upgrade requirements depending on where they connect and what constraints they influence. The second message is that entering a FERC Order 2023 cluster study without adequate preparation creates significant financial risk. Developers should perform preemptive CEII base case screening wherever access and applicable requirements permit. That means understanding the likely system constraints before the formal study begins. The third message concerns withdrawal penalties. Because the financial consequences can escalate substantially, developers need to be confident in their project before entering the process. The overall strategy can therefore be summarized in three ideas. First, understand the node. Second, understand the neighbors in the cluster. And third, understand the project's electrical impact before committing significant capital. Under the new environment, interconnection strategy has become a core engineering and investment decision. This slide converts the technical lessons into an actionable developer strategy. Before the study window, the first step is to obtain access to the applicable CEII information and utility planning models. Next, screen potential points of interconnection using defacts analysis against known or anticipated constraints. It is also useful to evaluate multiple project sizes. A small change in project capacity can sometimes determine whether a project crosses an upgrade threshold. Therefore, developers should not automatically assume that the maximum possible project size is the economically optimal size. Another critical preparation step is model validation. Developers should have accurate PSSE and PSCAD models ready before the formal study process begins. During the study, developers should actively participate in scoping meetings and verify modeling assumptions. They should also track the other projects in the cluster and assess the likelihood that those projects will remain in the process. As interim results become available, developers should review them carefully and submit specific engineering evidence when assumptions or results appear incorrect. After the study, capital planning becomes critical. Developers need to prepare for applicable execution deposits and monitor contingent facilities. They also need to understand that network construction schedules can extend over many years. Therefore, project financing, equipment procurement, construction sequencing, and commercial operation dates must all be aligned with the interconnection schedule. The developer playbook is essentially screen early, model accurately, participate actively, and plan financially for the resulting network upgrades. The final slide presents the engineering capabilities supporting this cluster strategy. The concept is described as having four seats at the table: the utility, the generator, the regulator, and the consultant. Each perspective provides a different part of the overall interconnection picture. The presentation highlights experience in grid operations, NERC compliance, renewable generation, power system studies, steady-state analysis, PSCAD, and substation engineering. The practical services highlighted include independent CEII base case screening, validated EMT and PSCAD modeling, cluster study shadowing and technical rebuttal, and owner's engineer substation design from 4 kV through 765 kV. The key value is The key value is bringing these capabilities together before and during the cluster study process. For developers, the objective is not simply to react to an interconnection study after the results are delivered. The objective is to understand the grid early, identify potential constraints, validate the project's electrical models, evaluate alternative points of interconnection, and prepare for the financial consequences of network upgrades. Under FERC Order 2023, successful interconnection strategy requires both regulatory awareness and deep engineering analysis. If you are developing generation, battery storage, renewable energy, or other inverter-based resources and need support with cluster strategy, CEII screening, PSCAD modeling, transmission studies, or substation design, Kentech Engineering can support the process from early development through interconnection and implementation. Thank you for watching this presentation on FERC Order 2023 Cluster Interconnection Strategy.

segments.text: Hello, my name is Alfonso Areti. I am
the renewable energy integration
manager at Luma. I would like to talk
to you about our distributed generation
project capacity map. To access this
map, all you need to do is locate our
Luma website and click on renewable
energy in the home section. This will
take you to this page, the letter D,
where you will be able to access the
link to the distributed generation
project capacity map. Clicking on this
link will take you to the map itself.
There you will find the disclaimer. You
must accept it in order to proceed with
using the map. It is worth noting that
the map contains two user guides, one
in Spanish and one in English. You can
access them by clicking on them. They
provide more details on how to use
these maps. The purpose of this video
is to provide you with a basic
familiarization with the map, and we
will refer to this user guide for more
details. Returning to the map, the map
has several segments and I want to
start by navigating it. In the upper
right corner, there is a magnifying
glass where you can place a particular
address to search for information about
that specific property. It also has
several layers that we will be
discussing that give you different
types of information, starting with the
voltage level layer, the GD penetration
layer, and the incremental hosting
capacity layer. In addition to this,
there will be a legend on the left side
that will change, that is, it is
dynamic depending on the layer that we
are using. Let's start with the voltage
level section. If you click on the
voltage level layer, the colors will
change in such a way that the different
feeders in the system can be shown
based on their voltage level. At first,
the blue color is for feeders that are
at 4000 V, the turquoise color is for

color is for feeders that are at 8 KB,
8000 V. And finally, our highest
voltage at the distribution level, the
13 KB, with an orange color. If you
increase the magnification, you can
zoom in, you will be able to verify
specific addresses and this information
. Otherwise, you can also click on one
of the feeders or a segment of the
feeder and it will identify the feeder
number, the primary voltage and the
substation to which that feeder is
connected. Moving on to the DG
penetration layer, it operates under
the same principle, that is, we have
the map of Puerto Rico that is divided
into different colors based on the DG
penetration of that feeder. The feeders
that are in green have a penetration
level between 0 and 10%. Those that are
in orange between 10 and 15%and those
that are in red have a penetration
greater than 15%. We also remember that
supplementary studies are necessary for
any feeder that has a penetration level
greater than 15%. The way to operate
this map is similar to the previous map
, where you can increase or zoom in on
any of the feeders. You can click on
one of the segments and it will give
you information about this feeder,
including the feeder number and the
current penetration of that feeder
based on the last time that number was
calculated. This information is usually
updated monthly. Finally, I also want
to show you the last layer, which has
to do with the incremental hosting
capacity. The incremental hosting
capacity tells us the additional
capacity that a feeder has to receive
additional services. This information
varies depending on the feeder segment
and there is limited information only
for those feeders that have already
been verified in the field. As we
continue to increase the number of
feeders verified in the field, we will
periodically publish and update each of
these feeders with new information. The
operating mode is similar to the
previous maps, we can increase or zoom
in on any of the available feeders and
click within any of our segments of
interest. And this will give you
additional information about the
capacity that can be added in that
segment. We have the feeder number, the
segment and the additional capacity
that can be received in that feeder.
This concludes the maps tutorial. I
hope this helps you make more informed
decisions when purchasing a renewable
energy system. Thank you very much.

metadata.title: Exploring How Hosting Capacity Analysis Can Inform Proactive Grid Planning and Cost Allocation
metadata.author: IRECUSA
metadata.shortDescription: In this workshop, we will discuss how proactive hosting capacity analysis can be integrated as an objective within distribution planning processes so that investment decisions consider the impact that new capital can or will have on the system's ability to accommodate new DERs. Additionally, we will describe a proposed alternative cost allocation framework that leverages proactive hosting capacity concepts, builds upon conventional utility rate making principles, and more equitably distributes the benefits and costs of grid upgrades to both interconnection customers and utility ratepayers. The workshop will include discussions with participants to help inform ongoing grid planning efforts in Maine.

metadata.title: ESB Networks Availability Capacity Heat Map
metadata.author: ESB Networks
metadata.shortDescription:
At ESB Networks we are committed to improving the experience of our customers. As part of this commitment, we have developed our interactive Capacity Heatmap. It contains capacity information on all our 3-phase LV, MV and HV DSO substations. It provides an interface that enables the easy identification of potential transformer capacity in the vicinity of your site. An excel file is available to download from the download section on this page.

We envisage that the map will be used to inform initial discussion between ourselves and our customers. Although we have taken steps to ensure the accuracy of the map, it cannot replicate the level of accuracy provided by the detailed assessment carried out as part of the formal application process.  Please read the accompanying notes and important details section to understand what the map does and does not provide.

If the Available Capacity Heatmap indicates that there is insufficient capacity to accommodate your development, please contact us to discuss the next steps. We will always work with customers to find solutions.

metadata.title: DIgSILENT PowerFactory Tutorial: Lecture 18, Hosting Capacity Analysis
metadata.author: Electrical Engineering - Power System
metadata.shortDescription:
Hosting capacity analysis evaluates the maximum amount of distributed energy resources, like solar panels, that a power grid can accommodate without compromising reliability or safety.
It identifies potential constraints such as voltage fluctuations, thermal overloads, and protection issues in electrical networks.
Utilities use simulation tools and data modeling to perform this analysis, often incorporating real-time grid data for accuracy.
The results guide infrastructure upgrades and policy decisions to support renewable energy integration.

metadata.title: “Data Colonialism”: Native Communities Fight AI Data Centers on Indigenous Land
metadata.author: Democracy Now!
metadata.shortDescription:
Support our work: https://democracynow.org/donate/sm-desc-yt

The artificial intelligence industry's data center boom is the latest chapter in a long history of environmental racism and resource exploitation in vulnerable Native communities, says Oglala Lakota and Northern Cheyenne activist Krystal Two Bulls, the executive director of Honor the Earth, an Indigenous-led environmental justice organization that is tracking over 100 proposed data center projects on tribal and rural lands. We speak to Two Bulls about the myriad impacts of what she calls a "modern-day iteration" of "settler colonialism," including noise pollution, cancers and respiratory illnesses, water depletion, energy grid overload and even "ecological collapse." As tech companies set their sights on Indigenous lands, Two Bulls says, "We're always the one that ends up having to sacrifice our relationship to land, air, water, our communities and our nonhuman relatives."

Democracy Now! is an independent global news hour that airs on over 1,500 TV and radio stations Monday through Friday. Watch our livestream at democracynow.org Mondays to Fridays 8-9 a.m. ET.

Subscribe to our Daily Email Digest: https://democracynow.org/subscribe

metadata.title: Building Hyperscale Data Centers: Site Selection, Long-Lead Gear & Ground Prep
metadata.author: MEP Engineer AJ
metadata.shortDescription:
Building a hyperscale data center or AI compute hub isn’t decided when the steel goes up. It’s decided in the dirt, months before vertical construction begins. A single data center campus can consume as much electrical power as a mid-sized city, meaning site selection, environmental permitting, and power grid interconnections carry multi-million-dollar stakes.

In this video, we break down the critical pre-construction and early civil phase of data center development. From evaluating high-capacity utility feeds and fiber diversity to navigating zoning, long-lead equipment procurement (generators, transformers, chillers), and pad grading, here is what it takes to prepare the ground for mission-critical infrastructure.

TIMESTAMPS:
0:00 - The High Stakes of Early Data Center Construction
0:46 - What is Early-Phase Construction?
1:20 - Hyperscale vs. Commercial Buildings: Power & Redundancy
1:50 - Strategic Site Selection & Business Alignment (Enterprise, Colocation, Hyperscale)
3:03 - Evaluating Land: Power Interconnection, Fiber Diversity & Soil Conditions
3:30 - Navigating Permits, Clean Air/Water Acts & Zoning Red Tape
4:24 - Pre-Construction Engineering & Modular Prefabrication
4:56 - Assembling the Team: MEP Engineers & Specialized General Contractors
5:36 - Early Civil Works Timeline: Earthwork, Drainage & Utility Trenching
6:08 - Supply Chain & Risk Management: Procuring Long-Lead Electrical & HVAC Gear
7:05 - Transitioning from Groundwork to Vertical Construction
7:45 - Future-Proofing Data Centers for AI & High-Density Compute

KEY TOPICS COVERED:
• Site Selection Criteria: Why proximity to high-voltage substations, diverse dark fiber pathways, and low-risk floodplains determine project viability.
• Regulatory & Utility Approvals: Managing environmental compliance (Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, stormwater runoff) and utility interconnection commitments before design freeze.
• Mitigating Supply Chain Risk: Why electrical switchgear, backup diesel/gas generators, and liquid cooling chillers require immediate early-procurement planning to avoid schedule slip.
• Early Civil Infrastructure: Grading, deep foundations, seismic reinforcement, and heavy underground utility duct banks needed before erecting the building envelope.

If you enjoy practical, in-depth breakdowns of commercial MEP engineering, industrial construction, and mission-critical infrastructure, subscribe to MEP Engineer AJ!

#DataCenter #MEP #CivilEngineering #ElectricalEngineering #ConstructionManagement #Hyperscale
