metadata.title: HV Transmission Line GIS Project | Connect Road Centerline to HVT Pole | Complete Practical Tutorial
metadata.author: Ram Khilawan
metadata.shortDescription:
⚡ HV Transmission Line GIS Project Series के इस वीडियो में आप सीखेंगे कि Road Centerline को HVT Pole से GIS में सही तरीके से कैसे Connect किया जाता है।

यह प्रक्रिया किसी भी Transmission Line GIS Project में बहुत महत्वपूर्ण होती है क्योंकि इससे Road Network और Pole Network के बीच सही Connectivity बनाई जाती है।

इस वीडियो में आप सीखेंगे:

✅ Road Centerline Preparation
✅ Line Connectivity Rules
✅ ArcGIS Editing Tools
✅ Practical GIS Workflow

यह वीडियो GIS Students, Survey Engineers, Electrical Engineers, GIS Professionals और Utility Mapping Projects पर कार्य करने वालों के लिए बेहद उपयोगी है।

यदि आप HV Transmission Line GIS Project शुरू से अंत तक सीखना चाहते हैं, तो इस पूरी प्लेलिस्ट को जरूर देखें।

लाइन है। यहां से एडिट में जाके हम प्रोजेक्शन दे देंगे। ये मैं प्रोजेक्शन दे रहा हूं। डब्ल्यूजीएस 1984 यूटीएम जोन 44 इसके बाद ओके करेंगे और प्रोजेक्शन के बारे में जानकारी चाहिए तो मैं ऑलरेडी वीडियो बना चुका हूं। आप प्लिस्ट में जाकर देख सकते हैं। ओके करेंगे। फिर ओके करेंगे। ये आपके पास क्रिएट हो जाएगी। यह रोड की लाइन की शेप फाइल आ गई आपके पास। इसकी आप अपने हिसाब से सिंबोलॉजी चेंज कर सकते हैं। जैसे भी चाहे जिस भी कलर में चाहे वह सिंबोलॉजी आप अपने से दे सकते हैं। देने के बाद फिर आपको पर्टिकुलर एक पॉइंट पे आना होगा। जहां से आपको क्रिएट करना स्टार्ट करना है। मैं ज़ूम कर लेता हूं। इसके बाद वर्ड इमेजरी खोलेंगे। यह आपके पास इमेज ओपन हो गई। अगर आपको मालूम ना हो तो इसके लिए आपको ऐड डाटा में जाना है। ऐड डाटा में जाएंगे। यह ऐड बेस मैप है। इस पे आप क्लिक करेंगे। इस पे क्लिक करने के बाद इमेजरी में क्लिक करेंगे। ऐड कर देंगे। यह वर्ड इमेजरी अपने आप ऐड हो जाएगी। यह जूम होने के बाद आपको पर्टिकुलर वर्क स्टार्ट करना है। यह हो गया। यह आपके पास रोड है। मेजर रोड है। मींस जिसे हम स्टेट हाईवे बोलते हैं। यह मेन रोड है। और इसके बाद यह विलेज के रोड दिए हुए हैं। तो, मैं एक-एक करके कैप्चर करता हूं। कैप्चर करने के लिए आपको स्टार्ट एडिटिंग में जाना है। स्टार्ट एडिटिंग करेंगे। जिस भी जगह आपकी फाइल रखी हुई है, वहां डिस्प्ले कराना है। इसे कराएंगे। कलर यहां से चेंज कर सकते हैं। जो भी कलर चाहिए यहां से आप टेक्स्ट का कलर ले लेंगे। अप्लाई करेंगे। ओके करेंगे। अब हम चेक करेंगे यहां से। यह जीरो सबस्टेशन का है। इसके बाद वन टू थ्री फोर इस तरीके से पूरी सभी सीक्वेंस से चेक करेंगे। क्या हमारा सीक्वेंस सही आ रहा है? ये है हमारा 39। यह 39 है और यह जीरो सबस्टेशन है। मींस हमारी जो भी आईडी डली हुई थी सर्वे से वह सभी सही है। अब हम इसे पर्टिकुलर पोल की आईडी में पॉपुलेट करा देंगे। राइट क्लिक करेंगे। ओपन करेंगे। यह ओपन होने के बाद अब हमें यह पोल की आईडी है। पोल की आईडी में अगर हमें थ्री डिजिट रखना है या फोर डिजिट रखना है वो आप पर डिपेंड करता है। आपको किस टाइप का रखना है। अगर थ्री डिजिट नंबर रखना है, फोर लिखना है या टी डब्ल्यू लिखना है, वह आप पर डिपेंड करता है। आपको क्या रखना है या प्रोजेक्ट की क्या रिक्वायरमेंट है? तो प्रोजेक्ट की यहां रिक्वायरमेंट है। आपको रखना है टीw स्लश और थ्री डिजिट होने चाहिए। थ्री डिजिट के लिए आपको यहां पहले राइट क्लिक करेंगे। यहां टी डब्ल्यू लिखेंगे। टी डब्ल्यू स्ल और जीरो लगा देते हैं ओके कर देंगे। ये हमारे पास TW जीरो हो गया। अब इस वैल्यू को यहां पापुलेट कराएंगे। राइट क्लिक करेंगे। फील्ड कैलकुलेटर में जाएंगे। अब हमें पोल आईडी एंड टेस्ट आईडी ओके करेंगे। यह हमारे पास कैलकुलेट हो गई। थ्री डिजिट में अगर आगे 100 आ जाएगा क्योंकि 100 प्लस तक है। मैक्सिमम 1000 के नीचे ही है सबस्टेशन टू सबस्टेशन इसलिए थ्री डिजिट रखा हुआ है। अब यहां थ्री डिजिट नहीं है। लेकिन यहां भी हमें थ्री डिजिट करना पड़ेगा। यह वन से ले न तक यहां भी हमें थ्री डिजिट ही रखना पड़ेगा सीक्वेंस के लिए। इसलिए हम इसे स्टार्ट एडिटिंग करेंगे। ओके करेंगे। अब इस पर हम वन जीरो बढ़ा देंगे। सभी में आप कैलकुलेट भी करा सकते हैं। मैं मैनुअली कर देता हूं। ज्यादा नहीं है। यह हो गए थ्री डिजिट। अब इसके बाद ये बचे हुए हैं दो जीरो जीरो वाले। ये हमारे सबस्टेशन है। तो सबस्टेशन का नेम पॉपुलेट करा देंगे। राइट क्लिक करेंगे। फिल कैलकुलेटर पर जाएंगे। अब यह टाइटल पर लिखा हुआ है। हम यहां से टाइटल सेलेक्ट करेंगे। ओके कर देंगे। यह हमारे पास सबस्टेशन आ गए। नेम अपने हिसाब से चेंज कर लेंगे। जैसे भी है अगर कुछ गलत है तो आप अपने हिसाब से नेम चेंज कर लेंगे। कैपिटल है, स्माल है वो आप देख लीजिएगा। कैसे रिक्वायरमेंट है उस तरीके से आपको करना है। यह आपकी पोल नंबरिंग हो गई। अब इसे हम डिस्प्ले करा के देखेंगे। राइट क्लिक करेंगे। प्रॉपर्टी पे जाएंगे। टेक्स्ट की जगह हम पोल आईडी लेंगे। ओके कर देंगे। इसे भी क्लोज कर देंगे। अब यहां से देखेंगे। यह सबस्टेशन है। सबस्टेशन है। पोल वन है। पोल टू है। मतलब हमारी सीक्वेंसिंग सही है। सीक्वेंसिंग सही 🌐 Exploring the Dynamics of Decentralized Data Centers, Hyperscale, and Edge Computing

🔍 In this insightful discussion, we dive into the evolving landscape of data center infrastructure, examining the growth potential and market dynamics across different scales - from decentralized data centers to hyperscale facilities and the emerging edge computing paradigm.

🌍 Discover how location, demand, and capacity are shaping the success of various data center models, and gain insights into the regional variations that are driving the prominence of tier two and tier three markets.

🔧 Learn about the challenges and opportunities in defining and deploying edge data centers, and explore strategies for meeting the rapidly growing demand for data center capacity.

 🌐 **Hyperscale vs Decentralized Data Centers** 🌞

Dive into the **global energy capacity** controlled by hyperscalers, which now accounts for a staggering **43% of the world's energy**! ⚡

💡 Discover why **decentralized data centers** are the future:

 - On-site energy generation 🌞

 - Reduced grid stress 🌐

 - Faster AI cluster growth 🤖

🔥 We also explore the concept of the **trillion-dollar cluster** needed to birth artificial superintelligence, requiring **100 gigawatts of power**—a game-changer for the industry! 🚀

🏗️ Learn how decentralized systems can:

 - Utilize curtailed wind energy 🌬️

 - Integrate district heating systems ♨️

 - Foster better community relations 🤝

📢 Join the conversation and stay ahead in the race to the electron! ⚡

Watch the full episode:
Ep. #40 Mark Bjornsgaard, Founder and CEO of Deep Green Technologies | Data Center Go-to-Market Podcast

metadata.title: Why AI Data Centers Are Heading to Rural America
metadata.author: Build Core
metadata.shortDescription:
Grab your airport posters at https://www.etsy.com/shop/GridFormLabs with code BUILDCORE for 10% off — thanks for supporting me!

AI feels invisible, but the infrastructure behind it is becoming impossible to ignore. Across the United States, a new generation of hyperscale data centers is being built for artificial intelligence, and many of the largest projects are moving away from traditional tech hubs and into rural America. These facilities need enormous amounts of electricity, huge buildable sites, faster grid connections, cooling systems, fiber routes, substations, backup generation, and room to expand. That changes where these projects can realistically be built.

But the story is not only about Big Tech. It is also about rural communities being asked to host some of the largest industrial projects in the country. These facilities can bring tax revenue, construction jobs, utility upgrades, new fiber infrastructure, and private investment, but they also raise questions about electricity, water use, land conversion, noise, construction impacts, and long-term local benefits. The point is not that data centers are good or bad. AI infrastructure has to be built somewhere. The question is whether every hyperscale AI project is actually the right fit for the place where it is being proposed.

metadata.title: Behind the Meter Generation: How Natural Gas Fuels AI Growth Until Nuclear Scales Up
metadata.author: ELK TRADING Co LLC | Natural Gas Trading
metadata.shortDescription:
The explosion of AI and cloud computing has created an unprecedented demand for reliable, low-cost power. Data centers—the backbone of AI growth—require enormous amounts of electricity, often in urban and suburban areas where grid limitations pose challenges. This is where Behind the Meter Generation (BTMG) comes in: on-site power generation that provides data centers with dedicated, scalable energy.

For the next several decades, natural gas will be the primary fuel driving BTMG for AI infrastructure, given its strategic advantages over other energy sources. The U.S. has abundant natural gas reserves, enabling stable pricing and long-term energy security. Unlike Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), which remain years away from widespread deployment, natural gas plants can be permitted and built much faster.

Recent deals, like Energy Transfer’s agreement with Cloudburst Energy (source), highlight how private energy providers are securing natural gas for hyperscale data centers. This allows AI growth to continue without waiting on large-scale grid expansions or nuclear advancements. While nuclear will likely take over in the 2040s, natural gas ensures that AI infrastructure doesn’t stall in the meantime.

As the U.S. leverages its energy advantage, policy leaders, AI firms, and energy providers must collaborate to streamline approvals for gas-fired BTMG facilities, ensuring America remains the leader in AI-powered innovation.

metadata.title: Behind the Meter: Powering AI at Gigawatt Scale
metadata.author: The Machine Room Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
AI infrastructure is increasing electricity demand at a speed and scale few industries have experienced before. In this episode, Kevin Brown speaks with Mandar Pandit, Chief Strategy and Growth Officer for Data Centers at GE Vernova, about how the energy sector is responding as individual data center campuses begin to require as much power as a small city. 

Mandar explains why limited grid capacity and lengthy interconnection timelines are leading more operators to consider behind-the-meter generation. By producing power on site, data centre developers can take greater control of their deployment schedules. However, this also means assuming responsibilities traditionally managed by utilities, from power generation and protection systems to grid stability and overall energy management. 

The conversation also explores the technologies that could support this growth more sustainably, including hydrogen-capable gas turbines, carbon capture and small modular nuclear reactors. Rather than viewing AI solely as a threat to the electricity system, Mandar argues that it is exposing existing weaknesses, accelerating innovation and encouraging data centre operators, utilities and technology providers to collaborate in new ways. 

Featured guest: Mandar Pandit, Chief Strategy and Growth Officer for Data Centers, GE Vernova 

Key quote: “The AI boom is highlighting the weaknesses in the system and showing us where, as an industry, we need to focus quickly.” 

Key takeaways:
- AI data center campuses are increasingly requesting hundreds of megawatts or more than one gigawatt of power at a single location. 
- Grid infrastructure and data center development operate on very different timelines, creating an urgent need for alternative power strategies. 
- Behind-the-meter generation can help operators gain faster access to power by producing electricity on site. 
- Operating behind the meter is not a simple solution, as data centre operators must also manage protection, control, stability and other utility-like responsibilities. 
- Gas generation, hydrogen, carbon capture and small modular nuclear reactors could all contribute to a more diverse power mix for AI infrastructure. 
- Growing data centre demand is stress-testing the energy system, exposing weaknesses and accelerating investment, collaboration and innovation. 

Follow or subscribe to The Machine Room on your preferred podcast platform for more conversations with the people building the energy and infrastructure systems behind AI.

segments.text: All right, let's dive right into an
explainer that completely flips how we
look at industrial power. We're pulling
this straight from the latest first
screens consulting report and we are
going to look at a massive shift
happening right now in how commercial
and industrial facilities manage their
electricity. And trust me, the financial
implications here, they're absolutely
massive. What if a battery could pay for
itself in just 5 years, all while
rescuing the national grid? That's the
exact question we're answering today.
We're going to bust the myth that
industrial batteries are just, you know,
glorified diesel generators. For a long
time, energy storage at a factory or a
hospital was basically just seen as an
emergency backup. But as we're about to
see, modern battery systems are active
profit generating assets. Get this, 20
to 30% of a facility's monthly power
bill is determined by just a few minutes
of PQs. It's kind of a shocking fact,
right? Imagine running a massive
manufacturing plant for 30 days
straight, but nearly a third of your
power cost is dictated by a single
random 15-minute window where all your
machines just happen to spin up at the
exact same time. It's a huge structural
cost problem, and it is begging to be
solved. To break down this massive
transition, we've structured our
explainer into six quick chapters. We'll
cover the costly power problem, the
behind the meter battery solution,
beating the demand charge, the brain
behind the battery, the financial
payback, and finally, fixing India's
duck curve. Let's get into it. Section
one, the costly power problem. Let's
pinpoint the immediate pain keeping
commercial facility owners awake at
night. So, what is a demand charge? It's
a fee based on the maximum electricity
demand recorded during your billing
period, usually measured in 15 or 30
minute intervals. The crucial point here
is that you aren't just paying for the
total energy you consume. You're
actually being penalized heavily for the
intensity of your demand spikes. If your
facility draws a massive surge of power
for just a 15-minute interval, the
utility company hits you with a premium
for that peak capacity, even if your
average use is super low the rest of the
month. Moving on to section two, the
behind the meter battery solution. This
brings us to the strategic frontier of
energy storage designed specifically to
eliminate those spikes. So, what does
behind the meter or BTM actually mean?
It's energy storage deployed on site at
commercial buildings or factories,
placing power control directly in the
consumer's hands. We need to be clear
here. We aren't talking about massive
utility substations. We're talking about
large batteries sitting right in your
facility's backyard. Behind the meter
means it's on your side of the utility
meter. It's your asset. You control the
power dynamics and costs rather than
relying entirely on the grid. India's
energy transition is shifting in a big
way from front of the meter grid
projects to behind the meter facility
solutions. Historically, India's storage
stock was all about central grids and
utility scale batteries. But now the
momentum has aggressively shifted.
Facilities are pairing rooftop solar
with their own on-site batteries to
manage local demand directly. Section
three, beating the demand charge. Let's
look at exactly how this technology acts
as an anchor to sync those exorbitant
monthly costs. Let's talk about the
actual math for a 5 MVA consumer before
and after installing a battery energy
storage system. The demand charge
shrinks from 82 cr down to.54 cr just by
shaving off 900 kW of peak demand. This
is real data from the first green model
for a large-scale industrial consumer.
By using the battery to supply power
during those intense 15-minute spikes,
the facility never pulls that peak load
from the grid. So, your energy charges
stay roughly the same, but your demand
charge absolutely plummets. When you
compare a before battery bill of 3.35
crore to an after battery bill of 3.01
core, you are looking at a pure 0.34
crore monthly savings. That is a 10.1%
bill reduction right off the top. It's a
massive operational cost saving. And the
best part, it all happens automatically
without the facility having to slow down
production or even turn off the lights.
But how does the system know when to act
to actually save you that money? That
brings us to section four, the brain
behind the battery. You see, you can't
just plug a giant lithium-ion box into a
factory and hope it figures things out.
The battery itself is just the brawn.
The real magic happens with the energy
management system or EMS. Think of it as
the brain of the whole operation. It
acts like an orchestra conductor,
monitoring the grid connection, tracking
rooftop solar generation, and deciding
moment by moment whether to charge the
battery, send power to critical loads,
or discharge to shave the peak. The EMS
operates on a brilliant four-step logic
loop to ensure your facility never
crosses that costly contract demand
threshold. First, it forecasts the load
using historical data to predict
tomorrow's energy needs. Second, it
detects the specific peak windows where
demand spikes are expected. Third, it
optimizes the charge and discharge
schedule, basically charging up at night
when electricity is cheap and
discharging during the peak. And fourth,
it always protects a minimum state of
charge reserve just in case there's a
sudden grid outage and you need
emergency backup. Section five, the
financial payback. Okay, so the tech
works beautifully, but does the business
case actually make sense for an
investor? Well, for a standard 2.5
megawatt system, the simple payback
period is an incredibly lean 5.1 years.
In the world of heavy industrial
infrastructure and large capital
expenditures, a payback period hovering
right around 5 years is highly
attractive, especially when you consider
this is for an asset that has a 12 to
15ear design life. Let's break down the
base case financial model. You start
with a gross capital expenditure of
14.50 50 cr rupees. But when you stack
the demand savings with tariff arbitrage
and offsetting diesel costs, things get
really interesting. The system captures
cheaper off- peak electricity to use
during expensive peak hours and replaces
dirty expensive diesel generators during
short outages. All of that yields a net
operating benefit of 2.89 cr rupees
every single year. That means you hit a
14.2% 2% project internal rate of return
generating positive operating cash flow
from year one. Finally, let's zoom out a
bit. Section six, fixing India's duck
curve. Let's see how thousands of these
individual factory decisions impact the
entire national power grid. You might
have heard of India's infamous duck
curve. It's the huge mismatch between a
massive surplus of midday solar power
and a massive demand spike that hits
right around 8:00 p.m. During the day,
there's so much solar power on the grid
that demand drops off. But as soon as
the sun sets, demand absolutely rockets
up to around 256 gawatt as everyone
turns on their lights and appliances.
Behind the meter batteries perfectly
balance this out. They charge during the
day, literally soaking up that excess
solar, and then discharge at night,
completely flattening that steep,
problematic curve. What's amazing is
that by simply acting in their own
financial self-interest to lower their
monthly bills, these commercial
facilities collectively create a massive
distributed flexibility resource that
stabilizes the entire national grid. If
we reach just 20% penetration of these
systems, we're looking at shaving up to
24 gawatt off the national peak demand.
Plus, we'd be shifting 58.3 gatt hours
of daily energy from low value periods
to high value periods. This directly
leads to an improved system load factor,
less stress on the grid, and way fewer
blackouts. There's a quote from the
report that really nails this whole
paradigm shift. Behind the meter battery
storage should be treated as a
performancedriven energy solution, not
as a battery commodity. It's so true.
You aren't just buying a box of
lithium-ion cells. You're investing in a
smart dynamic energy asset that
continuously negotiates with the grid to
save you money. The hardware stores the
energy, sure, but the smart dispatch
software is what actually monetizes it.
So, we leave you with this question. If
commercial facilities can transform from
grid burdens into profit generating
power assets, how does this redefine the
future of real estate and India's energy
independence? Think about that as you
consider your own energy strategies
moving forward. Because this transition,
it isn't just coming, it's already
sitting right there behind the meter.
The line between being a consumer of
power and a manager of power is totally
disappearing. I hope this explainer gave
you a really clear view of how energy
storage is completely reshaping
industrial power. Keep learning, stay
curious, and we'll catch you next time.

metadata.title: Big Power Needed Now! How Behind-the-Meter Generation can solve Grid Constraints & AI Power Demand
metadata.author: Collicutt Energy Services
metadata.shortDescription:
Data center power is changing — fast.

In this 2025 webinar, we break down how AI-driven demand, interconnection delays, and grid congestion are reshaping how large-scale data centers secure reliable power across North America.

As grid constraints intensify, developers are increasingly evaluating behind-the-meter generation, hybrid power strategies, and modular natural gas solutions to accelerate speed-to-power and maintain uptime.

In this session, we cover:

• Why Alberta built ~12 GW of load over 80 years — yet now faces ~20 GW in the interconnection queue
• Why grid connectivity is no longer guaranteed
• Behind-the-meter vs grid-connected data center strategies
• Natural gas vs turbines vs reciprocating engines
• Reliability modeling (99.9% uptime explained)
• Ramp-rate resilience for AI training & inference workloads
• Battery Energy Storage (BESS) integration
• Lead times and deployment timelines for 50–500+ MW projects
• Economic modeling: IRR, CapEx, OpEx comparisons

This webinar is designed for:
Data center developers, hyperscalers, AI infrastructure planners, power engineers, utilities, and energy investors navigating today’s grid-constrained markets.

Presented by Matthew Swinamer, Technical Sales Engineer at Collicutt Energy Services, specializing in distributed generation and scalable onsite power solutions for mission-critical infrastructure.

If you’re evaluating:
• Behind-the-meter data center power
• Natural gas power for AI workloads
• Distributed generation at scale
• Grid interconnection alternatives

this session provides a practical, engineering-based perspective.

metadata.title: Fast, flexible behind the meter power
metadata.author: Datacenter Dynamics
metadata.shortDescription:
In this discussion, Thomas Seeber of INNIO Group speaks with DCD to share insights on behind-the-meter power and the growing role of fast, flexible generation in unlocking new data center capacity.

Key topics covered:

Why behind-the-meter matters: How grid constraints are pushing operators to look at new power options.

Speed and flexibility: Why fast-deployable generation is gaining attention in constrained markets.

Unlocking capacity: How on-site solutions can help support growth where utility delivery is limited.

A changing power strategy: Why the industry is widening its view of how capacity can be secured.

To watch all of our video interviews, visit the DCD website: https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/videos/

For all the latest news, analysis and reports on the data center sector visit: https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/

Follow us on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/datacenterdynamics/

metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to Part 1 of our two-part series on powering data centers off the grid. In this episode, Dave Bell, our Vice President of Data Centers and Microgrids, dives into how we keep data centers running behind the meter using reliable natural gas solutions. He’ll explain the benefits of leveraging natural gas for consistent, resilient power and how this approach helps ensure reliability for critical operations.

Stay tuned for Part 2, where we’ll go even deeper into our infrastructure innovations.

metadata.title: TVA Interconnection Queue Reform Explained | New Cluster Process, Deposits & Costs
metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
TVA has fundamentally changed how large generators connect to its transmission system. The previous first-come, first-served queue has been replaced with a cluster-based interconnection process aligned with FERC Order 2023.

In this video, Keentel Engineering explains TVA’s new Large Generator Interconnection Procedure (LGIP) framework, including the annual cluster intake window, application requirements, study sequence, cost allocation methods, withdrawal penalties, and what developers need to prepare before entering the queue.

This guide covers:

• Why TVA moved from a serial queue to a cluster-based model
• How the 45-day annual cluster window works
• TVA LGIP application requirements and project readiness
• $25,000 application fee and study deposit structure
• Commercial readiness deposit requirements
• Feasibility Study, System Impact Study, and Facilities Study process
• Network upgrade cost allocation methods

📖 Read the full technical guide:
https://keentelengineering.com/tva-interconnection-queue-lgip

Chapters:

00:36 From Serial Queue to TVA Cluster Model
01:09 TVA Interconnection Entry Costs & Deposits
01:49 Cluster Study Process: Window to Agreement
02:34 Network Upgrade Cost Allocation
03:15 TVA Withdrawal Penalties & Cost Exposure
03:56 Withdrawal Penalty Exemptions
04:32 What TVA Queue Reform Means for Developers
05:15 Technical FAQs
06:30 Conclusion

Keentel Engineering helps renewable energy developers and utilities navigate TVA interconnection requirements through feasibility studies, POI analysis, power system studies, protection coordination, and grid compliance support.

Learn more:
https://keentelengineering.com

#TVA #TVALGIP #GeneratorInterconnection #FERCOrder2023 #GridInterconnection #RenewableEnergy

segments.text: Welcome to Keintel Engineering. Today
we're covering TVA's new cluster-based
interconnection queue. What changed,
what it costs to enter, how studies
sequence, and what it costs to exit. TVA
posted its revised large generator
interconnection procedures. On October
1st, 2024, effective November 1st, the
old serial first come first-s served
queue is gone, replaced by a cluster
process under FK order number 2023. If
you're developing generation in TVA
territory above 20 megawatts, this
framework now governs your timeline,
deposits, and cost exposure. Under the
old serial Q, projects were studied one
at a time in timestamp order. A single
withdrawal forced every downstream
project to be restudied. Speculative
filings with no real site control
clogged the line for serious projects.
The cluster model collects all requests
during a 45-day annual window and
studies them together. Every project in
that window is equally cued. No
advantage to filing earlier within it.
Earlier annual clusters outrank later
ones, but inside a cluster position is
flat. The competitive dynamic has
shifted from speed to readiness. Every
project pays a nonrefundable $25,000
application fee. Study deposits scale by
size. $150,000 for projects under 75
megawws. $200,000 for 75 to 199 megawws.
$300,000 for 200 megawws and above. On
top of that, a commercial readiness
deposit equal to twice the study deposit
is required at entry. A 200 megawatt
plus project is posting $925,000
before the first study begins. You also
need 100% site control at submission.
Full rights to develop, construct,
operate, and maintain the facility for
its expected operating life. The process
runs in defined phases. The 45day
cluster request window opens every
January 15th. A 60-day customer
engagement window follows. Scoping
meeting, Oasis posting of the anonymized
cluster list, and execution of the
cluster study agreement. Fail to execute
and your request is deemed withdrawn.
The cluster study runs 150 days, power
flow, stability, short circuit, and
alternative technology evaluation across
the whole group. Withdrawals can trigger
a cluster restudy at another 150 days.
The interconnection facilities study
adds 180 days of individual detailed
engineering. Then LGIA execution and
construction multi-year path even on
schedule. Three upgrade categories,
three allocation methods. Substation
network upgrades split per capita per
generating facility, not by megawws. Two
50 megawatt plants share equally with
one 300 megawatt plant at the same
substation bay. System network upgrades
allocate by proportional impact. Each
facilities share reflects how much it
drives the need for that specific
upgrade posted by category on Oasis. Two
identical plants at different POEs can
carry very different shares.
Interconnection facilities are directly
assigned to the customers using them
split per capita where shared. Funding
customers earn transmission credits
under the LGIA. Before the cluster study
starts, no penalty. After it begins,
costs escalate with progress. During or
after the cluster study, the floor is
twice your study deposit. During the
cluster restudy, the greater of twice
the deposit or 5% of allocated upgrade
costs. during the facility's study or
before LGIA execution the greater of
twice the deposit or 10% after executing
the LGIES or if the facility never
reaches commercial operation 20% of
allocated upgrade costs penalty funds
pull per cluster and are applied first
to remaining customers study costs then
to offset cost increases they absorbed
from projects that left three off-ramps
exist when TVA's own studies blow up
your economics the no material effect
exemption is always available. No
penalty if your exit doesn't materially
affect cost or timing for anyone
remaining in the cluster. The restudy
offramp, no penalty if your allocated
costs rose more than 25% between cluster
restudy reports. The facility study
offramp, no penalty if costs rose more
than 100% in your facility study report
compared to the prior cluster study
figure. These thresholds are your
protection against economics the studies
quietly destroy. Five takeaways. The
January window is a hard annual gate.
Miss it and you wait a year. Frontload
your readiness, site control, fees,
study deposit, and the two times
commercial readiness deposit are gating
requirements, not paperwork to tidy up
later. Model withdrawal exposure as a
real line item. The 25% and 100%
exemption thresholds are your planned
exit conditions if economics
deteriorate. Your costs are coupled to
your neighbors. Both per capita and
proportional impact allocations move
with cluster composition and storage and
partial service requests have real
flexibility. TVA will study storage at
your proposed charging assumptions and
injection limiting equipment allows
study below full capacity. When did the
new LGIP take effect? Posted October
1st, 2024. Effective November 1st, 2024.
Replacing the serial Q with a cluster
process under FIRK order number 2023.
What project size triggers the LGIP?
Generating facilities exceeding 20
megawatt 20 megawatt and below use the
small generating facility procedures.
How is Q position determined? All
requests in one window are equally cued.
No benefit to filing earlier within it.
Earlier annual clusters outrank later
ones. How do deposits escalate? The
commercial readiness deposit starts at
two times the study deposit, tops up to
5% of allocated costs before restudy and
10% before the facility's study. What's
in the cluster study report? Power flow
stability and shortcircuit results,
non-binding cost estimates, each
customer's allocated share, and
alternative transmission technology
evaluation. Can a project be modified
after filing? Up to a 60% decrease in
output is preapproved before returning
the executed cluster study agreement.
Any POI change is always a material
modification. Can Q position be
transferred? Yes. If the acquirer takes
over the facility, the POI stays the
same. Compliance is maintained and TVA
is notified. What is the difference
between ERIS and NRIS? ERIS delivers on
an as available basis using existing
capacity. NRIS builds upgrades for
native integration, allowing network
resource designation up to full output.
If you're developing a generating
facility larger than 20 megawatts
anywhere in Tennessee Valley Authority
territory, the interconnection rules
changed fundamentally in November 2024.
TVA replaced its old serial queue where
filing early gave you a competitive edge
with a cluster-based process aligned to
FK order 2023. Now there's one annual
intake window, 45 calendar days opening
every January 15th. Miss it and you wait
a full year. There's no rolling queue to
slip into anymore. To even submit a
valid request, you need to arrive ready.
That means 100% site control. Not in
progress, not pending. Done. A
non-refundable $25,000 application fee.
A study deposit scaled to your project
size up to $300,000.
And on top of that, a commercial
readiness deposit equal to twice the
study deposit. So a 250 megawatt project
is looking at nearly a million before a
single study runs. Once you're in, every
project in your annual cluster is
equally skewed. No advantage to filing
on day 1 versus day 44. That shifts the
competitive dynamic entirely away from
speed and toward readiness. Your cost
exposure depends heavily on what else is
clustered with you and where everyone
connects. Because system upgrade costs
follow proportional impact. And if you
need to exit, withdrawal penalties
escalate from two times your study
deposit up to 20% of your allocated
network upgrade costs after you've
executed an LGIA.
Though cost spike thresholds at 25 and
100% give you offramps if TVA's own
studies blow up your number. At Keenel
Engineering, we help developers in TVA
territory get Q ready. Feasibility
studies, POI analysis, deposit strategy
and interconnection application support.
For more information, visit
keintilengineering.com.

If the acquirer takes over the facility, the POI stays the same. Compliance is maintained and TVA is notified. What is the difference between ERIS and NRIS? ERIS delivers on an as available basis using existing capacity. NRIS builds upgrades for native integration, allowing network resource designation up to full output. If you're developing a generating facility larger than 20 megawatts anywhere in Tennessee Valley Authority territory, the interconnection rules changed fundamentally in November 2024. TVA replaced its old serial queue where filing early gave you a competitive edge with a cluster-based process aligned to FK order 2023. Now there's one annual intake window, 45 calendar days opening every January 15th. Miss it and you wait a full year. There's no rolling queue to slip into anymore. To even submit a valid request, you need to arrive ready. That means 100% site control. Not in progress, not pending. Done. A non-refundable $25,000 application fee. A study deposit scaled to your project size up to $300,000. And on top of that, a commercial readiness deposit equal to twice the study deposit. So a 250 megawatt project is looking at nearly a million before a single study runs. Once you're in, every project in your annual cluster is equally skewed. No advantage to filing on day 1 versus day 44. That shifts the competitive dynamic entirely away from speed and toward readiness. Your cost exposure depends heavily on what else is clustered with you and where everyone connects. Because system upgrade costs follow proportional impact. And if you need to exit, withdrawal penalties escalate from two times your study deposit up to 20% of your allocated network upgrade costs after you've executed an LGIA. Though cost spike thresholds at 25 and 100% give you offramps if TVA's own studies blow up your number. At Keenel Engineering, we help developers in TVA territory get Q ready. Feasibility studies, POI analysis, deposit strategy and interconnection application support. For more information, visit keintilengineering.com.

metadata.title: The Interconnection Queue Shrank. That's Not Good News
metadata.author: Stats in Motion
metadata.shortDescription:
Grid interconnection queue data from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory shows the queue shrinking, and it is being reported as the grid bottleneck finally easing. That reading is wrong, and the same dataset shows why: for every 1 GW that reached commercial operation in 2025, roughly 14 GW were withdrawn. A queue that drains because projects get abandoned is not a queue that is being processed.

The more interesting story is what battery storage developers are doing about it. Buying legacy solar projects to retrofit batteries onto an existing point of interconnection looks like a way to skip a wait that now runs more than five years. It trades a paperwork problem for a physics problem, because that interconnection was studied for one-directional midday export, not for a bidirectional asset that charges at night. Fault current, protection coordination and transformer thermal duty all change.

SOURCES
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, "Queued Up: 2026 Edition" (June 2026, data as of end of 2025): https://emp.lbl.gov/queues
FERC Order 2023 (July 2023) and Order 2023-A (March 2024).
FERC order directing PJM on co-located load, 2025-12-18.

Portions of the B-roll footage in this video were generated with AI. The analysis, script and sourcing are my own.

segments.text: The headlines are telling you the grid
connection bottleneck is finally easing.
They are pointing to the latest data
from Lawrence Berkeley National Lab
showing the total queue of projects
waiting to connect fell by about 10%
last year.
That reading is wrong. The queue isn't
being processed, it's being abandoned.
For every single gigawatt of new
generation that successfully connected
to the grid in 2025, a staggering 14
gigawatts were withdrawn.
Developers gave up. The storage queue,
which is critical for a reliable grid,
shrank by 16%.
That isn't a sign of efficient
processing, it is a sign of attrition.
The system is so slow and expensive that
projects are dying on the vine faster
than they can be built.
This is not a new problem, but it is
getting worse.
If we look at every project that entered
a queue between the year 2000 and 2020,
only 13% were actually built by the end
of last year.
75% were withdrawn. Federal regulators
tried to fix this with FERC Order 2023,
which forced grid operators to study
projects in clusters instead of one by
one.
But this data is the first real report
card on those reforms, and it suggests
the patient's health is not improving.
In response, some developers are trying
a new strategy.
Instead of waiting in line for a new
connection,
they are buying old solar farms just to
get their spot on the grid.
They then plan to add batteries to these
existing sites.
On paper, this looks like a clever way
to skip a wait that now runs more than 5
years.
In reality, it swaps a paperwork problem
for a physics problem.
An interconnection agreement for a solar
farm is not just a permission slip for a
certain number of megawatts.
It is a result of a study based on a
specific behavior, power flowing one way
out of the plant, peaking at midday, and
stopping at night. A battery is
completely different. It is
bidirectional. It charges from the grid,
often at night, acting as a load. Then
it discharges, acting as a generator,
often during the evening peak.
This reversal of power flow changes
everything for the equipment at that
connection point.
The original study made assumptions
about fault current, which is the surge
of electricity that happens during a
short circuit. A battery inverter
contributes to fault current differently
than a solar inverter.
The protective relays, the devices that
detect these faults and trip circuit
breakers, might not be calibrated to see
the fault correctly, or they may trip
when they are not supposed to. The
entire safety logic of the circuit can
become invalid.
It also creates new thermal stress. The
transformer connecting the project to
the grid was sized for a solar profile,
where it works hard during the day and
cools off at night. A battery that
charges all night and discharges all
evening forces that same transformer to
run hot for many more hours. That extra
heat shortens the life of the equipment
and can become the new lower limit on
how much power the project can actually
move.
This is where the engineering meets the
economics.
A developer might successfully buy a 40
MW solar site to add a battery, only to
find that the grid operator curtails its
output to 20 MW because of the thermal
limits on the transformer or voltage
issues on the line.
The binding constraint was never the
paper contract. It was the physical
capacity of the wires and switches at
that specific node on the grid. The
developers who make money will be the
ones who model the voltage profile and
check the protection settings before
they buy the asset.
So, the real story in this new data is
not that the queue is getting better. It
is that the market is finally repricing
where real, usable grid capacity exists.
The truly scarce asset is no longer a
spot in the queue. It's a physically
robust point of interconnection that's
already built. What I'm watching for
next is grid operators, like PJM was
recently ordered to do by FERC, getting
much stricter about these retrofit
applications. They will start demanding
the same detailed studies as new
projects because physics, not paperwork,
ultimately decides what can be built.

metadata.title: CAISO IPE 5.0 Explained | Cluster 16 Interconnection Changes | Solar & BESS Developers Guide
metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
CAISO Interconnection Process Enhancements 5.0 (IPE 5.0) introduces major changes to the CAISO interconnection process ahead of Cluster 16, impacting solar developers, battery energy storage systems (BESS), renewable energy projects, and Load Serving Entities (LSEs).

In this video, Keentel Engineering explains the complete CAISO IPE 5.0 reform, including updated intake scoring rules, commercial readiness deposit changes, WDAT distribution project requirements, energy-only project deliverability pathways, queue management updates, and what developers need to prepare before the Cluster 16 interconnection window opens.

You will learn:

• What changed under CAISO IPE 5.0
• How Cluster 16 interconnection scoring works
• New non-LSE affidavit requirements
• Commercial readiness deposit timing changes
• Updated allocation caps for LSE-supported projects
• How WDAT distribution projects are affected
• New deliverability options for operational energy-only projects
• Commercial viability criteria (CVC) updates
• Why the CAISO pre-application process was removed
• Key actions developers and utilities should take before Cluster 16

CAISO's latest reforms are designed to reduce queue delays, improve project readiness, and create a more efficient pathway for viable renewable energy projects. Understanding these changes is critical for developers working on solar, wind, battery storage, and other inverter-based resources seeking grid interconnection in California.

📖 Read the related engineering guide:
https://keentelengineering.com/caiso-ibr-model-review

Explore related services:

Utility Scale Solar Interconnection:
https://keentelengineering.com/utility-scale-solar-interconnection

Battery Energy Storage Engineering:
https://keentelengineering.com/service/utility-scale-battery-storage

Chapters:

00:00 Introduction: CAISO IPE 5.0 Overview
00:25 Background: IPE 2023 Foundation & Why IPE 5.0 Was Created
01:03 CAISO Intake Process Changes
01:59 Allocation Cap Updates & WDAT Distribution Projects
02:55 Deliverability for Operational Energy-Only Projects
03:52 Queue Management Changes & Commercial Viability Criteria
04:45 Topics Removed From IPE 5.0 Scope
05:30 What Developers Should Do Before Cluster 16
06:35 CAISO IPE 5.0 Technical FAQs

Keentel Engineering supports renewable developers, utilities, and project owners with CAISO interconnection studies, BESS engineering, grid studies, power system analysis, and compliance support.

Learn more:
https://keentelengineering.com

October 1st, 2026. IPE 2023 made
sweeping changes to CAISO's

Track 2 reduced Cluster 15 to a

resource needs. CAISO committed to
monitoring the process and returning to
address friction points. The Cluster 15
intake results from June 2025 and a FERC
informational report from July 2025
directly informed IPE 5.0. The goal:
remove friction, accelerate viable
resource onboarding, and have the
process ready for Cluster 16. Two intake
changes. First, the non-LSE affidavit.
The 25-point commercial interest award
previously required a non-LSE affidavit
specifically citing corporate
sustainability goals. IPE 5.0 removes
that requirement. The affidavit now only
needs to attest to the project's value
to the organization. The 25-point award,
the one project per cluster limit, and
CAISO's scrutiny of every affidavit
remain unchanged. This opens the door
for data centers and industrial
operators with economic, not just
sustainability, motivations. Second,
commercial readiness deposit timing.

interconnection request window, even for

ranking succeeds by the close of the
customer engagement window. Projects

more intake changes. The full allocation
election cap is revised to the lesser of
50% of the LSE's forecasted RA load
share or 500 MW calibrated to the 95th
percentile of projects that have reached
commercial operation. Small LSEs can now
support projects larger than their raw
allocation. Large LSEs are capped at 500
MW. Energy only projects face no cap.
Also new, WDAT distribution projects
must now compete in cluster intake

distribution project seeking

Same as transmission level projects. No

seek deliverability.

and 2030. CAISO's
solution, energy only projects from
cluster 15 and later that have reached
commercial operation may now seek TPD

cluster 14 and earlier.
Four eligibility requirements, in
commercial operation at the affidavit
submission date, executed RA a
procurement agreement with an RA

require the project to seek TPD and it

local deliverability constraint are not
eligible. Two queue management changes.
First, commercial viability criteria CVC

energy only when requesting COD
extensions beyond 7 years. Projects

queue entirely, no longer converted to
energy only. That conversion pathway is

extension limit was removed after
stakeholder pushback.

pre-application process is discontinued.

the 2027 affidavit due date. If your COD

procurement agreements now.
Load serving entities, review RA
portfolio gaps for 2029 and 2030. The
commercial operation pathway for cluster
15 and later energy only projects may
add deliverable capacity. Ensure
procurement agreements require TPD and
at least 5 years of RA procurement. My
cluster 15,
energy only project, can it now seek
deliverability?
Yes, after commercial operation through
the commercial operation allocation
group. Requires a 5-year RA agreement.
Projects behind a local constraint are
not eligible. My project COD is beyond 7
years. Will it be automatically
withdrawn? No.
CVC triggers only when you request a
future extension. Failing CVC means
withdrawal, not conversion to energy
only. We're a small LSE with limited
points. How does the new cap help? The
50% of forecasted RA load share
criterion lets you support projects
larger than your raw allocation. Again,
for municipal utilities and CCAs. We're
a WDAT developer seeking deliverability
in cluster 16. What changes? Confirm TPD
availability at your delivery point,
verify WDAT eligibility under the PTO's
tariff, and build a scoring strategy.
You now compete with transmission level
projects. How does the new deposit
timing affect planning?
The commercial readiness deposit is due
by close of the customer engagement
window only if your project advances
through scoring. Can a cluster 14 or
earlier energy only project seek TPD in
2027 without a PPA? Yes, one-time
accommodation for 2027. Beginning in
2028, a 5-year RA agreement is required
for all projects. Our COD extension was

Our latest discussion features Mike Netzer and David Liggitt, as they explore the topic of powered land in the data center industry.  

The Transformation of Data Centers:  

Take a journey through the history of data centers, highlighting the migration from rural markets to bustling cities such as Chicago, Phoenix, and Northern Virginia, fueled by cloud availability zones.
   
The New Era of Data Center Development:  

Discover the current focus on powered land. Developers are buying up land, supplying power, and selling it for profit. With an ever-growing demand for larger data centers, from 36MW to a staggering 500MW, the landscape is quickly changing.  

Navigating Challenges in Power Land Acquisition:  

Not everything is smooth sailing in the industry. Developers face hurdles in obtaining power for land development, as utility companies impose more stringent requirements and costs for site surveys and study plans.  

Balancing Opportunities and Risks:  

Enter the world of high stakes and high returns in the data center space. This long-term investment requires substantial capital and expertise, with shifting market dynamics focusing on alternative energy solutions and strategic workforce planning.  

Key Insights:  

The US data center market is booming and drawing in a crowd of investors and developers. To be successful, one must understand the landscape, differentiate real versus speculative projects, and make strategic decisions.

Senior Vice President of Advisory & Transaction Services at CBRE, Brant Bernet discusses the history, current key components, and future trends in data center site selection.

In the first episode of our series “Big Topics”, David is discussing data center site selection with an expert on this topic, Senior Vice President of Advisory & Transaction Services at CBRE, Brant Bernet. With decades of experience in data center real estate, Brant walks through the history of site selection, key considerations in site selection, and the future of data center site selection.

History of Data Center Real Estate

Innovation has improved the experience of site section in the data center real estate market. In earlier years of the industry, brokers would fly to proposed locations with a “toolbox” stocked with multiple items that are now all replaced by a smartphone. Tools such as Google Earth and Fiber Locator have reduced the need for physical tours and simplified connectivity research. 

Key Components of Data Center Site Selection

Colocation providers, hyperscale users, and crypto miners are driving data center real estate market development. The need for large land parcels and a pathway for the largest power requirements in industry history are creating challenges in site selection. Land parcels of this size can only be found in certain areas and are decreasing in volume which is pushing demand to secondary markets. Due to rising land costs in response to the pandemic and increasing power demand, clients have a desire to move quickly in site selection. To do so, clients are utilizing land banking and are seeking powered shells or sites to scale rapidly. Users are also less opposed to traditional risks when factors such as connectivity, location, and availability are in their favor.

Future Data Center Site Selection Trends

As costs go down, opportunities for renewable energy will be attractive to clients in the future. Improvements in construction and volume of demand will lead to the selection of sites previously not preferred. Tertiary markets will continue to take on the burden of growth in response to the unwavering demand. 

Please share and like this this video if you found this information helpful and be sure to stay tuned for our next episode on data center construction!

metadata.author: Académie Énergie — Efficacité & Électricité

In this video, we break down: Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS): sizing for peak shaving and arbitrage.
👉 Why it matters: Oversizing a BESS kills the ROI — cycling too deep degrades it faster than your model predicted.
We cover the key concepts, real-world numbers, common mistakes and actionable insights.
#energyefficiency #sustainability #renewableenergy #netzero #greenbusiness

there's this gut feeling, this

how does this even happen? Well, it's

hard enough to get a great return, but

and your investment along with it. And
that really brings us full circle. So,
the next time you're looking at a
proposal for a new battery project, just
ask yourself, is this model telling me

profit and tomorrow's degradation?

segments.text: The global installed capacity of utility
scale battery energy storage systems has
witnessed a dramatic expansion over the
past 5 years driven by the increasing
demand for renewable energy integration
and grid stability solutions.
This rapid deployment has however been
accompanied by several high-profile
failure incidents that have garnered
significant media attention and raised
safety concerns across the energy
sector.
Despite these challenges, the industry
has demonstrated remarkable progress in
addressing safety issues with the global
grids scale best failure rate declining
by 97% between 2018 in 2023.
This substantial reduction can be
attributed to the incorporation of
lessons learned from early failure
incidents into new system designs and
best practices.
The battery industry continues to engage
in extensive research and development
activities to enhance prevention and
mitigation measures, including
developing a deeper understanding of the
diverse causes of best failures.
The Electric Power Research Institute,
EPRI, has established the most
comprehensive compilation of stationary
best incidents through its best failure
incident database, which serves as the
primary source for understanding failure
patterns and root causes.
This database focuses on occurrences
that present wider public health and
safety risks rather than operational
failures that pose no additional danger
to personnel or equipment. As of the
current analysis, the database contains
81 incidents from 2011 to the present
with 26 incidents providing sufficient
information for detailed classification
and root cause analysis.
This classification system employs a
baxial framework that categorizes
failures by both root cause, design,
manufacturing, integration, assembly,
construction or operation and failed
element, cell/module, controls or
balance of system. This dual approach
enables a more nuanced understanding of
failure patterns and relationships
between different contributing factors.
The analysis of classified incidents
reveals that integration, assembly, and
construction emerges as the most common
root cause of best failures, accounting
for approximately 65% of all identified
faults. This finding challenges the
common assumption that lithium ion
battery cells constitute the primary
source of failures.
Instead, the balance of system BOS and
control systems account for the vast
majority of failed components with cells
representing only 11% of classified
incidents.
The BOS encompasses a wide range of
components including DC and AC wiring,
HVAC subsystems, safety elements such as
fire suppression systems, enclosures,
power conversion systems, transformers,
and thermal management systems.
Recent quality audits indicate that
nearly 50% of quality assurance issues
occur in the BOS with 26% of inspected
BES units exhibiting defects in fire
suppression systems and 18% showing
thermal management system defects.
Operational failures constitute the
second most common root cause accounting
for approximately 20% of classified
incidents.
Notably, the bulk of these operational
failures occurred during the 2018 to
2019 period when South Korea experienced
a significant wave of BES incidents.
Investigation of these failures revealed
that a substantial fraction occurred
when the state of charge exceeded 90%
suggesting that these failures could
potentially be attributed to
manufacturing or design issues related
to the cells.
However, due to insufficient evidence to
make definitive determinations, these
incidents were classified as operational
failures.
This highlights a broader challenge in
failure analysis. Manufacturing defects
often prove difficult to identify
conclusively due to the loss of physical
evidence after fire or explosion
incidents.
Design related failures, while less
common, have become increasingly
significant in recent years.
Three of the four design related
failures in 2023 resulted from the same
BOS design flaw affecting best products
in New York and Idaho where enclosure
design allowed water intrusion into the
battery compartment leading to loss of
isolation and subsequent thermal
runaway.
Manufacturing failures represent the
smallest category likely due to the
difficulty in definitively identifying
manufacturing defects as root causes
post incident.
However, it's worth noting that earlier
failures from 2018 to 2020 may have
involved cell or module manufacturing
defects as contributing factors as
evidenced by several product recalls
from major EV manufacturers during that
period citing manufacturing issues by
battery OEMs.
The timing of failures provides another
critical insight. Approximately 72% of
failures where system age is known occur
during construction, commissioning or
within the first two years of operation.
This concentration of failures in the
early life cycle phases underscores the
critical importance of integration,
assembly and construction as a risk
mitigation priority.
Many of these incidents occur during the
commissioning phase when monitoring and
communication systems are not yet
operational, allowing leaks or isolation
failures to escalate into large-scale
fires before detection and intervention
become possible.
South Korea's experience between 2018
and 2019 serves as a compelling case
study of rapid deployment without robust
safety standards.
During this period, 27 of the 30
incidents in the EPRI database occurred
in South Korea. The Korean government
had provided strong economic incentives
for best deployment, particularly when
paired with solar photovoltaic
generation, leading to explosive growth
in installed systems from 30 in 2013 to
This rapid expansion was not accompanied
by commenurate development of safety
standards and regulations, contributing
directly to the wave of failures that
followed. The Korean government's
subsequent investigation of the first
spade of fires and the government's
commitment to implementing safety
improvements demonstrated how early
failures can catalyze industry-wide
learning and improvement.
The surprise Arizona incident in 2019
represents another pivotal moment in BES
safety evolution.
This fire and explosion at a best
facility injured four firefighters and
prompted the release of multiple root
cause investigation reports to the
public. The incident marked safety as a
priority issue for the energy storage
industry in the United States and led to
increased scrutiny and safety safety
measures across the sector. The public
sharing of investigation details
represented a significant step toward
greater industry transparency, enabling
other operators and manufacturers to
learn from the incident and implement
preventive measures. The Elorn battery
facility fire in Moss Landing,
California on September 20th, 2022
provides a particularly instructive
example of dual root causes.
The investigation shared publicly by
Tesla, the best manufacturer and
integrator, and Pacific Gas and
Electric, the site owner, revealed that
rainwater intrusion through the
container had caused electrical arcing
within the system, leading to thermal
runaway.
A water ingress point in the enclosure
had been created when an umbrella valve
was dislodged during the improper
installation of a vent shield. As a
confounding factor, insulation loss
alarms were not properly escalated to
the operator. The industry must continue
to engage in regulatory development,
voluntary industry efforts, and focused
research initiatives to support
increased best safety and maintain
public confidence in this critical
energy infrastructure.

The Electric Power Research Institute, EPRI, has established the most comprehensive compilation of stationary best incidents through its best failure incident database, which serves as the primary source for understanding failure patterns and root causes. This database focuses on occurrences that present wider public health and safety risks rather than operational failures that pose no additional danger to personnel or equipment. Notably, the bulk of these operational failures occurred during the 2018 to 2019 period when South Korea experienced a significant wave of BES incidents. Investigation of these failures revealed that a substantial fraction occurred when the state of charge exceeded 90% suggesting that these failures could potentially be attributed to manufacturing or design issues related to the cells. However, due to insufficient evidence to make definitive determinations, these incidents were classified as operational failures. This highlights a broader challenge in failure analysis. Manufacturing defects often prove difficult to identify conclusively due to the loss of physical evidence after fire or explosion incidents. Design related failures, while less common, have become increasingly significant in recent years. Three of the four design related failures in 2023 resulted from the same BOS design flaw affecting best products in New York and Idaho where enclosure design allowed water intrusion into the battery compartment leading to loss of isolation and subsequent thermal runaway. Manufacturing failures represent the smallest category likely due to the difficulty in definitively identifying manufacturing defects as root causes post incident. However, it's worth noting that earlier failures from 2018 to 2020 may have involved cell or module manufacturing defects as contributing factors as evidenced by several product recalls from major EV manufacturers during that period citing manufacturing issues by battery OEMs. The timing of failures provides another critical insight. Approximately 72% of failures where system age is known occur during construction, commissioning or within the first two years of operation. This concentration of failures in the early life cycle phases underscores the critical importance of integration, assembly and construction as a risk mitigation priority. Many of these incidents occur during the commissioning phase when monitoring and communication systems are not yet operational, allowing leaks or isolation failures to escalate into large-scale fires before detection and intervention become possible. During this period, 27 of the 30 incidents in the EPRI database occurred in South Korea. metadata.title: How to Size BESS for Microgrid Applications
metadata.author: Storlytics Energy Storage
metadata.shortDescription:
Design a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) for behind-the-meter, front-of-the-meter and microgrid applications using site-specific load and renewable generation profiles in Storlytics. This video demonstrates how to use the Battery Profile Creator to develop a battery dispatch profile based on the operating requirements of a microgrid.
In this tutorial, you'll learn how to import load, solar, wind, and other generation profiles and configure how the battery should manage the site's net demand. The resulting dispatch profile defines when the battery charges and discharges to minimize or eliminate power imports and exports from the grid.
This workflow is particularly useful for energy engineers and developers designing self-sufficient microgrids or evaluating BESS operation based on real site demand and renewable generation profiles.

segments.text: No land, no project.
A single 200 megawatt solar plant needs 1,000 to 1,400 acres of land, more than twice the size of Central Park.
The Solar Energy Industries Association puts the rule of thumb at 5 to 7 acres per megawatt for utility scale solar. And not just any land.
It has to be flat, close to substations and transmission lines, and permittable.
Securing that land, site control, is the first gate of any project.
Lenders check it before anything else.
Without locked-up land, there is no permitting, no interconnection, no financing.
Today we walk through the commercial mechanics of site control, step by step.
Developers almost never buy the land outright.
They start with an option agreement.
An option is exactly what it sounds like: the right to choose. Typically for 2 to 3 years, the developer pays for the time to decide whether to build on that land.
During the option period, the developer runs environmental studies, permitting, the interconnection application, and a title review of the property.
If the results look good, the developer exercises the option and converts to a full lease.
If not, the agreement ends.
During the option period, the landowner can usually keep farming the land or using it as before.

Big projects sign options with dozens of landowners at once, and it can take months to a year to assemble the full site, because one missing parcel breaks the whole block. Sharing risk without locking up the whole property, that is the point of the option.
Money moves before construction ever starts.

First, the signing bonus: a one-time, upfront payment made when the option agreement is signed, the price of exclusivity while the developer studies the land. Second, the option fee: a smaller annual payment that keeps the option alive through the option period.
So the cash flow has three acts.
Signing bonus once at the start, option fees every year, and full lease rent only after the option is exercised.
Option fees are often structured to rise each year.
Here is where landowners need to be careful.

If the option money is too thin, the landowner is giving away years of exclusivity for almost nothing. U.S. land brokers advise landowners to get at least $1,000 to $2,000 per year in option consideration.
Never sign a deal that lets a developer tie up your land for years without paying for it.
Once the full lease kicks in, rent is set per acre per year.
Published industry data puts the common range at $250 to $2,000 per acre per year, and competitive markets like Texas can run above that.
A Purdue University survey found that a majority of landowners were offered $1,000 per acre per year or more.
Compare that to the $200 to $400 per acre that row-crop farming typically nets in a good year, and the appeal is obvious.
Rents vary enormously by region, so benchmarking against neighboring parcels matters.
Almost every lease also carries an annual escalator, usually 1.5 to 3 percent, compounding like inflation.
A quick example. One hundred acres at $1,000 per acre with a 2 percent escalator starts at $100,000 a year and passes $170,000 by year thirty.
How long does the lease run?
Typically around 30 years, with extension options of 5 to 10 years that can push it toward 40.
The math follows the hardware.
Panels last 25 to 30 years, power purchase agreements run 20 years or more, and project financing is built on those long cash flows.

Add 1 to 2 years of pre-construction diligence and about 1 year of decommissioning at the end, and the landowner is effectively signing up for more than three decades. When the agreement ends, the developer removes the equipment and restores the land.
That decommissioning obligation has to be in the contract, in writing. Ownership questions like title and mineral rights were covered in our Title special; this episode stays on deal structure.
Four practical points for the negotiating table.
First, lock in real option money from day one.
Exclusivity has a price, and it should be paid from the signing date. Second, fix the numbers: rent per acre, escalator percentage, in writing.
Third, count the total years, options and extensions included, and confirm the decommissioning clause.
Fourth, thirty years is a generational decision.
Tax and legal counsel is not optional, it is essential.
The best sites attract competing developers.
Do not rush. Compare at least two or three offers side by side before signing anything.

The term runs about 30 years, and decommissioning belongs in the contract.
Land is the first gate of every solar project.
That is the one thing to take away today.
This was Texas Energy ESSENTIALS, the Site Control episode.

metadata.title: Who Pays When an AI Data Centre Cannot Connect?
metadata.author: Beyound The Signal
metadata.shortDescription:
Britain now has 73 gigawatts of data centres waiting to connect to the grid — more than the country's entire peak demand of 45 gigawatts in 2025. In Texas the large-load queue has grown to over 230 gigawatts, against a record peak of 85. Grid connection waits can run five to ten years. So when an AI data centre cannot connect, or the grid has to be rebuilt around it, who actually pays?

This is Beyound The Signal. We look at how a connection works, why the queues exploded, who is being asked to pick up the bill, and the case that this can still be a genuine investment if the costs are assigned fairly.

The narration on this video is AI-generated.

Chapters
0:00 The 73-gigawatt queue
0:31 This is Beyound The Signal
0:44 How a connection works
1:49 Who is being asked to pay
2:54 The benefit side
3:47 Britain's queue
5:25 If they will not wait
6:36 Who pays?

Sources (every figure was checked against the opened original)
• Ofgem, “Curate – Demand Connections Reform” consultation, July 2026: contracted demand in the British queue rose from 41 GW (Nov 2024) to 125 GW (June 2025); about 73 GW across ~315 data-centre projects; peak GB demand in 2025 / 2025-26 was 45 GW (NESO Triad Data, cited by Ofgem); implied capex of £693 billion if the whole pipeline were built (~23% of UK GDP), presented as a warning not a forecast; at least 9 GW of transmission requests switched from batteries to data centres (May 2024–Aug 2025); proposed returnable commitment fee of £237,500–£712,500 per MW (2.5–7.5% of average capex) for projects over 40 MW; a 100 MW site would need to secure £23.8 million–£71.3 million; proposed milestones (customer, long-lead equipment, financial and technical readiness). https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/consultation/proposed-data-centre-connection-reforms
• Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, “Accelerating electricity network connections for strategic demand: government response”: earlier reforms deprioritised up to 300 GW of excess battery and solar projects; government intends to let NESO prioritise strategic demand, including data centres, and align later data-centre connections with regional targets. https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/accelerating-electricity-network-connections-for-strategic-demand
• International Energy Agency, “Key Questions on Energy and AI” (2026, CC BY 4.0): data-centre electricity use 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030 (~3% of global electricity); 17% growth in 2025, AI-focused use up 50% and projected to more than triple to ~465 TWh by 2030; five large technology companies’ capex exceeded $400 billion in 2025 and is expected to jump 75% in 2026; connection waits of five to ten years in many jurisdictions; transformer lead times 2–3 years, gas turbines around five years; Texas / ERCOT large-load queue ~63 GW (Dec 2024, around three-quarters data centres), 130 GW four months later, over 230 GW by Jan 2026, against a record peak of 85 GW, “not all these projects will be realised”; 5.6 GW of on-site gas for data centres under construction, more than 70 GW in development; more than one-third of new US gas capacity is on-site power for data centres; Tennessee example of 400 MW+ on-site turbines later scaled back once a 150 MW grid connection came online; SMR offtake pipeline 25 GW (end-2024) to 45 GW (end-2025), first projects around 2030; non-firm connections and demand response as a way to connect sooner. https://www.iea.org/reports/key-questions-on-energy-and-ai
• PJM Independent Market Monitor (Monitoring Analytics), Market Monitor Report to the Members Committee, 27 July 2026: data-centre load attributed $29.4 billion of capacity-market charges across the last four auctions (46.2% of those charges); $6.3 billion of $16.4 billion (38.2%) in the latest auction; first-half 2026 wholesale cost $103.40/MWh without that capacity-market impact and $114.50 with it (+$11.11, or 9.7%); the monitor notes that not all of the rise in capacity costs comes from data centres, and recommends taking data-centre load out of the main capacity auction so it procures its own supply. https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mc/2026/20260727-web/item-02---marketing-monitoring-report---presentation.pdf

Graphics are animated explainers, labelled conceptual or illustrative where they are not to scale. No real-event video clips are used; figures are shown with source tags on screen.

If this was useful, subscribe to Beyound The Signal for more.

metadata.title: Interconnection Queue Explained: The $3.5 Billion Waiting List
metadata.author: Andy Knows It
metadata.shortDescription:
The interconnection queue explained: the bureaucratic line that added roughly $3.5 billion to a single electricity auction in one American region. More than 2,000 gigawatts of generation are sitting in that line, and the median wait is over four years. Here is how the line works, why the federal fix did not fix it, and how a study queue becomes a line item on your power bill.

00:00 Intro
00:48 What the Queue Actually Is
02:37 How the Backlog Got This Bad
05:07 FERC Tries to Fix It
07:30 Why the Queue Still Doesn't Work
09:05 The $3.5 Billion Bill
11:03 Transmission Planning Is the Upstream Problem
12:25 How Other Grids Handle This
14:07 The AI Demand Wildcard
15:34 Takeaway

Most coverage of the energy transition treats permitting as the villain. The interconnection queue is the bigger and stranger bottleneck, and almost nobody outside the industry can describe how it actually functions. We walk through what the queue is, how the backlog got this bad, what the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) changed, and why the changes have not cleared the line. Then we get to the part that matters: the queue is not a paperwork problem, it is a cost allocation system, and every month a project waits is a decision about who eats the upgrade bill and who buys expensive power in the meantime. We also cover transmission planning as the upstream problem, how other grids handle the same queue, and what AI data center demand does to a line that is already four years deep. If you follow energy policy, grid infrastructure, or electricity prices, this is the interconnection queue explained one layer deeper than the version you have heard. The sun and the wind are not the bottleneck. The bill is.

Subscribe if you want the systems behind your bills explained properly, before the next rate increase shows up in your mailbox.
One question for the comments: should developers pay the full transmission upgrade cost, or should everyone on the grid share it? Make the case.

#energy #powergrid #electricity #infrastructure

segments.text: A bureaucratic wait list added about $3.5 billion to a single electricity auction in one American region.
That's $3.5 billion in one year at one auction and one region.
Multiply that by the entire country every year and you can see how it can become a huge problem.
But it wasn't a fuel shortage, a shortage of sun or wind.
It wasn't a shortage of people who want to build power plants that caused this problem.
It was just a line.
There are more than 2,000 gigawatts of generation sitting in that line right now.
And the median wait to get through it is over four years.
There's more capacity waiting to plug in than the entire United States currently produces.
So here's how that line works, why the fix for it didn't actually fix it,
and how the line turns into an item on your electricity bill.
Every power plant in this country, whether it's a wind farm, a gas plant, a nuclear station,
a battery sitting in a field, has to ask permission to connect to the power grid.
Not permission to exist, you can produce power off-grid.
You need permission to plug in.
So you file an interconnection request with the grid operator, and that operator runs a study.
The study asks one question.
If we let this project push power onto the network here, what else will break?
The study projects whether power lines will overload, voltage will sag,
or protection equipment will misfire, among other things.
Then the study comes back with a list of upgrades the network needs before it can safely carry your electricity.
And you pay for those upgrades as the generator.
The project that triggers the upgrade gets the bill.
For decades, that study happened one project at a time in the order they were received, first come, first served.
Which sounds fair, but is actually completely unworkable.
Because every new project in the study depends on the assumptions about every other project ahead of it in the line.
So if anything changes in front, everything behind it has to get re-studied.
And it's a huge scale we're talking about.
At the end of 2024, there were about 2,290 gigawatts of generating capacity sitting in American interconnection queues.
The entire installed generating fleet of the United States is somewhere around 1,200 gigawatts.
That's like if the waiting room was nearly twice the size of the building it was associated with.
Now, most of those projects are never going to get built, and they were never intended to.
The queue is part pipeline and part graveyard.
But even after you strip out the speculative filings, there's far more generation trying to connect to the grid than the system can ever process.
So the question is, how did that filing system get so backed up?
And stay with me, because in about three minutes, I'm going to show you the reform that was supposed to fix this,
and why the line is still too long even after the fix.
The interconnection queue got backed up because of two things pulling in the same wrong direction,
and both of those were baked into the original design of the line.
The first thing is the re-study cascade we just talked about,
where a change to a project ahead of you in line could trigger a fresh look at hundreds of other projects behind it,
