videos.full_text: I'm William Brangham and this is "Horizons." Artificial intelligence data centers are popping up across America. They're spurring innovation, but also fierce backlash because of their need for huge amounts of water and power. Is the AI revolution worth the price communities are paying? What we know about the impact of data centers, coming up next. ♪ Narrator: Support for "Horizons" has been provided by Steve and Marilyn Kerman and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. Additional support is provided by Friends of the News Hour. ♪ This program was made possible by contributions to your PBS station from viewers like you. Thank you. From the David M. Rubenstein Studio at WETA in Washington, here is William Brangham. Welcome to "Horizons." We're going to do a deep dive today into the controversies around the explosion of artificial intelligence data centers. If one is or has been built in your community, you likely know what I'm already talking about. Hundreds of billions of dollars are being spent right now constructing massive facilities to house and run the computers that are needed for the spiking demand for artificial intelligence. These centers are being built across the country with a particular concentration in Virginia, Texas, California, and Illinois. The biggest ones, so-called hyperscale plants like Meta's Hyperion plant in Louisiana, could have a footprint nearly as big as Manhattan. The leading tech giants, Meta, Google, Amazon, and OpenAI, among others, are in a breakneck race to get their centers up and running, each hoping to seize the advantage and become a dominant supplier of AI. Hey, hey, ho, ho, data centers have got to go! Brangham: But as those centers are being built, communities across the country are in open revolt, concerned about the large amounts of water and energy that these centers require. And it's a bipartisan backlash, with citizen activists pushing back at the speed of construction, the concern over pollution and rising utility bills, and the often opaque deals and tax breaks given to companies by their local officials. According to one poll, seven in 10 Americans would oppose a data center being constructed in their community, and the majority would support a national moratorium on building more. Given all of this, we wanted to examine the claims swirling around data centers to try and get a little clarity about their real impact. And for that, we turn to Michael Webber. He's a chair at both the LBJ School of Public Affairs and the Department of Mechanical Engineering, both at the University of Texas at Austin. He served as an officer and consultant for several tech and energy companies, including some in the AI business. And he's the author of the book "Power Trip, "The Story of Energy," which was also made into a multi-part series on PBS. Michael Webber, so good to have you on the program. I want to get into all these pros and cons and accusations and defenses about these data centers. But first off, just establish a baseline for us. What are these data centers? What are they for? Who's building them? That's a great question. So data centers, first of all, have been around for a while. They're not new, but the pace of their construction and their size is really capturing the attention because the last few years they've gotten a lot bigger and we're starting to use the tools in a more obvious way. By tools, I mean, like these AI tools. You might've used Claude or ChatGPT or something like that. And these tools are calling these data centers, which are these buildings that exist oftentimes outside of cities. And they've got big warehouses, big tilt wall construction. And so they're just large facilities, maybe it looks like a distribution center or something, but inside is filled with computer racks, just go on and on and on, these rows and rows of racks of computers that are stacked up and down. And those data centers fill these computers are answering our queries as we use these tools. We ask it like, "Make me a logo" or "Look something up for me" or "Help me analyze this data." That question we type into our computer is going over fiber optics towards that data center, calling all those computers to do a calculation and then giving this back some sort of reply. So those data centers are the place where those today, where those computations are made. I see, okay. I mentioned earlier that this 7 in 10 poll, people supporting a moratorium on building data centers. I want to put up this recent Quinnipiac poll, which showed that I believe it was 65% of people would oppose a data center in their community. And when asked why, 72% electricity costs, 64% said water use, 41% said noise. So I want to go through each of those individually. Let's start up with electricity. Data centers do gobble up a lot of energy. That is quite clear. A lot of people argue data centers mean in my community that my utility rates are going to go up. What's the truth to that? I mean, that's the concern and that's a fair concern. People are already nervous about electricity rates. Rates have been going up for years because of having to harden the system for hurricanes and wind storms or replace the system after wildfires in the Mountain West. So costs have already been going up for years. And now we have data centers who want a lot of electricity. So people are rightly concerned that rates will go up. And I think there's a lot of political or policy concern that retirees and grandmothers will have to pay higher rates to make really rich companies even richer. So there's a lot of concern and sensitivity about electric rates. There has always been concern about electricity rates. So that's not a new thing, but all the recent inflation concerns really show up in our electric bills. So there's a lot of concern. And the reasons why that's a valid concern is because these data centers consume a lot of electricity. And so if you have a big new consumer come in who's going to take a lot of electricity and maybe they can outbid you for it, they might bid the prices up. So that's a valid concern. Those same data centers are owned or operated or used by really rich companies. So maybe we can convince them to invest in making the grid better, which would drive down the rates for everybody. And the challenge is, we don't know which way it's going to go right now. Are the data centers and the hyperscalers and these data companies, are they going to invest to make electricity more affordable for all of us? Or are they going to compete with us for electricity and drive our rates up? That's the concern I think that they're stepping into with a lot of these local communities. I know that some of these data centers, when they're being built, are saying, "Look, "because of these concerns "and maybe because of local efficiency reasons, "we will build our own onsite "power plants that we will put "turbines and generators onsite to supply our own electricity." Does that alleviate this problem? It solves one problem, but introduces other problems. So if you're going to build what's called onsite power or behind the meter power generation, the meter being where the building occurs with the local utility, they might say, "Look, we'll build our own power plant. "So we're not going to charge you "or cause your rates to go up or anything like that." That might solve the problem of competing with all of us at peak times. And maybe we should just take a moment to say that peak times tends to be afternoons in August in the summer when everyone has their air conditioners on. We actually have an abundance of electricity almost the entire year, but there are a few hours each year where we don't have an abundance. And if they have onsite power generation, maybe that data center can disconnect from the grid or partially disconnect and use their own power plant. So they're not competing with us at peak times. And that's desirable in a variety of ways. The data center companies for the most part are actually trying to solve a different problem. They're trying to solve a speed to power problem where they want to get connected to electricity as soon as possible because they feel like they're in a race. And when they talk to the local utility, the utility might say, "Look, it's going to take us "four or five years to connect you to the grid." They'll say, "You know what? "We'll build our own power plant cause that's faster." So they're often trying to solve a speed to power issue. They can use that same equipment to reduce competition with all of us at peak times in those afternoons in August. And that solves a couple of problems, which is kind of nice. But now all of a sudden you got a power plant in your backyard and you might not want the noise or the fumes or the trucks delivering the fuel depending on what the fuel is. So there are other problems that come with the onsite power generation, but it does perhaps alleviate some pressure on electric rates. Right, that is another one of the issues that you just touched on, this idea of local pollution. Because those, if people haven't seen what a big electrical turbine is, it's like a jet engine and that there can be dozens of them, if not more on some of these big plants. That is something that maybe when you bought your property out in a rural stretch of the country, you weren't anticipating having a couple dozen jet engines firing up all the time in your backyard. Yeah, a couple of dozen jet engines or hundreds of these diesel generators. And diesel generators are especially noisy and fumy and all that kind of stuff. And you can imagine hundreds of them lined up at your fence line, do you want that? No one wants that. In fact, diesel generators have been outlawed in California and other places, because they're so dirty. And this is the challenge, like, "Hey, we'll build "behind the meter or onsite generation, "but is it going to be an onsite generation "at your fence line that you're comfortable with?" That's part of the conversation. Right. Okay. The next item on that Quinnipiac poll was people's concerns about water. Data centers, the NOCs use a ton of water, why? What are they using the water for? If you picture a data center as like a big white box, maybe it's got, power comes in, electricity comes in, and then two things go out from the chips. Photons go out, so you're taking electrons to photons. The chip is converting the electricity into photons, consider photons data or information packets, and generating heat, so the chip gets really hot in there. A lot of these chips and these computer servers interacts in these data centers. So electricity comes in, photons and heat goes out. And the heat's a real problem. You have to manage the heat so you don't destroy the equipment or damage the facility or anything like that. And so water is used for water cooling, for the most part, to cool these systems. If you're inside a data center, there's actually a lot of air cooling. They're blowing air over the computers and the racks and the chips, but more and more as the chips become more powerful, you need water cooling. You can't cool them fast enough with just air, so you have water cooling inside the facility. You also have to cool that water cooling. And that water cooling loop, imagine like a radiator in your car, which has a closed loop of just radiator fluid going around to cool your engine. It's that radiator's air cooled as you drive on a highway. If you take that water cooling loop inside your radiator, you have the same kind of thing in your data center. Sometimes you use a lake or a river or water to cool that water loop. And that's part of the tension. Like, "Wait, how much water are you going to use "to cool your facility? "Is it a one-time charge where you're loading up the water "in your closed loop cooling and then you're done? "Or are you going to use water every day "or every hour of every day "to cool the water loops for the data center?" So it's really around cooling the chips. And this is where there is a lot of opportunity for innovation and research. But if you go to a community that doesn't have much water, I'm thinking like West Texas, not much water, a lot of competition for that water, and you say, "We're going to build a data center, "we're going to create all these jobs "and we're going to take all your water," this is a real sensitive point for people because it's irreplaceable. So there's a lot of pressure and pushback on data centers. Like, "We need you to use air cooling wherever possible. "We need water efficiency, thermal efficiency, "reduce your water or do other things." And we can talk about what some of the other things are, but water is a very sensitive point. And I would say from Texas, water is a more sensitive point than electricity probably. We have pretty cheap electricity in Texas, we'd like to keep it that way, but the water feels even more scarce. So that's a real sore point. Right, I mean, one of the last programs we just did here on "Horizons" was about the Colorado River running dry and all these states in the American Southwest sucking more and more out of a diminishing resource. And if you're suddenly putting data centers on top of that, you can see why there's a lot of resistance to that. Yeah, but the same kind of comment with electricity, the data center companies are very rich. Maybe they can invest in more water efficiency or water production systems or wetlands restoration or desalination. They have the money and the desire to invest in water systems. They might end up improving the water system if we ask them to and they agree and everything else. So it doesn't just have to be that they're going to take all the water, it can be their part of the solution. I mean, you're touching again on a point that really does come up a lot of times where local communities look at the contracts that are signed. Oftentimes the companies will ask for non-disclosure agreements so that the deals themselves that the data center construction companies or the data center operators sign are really opaque. And people think, "What on earth is going on here? "Why are they speeding this through?" Like, are there examples of places where communities have said, "We want you to do this in the way "that doesn't harm our community?" Are there effective examples that you would point to to say, "Hey, here's an example "where we did one of these right?" There is actually a lot of good examples. And I think those are useful for us to know that, okay, we're not trapped in this negative path. We can look for a better opportunity. It's not the standard yet. It tends to be one-off examples. Meta has a water positive facility they're planning outside El Paso. Google has done a really clever project with renewables in Minnesota. Microsoft switched to air cooling outside of San Antonio. So you can think of the big hyperscalers. These are brand names we've all worked with or use or know. There are examples where they've done it in a really good way. It's not the default, it's not the standard, and so I think that's part of all of us working together to say, "Hey, the minimum standard "should be quite good." And then let's make it better as time goes on and we get more innovative. But the challenge is that where the locations are, they're not always within a jurisdiction where there's really clear authority about who regulates what. In fact, a lot of the development are in some of these unincorporated areas or maybe you have county commissioners or something, but you don't quite have like a city council and a mayor or something. So there's a lot of ambiguity sometimes about who's in charge or how to respond. And there's a lot of stealth that happens. It's not always for malicious, malign behavior. Sometimes the stealth is they're trying to get the land to build the data center and they don't want their competitors to know. So there is stealthy behavior as always happens in business. And that arouses a lot of suspicions because people are like, "What's going on? "What are you going to build? Where, why, why didn't I know? "And do we get to be part of the process "to help you make sure it's going to be "sort of harmonious with society?" So there are a lot of examples of bad actors that have done it in a sort of too quiet, too malicious way, maybe or dishonest way. And then some good examples. And I would say, well, let's push for the good examples. We know it's possible. Let's make that normal. Let's not make that the one-off exception. Right. One of the other concerns that we have seen this in a lot of local news reporting is the noise of these facilities. I mean, they are just quite enormous. And sometimes, if they are in proximity to where people live, that is just a cacophony that people do not want. What do we know about how loud these things are? They're loud. But there are a couple of different sources of the noise to pay attention to. One is if you're inside the data center. When I walk through data centers and I've been to many, you're often given ear protection, like earplugs or ear mitts or earmuffs or something of some sort to cover your ears because it's so noisy inside the data center from all the airflow. They have to push so much air through the facility to cool the chips and computers. It's quite noisy. So you hear the constant hum of the fans moving the air. That noise inside, you don't really hear outside though. There's sound insulation for the most part. Outside, you have a lot of generators. You mentioned those diesel generators, maybe those like aeroderivative jet engines that are bolted to the ground to give you power on site. Those diesel generators or gas generators or gas turbines, if those are all noisy, you'll hear that as well. And then there's all the truck noise and other things. There's people coming and going. Certainly during construction, there's a lot of noise. And so if you move to the rural countryside to get away from the city noise, and all of a sudden you've got a bunch of trucks and generators and fans and cooling towers, it's noisier, you can hear it. That can be solved usually by distance, by getting more land and having a little more space between you and the fence line, that would help if you have the space to do it. And that's one reason why they don't build in urban areas is the noise is, well, the land's expensive, but the noise is also a problem. But there's several sources for the noise. How much of this, Michael, do you think is a sort of mismatch between, we're doing all of this massive construction for the promise of the AI revolution, which right now, yes, we can use ChatGPT and all of that, and I can figure out a recipe or get an answer to some question that my son is asking me about. But the real revolution is still in the future and the present day madness is in people's backyards. Without a doubt. I think we're always suspicious of new stuff anyway. That's like kind of a human condition. But we've got this new stuff showing up. It's very visible, very loud. It might be expensive for electricity. It might take our water. So we've got all these concerns and we don't even know what it's good for. Maybe it's better cat videos, this kind of thing. And that's the challenge is the benefits of AI haven't really shown up in visible ways yet, but we should get better cancer treatments, we should be able to accelerate fusion reactor design. We should be able to optimize the grid. Like there are all these really good things we can get out of AI, but those haven't shown up in a very obvious, visible way yet. So we feel the impacts today, the benefits come later. That mismatch in time is a huge challenge because the benefits are kind of like, "Oh, "maybe I get a better search engine." There are benefits from the economic development of the jobs, but not all of us have a job at those companies or get those economic benefits. So there's a mismatch in who suffers, people in the rural countryside who now have a noisy or loud or whatever it is, data center, very visible, ugly ones, for example, versus who benefits, which are people later on, or maybe some shareholders. That mismatch in who benefits and who feels the impact and when we get the benefits and when we feel it, that's a huge problem. The best example today we're getting from AI that people might understand is these self-driving cars like Waymo, which are dramatically safer than human-driven cars. They're like 80% reduction in accidents and fatalities, other things. So that's all enabled by autonomy and artificial intelligence. That is a great example of AI making traffic safer. And that's one of the benefits we'll get. So that's one we kind of see now at small scale in some cities, but we really want all those other big benefits and then it will transform the world. But meanwhile, we're suffering the impacts of the fumes, the water, the electricity, the land, the noise, the light, the heat, everything else. And I think too, I want to put this poll up. This is a Pew Research poll about people's views of AI. According to Pew, half of Americans are, quote, "more concerned than excited "about the increased use of AI in daily life." And the same poll, a slightly smaller percentage think it will make it harder to think creatively, that it'll worsen our relationships, that it'll have a negative effect on the economy and on education. Do you think that that, again, is also part of the equation here, that people seem to think, "I'm going to get laid off by AI. "It's going to make my kids dumber. "Everyone's cheating on their homework with it. "Why are we building these massive data centers "to support all these things that I think of as negative?" Without a doubt, all these human condition concerns or ethical concerns, like what is AI? Why is it good? How is it going to change my relationship with my fellow neighbor or my family and everything else? These are real concerns. We see it at the universities. We already have to figure out how to deal with it, with cheating and everything else. So there are some downside risks, without a doubt. And I think that's true with every new technology. We said some of the same things with the arrival of the internet when I was in graduate school. And Wikipedia, was it cheating to use Wikipedia? People would argue just the arrival of computers decades before was cheating. You should have been able to do math with an abacus or your own by hand or a slide rule or something else. So we've had new tools come along. We had the same kind of fights every time. Socrates was concerned when writing was developed. He thought if we used writing instead of committing things to memory, it would make us weak as learners. So they were afraid of the new technology, writing. And so this is kind of a constant thing. We're always afraid of the new thing because we don't really understand the benefits yet. And there are downside risks for sure of all this. I think that like any tool that could be used for good or bad, you can use a hammer for good or bad. It's a tool. You can use AI for good and bad. And for the most part, humans will use it for good. And some people will use it for bad. That's a real ethical concern. But if you're worried about it's going to lay me off and make my kids stupid and take all our water and make our electricity more expensive, it's like, yeah, this is a big set of concerns. And I think that's on us to figure out on us or everyone who's developing AI to start, "Okay, is this a tool we can live with? "If so, do we need rules? "What are those rules going to be to ensure "it's safe for our children and everybody else?" So I think that's part of the conversation and a huge part of the concern. And kind of rightly so, I think we'll get through it because we'll start to see some good use cases, but it's really hard right now. Do you think the companies, again, you and... we both have been saying how they are all in a headlong rush to get to be first to market, to get these centers up to speed. Do you think that they appreciate and see this burgeoning opposition all over the country and they recognize, one, they have to address it more and maybe make the case more publicly to people as to here's why we're imposing on your communities. And two, here's what the possible benefits are. Do you think that they got that message and that they are doing that? I think they got the message and they're starting now. I also think they're very late. They did not start with that. So I feel like they have moved ahead longer. This is in a race. It feels like an arms race that there's only going to be a few winners and they want to be one of the few winners. So speed matters more than niceties or getting along well with your neighbors. And now they're finding out, actually getting along well with your neighbors is part of the condition for having speed because your neighbors can slow you down. So I think they're figuring it out kind of late. And this reminds me of the hydraulic fracturing or shale revolution that happened about 15 to 20 years ago where a lot of these oil and gas companies looking to produce shale moved into these rural communities with this new technology that would unlock a lot of domestic oil and gas from these shale formations. And they thought they'd be treated as heroes liberating us from the yoke of Middle Eastern oil and gas. And instead people got mad because of all the noise and trucks and everything else. The same kind of story. And they figured out a few years in like, "Oh, we need to go talk to the neighbors "and really sort this out "because they see us as a part of the problem "rather than part of the solution." AI companies see that now too. They thought they'd be heroes. "We're bringing in new tools, we're going to make you rich, "we're going to employ all these people, "we're going to beat the bad guys." And now they're finding out people perceive these companies as the bad guys. So they're having to play some catch up. And that's pretty typical. That often happens when there's a sort of a land rush or gold rush, so to speak, where they move quickly, make mistakes, then figure out, "Oh, we need to go back "and manage this better." So they've got the message, they're working on it. I don't think they've solved it yet. And this reminds me of the shale revolution. I've seen this before for oil and gas. There are, in this conversation about data centers, you inevitably will hear Elon Musk, Google, others talk about this, that, okay, maybe there are limits to what we can do on the land with regards to these data centers and we ought to go to outer space and build them up there. Explain the rationale why that might be feasible and why they would want to do that. Outer space or subsea, offshore and below water, right? So it strikes me as an engineer is just so difficult. Offshore is so much harder than onshore because you got to deal with the waves and the wind and the saltwater, the corrosion, the water tightness, everything else. And then that's easy compared to space. Space is really hard. Like these are really hard places to make things work. To be space rated means something different than to be suitable for fuse on land or offshore. So the idea that you might go offshore and below water or out into outer space and out of the atmosphere is driven by some sort of necessity, I think is what's happening, where they feel like it's just too slow to build the grid the way we need it. It's too hard to get the power we need. There are too many neighbors who complain. Let's go where there aren't neighbors who can complain, offshore or outer space. And so you can get a couple of things. Fewer people complain because you're out of sight, out of mind. You get your cooling for free. Deep space is quite cold, the ocean's quite cold. So it gets a lot of cooling. So that reduces your energy needs. But also you might be able to get solar power in space more easily than building a huge solar farm on the ground. Now, I'm skeptical. The engineering of that all seems really, really hard. But if you believe that the cost to go to space will drop, the cost for solar panels will drop, that the cost to expand the grid on ground will double, then it starts to look like space might make sense. If you think neighbors are always getting in your way, going offshore for the cooling water and to get away from the neighbors might make sense as well. That strikes me as really hard, frankly. But really smart people who are developing this, who are thinking about it, they're all looking at it. So I might be wrong on this, but I would say it's going to be easier to build it on earth, on ground than in space. But SpaceX and other companies are trying to drive down the lift costs to make it cheaper to go to space. Maybe it will make sense. Just in the last 30 seconds we have or so, you do believe though, you're optimistic, that we have enough agency to do it right here. Let's do it right. I mean, we can make these data centers power flexible, water positive, carbon negative, and really harmonious with the land. Let's just do it. Let's demand it of our partners. I say, let's do it that way. Michael Webber, it is always great to hear from you, but especially on such a controversial and confused and convoluted topic. You're such a clear voice on this. Thank you so much. Michael Webber at the University of Texas. Great to talk to you. Thank you. Thank you. And that is it for this episode of "Horizons." You can watch us on YouTube or listen wherever you get your podcasts. If you like what you hear, please subscribe and give us a rating. That single signal will help more people see this program. Thank you so much for watching. We'll see you next week. Narrator: Support for "Horizons" has been provided by Steve and Marilyn Kerman and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. Additional support is provided by Friends of the News Hour. ♪ This program was made possible by contributions to your PBS station from viewers like you. Thank you. ♪ You're watching PBS.

metadata.title: Data Center Electricity: Why AI Facilities Are Short on Power
metadata.author: BUILT BENEATH
metadata.shortDescription:
Data center electricity demand is growing faster than some parts of the grid can deliver power.
This Built Beneath documentary explains why AI facilities can have land, money, and chips, and still wait years for a grid connection.

In this episode of Built Beneath, we break down why access to power is becoming one of the biggest constraints on the AI infrastructure boom.

We cover:

• Why hyperscale AI data centers can require hundreds of megawatts of electricity  
• How 1-gigawatt AI campuses compare with traditional power demand  
• Why data centers can be built faster than the electric grid can expand  
• The growing importance of substations, transformers, and transmission lines  
• What’s happening in major data-center markets like Virginia and Texas  
• Why utilities are scrutinizing massive new data-center power requests  
• Transformer and electrical-equipment supply-chain constraints  
• Why natural gas, batteries, renewables, and nuclear power are entering the data-center race  
• Why “speed-to-power” is becoming as important as location and land  

AI may live in the cloud, but the cloud depends on physical infrastructure: power plants, turbines, transmission lines, substations, transformers, and the people who build them.

The next phase of the AI race may not be decided only by who builds the best model.

It may also be decided by who can secure the electricity to run it.

That’s what’s Built Beneath.

Subscribe for more documentaries about the money, infrastructure, construction, energy, and industrial systems behind technology.

#DataCenters #AI #Energy

metadata.title: America's Data Centers Are Becoming Their Own Power Plants
metadata.author: America2050
metadata.shortDescription:
America's data centers are entering a new era as technology companies begin building their own power systems to keep up with the explosive growth of artificial intelligence. With AI models, cloud computing, and massive server farms consuming unprecedented amounts of electricity, relying entirely on the traditional power grid is becoming a growing challenge. Could data centers soon operate like power plants of their own?

From on-site natural gas generators and advanced energy storage to fuel cells, dedicated power stations, and potential next-generation nuclear technology, companies are exploring new ways to secure the electricity they need. Instead of waiting years for grid connections and infrastructure upgrades, some data center developers are looking for ways to generate power directly at their facilities.

This shift could transform America's energy landscape. As AI demand accelerates, data centers are becoming more than buildings filled with computers. They are increasingly connected to major energy projects that could reshape how electricity is generated, delivered, and consumed across the country.

But this transformation also raises important questions. Will private power generation help ease pressure on America's electricity grid, or will it create new challenges involving fuel supplies, emissions, costs, and energy reliability? The decisions being made today could influence the future of both artificial intelligence and America's power infrastructure.

Watch until the end to discover why data centers are moving toward dedicated power systems and what this could mean for America's energy future. If you enjoy videos about AI, energy infrastructure, technology, and America's changing power grid, LIKE this video, SUBSCRIBE to the channel, and share your thoughts in the comments!

In December 2025, Denver's Boom Supersonic, the company building the Overture supersonic airliner, announced a 42 MW natural gas turbine called Superpower. It shares about 80% of its parts with Symphony, the engine designed for that airliner. Crusoe ordered 29 of them. That was a 1.21 GW order worth about 1.25 billion dollars. Boom said the revenue could help fund the airliner itself. Think about that. Money for AI power could have helped pay for the return of supersonic passenger flight. So, did it work? Here's what has actually been demonstrated. On the gas side, yes, at limited scale. Mid-2026, roughly 2 GW of on-site generation was operating across four projects, mostly XAIs. By the end of this year, Clean Air expects maybe 2.8 to 3.2. Abilene shows the hybrid reality. Its first 200 MW were energized in September 2025. The campus is planned for 1.2 GW with grid power plus a large on-site gas plant. Oracle has described that plant as backup. Other reports describe the turbines as a bridge before the grid catches up. The accounts differ. Fuel cells are another path. Bloom Energy's solid oxide fuel cells convert natural gas to electricity chemically instead of by burning it. The US Department of Energy puts their efficiency around 60%. Bloom says it can power an entire data center within 90 days. And its Oracle deal reportedly grew to 2.8 GW this April. Those are the company's claims. Deployment is still catching up. And then reality arrives. First, permits. Earlier this year, New Mexico blocked a gas pipeline meant to fuel a planned 2.45 GW power plant for one Open AI and Oracle campus. Clean Air's satellite analysis suggests the project will likely miss its 2027 target. In New Jersey, Nimbis is still seeking an air permit for a 400 MW plant, while most of its Microsoft compute depends on it. Second, neighbors. Virginia regulators had approved just one air permit for a campus with on-site gas as of July. One county rejected a huge complex outright. Third, supplier risk. In September, Crusoe dropped its Boom order. Crusoe says Boom was a great partner, but not the right fit today, and it still plans to use turbines, just proven ones. No superpower unit had been delivered. Boom says it still plans about 250 MW of deliveries next year to other sites, and a gigawatt in 2028. So, the question changed. It wasn't whether jet-derived power works. It was whether a new machine can be trusted when a billion-dollar campus depends on it. Fourth, the biggest number. Out of 90 GW announced, roughly 60% is still only announcements or early plans. So, what changes if this works? For the grid, it could ease the line. Every data center that powers itself is one fewer waiting for a transmission upgrade. For your bill, it's complicated. Analysts estimate data center demand already adds about 1.4 billion dollars a year to US residential electricity bills, concentrated in a few regions. Oracle says its Abilene setup will not affect local bills or supply. That's a company statement, and it's hard to check from outside. For aviation, it's strange and real. Companies that built engines for flight now find a second market that could help fund the next generation of aircraft. Boom's attempt shows both the upside and the risk. If everything on schedule happens, Clean View says up to 13 gigawatts could be online by the end of 2027. If permits and delays bite, it could be as low as five. So, back to the question. What has been proven? A data center can bring its own power, and it can happen fast. Memphis did it in months, and about 2 gigawatts are running now. What has not been proven? That 90 gigawatts will ever be built, that the new hardware is reliable at scale, or that communities and regulators will accept the emissions. What has to happen? Permits, pipelines, and turbines that actually arrive. And here's the implication worth watching. For decades, power plants came first and factories followed. AI is reversing that. The computer arrives first, and the power plant gets built beside it from whatever machines can be found. If engineers solve the permitting, supply, and reliability problems, this stops being a workaround for the grid. It becomes a new way of building America's infrastructure, one where the power plant is part of the build.

metadata.title: Solid-State Transformers & MVDC: Revolutionizing AI Data Center Power Systems | Keentel Engineering
metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
How will Solid-State Transformers (SSTs) and Medium-Voltage DC (MVDC) revolutionize power distribution for next-generation AI data centers?

As AI infrastructure expands toward hundreds of megawatts and even gigawatt-scale campuses, traditional power distribution architectures are facing new challenges. Solid-State Transformers (SSTs), MVDC distribution, and 800 VDC rack architectures are emerging as promising technologies for delivering efficient, reliable, and scalable power to high-density AI computing infrastructure.

Explore how Solid-State Transformers convert medium-voltage AC power into regulated DC power, reducing conversion stages, copper requirements, equipment footprint, and power distribution losses.

We also examine the critical electrical engineering challenges involved in integrating SST-based AI data centers with the utility grid.


Why Solid-State Transformers Matter for AI Data Centers

The growing power demand of AI accelerators and high-density computing racks is driving the transition toward advanced DC power distribution. SSTs provide a controllable interface between the utility grid and the data center, potentially enabling improved power management, reactive power control, energy storage integration, and more efficient power delivery.

However, successful deployment requires careful engineering of grid interconnection, protection coordination, dynamic performance, harmonic compliance, and MVDC system reliability.

How Keentel Engineering Supports Advanced Data Center Power Systems

Keentel Engineering provides electrical power systems consulting and engineering support, including:

• Utility and large-load interconnection studies
• Load flow and short-circuit analysis
• EMT modeling and PSCAD studies
• Grid stability and transient analysis
• MV and HV substation engineering
• Protection coordination and relay studies
• Harmonic and power quality analysis
• BESS integration and renewable energy studies
• NERC compliance and grid reliability assessments

From medium-voltage substations to 765 kV transmission systems, Keentel Engineering supports complex power infrastructure projects across the United States.

segments.text: Today's topic is beyond the box, how
solid state transformers and medium
voltage DC shape the grids that power US
AI data centers. This is a grid side
engineering guide. It covers three
things. How these campuses interconnect
with the utility. How we model them
using electromagnetic transient
simulation. And how we protect megawatt
scale DC systems.
The content is based on insights from
Kentech engineering. Over the next few
minutes, we'll look at why this problem
has changed, where the real engineering
risks sit, and how to manage them before
they become expensive.
Let's start with what has changed. In
the past, a data center was a passive
load. It sat behind a 60 hertz iron core
transformer, and its response to a fault
was predictable because it was governed
by physics, copper, iron, and magnetic
flux.
The future looks very different. A 1
gigawatt AI campus behaves like a
massive inverter based resource running
in reverse. Its behavior is set by
firmware, not physics.
That means the grid has to trust
software.
The catalyst came in July 2024 in
Northern Virginia. 1500 megawatts of
data center load dropped off in just 82
seconds, triggered by six successive
grid faults. As a result, NERC, ERCOT,
and utilities are rewriting the rules
for computational loads.
Models and performance commitments are
now mandatory.
This diagram shows the power path from
the grid down to the racks. Power moves
from the grid to the substation, then
through medium voltage AC collectors. At
the boundary line, it enters the
vendor's domain. There, an active front
end converts AC to DC. A medium
frequency transformer provides
isolation, and a DC to DC converter
feeds the medium voltage DC bus. That
bus supplies racks running at 800 volts
DC.
The scope of responsibility matters. The
vendor owns topology, silicon carbide
devices, and internal cooling. The
system engineer owns interconnection,
super harmonics, EMT models, and DC
fault protection.
Keen Tell Engineering does not design
solid state transformer hardware. This
guide covers the engineering physics
everywhere else. Regulators now ask for
specific things. In Texas, ERCOT Senate
Bill 6 sets mandates for loads above 75
MW including curtailment and remote
disconnect provisions.
In PJM and New York ISO, the pressure
comes from intense load clustering, new
co-location rules, and dense 345 kV
transmission constraints.
Across these markets, four deliverables
keep coming up. First, validated models.
EMT models in PSCAD and positive
sequence models, both based on actual
control code. Second, dynamic
commitments. Stated voltage and
frequency ride through curves.
Third, power quality. Harmonic and super
harmonic emission data at the point of
interconnection.
Fourth, protection logic. AC and DC
fault current contributions and blocking
behaviors.
The rule of thumb is that behavior is
assumed unless it is specified.
You must model the campus before you can
build it. This slide explains why EMT
modeling is essential. On the left, the
smooth gray curve is what a positive
sequence RMS model shows. It averages
out fast dynamics and misses control
instability. The jagged cyan trace is an
electromagnetic transient simulation. It
runs at microsecond resolution and
captures phase locked loop loss of lock,
silicon carbide switching, and real
control code. Here's the scenario. A
1,000 MW campus sits on a strong 345 kV
bus. A critical line trips and 800
megawatts of nearby solar and wind is
factored in. The short-circuit ratio
drops to about 3.9. Below a ratio of
three, current controllers become
critically unstable. The takeaway is
that positive sequence models cannot see
weak grid instability. Early EMT
screening prevents late-stage redesigns.
Now, we turn to DC protection.
In an AC system, a mechanical breaker
opens at the natural zero crossing,
which happens 120 times per second.
A DC fault has no zero crossing. To
interrupt it, you must either create one
or absorb massive energy.
Consider a pole-to-pole fault on a
medium-voltage DC bus. 20 converters at
2 mF each give 40 mF of capacitance.
At 6 kV DC, that stores 720 kJ. Those
capacitors discharge their peak current
in microseconds. That leaves a breaker
dilemma with three options.
Solid-state breakers act in
microseconds, but they have high
conduction loss and cost. Hybrid
breakers have low loss and are fast, but
the mechanical and electronic
integration is highly complex.
Converter blocking is cheap and simple,
but it takes down the entire bus section
instantly. This chart plots impedance
against frequency. Solid-state
transformers emit super harmonics
between 2 and 150 kHz. Within that band,
there is a sharp resonance peak near 50
kHz.
It happens in three steps.
First, aggregation. Low-order harmonics
from hundreds of modules stack up across
the campus. Second, resonance. Long
medium-voltage cable capacitance
combines with utility transformer
impedance and creates parallel
resonances. Third, amplification. When a
resonance aligns with fast silicon
carbide switching frequencies, small
currents produce massive voltage
distortion.
As a standards note, IEEE 519-2022
applies at the point of common coupling.
Mitigation requires coordinated filter
design and control interleaving across
the entire campus. Compliance falls into
four quadrants. The baseline
obligations, which come through the
utility, are FAC-001
and 002 for interconnection study data
and TPL-001 for contingency modeling. If
the campus exports power, it triggers
generator owner and operator
registration under NERC's inverter-based
resource rules. If you operate onsite
generation or battery storage, PRC-024
and PRC-029
impose strict voltage and frequency
ride-through performance.
After the build, MOD-026-2
requires model validation against
real-world field measurements.
The core insight is that compliance is
no longer a post-energization paperwork
exercise. Disturbance monitoring and
ride-through curves must be engineered
into the solid-state transformer
firmware on day one. Battery storage on
the MVDC bus can serve three different
jobs, and each one sizes the system
differently. For ride-through, you carry
500 MW for 2 seconds. That takes only
about 0.28 MW hours. So, power rating
and converter current limit drive the
design. For load smoothing, you absorb
plus or minus 100 MW of AI workload
swings at half a hertz. That is roughly
18 kW hours per half cycle, and power
rating and extreme cycle life drive the
design.
For peak shaving or backup, you replace
200 MW of grid supply for 4 hours. That
needs 800 MW hours, so total energy
capacity drives the design.
The strategic takeaway is that
connecting storage directly to the MVDC
bus saves conversion stages.
But, define the operational role before
sizing or you risk buying the wrong
system entirely. These three topics are
tied together.
Grounding architecture is the first. A
solid midpoint gives high fault current.
A high resistance or floating system
lets you operate through a first fault,
but it shifts pole voltages.
DC arc flash is the second.
IEEE 1584 doesn't cover DC, and massive
capacitor discharge energy makes
traditional AC calculations dangerously
inaccurate.
You need specialized NFPA 70E
alternative methods.
Insulation coordination is the third.
Fast transients from silicon carbide
switches cause partial discharge in
insulation that would easily survive
standard 60 hertz stress.
The central insight is that grounding
choices dictate both the insulation
rating and the DC protection strategy.
They cannot be engineered in isolation.
Here is the whole system in four zones.
Zone one is the utility interface from 4
to 765 kilovolts. Its concerns are
harmonic compliance under IEEE 519,
short circuit ratio, and interconnection
modeling.
Zone two is the substation and medium
voltage AC collectors, covering arc
flash, the grounding grid, AC
protection, and resonance mitigation.
Zone three is the boundary at the solid
state transformer. It covers
ride-through firmware, PSCAD modeling,
and silicon carbide insulation
coordination.
Zone four is the MVDC bus and storage,
covering DC fault interruption, battery
load smoothing, and NERC compliance for
exporting.
The key point is that a change in zone
four alters the physics in zone one.
Siloed engineering fails at the
boundary.
This is the project road map from phase
zero screening through phase six
operations.
Three gates control the schedule.
Gate [snorts] one is the model gate. No
interconnection application is submitted
without an accepted control code backed
EMT model.
Gate two is the specification gate. No
solid-state transformer hardware
purchase order without utility grid
performance KPIs explicitly written into
the contract.
Gate three is the protection gate. No
detailed MVDC design without an agreed
system-wide DC fault clearing
philosophy.
Each gate stops a known expensive
failure before it can spread to later
phases. This table lists what an owner
should demand from vendors, why and by
when. First, an EMT model with actual
control code for utility weak grid
stability studies by phase two.
Second, voltage and frequency
ride-through curves for NERC
applicability and the interconnection
application by phase one.
Third, DC fault current and capacitor
discharge data to design MVDC switchgear
and assess arc flash by phase two.
Fourth, firmware version control for
model management and NERC audit evidence
by phase four. Fifth,
hardware-in-the-loop factory acceptance
testing to prove weak grid stability
before shipping, also by phase four. Put
these items in the contract and treat
them as conditions of purchase. Two
examples show these gates working.
First, the Texas SCR save. A 600 MW
campus.
The interconnection had stalled because
nearby renewables pushed the campus
short-circuit ratio into unstable
territory.
Keentel mandated EMT modeling upfront
and adjusted the solid-state transformer
control parameters and transformer
impedance specifications at the same
time.
That restored the stability margin
before the equipment order and avoided a
multi-million-dollar late-stage
redesign.
Second, the New York protection save. A
250 MW campus.
Multiple vendors shared one MVDC bus
with no unified DC fault strategy. And
factory tests covered only baseline
efficiency.
Keentel wrote an interface control
document and required the factory
acceptance test to include partial
discharge tests and hardware-in-the-loop
grid simulator testing.
That caught insulation failures and
model discrepancies at the factory and
ensured first-pass utility approval. The
hardest engineering problems fall in the
gaps between silos. The solid-state
transformer vendor, the EPC, and the
utility each own a piece, but nobody
owns the seams.
Keentel Engineering covers those seams
with expertise from 4 to 765 kV, PSACD
and EMTDC modeling, NERC compliance, and
substation design.
We leave the converter hardware to the
designers. We make sure the grid, the
substation, and the regulators accept
what they built.
That is three decades of experience from
every side of the table and accountable
engineering.
To get in touch, call 813-389-7871
or email contact@keentelengineering.com.
Thank you.

metadata.title: When the Power Company Takes Your Land for a Data Center
metadata.author: The New York Times
metadata.shortDescription:
As data centers sprout across Georgia, the state’s utility providers are building new power lines to meet the demand for electricity. We speak with residents in Fayetteville, about 25 miles south of Atlanta, who say the new lines will run through their backyards and make it impossible to resell their homes at their current value.

Subscribe: http://bit.ly/U8Ys7n
More from The New York Times Video: http://nytimes.com/video
----------
Whether it's reporting on conflicts abroad and political divisions at home, or covering the latest style trends and scientific developments, New York Times video journalists provide a revealing and unforgettable view of the world. It's all the news that's fit to watch.

segments.text: This is Doug Fergus, and this is his backyard.
Last year, this high-voltage power line next to him
took out a quarter of it.
“We found this place that we love.
And then within a year, we’re told it’s going to be
changed totally.
And we just felt like a punch in the gut.”
A.I. data centers are coming to Georgia,
and they need a lot of electricity.
New power lines are going up to feed them,
sometimes in people’s backyards,
whether they like it or not.
Nearly 400 trees were cut down to make way for this
power line on Doug’s property.
“It was solid trees
like that all the way up to here.
And now we have this unobstructed view of
this new monstrosity.”
The state’s biggest utility company, Georgia Power,
says it offers fair compensation to homeowners
when it needs to build infrastructure
on their properties.
But many residents say the offers they’ve receive don’t
cover the property value they will lose from having a
power line built in their backyard.
“How’s it going?”
“Good, how about you?”
It’s Wednesday night.
Two dozen local residents are meeting at a church
to discuss another high-voltage transmission line
that will soon cut through their backyards.
“We chose the properties that we live on
because of the quality that the property offered us.
It is not about dirt and grass.
It is about the whole property.”
Some of them would move, but they say offers
Georgia Power has made aren’t enough
to start over again somewhere else.
“What if in a year or two from now, they going to come
and start another line?
Because all those data centers —
how do we know?”
“To me personally, I need replacement value.
I don’t want a penny over my — I want my dream here to have
my dream here.”
The statewide power line expansion
will deliver about 10 gigawatts of new energy,
enough to power twice the number of homes
currently in the state of Georgia.
Eighty percent of it will go to data centers.
“We have seen a lot of growth come in the state.
Much of it is data centers.
And it’s not only the hyperscalers and the
data centers, it’s the manufacturers,
it’s industrial, it’s commercial.
It’s also residential.”
To meet that demand, many more
transmission lines are needed.
In 2019, Georgia Power’s 10-year plan called for 24 miles
of new power lines.
Last year, that number ballooned to 1,065 miles.
“This infrastructure is actually benefiting
all the surrounding communities.
It will make anything through a storm and day-to-day
more resilient, more reliable because of these large
load users coming to our state.”
“There’s a lot of pressure to bring this new energy online
very quickly because states are currently competing
for the opportunity to attract these data centers,
even though the financial benefits of them for the state
has not actually yet borne fruit.”
“I feel like we can’t really plan for the future.
We don’t know where we’re going to live in a year.”
Rachael Maszk’s family bought their home four years ago.
“We definitely bought this house for the backyard.
We just knew there was going to be
enough room for chickens, for a garden, for fruit trees.”
Now, Georgia Power wants to use half of Rachael’s backyard
for a transmission line and is offering her $57,000.
“It’s a lot of money to us.
It would be a lot of money to, I think, any regular person.
But it isn’t enough money to cover the damage
to our property value that this will cause.”
During their negotiations over compensation,
Rachael said representatives from the company
discussed using eminent domain
to take her land.
Eminent domain gives utility companies power to seize
private property for public use without the owner’s
consent, if they pay fair compensation determined
by the courts.
“Eminent domain is always a last resort for our company.
In fact, we use it less than 1 percent of the time.”
“It feels like the only option is to reach a settlement with
them, and I don’t really see what leverage the
average person has in that situation.”
“Before the poles went in, it was such a wonderful country,
laid-back feel, rolling green grass landscape.
And now it’s like we’re like
inside an electric transfer station.
Doesn’t feel like home anymore.”
Doug reached a settlement with Georgia Power
after more than a year of negotiating.
He used that compensation to pay down half of his mortgage,
but is reconsidering where to live out his retirement.
“There’s really no amount of money that could erase all
this and make it go back the way it was.”

metadata.title: Sustainable Data Centers: microgrid-enabled and battery energy storage powered systems
metadata.author: Digital Infrastructure Network
metadata.shortDescription:
Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are gaining momentum in the data center industry for their emission-free operation, back-up power capabilities, ability to optimize renewable energy generation and participation in new ancillary services.

In ABB session we are focusing on BESS within a microgrid-enabled data center and how it can support a more sustainable backup power and allows to be in charge of the energy mix, from Hyperscale to Enterprise customer.

About Digital Infra Network
Digital Infra Network is one of the media brands of RockScar Media. Sharing Sustainable Digital Infrastructure Thinking via interviews and presentations from leading operators, consultants and solution providers: We cover multiple topics across the year, providing ongoing access to information, advice and ideas to assist you in fully understanding the Digital Infrastructure Energy Transition and what is required to enable Sustainable Digital Transformation.

Join us as we explore the latest technologies, strategies, and best practices that are shaping the future of business. Visit:
RockScar: https://rockscarmedia.com/
Digital Infra Network: https://digitalinfranetwork.com/
Net Zero Professional: https://netzeroprofessional.com/
Connected Energy Solutions: https://connectedenergysolutions.co.uk/
Connected Technology Solutions: https://connectedtechnologysolutions.co.uk/

metadata.title: Why Big Tech Can't Build AI Data Centers Fast Enough
metadata.author: Data Center Sales & Marketing Institute (DCSMI)
metadata.shortDescription:
https://www.dcsmi.com/briefing Subscribe to the Data Center GTM Briefing


⚡ In episode 206 of the Data Center Go-to-Market Podcast, you’ll join Joshua Feinberg and Mark Caskey, founder and CEO of Steel Nation, to learn why grid constraints are driving data centers toward behind-the-meter power, what makes natural gas and generation equipment difficult to secure, and how pipelines, permitting, and regional resources affect project timelines. Mark also shares how Steel Nation found its niche in energy infrastructure and what he sees ahead for natural gas, battery storage, and small nuclear reactors. 🏗️

Ep. 206 Mark Caskey, CEO/Founder of Steel Nation | Data Center Go-to-Market Podcast

0:00 Data Center Power Constraints & Intro
1:04 Introducing Mark Caskey, CEO/Founder at Steel Nation
1:50 Mark Caskey's Data Center Energy Background: Oil, Gas, Coal, and Nuclear
6:24 Data Center Power Moratoriums, Grid Shortages, and Launching Steel Nation Microgrids
10:35 The Biggest Data Center Microgrid Go-to-Market and Behind-the-Meter Regulatory Challenges
12 52 Educating Data Center Decision Makers on Behind-the-Meter Power
18:45 Data Center Site Selection and Natural Gas Pipelines vs. Railroad Rights-of-Way
20:50 Why Fiber Optic Infrastructure Drives Data Center Locations
23:00 Subscribe to the Data Center GTM Briefing
23:57 How Steel Nation Pivoted from Turbine Enclosures to Switchgear
27:15 Partnering Directly with Natural Gas Providers for Data Center Infrastructure
30:41 The Reality of Solar & Wind vs. Base Load Energy for Data Centers
32:35 Data Center Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) & Mini Nuclear Reactors
35:31 What Sales Professionals Misunderstand About Data Center Buyers
38:04 Turbines Located Inside Data Center Buildings Became Competitively Obsolete
42:21 Reaching the Real Economic Decision-Maker in Data Center GTM
44:29 The Next 12–24 Months: Grid Independence and Data Center Power Predictions

49:19 Subscribe to the Data Center GTM Briefing

metadata.title: Battery Forum: Grid-Forming BESS Architectures for AI Data Center Power Quality with Lyten
metadata.author: Volta Foundation
metadata.shortDescription:
AI data centers are creating new challenges for power quality and grid stability as rapidly fluctuating AI workloads place increasing demands on energy infrastructure.

In this Battery Forum session, Jongwon JP Park of Lyten examined how grid-forming battery energy storage systems (BESS) can help manage extreme load fluctuations and improve power quality in AI data centers.

Using simulated hyperscaler load profiles, JP discussed how Lyten's Voltpack Mobile System can stabilize rapid power oscillations and address challenges that conventional BESS architectures may struggle to manage.

Watch the full session to learn more about grid-forming BESS, AI data center power management, and next-generation energy storage solutions.


For more insights and updates:
- YouTube channel:  ⁨@voltafoundation⁩  
- LinkedIn page: https://www.linkedin.com/company/volta-foundation

metadata.title: Data center solutions: Types, design, and infrastructure explained | Eaton PSEC
metadata.author: Eaton
metadata.shortDescription:
Data centers are the foundation of our digital world and rely on complex networks of servers, storage systems, and communication infrastructure operating continuously. To that end, data centers require power, cooling, security, and reliability to always keep the information available. 

Data centers power today's digital world, from cloud computing to AI. Discover data center types, reliability tiers, redundancy, infrastructure design, and how Eaton solutions help deliver the uptime, scalability, and performance modern facilities demand.

Shaunta Mason, Eaton Area Sales Manager, explains the data center types and unique roles they play in our connected world. Learn about 
• Managed and hosted
• Enterprise
• Colocation or multi-tenant 
• Edge
• Hyperscale 
• Cloud

We also discuss data center considerations, reliability tiers, redundancy systems, and the role of major industry organizations and standards that influence the design, construction, operation, and safety of data centers. 
Learn how Eaton supports modern data center infrastructure and how we’re partnering with chip manufacturers to develop solutions that high density computing environments. 

Walk away with a better understanding of how these facilities operate and why they are essential to supporting the technologies that power our connected world.

00:16
01:26 Types of data centers
04:57 Data center redundancy 
07:26 Data center configurations 
09:01 Eaton’s data center role
10:36 Conclusion

segments.text: Have you ever stopped to think about how much of your daily life
depends on web based systems?
From social media and online shopping to emails and apps.
Every one of these actions connect to a vast digital network.
Behind the scenes, all this activity relies on a global network
of computers and servers that communicate through miles of fiber optic and copper cables.
It's fascinating to realize just how much physical hardware
is involved in something we often think as intangible.
Data centers house these systems, providing the power, cooling,
and security needed to keep everything running smoothly.
But data centers aren't just about convenience.
They're the backbone of industries like finance, healthcare, and manufacturing.
Not just the delivery of critical information, but also storing and data processing.
With artificial intelligence becoming a bigger part of our lives.
The demand for fast, secure and always available data is skyrocketing.
That's why the design and infrastructure of data centers matter now more than ever.
They're not just buildings, they're the foundation of our digital future.
Data centers come in various shapes, sizes,
and configurations, each designed to meet different needs.
Let's break them down in a way that's easy to understand.
The typical size of a data center tends to start around
one megawatt, which is 1000 kW.
On average, one single household can consume 3 to 5 kW of power.
This level of power consumption can compare to hundreds,
even thousands of homes, depending on the type and service.
The power consumption of data centers varies.
Let's take a look at different types of data centers.
First, our manage and hosted data centers that offer data center as a service.
Small businesses that want to grow their online presence but lack the resources
to build their own facility can rent space and services from a provider.
The provider handles the infrastructure while the business focuses on
its customers.
These data centers can have customers that may only require
5 to 10kW, or the equivalent of 1 to 2 homes.
Enterprise data centers are built on and operated
by a single organization, like a bank or a large corporation such as Eaton.
For example, a national bank offering online banking might run
its own data center to ensure secure and reliable access to customer accounts.
Everything is managed in-house to support core business operations.
Co-location or multi-tenant data centers are like shared
office spaces, but for servers.
Businesses lease space in a facility that provides power, cooling and security.
The company brings its own equipment, but the infrastructure is shared.
It's a great option for organizations that want control
over their hardware, without the costs of building a full data center.
Edge data centers are smaller facilities located closer to users, designed
to reduce latency and improve performance by processing data near its source.
Ever notice how your music or video stream pauses less when you're close to a city?
That's thanks to edge data centers.
Hyperscale data centers are the giants massive facilities built
to support the needs of the tech industry and cloud providers.
They house thousands of servers and are optimized
for scalability, efficiency, and high volume data processing.
These data centers are size from 50 MW to over 100 MW.
Cloud data centers store your information across multiple locations
so you can access it from anywhere, even if one center goes offline.
Your data stays safe and available.
If you've ever backed up your phone's content to the cloud,
you've used one of these.
Designing a data center involves several critical considerations,
starting with asking the right questions.
Here are some key aspects to think about.
Location. Location. Location.
Where you build a data center is crucial.
Here are things to consider.
Is the area prone to natural disasters?
Is there reliable access to power?
Is fiber connectivity readily available?
Can the site support future growth?
Are there local regulations or zoning laws that could impact operations?
Standards like TIA-942-A help guide these decisions,
offering best practices for site selection and infrastructure planning.
Built in redundancy is essential for ensuring
reliability and availability.
Data centers often have redundant
utility connections, with multiple power lines feeding into the building
from the utility in the event one becomes unavailable.
Backup power, including generators, uninterruptible power systems, and various
forms of battery energy storage systems in the event of a power disturbance.
Redundant cooling systems incorporating multi-layer HVAC system designs,
including water cooling technology, are also designed for resilience.
Duplicate network paths utilizing various communication
paths and networks for consistent information delivery.
This redundancy ensures that if one fails, the remainder of the system
maintains continuous operation. From power generation to load distribution
each system can have various levels of redundancy tier levels.
Measuring reliability.
The Uptime Institute created a tier system
to compare data centers based on their reliability.
Tier one: Basic setup, no redundancy.
Tier two: Some redundant components.
Tier three: Concurrently maintainable without the need to shut down.
and Tier four: Fully fault-tolerant, highest level of reliability.
For example, most hyperscale data centers are designed
and rated as tier four operations.
Ensuring up time of 99.995%,
which is under 30 minutes of downtime a year.
Uptime Institute is the only organization
that can provide official certification of these tiers.
Several organizations
provide standards that shape how data centers are built and operated.
Some of the most influential standards include
IEEE, UL,
ASHRAE, NFPA,
NEC,
and AHJ, the local authority having jurisdiction.
These standards ensure that data centers
are designed to be safe, efficient, and reliable.
Data centers are designed and built based on local requirements as well,
which vary based on location, location, location.
Now that we've covered the big picture decisions like
where to build and how to ensure reliability, let's shift
gears and talk about how data centers are configured
to meet specific performance, space and operational needs.
System redundancy is key.
It's about having backup systems in place so that if something fails,
operations keeps running smoothly.
When discussing design considerations, you might hear terms like
N, N+1, 2N, and 2N+1,
But what does that really mean? Let's break it down.
N is the baseline. It's the minimum number of components,
like power supplies or cooling units,
needed to keep the data center running under normal conditions.
Including generators to network components, as discussed earlier.
N+1 means you have one extra component in operation.
If one fails, the system continues to be supported
with redundant components.
2N takes it a step further.
You have a fully operational, duplicate system ready to go.
If the primary system goes down, the secondary one takes over
without missing a beat.
2N+1 is the gold standard.
It consists of a fully redundant system, plus an extra component,
designed for the highest level of fault tolerance and availability.
These configurations are how data centers meet their tier classifications, ensuring
they deliver the level of uptime their users expect.
At Eaton, we work closely with the data center industry to support the infrastructure
behind this growing demand for speed, scale and reliability.
Our uninterruptible power supplies are designed to deliver efficient,
reliable backup power while minimizing the space required to support system
expansion from small projects to hundreds of megawatts.
Whether you're scaling for a large solution, reducing equipment
footprint, or monitoring performance, we offer solutions that include
a variety of energy storage alternatives to support your configurations.
We're also partnering with chip manufacturers
to develop solutions that support high density computing environments.
Think one megawatt racks for AI workloads.
Our chip-to-growth strategy focuses on optimizing both white space, where the IT
lives, and gray space, where the power distribution lives, to support it.
Not only do we support the power quality infrastructure of data centers with UPS,
but we are also aligned with meeting the power distribution,
metering, and monitoring demands of our growing data generated markets.
With growing and innovative technology on the horizon, we are planning to see
a massive growth in the data center market by more than 10% in the next 10 years.
Lastly, with features like EnergyAware UPS,
we're helping data centers not only manage large electrical load during faults,
but also contribute to renewable energy efforts
and even generate revenue from those investments.
As we've seen, data centers are far more than just buildings filled with servers,
they're the digital backbone of our connected world.
From supporting everyday conveniences to powering the future of AI,
their design, reliability and infrastructure
are critical to keeping our world running.
To interact with some of our data center products, or to learn more about our capabilities
in designing and building data centers for today's modern needs,
contact us or your local Eaton representative to schedule a visit
to one of our Power Systems Experience Centers today.

metadata.title: Understanding BESS Fire Testing for Data Centers | TCA 18
metadata.author: UL Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
Data centers depend on battery energy storage systems (BESS) to help maintain critical operations. But as these systems store more energy, understanding fire risks becomes increasingly important. 

In this episode of The Code Authority®, LaTanya Schwalb, principal engineer at UL Solutions, discusses how updated requirements in NFPA 855 (Standard for the Installation of Stationary Energy Storage Systems) and UL 9540A (Test Method for Evaluating Thermal Runaway Fire Propagation in Battery Energy Storage Systems) address large-scale BESS fire testing. 

She breaks down how the testing works, what has changed in UL 9540A, Edition 6 and how test data can help authorities having jurisdiction (AHJs) evaluate BESS installations in data centers. 

Explore, learn and connect with us:
At UL Solutions, we’re dedicated to advancing safety science across various industries. Our channel provides insights into safety standards, sustainability, security and much more. Discover our thought leadership content, get to know our subject-matter experts and catch behind-the-scenes looks at our pioneering testing, inspection, certification, software and advisory services.
