segments.text: You finished building a solar farm.
But you can't sell a single electron, because you're not connected to the grid.
To connect, you file an application and take a number in a line called the interconnection queue.
Right now, that line holds nearly two thousand generation projects totaling four hundred thirty-two gigawatts.
That's more than five times Texas's all-time peak demand.
And nationally, the median project spends five years in that line before it ever generates power.
Today: how to read the queue.
The interconnection queue is simply the ordered list of generation projects waiting to connect to the grid.
In Texas, you file your application with ERCOT, the grid operator, and each project is assigned a unique tracking number, the GINR, the Generation Interconnection Request number.
That one number lets you follow the project's entire journey: its capacity in megawatts, its fuel and technology, its point of interconnection, and exactly which stage it has reached.
ERCOT publishes the list every month, so anyone can see who's at the front of the line, and who's dropped out.
The public file is called the GIS Report, Generator Interconnection Status, published monthly as a spreadsheet.
Reading it is straightforward.
Each row is one project; follow the columns: project name, point of interconnection, fuel and technology, capacity, expected in-service date, and status.
Statuses fall into three buckets.
Active, the study is moving forward.
Inactive, the project is paused, usually because required information wasn't submitted in time.
Withdrawn, the project has left the queue.
One thing to remember: the queue is a snapshot.
New projects enter and others drop out every month, so always cite the date alongside the number.
Once you're in line, the studies begin.
First comes the Screening Study, a high-level review ERCOT performs itself, with a target of about three months.
It asks the big-picture question: can this project connect without major problems, and what transmission upgrades might be needed?
If needed, a stability review, the SSR, follows.
Then comes the Full Interconnection Study, the FIS, performed by the transmission service provider, the TSP, with a target of about ten months.
This is where the required facilities and their costs get nailed down.
After that: negotiating the Interconnection Agreement, the IA, about six months, then an ERCOT compliance review of about three months, and finally construction and commercial operation.
Studies and agreements alone add up to roughly nineteen months on paper, and in practice, usually more.
Why longer?
First, sequential processing.
ERCOT studies projects one at a time, in the order they applied.

Other regions group projects into cluster studies; ERCOT doesn't, which makes it relatively fast, but when a project ahead of you withdraws, the results for everyone behind it can shift, triggering restudies.
Second, financial security.
ERCOT studies first, then sets the deposit amount.
Once the study lands, you post security to move forward, and if you can't, you're out of the line.
Third, attrition.
Projects drop out when the money or the economics don't work, and each withdrawal can force restudies that stretch the timeline for everyone else.
Nationally, fewer than one in five queued projects ever reaches commercial operation.
One more thing to know: the queue for large loads, data centers and the like, is moving to batch studies starting in 2026.
The generation queue and the load queue are separate conversations.
All of this is public.
First, the GIS Report, downloadable monthly from ercot.com as a spreadsheet, with project-level status, capacity, and expected online dates.
Second, ERCOT board materials.
The System Planning Update presented to the board summarizes total queue size and the fuel mix; the four-hundred-thirty-two gigawatt figure and the fuel breakdown in this video come from there.
Third, the same files are listed in ERCOT's Market Information System report library.
Search "GIS Report" on ercot.com.
And when you quote a number, always quote its date.
The queue is a living number that changes every month.
Three takeaways for developers.
First, don't take the headline number at face value.
Only a fraction of four hundred thirty-two gigawatts will ever get built.
Look at how solid the projects ahead of you are, and price in the attrition.
Second, understand ERCOT's philosophy: connect and manage.
ERCOT leans toward letting projects connect and managing congestion operationally.
Connection may be fast, but your output can be curtailed when the wires are full, and that hits revenue directly.
Third, watch the gas queue.
It nearly doubled in a year, from twenty-six to forty-eight gigawatts between October 2024 and October 2025, a clear signal of demand for firm, dispatchable capacity.
For the technical review process and the capital game behind it, see our Interconnection ESSENTIALS episode.
It pairs with this episode.
To recap: the interconnection queue is the line every generation project stands in to reach the grid.
One GINR number tracks the whole journey, and the monthly GIS Report tells you where everyone stands.
Follow the stages, screening, full study, agreement, and even a long line starts to reveal its opportunities.
This has been Texas Energy ESSENTIALS.

Picture the power grid is a vast and intricate web,

regional power markets.

Regional Transmission Organizations.
ISOs tend to cover single states or smaller regions,
while RTOs tend to cover larger multistate or multi-province areas.
There are also some regions that aren't covered by ISOs and
RTOs, but we don't need to worry about these for now.
For almost all regions that are covered by ISOs and RTOs,
their market operations are overseen by the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission (or FERC).
FERC is an independent agency of the US government,
whose goal is to oversee the interstate transmission of
electricity and natural gas.
However, ISOs and RTOs are individually responsible for coordinating
and operating the power grids within their respective regions.
As of early 2024, there are nine ISOs and RTOs in North

ERCOT is an ISO - and, crucially,

This is because ERCOT has no synchronous AC ties to the

segments.text: Welcome to KeenTel Engineering. In this
presentation, we're breaking down how
the Electric Reliability Council of
Texas actually works. We'll cover the
wholesale power market, how electricity
prices are set in real time, and what
keeps the Texas grid running
independently from the rest of the
country. Let's dive in. ERCOT is unlike
any other grid operator in the United
States. It powers about 90% of Texas,
over 26 million customers, and it
operates completely outside federal FERC
jurisdiction. That independence means
Texas sets its own rules. And one of the
biggest rules, there's no capacity
market. Generators only get paid for
power they actually produce. That keeps
the market competitive, but it also
means prices can spike hard when demand
peaks. To understand ERCOT, you need to
know the four main players. First,
transmission service providers, they own
the physical wires. Then, resource
entities, the generators, whether that's
wind, solar, gas, or nuclear.
Next, qualified scheduling entities, or
QSEs. They're the middlemen who submit
bids and handle settlements. And
finally, load serving entities, the
retail suppliers who deliver power to
homes and businesses. Each plays a
distinct role in keeping the market
balanced. ERCOT uses a nodal pricing
model called LMP, locational marginal
pricing. Every 5 minutes, prices are
recalculated at roughly 900 points
across the grid. The price is made up of
three components. System lambda, the
base cost of the next unit of power
statewide, a congestion component that
adjusts for transmission bottlenecks,
and a price adder that kicks in when
reserves get tight. When reserves drop
below 3 gigawatts, prices can hit the
$5,000 per megawatt hour cap. ERCOT runs
two markets simultaneously. The
day-ahead market lets generators and
buyers lock in commitments the day
before, with hourly granularity and
co-optimized energy and ancillary
services. Then, there's the real-time
market, powered by the SCED algorithm,
which dispatches every 5 minutes, 24
hours a day, 365 days a year.
Settlements happen every 15 minutes
using the average of three 5-minute
prices. Real-time is where the action
truly happens. Beyond energy, ERCOT
procures four ancillary services to keep
grid frequency stable at exactly 60
hertz. Regulation handles small
continuous deviations automatically.
Responsive reserve service kicks in fast
during major events like a generator
tripping offline. ECRS, the ERCOT
contingency reserve, provides rapid
response to large disturbances. And
non-spinning reserves are offline units
that can come online quickly when the
system tightens. Together, these are the
grid's safety net. Because ERCOT has no
capacity market, generators must recover
all their costs through market revenues
alone. That's why power purchase
agreements, PPAs, are so critical.
Generators use them to secure
predictable revenue and finance new
projects. Buyers lock in stable prices
over 10 to 20-year periods. And the
system benefits because PPAs encourage
new generation to be built exactly where
it's needed. One important detail. In a
PPA, you're not receiving the actual
electrons from that plant. It's a
financial arrangement layered on top of
how the grid physically operates.
ERCOT's energy-only nodal design is
elegant in theory. Prices always reflect
real-time scarcity, investment follows
value, and competition keeps long-run
costs down. But it comes with built-in
volatility. Without a capacity market
backstop, tight supply can send prices
to $5,000 per megawatt-hour almost
instantly. And as Texas continues
leading the nation in wind and solar,
managing that intermittency on an
isolated grid is ERCOT's defining
challenge going forward. To learn more,
visit keentelengineering.com.

Texas power is different. An energy-only market with no capacity market, scarcity pricing that spikes when power runs short, the ORDC that prices reserves automatically, a different price at every node via LMP, and the QSE as the market's gatekeeper — the ERCOT market structure explained in an ESSENTIALS-level class.

5. Nodal market · LMP (Locational Marginal Pricing)
6. QSE (Qualified Scheduling Entity) and settlement — who trades
7. Closing

segments.text: On July twenty-second, twenty twenty-six, Texas set a new all-time record for electricity demand: ninety-one point one gigawatts.
The organization managing that power is ERCOT, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, serving roughly ninety percent of the state's electric load, more than twenty-seven million customers.
And it runs unlike any other power market in America, because the Texas grid is, for all practical purposes, an island, barely connected to neighboring states.
Today, we're breaking down the structure of the ERCOT market.
Start with the biggest difference.

In most U.S. power markets, generators get paid twice: once for the electricity they produce, and again, through a capacity market, just for standing by, ready to run. PJM, MISO, New York, and New England all run capacity markets. ERCOT has none.
Texas generators earn money only when they actually produce electricity.
That's what makes it an energy-only market.
Plants sell cheap most of the year, and must earn the bulk of their annual revenue in a tiny handful of high-demand hours.
A study of twenty nineteen found that simple-cycle gas peakers earned about ninety percent of their real-time market value in just one percent of the hours that year.
For an energy-only market to work, one thing is essential: when power runs short, prices must be allowed to spike.
That's scarcity pricing.
In August twenty nineteen, ERCOT's real-time price hit the nine-thousand-dollar-per-megawatt-hour cap on two separate days, more than two hundred times the typical price.
The extreme case was Winter Storm Uri in February twenty twenty-one. With blackouts spreading, Texas regulators directed ERCOT to hold prices at nine thousand dollars.
Retail providers were buying power at nine thousand dollars a megawatt-hour and selling it to customers at around ninety dollars.
Several went bankrupt.
After Uri, the system-wide offer cap was cut to five thousand dollars per megawatt-hour, effective January twenty twenty-two.
But you can't have humans setting emergency prices every time. So ERCOT automates it with the ORDC, the Operating Reserve Demand Curve, introduced in June twenty fourteen.

The logic is simple: as operating reserves decline, an automatic price adder is applied to the real-time energy price. When reserves fall to the minimum contingency level of about three thousand megawatts, the adder climbs to VOLL, the Value of Lost Load, currently capped at five thousand dollars per megawatt-hour.
And since late twenty twenty-three, there are minimum adders: twenty dollars when reserves slip below sixty-five hundred megawatts, ten dollars below seven thousand.
The ORDC turns tightening reserves into a price signal before anyone has to intervene.
Next: where prices are set.
On December first, twenty ten, ERCOT switched to a nodal market.
More than four thousand electrical nodes across Texas now each get their own real-time price.
Each nodal price has two parts: the cost of energy itself, and the cost of transmission congestion.
Power is cheap at nodes near West Texas wind farms and expensive in congested cities.
These nodal prices are called LMP, Locational Marginal Pricing.
Those price differences are a map of where the grid needs more transmission.
So who actually trades in this market?
Only one kind of entity deals directly with ERCOT: the QSE, the Qualified Scheduling Entity.
Every generator and every retail provider must go through a QSE to submit bids, send real-time telemetry from their plants, and settle payments with ERCOT.
QSEs pass ERCOT's qualification process and post collateral for settlement.
For market participants, the QSE is the gatekeeper to the market.
To recap: ERCOT is an energy-only market with no capacity market. Scarcity pricing is the investment signal.
The ORDC generates that signal automatically.
Nodal LMP sets a different price at every location.
And the QSE is the gatekeeper for every trade.
Texas demand topped ninety-one gigawatts this year.
Once you understand this structure, Texas power news reads differently.
This has been US Energy Weekly's one-oh-one series.

metadata.author: Modo Energy
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how prices are determined in ERCOT, a nodal power market with around 17,000 nodes. Find out about Locational Marginal Prices (LMPs), Settlement Points, and the role of System Lambda in shaping electricity prices across the system.

You can learn more about ERCOT and the GB power systems here: https://modoenergy.com/research

Follow our LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/modo-energy-usa/

#powersystem #systemlambda #nodalpowermarket #LMP #ERCOT #settlementpoints #explainervideo

segments.text: Welcome back to The Energy Academy.
Over the next couple of episodes,
we'll be looking at how prices are determined in ERCOT.
As we mentioned previously, ERCOT is a nodal power market.
This means that the price of power differs across various
locations - and these locations are known as "nodes".
The different prices at these nodes are known as Locational
Marginal Prices, or LMPs.
LMPs simply reflect the value of producing an additional unit
of power at a given node.
As of early 2024, there are around 17,000 nodes in
ERCOT. And just under 900 of these have a unique LMP.
These nodes with a unique LMP are known as "Settlement
Points".
Most Settlement Points represent a single resource,
in the form of a "resource node" -
something like a battery energy storage system, a wind farm,
a combined cycle gas generator, etcetera.
Basically, a transmission-connected resource that participates in
wholesale markets and can respond to dispatch instructions.
Some Settlement Points don't just represent a single node.
Instead, they're aggregations of nodes - called "load zones",
or "trading hubs".
Every five minutes,
ERCOT produces a unique LMP for each of them.
But, how are these prices formed?
Well, the main component of prices across ERCOT is something
called the "System Lambda".
System Lambda is just cost of procuring the next cheapest
unit of energy across the entire system.
So, say that demand is 50 GW across the entire state.
The sun is shining, the wind is blowing,
and demand is being met by a combination of wind and solar,
nuclear, and a bit of coal generation on top.
As the most expensive generator being used in this case,
the coal plant determines the System Lambda.
Now, imagine the sun sets and solar generation drops off.
And, at the same time, demand rises slightly.
This means that ERCOT may now need to use slightly more
expensive generation in order to meet demand.
So, ERCOT turns up some natural gas plants.
And, because natural gas is generally a more expensive form
of generation, System Lambda increases.
Now, this scenario is a crazy oversimplification.
In fact, determining System Lambda is a much more complex and nuanced
process than this.
It takes into account factors such as: resource ramp rates,
system frequency,
and the bid and offer curves of individual resources.
System Lambda is simply the first component in determining
the LMP at every Settlement Point.
The second is transmission congestion.
In the next episode,
we'll discuss exactly how the cost of alleviating congestion
is factored into LMPs.
See you there.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Data Center (Why 65% Full Means Bankrupt)
metadata.author: Your Finance Uncle
metadata.shortDescription:
This video breaks down the real economics of owning a data center, covering construction costs per megawatt, colocation pricing, power and cooling expenses, and the break-even utilization rate that determines profit or bankruptcy. Learn how data center investment, hyperscale facilities, wholesale colocation, and retail colocation models generate revenue through rack rental, cross-connect fees, managed services, and metered electricity billing. We explore real-world data center construction costs, grid capacity constraints, power purchase agreements, generator backup systems, PUE (power usage effectiveness), and uptime SLA penalties that shape long-term profitability in this multi-billion-dollar AI-driven infrastructure boom. Whether you're researching data center investing, colocation business models, data center REITs, or how to build a data center from the ground up, this video explains the capital costs, risks, and financial realities behind one of the fastest-growing sectors in real estate and technology.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER: This video is for informational and educational purposes only and does not constitute financial, investment, legal, or business advice.

segments.text: Okay, so you want to own a data center,
rent out server racks, sign contracts
with tech giants, and collect fees every
single month for decades. Rows of
blinking machines, a waiting list of
companies begging for space. It looks
like the closest thing to a guaranteed
money printer in modern business. Here's
the problem. Almost none of that is
true. And the part that is true is far
more brutal than the marketing suggests.
What you're actually signing up for is a
business that blends industrial
construction, power grid engineering,
real estate speculation, and a customer
relationship built on uptime guarantees
measured in minutes, not months. Some
people who buy into this business become
extraordinarily wealthy. Others sink
hundreds of millions into a building
that never fills, and they lose it
slowly, in a way that looks fine right
up until it doesn't. So, let's take this
apart the way an operator actually has
to see it, not the way it looks from a
glossy investor deck. First, a quick
note on what kind of data center we're
even talking about, because the model
changes everything. Hyperscale
facilities built and owned entirely by
companies like Amazon or Google never
touch the open market at all. Wholesale
colocation leases entire buildings to
single large tenants for years at a
time. Retail colocation rents out
individual racks and cages to smaller
businesses. The purest version of this
business, the one where every dollar of
risk sits on one operator's shoulders,
is the independently developed wholesale
or retail colocation facility. That's
the version we're breaking down here,
because that's the version where the
economics cut both ways. The scale of
this market is worth sitting with for a
second. Global data center spending is
projected to cross $1 trillion this year
alone, driven heavily by artificial
intelligence workloads. A genuinely
enormous industry hiding behind a
windowless building on the edge of a
highway. Let's start with the part
almost nobody thinks about first, the
power underneath the building. A data
center does not begin with a server. It
begins with an electricity negotiation,
and that negotiation alone can kill the
entire project. Before you even design a
floor plan, you need to secure a
substation and confirm the local grid
can actually deliver enough power. A
single modern hyperscale campus can
require hundreds of megawatts, roughly
the output of a small city. In many
major markets like Northern Virginia,
utilities now quote multi-year waits
just to get power delivered. That
waiting list alone can push a project
back 3 to 5 years before a single wall
goes up. And it's not just about whether
power exists, it's about whether the
utility will commit to it contractually.
Because a data center without a
guaranteed power allocation is legally
worthless the moment demand spikes
elsewhere. Land near major fiber routes
and substations commands a steep
premium, sometimes many multiples of
ordinary industrial land nearby. Push
further from those routes and land gets
cheaper, but now you've traded cash for
latency, and latency is the one thing
enterprise tenants will not accept. Now,
here's where it gets genuinely
expensive. Say you've secured land and
locked in a power agreement. Building an
actual data center is nothing like
building a warehouse, and the price tag
proves it instantly. Industry estimates
commonly put construction costs
somewhere between 7 and 12 million
dollars per megawatt of critical IT
capacity, depending on redundancy level
and region. A modest 10 megawatt
facility, small by hyperscale standards,
can run well past 100 million dollars
before a single server is racked. Push
into a large hyperscale campus north of
100 megawatts, and total development
costs can climb past 1 billion dollars.
And that's before a single specialty
system gets added. Redundant power
infrastructure, the uninterruptible
power supplies and backup generators,
alone can add tens of millions of
dollars. Precision cooling systems,
whether traditional chillers or newer
liquid cooling for AI workloads, add
tens of millions more. Fire suppression
systems designed specifically for
electrical fires, raised flooring,
biometric security, and seismic bracing
in earthquake zones are none of them
optional. On top of the physical build,
you budget for network fiber
connectivity, generator fuel storage
compliant with environmental
regulations, and engineering fees that
commonly eat another 15 to 20% project
cost. On a $200 million bill, that's
another $30 million that rarely shows up
in the headline number people quote each
other.
One real pattern shows up constantly
across this industry. A developer locks
in a construction budget, then spends 18
months securing permits and utility
approvals.
During that window, steel prices move,
generator lead time stretch past 2 years
amid global supply shortages, and
transformer costs climb sharply due to
demand from renewable energy projects
competing for the same components.
That gap doesn't come from
mismanagement. It comes from something
far more ordinary. The years it takes to
plan a data center are years in which
materials, labor, and equipment simply
don't sit still.
So, here's the first trap. The number in
your head when you decide to build is
never the number you actually pay.
Construction costs across the industrial
sector have climbed sharply over the
past several years nationally, and

metadata.title: Stargate’s $1 Land Option: Who Pays for the $15 Billion Build?
metadata.author: Systems Leverage
metadata.shortDescription:
A Texas ground lease gives one Stargate project company a $1 option to buy the land under the first two buildings starting in 2039. Follow the documents behind that clause, the construction financing, and what the Abilene build means for neighbors, businesses, and taxpayers.

The $1 is an option price. The $15 billion figure is the announced eight-building venture. This investigation separates the commitments on paper from the money and jobs local records can verify.

Sources
SEC exhibit, Abilene DC 1 financial statements: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1944366/000194436626000020/exhibit993-2025abelinedc1l.htm
Initial financing: https://www.nmrk.com/insights/press-releases/newmark-arranges-2-3-billion-construction-financing-for-206-mw-build-to-suit-data-center
Phase two financing: https://www.nmrk.com/insights/press-releases/newmark-facilitates-7-1-billion-construction-loan-to-develop-ai-data-center
City of Abilene tax abatement records: https://abilenetx.gov/2476/Tax-Abatements
WTOC local reporting and interview excerpts: https://www.wtoc.com/2026/10/26/ai-next-door-what-abilene-learned-living-by-stargate-what-effingham-could-see/

Reporting through November 20, 2026. AI tools assisted production. Thumbnail is an editorial treatment.

#Stargate #AIInfrastructure #SystemsLeverage

metadata.author: Ryne Ogren
metadata.shortDescription:
What is a substation and why are they important for data centers? In this video I breakdown one of the major bottlenecks in the data center development industry. If you found value, please like and subscribe!

🔗 Learn more: https://prrpartners.com

If you're new to my channel, my name is Ryne Ogren. I'm a partner at PRR Partners, where we specialize in power infrastructure and data center development. We help landowners, developers, and utilities navigate complex data center deals from site selection to power procurement to capital formation.

How I got here…

Started as a private equity investor acquiring marketing agencies. That's where I learned how to structure deals and market effectively.

Got involved in a commercial real estate deal that turned into a data center project. That's when everything changed. I saw the massive opportunity in the intersection of real estate, power infrastructure, and technology.
Pivoted to focus exclusively on data center development and power infrastructure.

Founded PRR Partners to help others navigate this complex industry. We're dealmakers. We put sites under control, assemble partnerships, connect the dots, and get deals done.

Today: PRR Partners is a multi faceted firm. We do site selection, interconnect strategy, power generation strategy, due diligence, capital formation, and partner introductions. Sometimes we consult. Sometimes we take equity positions. Sometimes we assemble the entire deal. 

Our reputation in the industry is growing exponentially, and we're helping more landowners and developers capitalize on the data center boom every day.

The data center industry is a $300+ billion market. Understanding who the players are and how they make money is the first step to positioning yourself in it.

To all the landowners, developers, and dealmakers out there: you're in the middle of writing your own story. The bigger the challenge, the more epic the outcome.

You either get an epic deal or an epic lesson. Both mean you win.

Keep crushing. May your deals be greater than your obstacles.

Never quit,
Ryne

The information shared here is not a guarantee of success. Your results may vary.

What is PUE in a data center? This visual guide to Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) shows how two AI data centers can run the same 100 MW IT load while one draws 30 MW less from the grid.

PUE = total data center energy ÷ IT equipment energy, measured over the same period. A PUE of 1.50 means 0.50 kWh of overhead for every 1 kWh used by IT. At 1.20, that drops to 0.20 kWh.

• Same IT load: At a steady 100 MW of IT, a PUE of 1.50 means 150 MW at the meter. At 1.20, it means 120 MW. If that 30 MW gap holds for a year at US$0.10/kWh, that’s US$26.28 million less in energy charges, before upgrade costs.
• Same site power limit: Under a fixed 150 MW site limit, the potential IT power budget rises from 100 to 125 MW. That assumes the lower PUE holds at the higher load and the cooling and electrical systems can support it at peak conditions.

See how cooling, fans, pumps, and power conversion losses affect facility overhead. Pair PUE with energy per useful computing task to judge how efficiently the racks do work.

CHAPTERS
00:00 Same IT load, different grid draw
00:31 What PUE measures and how to calculate it
00:59 Same IT load, lower electricity costs
01:34 Same site power limit, more room for IT
02:00 Where to reduce cooling and power losses
02:23 A lower bill, more racks, or both

https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLYmfSHo5dsrE

Previous episode — Why AI Data Centers Are Moving to 800 VDC:

https://www.iso.org/standard/30134-2

metadata.title: AI Without New Data Centers?
metadata.author: Founders Explain The World
metadata.shortDescription:
Rodrigo Liang, co-founder and CEO of SambaNova, explains how AI inference — our biggest use case today — can run in existing data centers. Drawing from 30 years in chip design and nearly a decade leading SambaNova, Liang explains how their Reconfigurable Dataflow Unit (RDU) chips and racks can cut AI inference costs by 10x. And they can be installed in existing data centers, so we don’t have to build so many new ones. Liang's dream is for every person in every country to be able to access and get the full benefits from using AI, and he says that can only happen if we bring the cost and energy use down. 

See this episode's accompanying Substack post here: https://dynamoinyourinbox.substack.com/p/the-11-billion-chip-company-betting 

Editor's Note: This interview was recorded on October 22, 2026.

metadata.title: How Modular Manufacturing Accelerates Data Center Deployment | Hyper
metadata.author: JSA TV: Tech & Telecom News
metadata.shortDescription:
For AI and hyperscale data center projects, securing powered land is only part of the challenge. Once power is available, the focus quickly shifts to how fast new capacity can be built, commissioned and generating revenue.

At YOTTA 2026, JSA TV spoke with Matt Caldwell, Director of AI & Hyperscale] at Hyper, about how modular, prefabricated construction can accelerate data center deployment without compromising quality.

Matt explains how Hyper’s model provides dedicated manufacturing capacity for hyperscale, colocation and neocloud developers, helping reduce competition for traditional manufacturing slots while supporting development across large-scale campuses. He also discusses how repeatable factory processes, trained labor and quality assurance can improve both deployment speed and reliability.

#JSATV #YOTTA2026 #DataCenters #AIInfrastructure #Hyperscale #ModularConstruction #DigitalInfrastructure

With billions of people and tens of billions of devices online today, there’s never been a bigger need for computing infrastructure and data facilities.

Hyperscale Data Centers: The Way of the Future

With billions of people and tens of billions of devices online today, there’s never been a bigger need for computing infrastructure and data centers. What’s paving the way for companies to scale operations faster than ever before? Hyperscale data centers.

What Is a Hyperscale Data Center?

A data center is a building that houses an organization's servers and IT equipment. A private, or enterprise data center serve strictly as a resource for the businesses that own them. A multi-tenant, or colocation data center is used as a means of providing infrastructure services to the public.

When people refer to hyperscale data centers, they are usually referring to both the customer and the size of the facility. Tag Greason, Chief Hyperscale Officer at QTS, defines hyperscale companies as those that build or lease 20+ MW at once or expand to that level over time in 1–3 MW increments. Only a small number of companies make these large commitments—primarily cloud service providers like Amazon (AWS), Microsoft (Azure), Facebook, and Google (GCP). Several dozen others, including SaaS companies such as SAP, Salesforce, Workday, Uber, Lyft, and Twitter, may grow into the 15–20 MW range over time.

A hyperscale data center is either built by a hyperscale company or designed specifically to meet one’s needs, often in partnership during the pre-leasing process.

The Rise of Hyperscale

As our world becomes increasingly technological and the demand for storage and compute services has grown, so has the need for facilities to handle these needs. 

Two trends have driven the need to large-scale IT infrastructure. When cloud computing platforms began to emerge in the late 2000s, they acted as demand aggregators for businesses who were looking to convert their on-premises IT workloads. Cloud platforms allow users to provision resources and scale quickly, often remotely and near-instantaneously. And the companies who provide these services could then forecast future growth and “buy in bulk” to meet that demand. 

Additionally, the rapid rise of SaaS, streaming, and social media further drives growth in the industry. All three of these types of companies need massive amounts of storage, compute, and bandwidth to meet their customers needs. 

Who Are the Hyperscale Users?

There are now three times as many large-scale data centers being operated by hyperscale providers as there were in 2013. And it’s not hard to imagine which companies might be at the top of that list.

Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and IBM all have hyperscale data centers in every major region of the world, and other top players like Facebook, Apple, Oracle, and Chinese cloud giant Alibaba aren’t far behind. These A-listers can take down over 70 megawatts and hundreds of thousands of square feet at a time.

Next in line are companies with lower present requirements, but who still want the ability to grow a few megawatts at a time. Among their ranks are companies like Salesforce, SAP, Dropbox, Twitter, Uber, and Lyft.

Hyperscale Over Colocation?

As noted above, the largest consumers of data centers all employ a build and lease strategy. This is dependent on many factors, such as timing, cost, future needs, and others. These colocation providers have become increasingly creative in pursuing hyperscale companies, ranging from basically being the development arm for them to designing to their specifications or delivering just a powered shell and letting the user provide the internal equipment.

metadata.title: How Hyperscale Data Centers Work – The Factories Of The Digital World.
metadata.author: Mini Leviathan
metadata.shortDescription:
How Hyperscale Data Centers Work Explained Simply.

Learn how hyperscale data centers use thousands of servers, advanced networking systems, massive power infrastructure, and automation technology to support cloud computing and AI services.

This video explains hyperscale facilities, cloud computing, data centers, server infrastructure, networking technology, internet services, AI computing, distributed systems, and modern digital infrastructure in a clear beginner-friendly way.

Discover how some of the world's largest computing facilities power the internet, streaming services, artificial intelligence, and cloud platforms.

A calm and easy-to-understand breakdown of hyperscale data center technology and large-scale computing systems.

@MiniLeviathanVideos 

how hyperscale data centers work, hyperscale data centers explained, cloud computing explained, data centers explained, server infrastructure explained, distributed computing explained, internet infrastructure explained, networking technology explained, ai computing explained, cloud platforms explained, digital infrastructure explained, server farms explained, tech explained, modern computing explained, hyperscale facilities.

segments.text: How hyperscale data centers work.
Every time you stream a movie, save a
photo to the cloud, ask an AI a
question, or send an email, something
happens behind the scenes.
A computer somewhere processes that
request.
Now imagine serving not one person,
not 1,000 people,
but millions of people simultaneously.
That requires an extraordinary amount of
computing infrastructure.
This is where hyperscale data centers
come in.
These facilities are among the largest
and most powerful computing environments
ever built.
So today we're going to explore how
hyperscale data centers work.
Chapter one, what makes a data center
hyperscale? A data center is simply a
building that houses computing
equipment. A hyperscale data center
takes that concept to a much larger
scale.
These facilities often contain tens of
thousands of servers,
sometimes even hundreds of thousands.
They are designed to support massive
cloud services, AI workloads, video
streaming platforms, social networks,
and enterprise applications.
Scale is the defining characteristic.
Everything is built to handle enormous
demand.
Chapter two, rows and rows of servers.
Inside a hyperscale facility, servers
are organized into racks.
Each rack contains multiple computers.
The servers perform different tasks.
Some store data.
Some process applications.
Others handle networking or AI
workloads.
Together, they function as a giant
distributed computing system.
Instead of relying on one powerful
machine, the workload is spread across
thousands of smaller systems.
Chapter 3, networking at massive scale.
Moving data is just as important as
processing it.
Hyperscale facilities contain extensive
networking infrastructure.
Switches,
routers,
fiber optic connections,
and specialized networking hardware.
Data must travel rapidly between
servers.
If networking becomes a bottleneck,
performance suffers.
As a result, networking is often one of
the most critical parts of the entire
facility.
Chapter 4, power and cooling.
Computers consume electricity.
Lots of electricity.
A hyperscale facility may use as much
power as a small town.
Reliable electrical infrastructure is
essential.
Power distribution systems deliver
electricity throughout the building.
Backup generators and battery systems
provide redundancy.
Cooling systems remove heat generated by
the equipment.
Without cooling, servers would quickly
overheat.
And computers generally perform best
when they are not attempting to become
space heaters.
Chapter 5, automation and efficiency.
Managing thousands of servers manually
would be nearly impossible.
Automation software monitors hardware
health, allocates workloads, and
responds to failures.
If a server stops working, other systems
can often take over automatically.
The goal is maintaining reliability
while operating at enormous scale.
This combination of automation,
computing power, networking, and
infrastructure makes hyperscale
facilities possible.
To wrap up,
hyperscale data centers work by
combining massive numbers of servers,
advanced networking systems, reliable
power infrastructure, and sophisticated
automation.
These facilities provide the computing
resources behind many of the digital
services people use every day.
Together, they form a critical part of
modern internet infrastructure.
This has been a Mini Leviathan
production. If you enjoyed it, check out
our other videos. See you in the next
one.

metadata.title: Behind-the-meter electricity: what does it mean?
metadata.author: Modo Energy
metadata.shortDescription:
Imagine your energy meter sits on your front door - everything behind the door (in your house or your business or building or community) is 'behind-the-meter' energy. It can be used onsite without passing through the meter. Traditionally, this meant stuff you could switch on and off - kettles, TVs, etc. - but as our energy system becomes increasingly decentralised, it also refers to stuff like domestic solar panels and battery energy storage systems.

Head to https://modo.energy/ to find out more.

metadata.title: The 5-Year Queue Behind Your Chatbot
metadata.author: THE PHYSICAL LAYER
metadata.shortDescription:
Your chatbot answers in seconds. The power plants that could run it wait for years. This is the queue standing between new electricity demand and new electricity supply.

A chatbot can answer in seconds, but the electricity behind it cannot be switched on that quickly. Before a new power plant can send power to the grid, it must join a queue, be studied, and reach an interconnection agreement — a process that now takes years.

At the end of 2025, about 8,200 generation and storage projects were actively seeking a grid connection, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Queued Up: 2026 Edition. Together they requested about 2,061 GW — 1,312 GW of generation plus about 749 GW of storage. The queue shrank about 10 percent, mainly through withdrawals, from a peak near 2,600 GW at the end of 2023. About 549 GW has a draft or signed interconnection agreement but is not yet operating.

The wait is long, and most of the queue never gets built. The median project built in 2025 spent more than five years from request to operation (regions with available data). Of the capacity requested in 2000-2020, only 13 percent was operating by the end of 2025, about 75 percent had been withdrawn, and 10 percent was still active.

Demand is not waiting. US data centres used 176 TWh in 2023 (4.4 percent), up from 58 TWh in 2014. DOE/LBNL modelled 325-580 TWh by 2028 — a projection, not a measurement. FERC Order 2023 reform is under way, but it is too early to measure its full impact.

Note on visuals: visuals are photorealistic AI-generated images with cinematic motion, not photos of real power plants, substations or control rooms. Charts/diagrams are labelled schematics. Where a figure is a projection, the video says so.

- US DOE / LBNL 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (primary)
- FERC Order No. 2023
- 61-month median verified 12 Nov 2026 against the primary LBNL slide deck, valid in-service date for only 73 percent of operational projects

instant, weightless, like it comes from
nowhere.

to deliver electricity every second of
every day. Here's the problem nobody
sees. The computers are getting faster,
and the demand for electricity is rising
fast, but the new power plants that
could meet that demand are not arriving
fast at all.

watt, it has to wait in line in the
United States now for years.

queue, the waiting list for the American

precise because this is where most
explanations go wrong. The

Data centers connect through a separate

different. It is the list of power
plants and storage projects that want to

grid. Here's how it works in simplified
form.
A developer proposes a solar farm, a
wind farm, a gas plant, or a battery
project.
Before it can be built and connected,
the grid operator has to study it.
Will the local lines cope with the extra
power?
What upgrades are needed? A new
substation, a re-conducted line, a
transformer?
And who pays for those upgrades? Until
the studies are done and an agreement is
signed, the project waits. Across more
than 50 grid operators, that waiting
list is the interconnection queue. So
when you hear a huge number for the
queue, remember what it counts, proposed
generation and storage, not operating
power plants and not data centers
themselves. At the end of 2025, about
8,200 projects were actively seeking a
grid connection in the United States,
according to Lawrence Berkeley National
Laboratory's queued up 2026 edition
published in May 2026. Together, those
represented 1,312
gigawatts of generation and about 749
gigawatts of storage. Added together,
that is about 2,061
gigawatts of requested capacity. The
queue shrank about 10% on the year
before, mainly through withdrawals, not
building, from a peak near 2,600
gigawatts at the end of 2023.
What is in the queue has also changed.
Solar is still the largest single share
at 773 gigawatts, but that is down 19%
on the year before.
Storage is 749 gigawatts, down 16%
Wind is 220 gigawatts, down 19%
Natural gas, by contrast, rose sharply,
up 86% to 253 gigawatts.
One more number matters. About 549
gigawatts of capacity already has a
draft or signed interconnection
agreement, but has still not reached
commercial operation.
That includes 256 gigawatts of solar,
161 gigawatts of storage, 76 gigawatts
of wind, and 45 gigawatts of gas. So why
does a study take years?
Because the grid is a shared machine and
every new connection changes it for
everyone else. First, the studies
themselves are complex. An operator has
to model what happens when a new plant
injects power at a particular point
under normal conditions and under fault
conditions.
Second, the upgrades are physical.
A study might conclude that a line needs
to be rebuilt, a substation expanded, or
transformer replaced.
They are steel, copper, concrete, and
long manufacturing lead times, a subject
for video four on the transformer
weight.
Third, the old process studied projects
one by one in the order they arrived.
That meant a single slow or speculative
project could hold up the projects
behind it.

studying projects that would never be
built. The result in Berkeley Lab's own
summary is stark.

operation.

and it has roughly doubled since the
early 2000s, even as the technology
being connected has got cheaper and

second surprise.

power plant. Berkeley Lab found that of
the capacity that submitted
interconnection requests from 2000 to
2020, only 13% had reached commercial
operation by the end of 2025.

was still active. That does not mean the
queue number is fake. It is not a
forecast. Developers submit more

hold a place in line, test several
sites, or because a study may reveal an
expensive upgrade.

shrinks, part of why it fell in 2025.

future supply. It is a pipeline with a
very high dropout rate, not a warehouse
waiting to be switched on. That dropout
rate also makes the system harder to
plan. Grid operators have to study a
large number of speculative projects to

actually be built, and that study
workload is itself part of the delay.

careful about what it claims. Its 2026
edition notes that FERC order 2023 and

implemented, that these are important
measures to reduce bottlenecks, and that

queue to clear. A United States
Department of Energy report produced by

the United States used 176 terawatt
hours of electricity in 2023, about 4.4%
of total electricity in the United
States,

plants to wires and the wires to each
other.

your local grid, and your chatbot are

years ago.

supply can connect, existing capacity

sharper.

worth watching correctly.

number.

much has actually been built? And how

agreement but not operating. 13% built
from two decades of requests and more
than five years for the typical project
that made it through. The chatbot will
keep answering in seconds. The question

can keep up. And right now, the queue
says it is struggling to. So next time
an answer appears instantly, remember
the line behind it. Power plants and
batteries waiting for studies, upgrades,
and agreements while demand keeps
rising. That line, generation to study
to upgrade to grid is the physical
layer. In the next video, we follow the
queue to its most physical bottleneck,
the transformer, the quiet box of steel
and copper that every new connection
needs and why waiting for one can now
take years.

metadata.title: Waiting for Power  Why New Electricity Gets Stuck Before It Reaches the Grid
metadata.author: The Pharos Project
metadata.shortDescription:
More than 2,500 gigawatts of new power plants, large power users and batteries are stalled in grid connection queues worldwide, according to the International Energy Agency. In the United States, the median project that was built in 2025 waited 61 months between asking to connect and switching on. Most of the capacity in line never gets built.

In this deep dive, we ask why connecting new electricity generation and storage to the grid takes so long, in so many countries. We follow a project through the interconnection queue (studies, upgrade costs, and withdrawals that force other projects to be studied again), compare how long the wires take with how long the plants take, and look at fixes in the United States, Germany and Great Britain, whether they are working, and the strongest case for caution. Then we look at three ways ordinary people can contribute, with the evidence and the limits for each.

Early access to each episode and its research brief: https://www.patreon.com/ThePharosProject

segments.text: At the end of 2025, about 2,61 gawatts
of generation and storage capacity were
actively seeking a connection to the
electric grid in the United States. Most
people assume that building new power
capacity is a matter of manufacturing
solar panels, assembling wind turbines,
or installing batteries. But when a
developer finishes planning a facility,
they cannot simply plug it in and send
electricity to consumers.
Instead, they enter an interconnection
queue where projects wait for years
while grid operators run technical
studies. The shortage is not only in
power plants. It is in the wires and in
the process of connecting to them. So,
why does connecting new electricity
generation and storage to the grid take
so long in so many countries? The
International Energy AY's electricity
2026 report forecasts that global
electricity demand will grow by an
average of 3.6% 6% a year through 2030
at least two and a half times as fast as
overall energy demand and the agency
names grid capacity as a critical
bottleneck. To see why, you have to look
at the gate where new power meets the
existing grid.
Start with how long the wait is. In the
United States, the median time from an
interconnection request to a signed
interconnection agreement was 45 months
That is nearly 4 years. and a signature
is not the finish line. The median
project that was actually built in 2025
took 61 months from request to
commercial operation.
In 2015, that took 36 months. In 2008,
22 months. Most requests never get that
far. Of the capacity requested between
2000 and 2020, about 13% had come online
by the end of 2025 and 75% had been
withdrawn.
Lawrence Barkley National Laboratory,
which tracks these cues, reports that
withdrawal rates exceed 40% even after a
developer signs an interconnection
agreement. So, the wait is long and so
is the list of projects that give up
along the way. You might expect this to
be a problem for one kind of energy. It
is not. In 2025, ceued natural gas
capacity in the United States rose 86%
to 253 gawatt, while ceued solar,
storage, and wind each fell by 16 to
Every kind of generator is in the same
line. The total American queue fell 10%
from 2024, and it sits below its peak of
nearly 2600 gawatt at the end of 2023.
Over 750 gawatts of capacity withdrew in
2025 by Barclay Labs estimate.
Worldwide, the International Energy
Agency reports that more than 2500
gawatt of renewable large load and
storage projects are stalled in grid
connection cues. A smaller American
queue sounds like progress. But why did
it shrink and did anything get connected
faster? We will come back to that.
First, what happens between applying and
signing? When a developer applies, the
grid operator runs a series of
interconnection studies. The studies
establish what new transmission
equipment or upgrades may be needed, and
then they assign the cost of that
equipment. Only then can the developer
sign an interconnection agreement, which
is effectively a contract between the
developer and the transmission provider.
Who pays for the upgrades depends on
where you are. In the mid-continent
independent system operator, PJM
interconnection ISO New England, the New
York ISO, and the Southwest Power Pool,
the generator pays for network upgrades.
The California ISO uses a crediting
approach. In Texas, under a connect and
manage approach, generators do not pay
for network upgrades.
Now, follow the money. Barkley Lab
reports that limited available
transmission capacity has resulted in
high interconnection upgrade costs which
contributes to high withdrawals and may
deter developers from submitting new
requests. Separately, when a project
withdraws late in the process, it can
trigger resties for other projects in
the queue, increasing delays. Later
stage withdrawals can also lengthen
study durations.
Put the two together and you get what
looks like a loop. That is our reading,
not Barkley Labs. High costs push
projects out and a late exit can reopen
the studies of the projects that stay.
Underneath the loop is a mismatch in
speed. The wires take longer than the
plants they serve. The International
Energy Agency says that planning,
permitting, and completing new grid
infrastructure can take anywhere from 5
to 15 years. Solar and wind projects
take 1 to 5 years and data centers 1 to
three. The agency also says that grid
investment has lagged well behind
investment in generation capacity and
that many power systems already face
rising curtailment caused by congestion.
To meet demand through 2030, it says
annual grid investment would need to
rise by about 50% from today's $400
billion.
In the United States, regulators have
tried to fix the process itself. On July
28th, 2023, the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission issued order
number 2023.
The commission said that under the old
process, customers had an incentive to
submit speculative interconnection
requests that contribute to
interconnection study backlogs. The
order replaces studying requests one at
a time in the order they arrive with a
first ready, first served cluster study
process where groups of projects are
studied together. Developers must show
90% site control when they apply and
must post deposits that rise toward 20%
of their estimated network upgrade
costs. A developer that withdraws can
face a penalty that grows as the project
advances, reaching 20% of its network
upgrade cost once it has signed, with
certain exceptions.
And the transmission providers face
penalties of their own, $1,000 for each
business day they miss a cluster study
deadline up to a cap once the new rules
phase in. Did it work? The evidence so
far is mixed and it is mostly about the
size of the queue, not its speed.
Barkley Lab lists several reasons the
American Q shrank in 2025.
Most balancing areas have moved to
cluster studies. Higher deposits and
withdrawal penalties came in. Several
grid operators paused or capped new
requests. ISO New England and the New
York ISO accepted none in 2025. And the
mid-continent operator capped total Q
capacity. High upgrade costs and the
looming expiration of federal tax
credits may also have pushed developers
to cancel. So, a smaller queue is partly
a sign of reform and partly a sign that
the door was closed for a while. The
median weight for an interconnection
agreement, meanwhile, increased to 45
months. A June 2026 review of seven grid
operators by the firm Grid Strategies
found that all seven regions have made
meaningful progress in the last 18
months. Progress though is not the same
as speed. Some grid operators have
responded by building a fast lane. In
May 2025, PJM Interconnection selected
51 projects out of 94 applications for a
one-time fast track that it described as
an opportunity for shovel ready
resources. The 51 projects total about
11.8 gawatt of selected capacity or
about 9.4 gawatt counted as unforced
capacity. By our arithmetic from PJM's
figures, about 69% of the selected
capacity is natural gas, 19% is battery
storage, and 12% is nuclear. PJM expects
90% of them to be running by 2030 and
all of them by 2031.
A fast lane solves the problem for the
projects inside it. But it raises a new
question. Who gets in? Is this only an
American problem? No. In Germany,
network operators received 9,710
applications in 2024 to connect battery
storage at medium voltage level and
above, together totaling about 400 gaw.
By contrast, the AY's November 2025
report counts 921 battery storage
facilities connected with about 2.3
gawatt of netrated capacity. Germany's
Bundisnet Sagger cautions that not all
projects will necessarily be
implemented.
In Great Britain, the National Energy
System operator reported that the old
queue held more than 700 gawatts of
generation and storage projects.
After a reform approved by the
regulatory in April 2025, the operators
reformed Q published in December holds
283 gawatt of generation and storage
plus 99 gaw of transmission connected
demand.
Q rules differ from country to country,
including who pays for upgrades,
but the pattern is similar. Far more
projects are to connect than are
connected.
It is worth being clear about what these
numbers do and do not show. First, Q
figures measure requests, not
construction.
Barkley Lab says that most of the
proposed capacity will not be built and

Most people assume that building new power capacity is a matter of manufacturing solar panels, assembling wind turbines, or installing batteries. But when a developer finishes planning a facility, they cannot simply plug it in and send electricity to consumers. Instead, they enter an interconnection queue where projects wait for years while grid operators run technical studies. The shortage is not only in power plants. It is in the wires and in the process of connecting to them. So, why does connecting new electricity generation and storage to the grid take so long in so many countries? The International Energy AY's electricity 2026 report forecasts that global electricity demand will grow by an average of 3.6% 6% a year through 2030 at least two and a half times as fast as overall energy demand and the agency names grid capacity as a critical bottleneck. To see why, you have to look at the gate where new power meets the existing grid. Start with how long the wait is. In the United States, the median time from an interconnection request to a signed interconnection agreement was 45 months in 2025. That is nearly 4 years. and a signature is not the finish line. The median project that was actually built in 2025 took 61 months from request to commercial operation. In 2015, that took 36 months. In 2008, 22 months. Most requests never get that far. Of the capacity requested between 2000 and 2020, about 13% had come online by the end of 2025 and 75% had been withdrawn. Lawrence Barkley National Laboratory, which tracks these cues, reports that withdrawal rates exceed 40% even after a developer signs an interconnection agreement. So, the wait is long and so is the list of projects that give up along the way. You might expect this to be a problem for one kind of energy. It is not. In 2025, ceued natural gas capacity in the United States rose 86% to 253 gawatt, while ceued solar, storage, and wind each fell by 16 to 19%. Every kind of generator is in the same line. The total American queue fell 10% from 2024, and it sits below its peak of nearly 2600 gawatt at the end of 2023. Over 750 gawatts of capacity withdrew in 2025 by Barclay Labs estimate. Worldwide, the International Energy Agency reports that more than 2500 gawatt of renewable large load and storage projects are stalled in grid connection cues. A smaller American queue sounds like progress. But why did it shrink and did anything get connected faster? We will come back to that. First, what happens between applying and signing? When a developer applies, the grid operator runs a series of interconnection studies. The studies establish what new transmission equipment or upgrades may be needed, and then they assign the cost of that equipment. Only then can the developer sign an interconnection agreement, which is effectively a contract between the developer and the transmission provider. Who pays for the upgrades depends on where you are. In the mid-continent independent system operator, PJM interconnection ISO New England, the New York ISO, and the Southwest Power Pool, the generator pays for network upgrades. The California ISO uses a crediting approach. In Texas, under a connect and manage approach, generators do not pay for network upgrades. Now, follow the money. Separately, when a project withdraws late in the process, it can trigger resties for other projects in the queue, increasing delays. Later stage withdrawals can also lengthen study durations. metadata.title: NERC Compliance Engineering: Reliability Standards, IBR Requirements & Power System Compliance
metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
NERC compliance is becoming increasingly important for electric utilities, renewable energy developers, solar and wind power plants, battery energy storage systems (BESS), transmission owners, and large-load facilities.

Explore the engineering behind NERC Reliability Standards and compliance requirements, explaining how power system engineering, protection systems, inverter-based resources (IBRs), grid reliability, and technical documentation contribute to a successful compliance program.

Following FERC Order No. 901, new and revised NERC requirements are bringing greater attention to inverter-based resource performance, disturbance monitoring, ride-through capabilities, model validation, and unexpected event mitigation.


Why NERC Compliance Engineering Matters

NERC compliance is not just about maintaining documentation. It requires technically accurate engineering studies, validated simulation models, properly configured protection systems, inverter performance verification, disturbance monitoring, and reliable compliance evidence.

Keentel Engineering supports clients with NERC compliance assessments, power system studies, protection and control engineering, EMT/PSCAD modeling, model validation, renewable energy integration, and transmission and substation engineering.


Who Should Watch This Video?

Electrical and power systems engineers

NERC compliance managers and consultants

Solar and wind energy developers

Battery energy storage system (BESS) developers

Generator Owners (GO) and Generator Operators (GOP)

Transmission Owners and Transmission Planners

Electric utilities and distribution providers

Data center and large-load developers

Renewable energy investors and project owners


Explore our engineering expertise in power system studies, grid interconnection, renewable energy, transmission and substation design, protection systems, and NERC compliance.

reality. It's a technical architecture
for three groups, generator owners,
transmission operators, and large loads.
All three are working through FERC order
901 and the new category two
registrations.
The presentation comes from Kinetel
Engineering, a power system engineering
firm working from 4 kV all the way up to
kV.
The central idea is that this new
compliance world is at its core an
engineering problem, not a paperwork
problem.
Let's start with why. Think of the RSAW,
the Reliability Standard Audit Worksheet
as an iceberg.
Above the water line is what most people
see, paperwork, timelines, and
attestations.
That's the visible part of compliance.
Below the water line is where the real
work lives, and it's far bigger.
We call it compliance engineering, and
it has five major pieces.
First, EMT models built in PSCAD,
detailed inverter simulation, grid
interaction analysis, and critical
transient data.
Second, short circuit studies,
two-phase and ground fault calculations
and fault contribution levels.
Third, relay coordination under PRC-27,
setting verification, selectivity
studies, protection zones, and the risk
of misoperation.
Fourth, PSMP databases under PRC-005,
maintenance records, testing histories,
and asset inventories where data gaps
are the main risk.
And fifth, high resolution event data,
oscillography, sequence of events, PMU
integration, and root cause evidence.
The call out at the top right sums it
up. Most audit findings are evidence
failures, not engineering failures.
And the evidence that makes a program
defensible is engineering evidence.
Here how we got here in four steps.
In October 2023, FERC order 901 directed
NERC to develop reliability standards
for inverter-based resources or IBRs.
In February 2025, FERC approved PRC
covering disturbance monitoring and PRC
covering unexpected event mitigation.
In July 2025, FERC order 909 approved
the IBR ride-through standard along with
PRC
And in October 2025, the NERC board
adopted MOD 032-2,
the modeling data standard which now
includes distributed energy resources.
The warning box at the bottom is the key
message. The impact lands entirely on
engineering. A ride-through requirement
is met by inverter settings. A model
validation requirement is met by EMT
simulations.
And thousands of megawatts of smaller
solar, wind, and battery plants are now
effectively bulk electric system
entities. The first question is whether
you're even in scope.
This funnel walks through the category
two decision.
Start with a non-BES inverter-based
resource, solar, wind, or battery.
Question one.
Is the aggregate nameplate capacity 20
megavolt amperes or more?
If not, you're unregistered, but you
should monitor for expansion.
If yes, question two.
Is the common point of interconnection
60 kilovolts or higher?
If not, you're still unregistered.
If both answers are yes, the alert
applies.
Category two registration is required.
Now look at the worked example on the
right because it shows the trap.
Site B is an 18 megavolt ampere solar
plant at a 115 kilovolt point of
interconnection. Today, it's not
registered.
Then someone adds a 4 megavolt ampere
battery behind the same transformer.
The aggregate jumps to 22 and the plant
instantly crosses the threshold into
strict compliance.
A modest capacity addition changes your
regulatory status overnight. Once you
know you're registered, the next
question is which standards apply to
you. This matrix maps roles to
standards.
Under protection, PRC-019,
and PRC-025
and PRC-027
apply to both generator owners and
transmission owners. Under ride through,
PRC-024
and PRC-029
apply to generator owners. Under
monitoring, PRC-028
and PRC-03 also apply to generator
owners. And under modeling, MOD-026
and MOD-032 apply to generator owners
and planning coordinators.
For large loads, modeling is flagged as
an emerging requirement. We'll come back
to that. The takeaway is at the bottom.
Applicability is the first engineering
decision.
A wrong BES or category two
determination undermines the entire
operational architecture.
Now we get into the standards
themselves, starting with PRC-019-2,
which I like to call the limiter versus
relay race. The chart plots reactive
power against active power. The blue
region is the plant's controller or
limiter boundary. For example, an
underexcitation limiter.
The orange band outside it is the
protective relay trip zone. For example,
a loss of field relay.
The engineering rule is simple to state.
The plant's internal limiters, meaning
controller reactive limits and inverter
current limits, must physically act
before the protective relays trip the
unit. The limiter has to shield the
relay trip zone.
The evidence required is a PQ or RX plot
proving that the limiters keep the unit
inside its capability so it doesn't
disconnect prematurely during system
stress.
Next is ride through.
On the left, the blue box is the NERC no
trip zone.
The orange line shows a plant's voltage
response over 3 seconds.
can see the failure point.
The inverter's undervoltage setting lets
the voltage dip into the restricted
zone, which is not allowed.
On the right, the comparison matrix
separates two standards that people
often confuse.
PRC-024
covers settings. It applies to
synchronous machines and type 1 and 2
wind, and it proves that protective
relays won't trip inside the boundary.
PRC-029 covers performance. It applies
to IBRs and proves that the plant
actually rides through.
That means accounting for inverter
firmware, momentary cessation, and phase
lock loop response.
One more point shown at the bottom.
When low voltage ride through becomes
high voltage ride through,
a plant that rides through a voltage dip
can still trip on the high voltage spike
that follows fault clearing.
You have to engineer for both halves of
the event. PRC-25-2
is about relay loadability. The picture
shows the path from the inverters
through the collector to the main
transformer and the point of
interconnection.
The threat is relays tripping heavily
loaded lines during stress conditions,
for example, field forcing after a
nearby fault, which can cause cascading
failures.
Here's the worked example.
A 230 megavolt ampere solar plant at 138
kilovolts has a rated current of 962
amps.
Attachment 1 requires the relay pickup
to exceed 130% of that, which is 1,251
amps.
A relay set at 1,100 amps fails, and it
must be raised.
And a warning, the most common PRC-25
problems are population errors, load
response of relays that were never
identified, auxiliary transformers that
were overlooked, or IBR collector relays
added after the original review.
The math is usually right. The inventory
is usually what's wrong. This slide
shows why monitoring resolution matters.
On the left is a 4-second SCADA
historian. It's marked non-compliant,
and you can see why. A 200-millisecond
voltage dip simply falls between the
samples and is missed entirely.
On the right is a PRC-028 dynamic
disturbance recorder, which captures
that same 200-millisecond fault event
accurately, waveform and all. Below the
triggers and the engineering reality. A
PRC-030 analysis is triggered by an
unexpected change in real power of 20 MW
or more and 10% or more of gross
nameplate within 4 seconds.
The engineering challenge is that a
PRC-030 root cause analysis is only as
good as the PRC-028 equipment that
captured the event. This leads to one of
the most practical ideas in the deck.
Build one data architecture, not one per
standard.
At the center is the PRC-028
high-resolution recorder architecture,
and it feeds three things.
PRC-030 gets the millisecond data needed
for 90-day root cause analyses and
corrective action plans.
MOD-026 gets real recorded disturbances
to benchmark and verify dynamic PSSE,
PSLF, and
and MOD-033 gives planning coordinators
dynamic comparisons to validate the
wider grid model.
The closing line says it well.
Architectural engineering is the only
defense against overlapping mandates.
Let's look at two real-world style case
studies. The first is an independent
power producer with four solar plants
between 22 and 60 MVA,
newly registered as a category two
generator owner and operator. The
diagnostic found two things. First, a 60
MVA plant that a planned 20 MVA ampere
storage addition would instantly push
into full BES status. Second, inverter
under-voltage stages with non-compliant
distribution-style short delays. The
root cause was that plant controllers
had no defined freeze or hold behavior
during faults, and there was no
high-resolution recording capable of
resolving 4-second output changes. The
delivered evidence had three parts,
facility applicability memos with
nameplate schedules, a ride-through
settings inventory screened against NERC
envelopes, and PRC-28 monitoring designs
with compliance calendars. The second
case involves a 200 megawatt 800
megawatt hour battery storage plant.
It was discharging at 160 megawatts
during a distant 345 kilovolt fault,
and its output collapsed to 95
megawatts.
That loss exceeded the PRC-030 threshold
of 20 megawatts.
21 of 52 power conversion systems
tripped on DC link over-voltage alarms
30 milliseconds after the fault cleared.
The root cause was in the plant
controller. It wound up during the
fault, then commanded maximum reactive
output on recovery.
That pushed terminal voltages higher,
which coincided with the DC link
overshoot and caused the trips.
The delivered evidence included a PSCAD
replication pinpointing the firmware
flaw
and a corrective action plan with an
extended controller freeze and revised
DC chopper settings.
It also included an updated MOD-026
verified model reflecting the fixed
settings. It's a good example of one
event flowing through monitoring, root
cause, and modeling. Now to the
frontier, which is large computational
loads such as data centers. The threat
is that large loads disconnecting
simultaneously after transmission faults
behave like large generators in reverse,
and that poses massive grid stability
risks. The engineering response is that
utilities now treat large data centers
as high impact loads and enforce
generation-like requirements.
The requirements include FAC 001 for
interconnection, FAC 002 and TPL 001 for
dynamic models and ride-through, and MOD
032 for load composition data. The
takeaway is that large load developers
must design for grid stability from day
one and prepare for imminent formal
registration criteria.
Here's how to put it all together as a
seven-step lifecycle centered on
accountable engineering.
Step one,
register in scope,
confirm BES or category two status and
map facility applicability.
Step two, assess gaps.
Compare existing models and settings to
RSAW requirements.
Step three, program design.
Write the PSMP, PRC 030 and MOD 032
procedures.
Step four, engineering. Perform the
loadability, coordination, and EMT
dynamic studies.
Step five, evidence. Package the data
strictly in RSAW order.
Step six, audit.
Conduct mock audits and train your

And step seven, sustain. Enforce

updates.
Then the loop closes. Step seven feeds
back to step one
because a plant addition, a firmware
update, or a settings change can reopen
the whole cycle.
It's continuous improvement. Under the
leadership of Sandeep Sunny R. Patel, an
IEEE senior member, Kental Engineering
brings three decades of battle-tested
expertise to the grid's most complex
challenges.
That comes down to three things.
Engineering-led compliance from 4 kV to

and FERC order 901 mandates,
and audit-ready evidence built by the
engineers running the studies.
Three decades, every side of the table,
one standard,
accountable engineering.
To reach the team, visit
www.keentelengineering.com,
or email contact@keentelengineering.com.
