In February 2025, FERC approved PRC 028-1 covering disturbance monitoring and PRC 030-1 covering unexpected event mitigation. In July 2025, FERC order 909 approved PRC 029-1, the IBR ride-through standard along with PRC And in October 2025, the NERC board adopted MOD 032-2, the modeling data standard which now includes distributed energy resources. The warning box at the bottom is the key message. The impact lands entirely on engineering. A ride-through requirement is met by inverter settings. A model validation requirement is met by EMT simulations. And thousands of megawatts of smaller solar, wind, and battery plants are now effectively bulk electric system entities. The first question is whether you're even in scope. This funnel walks through the category two decision. Start with a non-BES inverter-based resource, solar, wind, or battery. Question one. Is the aggregate nameplate capacity 20 megavolt amperes or more? If not, you're unregistered, but you should monitor for expansion. If yes, question two. Is the common point of interconnection 60 kilovolts or higher? If not, you're still unregistered. If both answers are yes, the alert applies. Category two registration is required. Now look at the worked example on the right because it shows the trap. Site B is an 18 megavolt ampere solar plant at a 115 kilovolt point of interconnection. Today, it's not registered. Then someone adds a 4 megavolt ampere battery behind the same transformer. The aggregate jumps to 22 and the plant instantly crosses the threshold into strict compliance. A modest capacity addition changes your regulatory status overnight. Once you know you're registered, the next question is which standards apply to you. This matrix maps roles to standards. Under protection, PRC-019, PRC-023, and PRC-025 and PRC-027 apply to both generator owners and transmission owners. Under ride through, PRC-024 and PRC-029 apply to generator owners. Under monitoring, PRC-028 and PRC-03 also apply to generator owners. And under modeling, MOD-026 and MOD-032 apply to generator owners and planning coordinators. For large loads, modeling is flagged as an emerging requirement. We'll come back to that. The takeaway is at the bottom. Applicability is the first engineering decision. A wrong BES or category two determination undermines the entire operational architecture. Now we get into the standards themselves, starting with PRC-019-2, which I like to call the limiter versus relay race. The chart plots reactive power against active power. The blue region is the plant's controller or limiter boundary. For example, an underexcitation limiter. The orange band outside it is the protective relay trip zone. For example, a loss of field relay. The engineering rule is simple to state. The plant's internal limiters, meaning controller reactive limits and inverter current limits, must physically act before the protective relays trip the unit. The limiter has to shield the relay trip zone. The evidence required is a PQ or RX plot proving that the limiters keep the unit inside its capability so it doesn't disconnect prematurely during system stress. Next is ride through. On the left, the blue box is the NERC no trip zone. The orange line shows a plant's voltage response over 3 seconds. can see the failure point. The inverter's undervoltage setting lets the voltage dip into the restricted zone, which is not allowed. On the right, the comparison matrix separates two standards that people often confuse. PRC-024 covers settings. It applies to synchronous machines and type 1 and 2 wind, and it proves that protective relays won't trip inside the boundary. PRC-029 covers performance. It applies to IBRs and proves that the plant actually rides through. That means accounting for inverter firmware, momentary cessation, and phase lock loop response. One more point shown at the bottom. When low voltage ride through becomes high voltage ride through, a plant that rides through a voltage dip can still trip on the high voltage spike that follows fault clearing. You have to engineer for both halves of the event. PRC-25-2 is about relay loadability. The picture shows the path from the inverters through the collector to the main transformer and the point of interconnection. The threat is relays tripping heavily loaded lines during stress conditions, for example, field forcing after a nearby fault, which can cause cascading failures. Here's the worked example. A 230 megavolt ampere solar plant at 138 kilovolts has a rated current of 962 amps. Attachment 1 requires the relay pickup to exceed 130% of that, which is 1,251 amps. A relay set at 1,100 amps fails, and it must be raised. And a warning, the most common PRC-25 problems are population errors, load response of relays that were never identified, auxiliary transformers that were overlooked, or IBR collector relays added after the original review. The math is usually right. The inventory is usually what's wrong. This slide shows why monitoring resolution matters. On the left is a 4-second SCADA historian. It's marked non-compliant, and you can see why. A 200-millisecond voltage dip simply falls between the samples and is missed entirely. On the right is a PRC-028 dynamic disturbance recorder, which captures that same 200-millisecond fault event accurately, waveform and all. Below the triggers and the engineering reality. A PRC-030 analysis is triggered by an unexpected change in real power of 20 MW or more and 10% or more of gross nameplate within 4 seconds. The engineering challenge is that a PRC-030 root cause analysis is only as good as the PRC-028 equipment that captured the event. This leads to one of the most practical ideas in the deck. Build one data architecture, not one per standard. At the center is the PRC-028 high-resolution recorder architecture, and it feeds three things. PRC-030 gets the millisecond data needed for 90-day root cause analyses and corrective action plans. MOD-026 gets real recorded disturbances to benchmark and verify dynamic PSSE, PSLF, and and MOD-033 gives planning coordinators dynamic comparisons to validate the wider grid model. The closing line says it well. Architectural engineering is the only defense against overlapping mandates. Let's look at two real-world style case studies. The first is an independent power producer with four solar plants between 22 and 60 MVA, newly registered as a category two generator owner and operator. The diagnostic found two things. First, a 60 MVA plant that a planned 20 MVA ampere storage addition would instantly push into full BES status. Second, inverter under-voltage stages with non-compliant distribution-style short delays. The root cause was that plant controllers had no defined freeze or hold behavior during faults, and there was no high-resolution recording capable of resolving 4-second output changes. The delivered evidence had three parts, facility applicability memos with nameplate schedules, a ride-through settings inventory screened against NERC envelopes, and PRC-28 monitoring designs with compliance calendars. The second case involves a 200 megawatt 800 megawatt hour battery storage plant. It was discharging at 160 megawatts during a distant 345 kilovolt fault, and its output collapsed to 95 megawatts. That loss exceeded the PRC-030 threshold of 20 megawatts. 21 of 52 power conversion systems tripped on DC link over-voltage alarms 30 milliseconds after the fault cleared. The root cause was in the plant controller. It wound up during the fault, then commanded maximum reactive output on recovery. That pushed terminal voltages higher, which coincided with the DC link overshoot and caused the trips. The delivered evidence included a PSCAD replication pinpointing the firmware flaw and a corrective action plan with an extended controller freeze and revised DC chopper settings. It also included an updated MOD-026 verified model reflecting the fixed settings. It's a good example of one event flowing through monitoring, root cause, and modeling. Now to the frontier, which is large computational loads such as data centers. The threat is that large loads disconnecting simultaneously after transmission faults behave like large generators in reverse, and that poses massive grid stability risks. The engineering response is that utilities now treat large data centers as high impact loads and enforce generation-like requirements. The requirements include FAC 001 for interconnection, FAC 002 and TPL 001 for dynamic models and ride-through, and MOD 032 for load composition data. The takeaway is that large load developers must design for grid stability from day one and prepare for imminent formal registration criteria. Here's how to put it all together as a seven-step lifecycle centered on accountable engineering. Step one, register in scope, confirm BES or category two status and map facility applicability. Step two, assess gaps. Compare existing models and settings to RSAW requirements. Step three, program design. Write the PSMP, PRC 030 and MOD 032 procedures. Step four, engineering. Perform the loadability, coordination, and EMT dynamic studies. Step five, evidence. Package the data strictly in RSAW order. Step six, audit. Conduct mock audits and train your subject matter experts. And step seven, sustain. Enforce management of change triggers for updates. Then the loop closes. Step seven feeds back to step one because a plant addition, a firmware update, or a settings change can reopen the whole cycle. It's continuous improvement. Under the leadership of Sandeep Sunny R. Patel, an IEEE senior member, Kental Engineering brings three decades of battle-tested expertise to the grid's most complex challenges. That comes down to three things. Engineering-led compliance from 4 kV to 765 kV, deep expertise in IBRs, EMT modeling, and FERC order 901 mandates, and audit-ready evidence built by the engineers running the studies. Three decades, every side of the table, one standard, accountable engineering. To reach the team, visit www.keentelengineering.com, call 813-389-7871 or email contact@keentelengineering.com.

metadata.title: One solar farm was handed a $598 million bill to plug in
metadata.author: Wattlore
metadata.shortDescription:
Interconnection queue explained, with one real bill. In August 2021, a PJM grid study said a 51 MW solar project in Cumberland County, New Jersey, was responsible for about $598.5 million to connect, almost all of it upgrades to the grid itself. That is a study-stage estimate for one project, not a final bill.

So why does a solar farm wait years and face a bill like that just to plug in? We stand in the waiting line (about 2,061 GW of proposed plants at the end of 2025, against 1,374 GW already running), follow an example solar-plus-battery farm through the three old studies, open the bill, meet the projects that quit and see how each exit can move the bill for the ones still waiting. Then FERC Order No. 2023 and PJM's first round under the new rules.

This video explains the US interconnection process. Our example farm is made up. It makes no forecast and is not advice of any kind.

SOURCES (what we checked)
Every number in the video, with what we took from each source. Costs, queue sizes and waits name their year and who counted them.

A $598 MILLION BILL TO PLUG IN
PJM System Impact Study, queue project AG1-129 (Aug 2021): a 51 MW New Jersey solar project allocated $598.5 million, $592.1 million of it network upgrades https://www.pjm.com/pub/planning/project-queues/impact_studies/ag1129_imp.pdf
Photo: File:A photovoltaic power station in the United States (36130544874).jpg (Photo by Chris Allan. – U.S. Department of Energy from United States, Public domain, 2017-08-01) https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_photovoltaic_power_station_in_the_United_States_(36130544874).jpg
FERC Order No. 2023 (Federal Register, Sep 2023): the old first-come, first-served process and its three studies; 68% of 2022 studies late; restudy cascades; the new cluster rules, deposits, withdrawal penalties and study-delay penalties https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2023-09-06/html/2023-16628.htm

WHAT IS THE INTERCONNECTION QUEUE
Berkeley Lab, Queued Up 2026 (June 2026): about 2,061 GW in US queues at end-2025, against a 1,374 GW fleet; 13% of 2000-2020 capacity built; a 61-month median wait for 2025 plants; reforms too new to judge https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-06/queued_up_2026_edition.pdf

WHO PAYS FOR GRID UPGRADES
Photo: File:High voltage transmission towers and lines.jpg (Stefan Andrej Shambora (St_A_Sh), CC BY 2.0, 2007-04-30) https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:High_voltage_transmission_towers_and_lines.jpg

PJM'S NEW INTERCONNECTION PROCESS
Berkeley Lab, Queued Up 2025 (Dec 2025): PJM's move from first-come, first-served to first-ready, first-served cluster cycles, approved by FERC in Nov 2022 https://emp.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/Queued%20Up%202025%20Edition%20-%2012.15.2025.pdf
PJM news release (3 Aug 2026): 715 projects, 201.5 GW, qualified for Cycle 1 of the reformed process, led by gas and storage; no backlog left; 51 GW signed but many not being built https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/newsroom/2026-releases/20260803-over-700-new-generation-projects-accepted-into-first-cycle-of-reformed-interconnection-process.pdf

WILL THE QUEUE GET SHORTER
Photo: File:ERCOTOperator 2.jpg (Dpysh w, CC BY 3.0, 2012-10-03) https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ERCOTOperator_2.jpg
Photo: File:Norris Dam Electrical Substation - Norris, Tennessee - March 8, 2015.jpg (David Ratledge, CC BY 4.0, 2015-03-08) https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Norris_Dam_Electrical_Substation_-_Norris,_Tennessee_-_March_8,_2015.jpg

MORE
Berkeley Lab, Interconnection Cost Analysis in the PJM Territory (Jan 2023): completed projects averaged $84/kW in 2020-22, withdrawn ones $599/kW (94% network upgrades); withdrawn solar's $559/kW was 36% of installed cost https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/berkeley_lab_2023.1.12-_pjm_interconnection_costs.pdf

0:00 A $598 million bill to plug in
0:57 What is the interconnection queue
2:10 How long interconnection takes
3:29 Who pays for grid upgrades
5:01 Why projects drop out
6:31 FERC Order 2023 explained
7:40 PJM's new interconnection process
8:42 Will the queue get shorter

The narration voice in this video is AI-generated (altered or synthetic content).

How we make it: the narration voice is AI and the thumbnails are made with AI tools; the animation is drawn by us in code, scene by scene, any real photo is credited on screen, and every source above was read and checked by us. Spotted a mistake? Tell us in the comments and we will pin the fix.

segments.text: Five hundred and ninety-eight million dollars To plug in one solar farm
That's what a grid study said one solar farm in New Jersey would owe back in
August twenty twenty-one
Fifty-one megawatts of panels in Cumberland County
And here's the strange part The farm's own connection its own wire to the grid came
to six point four million
Almost all the rest about five hundred and ninety-two million was for
upgrades to the grid itself
Now my first guess was that the panels cost the most
They're the thing you see Rows and rows of glass in a field
So why does a solar farm have to wait years and face a bill like
that just to plug in
To find out we'll stand in a waiting line bigger than every power plant in
America put together
We'll follow one farm through three studies that keep running late
We'll open that bill and see what's really in it
And we'll meet the projects that quit and see why each one that quits can raise the
bill for the ones still waiting
Under the federal rules a new power plant over twenty megawatts can't just plug
in It has to ask
It sends a request to the company that runs the power lines and it joins a line
That line has a name the interconnection queue Interconnection just
means plugging in
Think of it as a ticket Not a ticket to connect A ticket to be studied
So how long is the line
Berkeley Lab a United States national lab counts it
At the end of twenty twenty-five more than eight thousand two hundred proposed plants
were waiting across the country
Together they add up to about two thousand and sixty gigawatts A gigawatt is
a huge amount of power
And here's the bit that stopped me
Every power plant already running in the United States adds up to about one
thousand three hundred and seventy gigawatts
So the line of plants waiting is about one and a half times bigger than
everything already built
What's in it Mostly sunshine and batteries
About seven hundred and seventy gigawatts of solar About seven hundred and fifty of
storage and almost all of that storage is batteries
Nearly half of that solar and storage comes as a pair a solar farm with a
battery right beside it
So let's follow one of those from the day it takes its ticket
I'll call it Meadow Solar It's our own made-up example a solar farm
with a battery beside it
Under the old rules Meadow Solar sends in its request with a ten thousand dollar
deposit and it gets that back if it leaves
Its place in line is set by one thing the time and date its request arrived First
come first served
Then come the studies Three of them one after another
The first is a quick look could this plant even fit here
The second is the big one Engineers model the whole grid with the
new plant switched on
They look for wires that would run too hot faults that would hit too hard and
anything that could go unstable
The third is called the facilities study
On paper each study was meant to take somewhere between a month and a
half and six months
In practice In twenty twenty-two sixty-eight percent of these
studies came out late
That's more than two out of every three
So here's what the wait looks like
A typical project built in twenty oh eight went from its request to switching on
in under two years
A typical project built in twenty twenty-five took sixty-one months Just
over five years
And a solar farm with a battery like Meadow Solar tends to wait longer than a
battery or a gas plant on its own
So Meadow Solar waits maybe for years And then the study comes
back with a bill
To see what's on a bill like that let's go back to our real farm in New Jersey
Its study came from PJM the grid operator that checked whether it could connect
And the bill has two parts
Part one is the farm's own connection its own wire Six point four million dollars
Part two is what the study calls network upgrades
That means new or bigger parts of the main grid needed to keep the grid reliable once
the new plant is on it
And the study says the farm may be responsible for the cost of building them
What's on that list Power lines rebuilt Old lines strung with new wire
Some of them are big high-voltage lines at two hundred and thirty thousand volts
One whole line would be rebuilt with new poles
That's what most of the five hundred and ninety-eight million was for
Here's a way to feel how big that is
Split the bill over the farm's size and it comes to more than eleven thousand dollars
for every kilowatt
Now compare Berkeley Lab looked at what it costs projects to get connected
Recent projects that made it through every study averaged about eighty-four
dollars a kilowatt
The ones that gave up and left the line averaged about six hundred
And for those upgrades to the wider grid were ninety-four percent of the cost
Berkeley Lab says those costs are likely a key reason they left
So my guess was wrong In that bill the big number was never the farm It was the grid
A grid with little room left where one more farm means rebuilding
the roads it drives on
Now here's what surprised me most
Most of the plants in that line will never be built
Berkeley Lab followed everything that asked to connect from the year two
thousand to twenty twenty
By the end of twenty twenty-five only thirteen percent of that
power had switched on
Seventy-five percent had walked away
And even plants that signed the final deal to connect Forty-one percent of that
power still left
Why so many Because a ticket was cheap
The federal regulator FERC found that the old rules had no meaningful money on the
line to get in or to stay in
So developers sent in several requests at several spots on the grid knowing not
all of them would be built
It was a way to shop around find the spot where the grid bill comes back lowest and
go ahead with that one
And here's how one exit can cost someone else
Remember the old line goes in order
PJM's study for our New Jersey farm spells out the rule The cost of an upgrade starts
with the first project in line that makes it needed
So if a project ahead of you leaves its share of the bill can land on you
An exit can mean a restudy the engineers run the grid again
without the plant that left
FERC found these restudies can push other projects' costs way up
and push their dates back
And a bigger bill can make the next project quit Which can set
off another restudy
That's why the study told our New Jersey farm in plain words that its
cost could still change
So on the twenty-eighth of July twenty twenty-three FERC changed the rules
Its name Order twenty twenty-three
First come first served is out Now it's first ready first served
Instead of one long line projects are studied in groups called clusters
Everyone in a group is equal Nobody is ahead of anybody
And the bill for an upgrade is split by how much each plant actually
adds to the need for it
To get in you now have to show you control the land
You pay deposits that grow as you go tied to your share of the grid bill
And if you quit late it costs you
Walk away after you've signed your deal to connect and you pay a penalty twenty
percent of what your grid upgrades were estimated to cost
So the ticket isn't cheap anymore
But the rule cuts both ways
The grid operators get deadlines too A cluster study has to be done within a
hundred and fifty days
Miss a deadline and they pay a fine for every working day they're late
A thousand dollars a day for a late cluster study and up to two thousand five
hundred a day for the last one the study that works out what gets built
So now both sides have something to lose
That was the federal rule Now back to PJM the grid operator that studied
our New Jersey farm
PJM had already started switching to first ready first served and FERC approved its
plan in November twenty twenty-two
When the switch began a lot of projects left PJM's line
Then PJM announced who qualified for the first round of its new system
Seven hundred and fifteen projects got in more than two hundred
gigawatts between them
And PJM says nothing is left over from the old line No backlog
Each project is meant to take one to two years to study depending on how much
it changes the grid
Here's the twist The biggest share of that first round isn't solar
It's natural gas almost a hundred gigawatts Solar on its own under twelve
And getting through the study still isn't the finish line
PJM has fifty-one gigawatts of plants that have already signed their deals to connect
It says many of them aren't being built at all or are slowed by state permits and
supply chain backlogs
So does the new system work
Berkeley Lab's answer it's too early to measure
They call the reforms important But their full effect can't be measured yet
And some places were already faster Texas with its own grid operator called ERCOT
and the regions without a big grid operator tend to connect plants sooner
So here's where I've landed
I thought the panels cost the most
Now I think the hardest part of building a solar farm is the plug
A grid with little room left A line of thousands all waiting on the same studies
A bill for upgrades that can dwarf the farm's own wire
And for years every plant that left could change the price
for the ones still waiting
The new rules put deadlines and penalties on both sides
Whether the line actually gets shorter it's still too early to tell That's the
part I'll be watching
Every source is in the description
So tell me when a new power plant needs a bigger grid who should pay for it

In the data center industry, staying current on evolving development models is critical—and Powered Shells are gaining significant attention. We sat down with industry experts David Liggitt and Mike Netzer to discuss the rise of Powered Shell data centers and how they help meet growing demand for efficient, adaptable infrastructure. This overview covers the history of Powered Shells, what they include (and don’t), and why the model is attractive in today’s market.

What is a Powered Shell?
A Powered Shell is a purpose-built, secure data center facility that includes the building, site power, and connectivity options (such as proximity to fiber providers), but excludes key IT infrastructure like UPS systems, generators, and cooling—so end-users can install their own components. This differs from Turnkey Data Centers, which include all required IT equipment for immediate operation. Powered Shell leases are typically priced by square footage rather than per kilowatt (kW).

Why are Powered Shells gaining popularity now?

* Hyperscale investment: Amazon ($100B), Microsoft ($80B), Google ($75B), and Meta ($60–80B) are making massive investments in data center infrastructure, increasing demand for scalable approaches like Powered Shell development.
* Speed to market: Powered Shells can help bring capacity online faster by allowing end-users to install critical infrastructure and operations on their own timeline.
* Flexibility and customization: End-users can choose and manage their own IT, power, and cooling (including liquid cooling or custom design requirements).
* Capital allocation efficiency: Powered Shells reduce upfront capital demands versus building a full Turnkey facility while still providing a secure, scalable solution.

What does a Powered Shell include?
Included: physical building (often designed with hardened shells for security), power infrastructure to the site, and proximity to fiber providers for connectivity.
Excluded: UPS systems, generators, cooling systems, and other advanced IT infrastructure. End-users equip and operate the facility to match their requirements.

Geographic trends and market adoption
Powered Shell developments have historically been concentrated in Northern Virginia, which accounts for about 100 of the 130 Powered Shell deals tracked globally. The model is gaining traction in other regions due to constraints around land availability, power, and evolving end-user needs. Internationally, Europe is worth watching; for example, a recent €200B investment in France for AI and data center infrastructure highlights growing demand beyond the U.S.

Looking ahead
As deals grow in size—often exceeding hundreds of megawatts—hybrid models combining Powered Shell and Turnkey facilities are becoming more common. These arrangements help developers balance capital allocation while meeting diverse client needs. Powered Shells can also be an entry point for industrial developers entering the data center market by leveraging large-scale site-building expertise.

Final thoughts
Powered Shell data centers offer operational flexibility, scalability, and efficient capital deployment for hyperscale companies, developers, and operators. Want to stay ahead of the curve? Reach out to our team to explore market trends, gain deeper insights, and make informed decisions in the data center space.

metadata.title: The Real Product of a Data Center Isn't Data
metadata.author: Break Even
metadata.shortDescription:
A data center looks like a tech business. It isn't. It's a power company wearing enough concrete and cooling to survive the heat — and it might be the best real-estate business on Earth right now.

In this episode we break down exactly how data centers make money in 2026: why leases are quoted in dollars-per-megawatt instead of square feet, why Northern Virginia's vacancy rate collapsed to 0.3%, how a single Applied Digital lease is worth up to $18.2 billion, and why "speed to power" has quietly become the most valuable asset class in infrastructure.

By the end you'll understand why the asset you named isn't the real asset — the real asset is control over an essential system nobody can opt out of.

⏱️ Chapters
0:00  The question that actually matters
0:43  Three sizes, three completely different businesses
2:29  Where the money really comes from
4:23  The number that breaks people's brains
4:50  The hidden mechanic: renting power nobody else can get
7:45  So why do owners still lose money?
9:57  The risk buried inside the whole boom
12:02 What a data center actually is
13:18 How much you actually make
14:31 The only rule that matters

📊 Every figure is sourced from real reports (CBRE, JLL, Goldman Sachs, Uptime Institute, PJM, Applied Digital filings).

🔔 Subscribe for more on the systems that run the world — how they make money, and what happens when they break.

#datacenter #AI #artificialintelligence #infrastructure #investing #powergrid #datacenters #techexplained #aiboom #breakeven

metadata.title: How Battery Storage Makes Money in EU Electricity Markets — BESS Explained
metadata.author: learnBESS
metadata.shortDescription:
A battery storage plant earns in three ways: energy arbitrage, balancing services, and capacity payments where a capacity mechanism exists.

Underneath every stream sit two roles the industry rarely defines: the balance responsible party (BRP), which settles the plant's own imbalance, and the balancing service provider (BSP), which is paid to resolve the system's. In practice one Route to Market (RTM) provider fills both.

The EU sets the frame. The detail — balancing prequalification, imbalance pricing, network tariffs, capacity mechanisms — is national. That's why identical hardware earns different revenue in different countries.

The BRPs that cause imbalances pay, indirectly, the BSPs that resolve them. They're two ends of the same transaction. In practice, one route to market provider or RTM usually fills both roles under a single contract. It trades the asset, submits the schedules, carries the imbalance position, and sells the balancing services. The European Union sets the frame. The detail is national. Balancing pre-qualification, imbalance pricing, network tariffs, and whether a capacity mechanism exists at all. That's why two BESS plants with identical hardware earn different revenue in different European countries. A BESS plant's revenue is market-based. A single stream rarely justifies the investment on its own. Arbitrage, balancing, and capacity are stacked, and the RTM provider is the one that executes it. Read the full article on learnbess.com. Link in the description. Subscribe for more BESS explainers.

metadata.shortDescription:
How do you price the risk of a battery you can’t see inside?

In this conversation, Antonio Mazza (CEO, ClearSpot.ai) talks with Zamiyad Dar, Co-Founder of Avikala Power, about the real risks and opportunities of battery energy storage (BESS).

In this episode:

• Why insurers and lenders struggle to price battery risk, and why monitoring data is the missing piece
• Degradation: how the way a battery is operated changes its life and its insurance cost
• Merchant storage: why it works for only a few owners, and how a new transmission line can wipe out revenue
• Tolling agreements, capacity PPAs and utility-operated batteries
• A new use case: batteries that help data centers and large loads connect to the grid faster through flexible interconnection
• What data centers need from storage, and how that differs from grid-scale projects
• Taking over a storage portfolio? The first things to check: past operation compared with the manufacturer’s limits, how consistent the revenue was, and proper data monitoring

If you work in energy storage, insurance, finance or asset management, this one is for you.

metadata.title: Civil Engineering Design for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in Australia
metadata.author: Civil and Structural Engineer
metadata.shortDescription:
A comprehensive overview of the civil engineering framework required to design and deliver large-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) within the Australian landscape. It offers information on the technical integration of foundational inputs, such as swept-path analysis for access roads, stormwater drainage design, flood resilience, and the critical management of fire-water containment systems. By exploring site-specific challenges—from geotechnical soil stabilization to sustainable earthworks—the article serves as a practical guide for engineers and developers navigating the physical infrastructure needs of Australia’s rapidly evolving renewable energy sector.

#RenewableEnergy #CivilEngineering #EnergyStorage #BESS #AustraliaEnergy #Sustainability #Infrastructure #GridStability #StormwaterManagement #PavementDesign #GeotechnicalEngineering #NetZeroAustralia #ConstructionAU #RenewableEnergyAustralia

segments.text: As the Australian energy network
integrates higher levels of wind and
solar generation, it relies on battery
energy storage systems or BES, these
grids scale batteries are tasked with a
specific job, stabilizing voltage and
shifting stored energy into the network
during peak demand periods. Inside these
enclosures, highly advanced electrical
engineering manages gawatt of power. But
the performance of those internal
lithium ion cells is entirely dependent
on a hidden highly vulnerable variable,
the physical ground they sit on. A best
facility survival requires strict
environmental isolation. If the ground
shifts, if water pools or if heavy
equipment fractures the access routes,
the electrical hardware will fail. The
physical backbone of the site, the civil
engineering, maintains the structural
integrity necessary for the battery to
function. This civil infrastructure must
act as a fortress against three primary
physical threats. Extreme regional flood
events, massive temporary mechanical
loads from construction cranes, and the
highly hazardous chemical runoff
produced in the event of a battery fire.
To understand how this physical
isolation is achieved, we will build a
theoretical best site from the ground
up. We will start with raw topological
data and planning documents and piece by
piece construct a fully fortified
facility. Mastering this unglamorous
civil backbone is the absolute
prerequisite for the longevity of these
facilities. You secure Australia's
transition to a clean energy grid by
first securing the dirt beneath it.
Before a single trench is dug, the
site's geometry is defined by strict
regulatory and technical documents. The
principal project requirements or PPR
act as the overarching specification for
all design choices. Parallel to this is
the traffic impact assessment or TIA
which identifies the specific volumes
and turning needs of all vehicles
entering the site. The TIA dictates that
massive oversized equipment delivery
vehicles will need to navigate the
compound. To ensure they can do this
safely, engineers run a swept path
analysis using specialized modeling
software to simulate exactly how large
vehicles maneuver through corners and
critical equipment zones. Heavy loaders
require wide sweeping paths to clear
intersections safely. Emergency vehicles
dictate perimeter approach routes and
strict turning radi around fire tanks.
Construction also requires precise
parking. 10 temporary angled bays
measuring 2.4 x 5.4 4 m separated by a
6.2 m circulation aisle. Once the
facility is built and enters its
operational stage, almost all of this
heavy vehicle traffic disappears.
Maintenance personnel only require
minimal parking capacity for routine
checks. The sprawling geometry of a best
site is a direct response to the extreme
spatial demands of construction
logistics and emergency response
protocols rather than its daily
operational needs. Many Australian
renewable energy sites are positioned on
perfectly flat terrain. While flat
ground simplifies some aspects of
construction, a lack of natural
elevation creates a severe risk of
stagnant ponding. If water gathers
beneath high voltage equipment, the
facility fails. To solve this, engineers
impose a subtle minimum grade across the
entire site. Sloping the earthworks
between.5 and 1.0% 0% is enough to
promote efficient water runoff without
requiring expensive massive volumes of
imported soil. However, runoff is only
one part of the equation. Regional flood
mapping dictates strict resilience
mandates. The critical electrical
components must be elevated to survive
rare extreme flooding events. Platforms
must sit entirely above the local 1% AE
flood level, which here sits at 181.5 m.
Furthermore, the design raises the
platform an additional 300 to 500 mm, an
elevation buffer known as freeboard to
protect against unexpected hydraulic
variables. Elevating the platforms
protects them from rising water. But the
site must also manage overland flow,
large volumes of storm water traveling
horizontally across the landscape from
external neighboring properties. To
manage this, an earth berm called a wind
row is placed along the site's edge.
This structure physically intercepts
external overland flows and diverts them
around the perimeter, ensuring water
never traverses the battery platforms
during major storms. In diverting this
water, the site must comply with the
strict no worsening rule. By law, the
project's internal grading and wind row
placement cannot increase the depth or
flow velocity of flood waters on
neighboring lands. Engineers use
geotechnical reports to map out exact
top soil stripping and bench
adjustments. By carefully balancing the
volume of dirt cut from high areas with
the fill needed for low areas, they
drastically reduce the need to truck in
costly imported soil. The earthworks of
a best site form a precise hydraulic
defense mechanism. Every slope and
elevation is calculated to keep high
voltage equipment dry under the worst
statistical weather events on record.
With the site properly elevated and
graded, the internal drainage network
must manage the water falling directly
onto the compound. This requires
splitting all runoff into two highly
controlled, entirely separate systems.
First, engineers estimate peak clean
water discharge using the rational
method. They base these internal
hydraulic calculations on a 10% AE storm
event, a heavy rainfall scenario with a
10% chance of occurring annually. This
visualization demonstrates varying
runoff speeds based on surface
materials. Rain hitting a solid
enclosure with a coefficient of 1.0
converts instantly to surface flow. In
contrast, rain hitting crushed rock with
a coefficient of 7 partially absorbs
into the ground, slowing the water down.
Clean rainwater is predictable, but the
most critical environmental threat to
the site is a battery fire. If a fire
occurs, the water used to extinguish it
becomes highly contaminated with
hazardous materials, including toxic
lithium compounds. Regulatory permits
strictly require that this contaminated
fire is completely isolated from the
clean storm water network. It cannot be
allowed to leave the site and enter
local ecosystems. This smart valve
system seals off clean drainage paths,
forcing all toxic fire water into a
dedicated retention pond. This pond is
strictly sized to hold the entire volume
of emergency firewater tanks, plus a 0.3
m freeboard safety margin to guarantee
safe containment. While the retention
pond waits for an emergency, the clean
storm water detention basin works
constantly during rainfall. It uses
specific lowflow and high- flow
orififices to regulate the speed of the
clean water, matching the discharge rate
exactly to the legal point of discharge
permitted by local authorities. If a
storm drops more clean water than the
design capacity allows, a built-in
overflow we activates, it safely conveys
the surplus water over a rock beach
spillway, entirely preventing erosion as
the water moves downstream. This dual
drainage infrastructure operates as an
environmental firewall. It guarantees
the site will never inundate itself
during a storm while completely
isolating local ecosystems from
catastrophic chemical contamination.
Below the grading and drainage lies the
issue of structural density. Designing
the pavement for a best site reveals a
counterintuitive reality about
loadbearing. The absolute maximum
structural stress inflicted on the
ground occurs during the temporary
construction phase. The weight of
concrete mixers, semi-trailers, and
massive cranes delivering pre-fabricated
enclosures exerts extreme downward force
far exceeding any traffic the site will
see once operational. To prevent the
access roads from collapsing under this
weight, engineers calculate equivalent
standard axle or ESA loadings. By
projecting the exact movements of the
heavy construction fleet, they determine
the specific pavement thickness required
to support them. This becomes an
immediate problem when geotechnical data
reveals weak subgrade soils on site.
Areas identified with a California
bearing ratio or CBR of less than 3%
lack the mechanical strength to
withstand heavy machinery and require
intensive stabilization. To stabilize
those weak areas over a subgrade with a
CBR of less than 3%, engineers lay a
stabilization geo fabric followed by a
granular subbase, a thick crushed rock
base layer, and finally a sacrificial
wearing course designed to absorb
surface degradation. Once the structural
loads are accounted for, the focus
shifts to securing the high value
equipment that sits on top of it.
Millions of dollars of sensitive
electrical infrastructure demand strict
standardized protection. The entire
battery compound is enclosed by a 2.1 m
chain wire mesh fence topped with three
strands of barbed wire. Additional 1.8 m
fencing encloses the storm water and
firewater ponds, ensuring public safety
and preventing unauthorized access to
deep water. With the robust pavement
strata bearing the mechanical load and
the standardized fencing securing the
perimeter, the physical isolation of the
site is finalized. Looking at the
completed site, the underlying
engineering is clear. The elevated
earthworks, the dual drainage pipe
networks, and the stabilized pavements
interlock as a single unified physical
system. When developers underestimate
flood impacts on flat sites, the results
are expensive. Skipping minor grading
adjustments leads directly to
catastrophic water ponding beneath high
voltage equipment after minimal
rainfall. Similarly, when engineers fail
to properly account for the massive
temporary ESA loadings of construction
cranes, the roads fracture before the
battery is even plugged in, delaying
deployment and adding massive
remediation costs. Success relies
entirely on holistic data integration. A
single geotechnical soil sample
simultaneously dictates how much earth
can be safely cut, the absorption rate
of the drainage system, and the physical
depth of the concrete foundations. The
site's long-term sustainability depends
on maintaining these systems over
decades. Drainage assets must be cleared
of debris, swailes kept free of
sediment, and native vegetation buffers
maintained to support local
biodiversity.
The electrical engineering inside the
battery shifts the power, but the civil
engineering ensures the battery survives
long enough to do it. Rigorous, precise
site design provides the literal
foundation that allows Australia's
high-capacity renewable energy grid to
operate safely and reliably.

🔋 Largest Operational & Major BESS Projects Worldwide
🇺🇸 United States
1. Edwards & Sanborn Solar + Storage (California, USA)
• ~3,287 MWh BESS (largest operational) paired with 875 MWdc solar PV. Operates to stabilise grid, store renewable output, and provide peak energy.

2. Blythe/McCoy/Arlington Complex (California, USA)
• ~3,248 MWh BESS capacity supporting grid flexibility and renewable integration.

3. Moss Landing Energy Storage Facility (CA, USA)
• ~1,800 MWh BESS used for frequency regulation & peak load management.

4. Victorian Big Battery (Victoria, AUS)
• ~450 MWh / 300 MW battery facility, supports grid stability.

5. New England Solar + Storage / Waratah Super Battery (NSW) (development focus)
• Large-scale BESS projects supporting solar + renewables integration (e.g., ~2,800 MWh for New England Solar BESS).

6. Songino Battery Storage Power Station (Ulaanbaatar)
• 80 MW / 200 MWh operational BESS supporting grid integration of intermittent renewables.

7. Tsengeg Battery at Borkh Solar Power Plant
• 3.6 MW BESS paired with 5 MW PV plant — smaller yet important for local grid stability.

8. Kenhardt Solar + BESS (Northern Cape)
• 225 MW / ~1,140 MWh BESS supporting solar output smoothing and firming.

9. Quillagua Solar + 1.2 GWh BESS
• One of Latin America’s largest hybrid solar + battery facilities delivering up to 6+ hours of stored clean power.

10. Blackhillock Battery Storage (Scotland, UK)
• 200+ MW operational battery installation (expanding to ~300 MW), helping absorb wind surpluses and stabilise grid.

segments.text: The global installed capacity of utility
scale battery energy storage systems has
witnessed a dramatic expansion over the
past 5 years driven by the increasing
demand for renewable energy integration
and grid stability solutions.
This rapid deployment has however been
accompanied by several high-profile
failure incidents that have garnered
significant media attention and raised
safety concerns across the energy
sector.
Despite these challenges, the industry
has demonstrated remarkable progress in
addressing safety issues with the global
grids scale best failure rate declining
by 97% between 2018 in 2023.
This substantial reduction can be
attributed to the incorporation of
lessons learned from early failure
incidents into new system designs and
best practices.
The battery industry continues to engage
in extensive research and development
activities to enhance prevention and
mitigation measures, including
developing a deeper understanding of the
diverse causes of best failures.
The Electric Power Research Institute,
EPRI, has established the most
comprehensive compilation of stationary
best incidents through its best failure
incident database, which serves as the
primary source for understanding failure
patterns and root causes.
This database focuses on occurrences
that present wider public health and
safety risks rather than operational
failures that pose no additional danger
to personnel or equipment. As of the
current analysis, the database contains
81 incidents from 2011 to the present
with 26 incidents providing sufficient
information for detailed classification
and root cause analysis.
This classification system employs a
baxial framework that categorizes
failures by both root cause, design,
manufacturing, integration, assembly,
construction or operation and failed
element, cell/module, controls or
balance of system. This dual approach
enables a more nuanced understanding of
failure patterns and relationships
between different contributing factors.
The analysis of classified incidents
reveals that integration, assembly, and
construction emerges as the most common
root cause of best failures, accounting
for approximately 65% of all identified
faults. This finding challenges the
common assumption that lithium ion
battery cells constitute the primary
source of failures.
Instead, the balance of system BOS and
control systems account for the vast
majority of failed components with cells
representing only 11% of classified
incidents.
The BOS encompasses a wide range of
components including DC and AC wiring,
HVAC subsystems, safety elements such as
fire suppression systems, enclosures,
power conversion systems, transformers,
and thermal management systems.
Recent quality audits indicate that
nearly 50% of quality assurance issues
occur in the BOS with 26% of inspected
BES units exhibiting defects in fire
suppression systems and 18% showing
thermal management system defects.
Operational failures constitute the
second most common root cause accounting
for approximately 20% of classified
incidents.
Notably, the bulk of these operational
failures occurred during the 2018 to
2019 period when South Korea experienced
a significant wave of BES incidents.
Investigation of these failures revealed
that a substantial fraction occurred
when the state of charge exceeded 90%
suggesting that these failures could
potentially be attributed to
manufacturing or design issues related
to the cells.
However, due to insufficient evidence to
make definitive determinations, these
incidents were classified as operational
failures.
This highlights a broader challenge in
failure analysis. Manufacturing defects
often prove difficult to identify
conclusively due to the loss of physical
evidence after fire or explosion
incidents.
Design related failures, while less
common, have become increasingly
significant in recent years.
Three of the four design related
failures in 2023 resulted from the same
BOS design flaw affecting best products
in New York and Idaho where enclosure
design allowed water intrusion into the
battery compartment leading to loss of
isolation and subsequent thermal
runaway.
Manufacturing failures represent the
smallest category likely due to the
difficulty in definitively identifying
manufacturing defects as root causes
post incident.
However, it's worth noting that earlier
failures from 2018 to 2020 may have
involved cell or module manufacturing
defects as contributing factors as
evidenced by several product recalls
from major EV manufacturers during that
period citing manufacturing issues by
battery OEMs.
The timing of failures provides another
critical insight. Approximately 72% of
failures where system age is known occur
during construction, commissioning or
within the first two years of operation.
This concentration of failures in the
early life cycle phases underscores the
critical importance of integration,
assembly and construction as a risk
mitigation priority.
Many of these incidents occur during the
commissioning phase when monitoring and
communication systems are not yet
operational, allowing leaks or isolation
failures to escalate into large-scale
fires before detection and intervention
become possible.
South Korea's experience between 2018
and 2019 serves as a compelling case
study of rapid deployment without robust
safety standards.
During this period, 27 of the 30
incidents in the EPRI database occurred
in South Korea. The Korean government
had provided strong economic incentives
for best deployment, particularly when
paired with solar photovoltaic
generation, leading to explosive growth
in installed systems from 30 in 2013 to
This rapid expansion was not accompanied
by commenurate development of safety
standards and regulations, contributing
directly to the wave of failures that
followed. The Korean government's
subsequent investigation of the first
spade of fires and the government's
commitment to implementing safety
improvements demonstrated how early
failures can catalyze industry-wide
learning and improvement.
The surprise Arizona incident in 2019
represents another pivotal moment in BES
safety evolution.
This fire and explosion at a best
facility injured four firefighters and
prompted the release of multiple root
cause investigation reports to the
public. The incident marked safety as a
priority issue for the energy storage
industry in the United States and led to
increased scrutiny and safety safety
measures across the sector. The public
sharing of investigation details
represented a significant step toward
greater industry transparency, enabling
other operators and manufacturers to
learn from the incident and implement
preventive measures. The Elorn battery
facility fire in Moss Landing,
California on September 20th, 2022
provides a particularly instructive
example of dual root causes.
The investigation shared publicly by
Tesla, the best manufacturer and
integrator, and Pacific Gas and
Electric, the site owner, revealed that
rainwater intrusion through the
container had caused electrical arcing
within the system, leading to thermal
runaway.
A water ingress point in the enclosure
had been created when an umbrella valve
was dislodged during the improper
installation of a vent shield. As a
confounding factor, insulation loss
alarms were not properly escalated to
the operator.
Two days after the initial insulation
alarms were recorded, smoke and fire
were reported to the fire department.
Appropriate reporting of the insulation
loss alarms could have prevented
escalation of the initial failure into a
fire that consumed the entire BES unit.
Consequently, the root cause was
classified as both an integration,
assembly, and construction failure in
the BOS and a design failure of the
control system. The Victoria Big Battery
incident in Australia during 2021
demonstrates another critical aspect of
BES failure analysis.
During commissioning, a leak in the
coolant system led to a fire that spread
across two best units.
This incident exemplifies BOS failure
due to assembly quality issues and
underscores the critical importance of
proper commissioning procedures,
monitoring and hazardous assessments
during this vulnerable phase. The fact
that monitoring and communication
systems were not yet online during
commissioning allowed the coolant leak
to cascade into a major incident before
detection.
The operational challenges facing the
best industry are multifaceted and stem
largely from the rapid pace of
deployment and market expansion.
The industry is experiencing significant
growth with many new entrance bringing
products that lack long operational
histories.
This creates a substantial knowledge gap
particularly in integration and assembly
practices where proper training and
experience are essential for safe and
reliable operation.
The best supply chain involves
components from multiple suppliers which
are not necessarily designed to work
together, creating potential for
incompatible interfaces and unexpected
interactions between components.
The diversity of product architectures,
thermal management approaches, and
system designs further complicates
integration efforts.

videos.full_text: The global installed capacity of utility scale battery energy storage systems has witnessed a dramatic expansion over the past 5 years driven by the increasing demand for renewable energy integration and grid stability solutions. This rapid deployment has however been accompanied by several high-profile failure incidents that have garnered significant media attention and raised safety concerns across the energy sector. Despite these challenges, the industry has demonstrated remarkable progress in addressing safety issues with the global grids scale best failure rate declining by 97% between 2018 in 2023. This substantial reduction can be attributed to the incorporation of lessons learned from early failure incidents into new system designs and best practices. The battery industry continues to engage in extensive research and development activities to enhance prevention and mitigation measures, including developing a deeper understanding of the diverse causes of best failures. The Electric Power Research Institute, EPRI, has established the most comprehensive compilation of stationary best incidents through its best failure incident database, which serves as the primary source for understanding failure patterns and root causes. This database focuses on occurrences that present wider public health and safety risks rather than operational failures that pose no additional danger to personnel or equipment. As of the current analysis, the database contains 81 incidents from 2011 to the present with 26 incidents providing sufficient information for detailed classification and root cause analysis. This classification system employs a baxial framework that categorizes failures by both root cause, design, manufacturing, integration, assembly, construction or operation and failed element, cell/module, controls or balance of system. This dual approach enables a more nuanced understanding of failure patterns and relationships between different contributing factors. The analysis of classified incidents reveals that integration, assembly, and construction emerges as the most common root cause of best failures, accounting for approximately 65% of all identified faults. This finding challenges the common assumption that lithium ion battery cells constitute the primary source of failures. Instead, the balance of system BOS and control systems account for the vast majority of failed components with cells representing only 11% of classified incidents. The BOS encompasses a wide range of components including DC and AC wiring, HVAC subsystems, safety elements such as fire suppression systems, enclosures, power conversion systems, transformers, and thermal management systems. Recent quality audits indicate that nearly 50% of quality assurance issues occur in the BOS with 26% of inspected BES units exhibiting defects in fire suppression systems and 18% showing thermal management system defects. Operational failures constitute the second most common root cause accounting for approximately 20% of classified incidents. Notably, the bulk of these operational failures occurred during the 2018 to 2019 period when South Korea experienced a significant wave of BES incidents. Investigation of these failures revealed that a substantial fraction occurred when the state of charge exceeded 90% suggesting that these failures could potentially be attributed to manufacturing or design issues related to the cells. However, due to insufficient evidence to make definitive determinations, these incidents were classified as operational failures. This highlights a broader challenge in failure analysis. Manufacturing defects often prove difficult to identify conclusively due to the loss of physical evidence after fire or explosion incidents. Design related failures, while less common, have become increasingly significant in recent years. Three of the four design related failures in 2023 resulted from the same BOS design flaw affecting best products in New York and Idaho where enclosure design allowed water intrusion into the battery compartment leading to loss of isolation and subsequent thermal runaway. Manufacturing failures represent the smallest category likely due to the difficulty in definitively identifying manufacturing defects as root causes post incident. However, it's worth noting that earlier failures from 2018 to 2020 may have involved cell or module manufacturing defects as contributing factors as evidenced by several product recalls from major EV manufacturers during that period citing manufacturing issues by battery OEMs. The timing of failures provides another critical insight. Approximately 72% of failures where system age is known occur during construction, commissioning or within the first two years of operation. This concentration of failures in the early life cycle phases underscores the critical importance of integration, assembly and construction as a risk mitigation priority. Many of these incidents occur during the commissioning phase when monitoring and communication systems are not yet operational, allowing leaks or isolation failures to escalate into large-scale fires before detection and intervention become possible. South Korea's experience between 2018 and 2019 serves as a compelling case study of rapid deployment without robust safety standards. During this period, 27 of the 30 incidents in the EPRI database occurred in South Korea. The Korean government had provided strong economic incentives for best deployment, particularly when paired with solar photovoltaic generation, leading to explosive growth in installed systems from 30 in 2013 to 947 in 2018. This rapid expansion was not accompanied by commenurate development of safety standards and regulations, contributing directly to the wave of failures that followed. The Korean government's subsequent investigation of the first spade of fires and the government's commitment to implementing safety improvements demonstrated how early failures can catalyze industry-wide learning and improvement. The surprise Arizona incident in 2019 represents another pivotal moment in BES safety evolution. This fire and explosion at a best facility injured four firefighters and prompted the release of multiple root cause investigation reports to the public. The incident marked safety as a priority issue for the energy storage industry in the United States and led to increased scrutiny and safety safety measures across the sector. The public sharing of investigation details represented a significant step toward greater industry transparency, enabling other operators and manufacturers to learn from the incident and implement preventive measures. The Elorn battery facility fire in Moss Landing, California on September 20th, 2022 provides a particularly instructive example of dual root causes. The investigation shared publicly by Tesla, the best manufacturer and integrator, and Pacific Gas and Electric, the site owner, revealed that rainwater intrusion through the container had caused electrical arcing within the system, leading to thermal runaway. A water ingress point in the enclosure had been created when an umbrella valve was dislodged during the improper installation of a vent shield. As a confounding factor, insulation loss alarms were not properly escalated to the operator. Two days after the initial insulation alarms were recorded, smoke and fire were reported to the fire department. Appropriate reporting of the insulation loss alarms could have prevented escalation of the initial failure into a fire that consumed the entire BES unit. Consequently, the root cause was classified as both an integration, assembly, and construction failure in the BOS and a design failure of the control system. The Victoria Big Battery incident in Australia during 2021 demonstrates another critical aspect of BES failure analysis. During commissioning, a leak in the coolant system led to a fire that spread across two best units. This incident exemplifies BOS failure due to assembly quality issues and underscores the critical importance of proper commissioning procedures, monitoring and hazardous assessments during this vulnerable phase. The fact that monitoring and communication systems were not yet online during commissioning allowed the coolant leak to cascade into a major incident before detection. The operational challenges facing the best industry are multifaceted and stem largely from the rapid pace of deployment and market expansion. The industry is experiencing significant growth with many new entrance bringing products that lack long operational histories. This creates a substantial knowledge gap particularly in integration and assembly practices where proper training and experience are essential for safe and reliable operation. The best supply chain involves components from multiple suppliers which are not necessarily designed to work together, creating potential for incompatible interfaces and unexpected interactions between components. The diversity of product architectures, thermal management approaches, and system designs further complicates integration efforts. Untangling the various equipment you might see in an electrical substation.

In many ways, the grid is a one-size-fits-all system - a gigantic machine to which we all connect spinning in perfect synchrony across, in some cases, an entire continent. segments.text: When you plug in an electric device, it’s easy not to even consider where the electricity
actually comes from.
The simple answer is a power generating station, also known as a power plant, usually someplace
far away.
But the reality is much more complicated than that.
Generation is only the first of many steps our power takes on its nearly instantaneous
journey from production to consumption.
The behaviour of electricity doesn’t always follow our intuitions, which means the challenges
associated with constructing, operating, and maintaining the power grid are often complicated
and sometimes unexpected.
Many of those challenges are overcome at facility which, at first glance, often looks like a
chaotic and dangerous mess of wires and equipment, but which actually serves a number of essential
roles in our electrical grid, the substation.
I’m Grady and this is Public Works, my video series on infrastructure and the humanmade
world around us.
This video is sponsored by NordVPN.
Visit NordVPN.com/practicalengineering to get 75% off a 3-year plan. More on that later.
As simple as it is to imagine, the power grid isn’t just an interconnected series of wires
to which all power producers and users collectively connect.
In reality, the electricity normally makes its way through a series of discrete steps
on the grid normally divided into three parts: generation, or production of electricity;
transmission, or moving that electricity from centralized plants to populated areas; and
distribution, or delivering the electricity to every individual customer.
If you consider the power grid a gigantic machine (and many do), substations are the
linkages that connect the various components together.
One of the cool parts about our electrical infrastructure is that most of it is out in
the open so anyone can have a look.
I’m somewhat of an infrastructure tourist, a regular beholder of the constructed environment,
and my goal is for you too to be able to mentally untangle this maze of modern electrical engineering
so that the next time you feast your eyes on a substation, you’ll be able to appreciate
it as much as I do.
Originally named for smaller power plants that were converted for other purposes, “substation”
is now a general term for a facility that can serve a wide variety of critical roles
on the power grid.
Those roles depend on which parts of the electrical grid are being connected together and the
types, number, and reliability requirements of the eventual customers downstream.
And the first and often simplest of these roles is switching.
The general layout of a substation consists of some number of electric lines (called conductors
if you want to fit in with the electrical engineers) coming into the facility.
These high voltage conductors connect to a series of some or many pieces of equipment
before heading out to their next step in the power grid.
As a junction point in the grid, a substation often serves as the termination of many individual
power lines.
This creates redundancy, making sure that the substation stays energized even if one
transmission lines goes down.
But, it also creates complexity.
The connections to these various devices are called buses, often rigid, overhead conductors
that run along the entire substation.
The arrangement of the bus is a critical part of the design of any substation because it
can have a major impact on the overall reliability.
Like all equipment, substations occasionally have malfunctions or things that simply require
regular maintenance.
To avoid shutting down the entire substation, we need switches that can isolate equipment,
transfer load, and control the flow of electricity along the bus.
This may seem obvious, but turning on and off high voltage lines isn’t as simple as
flipping a light switch.
At high voltages, even air can act like a conductor, which means even if you create
a break in a line, electricity can continue flowing in a phenomenon known as an arc.
Not only does arcing defeat the purpose of a switch, it is incredibly dangerous and damaging
to equipment.
So, switching in a substation is a carefully-controlled procedure with specially-designed equipment
to handle high voltages.
Disconnect switches are often just called switchgear in addition to the equipment that
serves another important role in a substation: protection.
I mentioned earlier that much of our electrical infrastructure is exposed and out in the open.
That’s nice for people like me who enjoy having a look, but it also means being vulnerable
to an endless number of things that can go wrong.
From lightning strikes to rogue tree limbs, windstorms to squirrels, grid operators contend
with so many threats to their infrastructure on a day by day basis.
When something causes a short circuit on the power grid, also called a fault, it can severely
damage power lines and other equipment.
Not only that, because of the overwhelming complexity of the power grid, faults can and
do cascade in unexpected and sometimes uncontrollable ways, leaving huge populations without power
for hours or days.
Many of the ways we protect equipment from faults are handled at a substation.
One of the most common types of electrical fault is a short circuit to ground.
This type of fault creates a low-resistance path for current to flow and leads to an overload
of power lines and equipment.
The simplest way to protect against this type of fault is with a fuse, a device that physically
burns out at a certain current threshold.
Fuses are dead simple and don’t require much maintenance, but they have some disadvantage
too.
They’re one-time use and can’t be used to interrupt current for other types of faults.
On the other hand, circuit breakers are a class of devices that serve similar roles
as fuses, but provide more sophistication for dealing with a wide variety of faults.
Like disconnect switches, circuit breakers need to be carefully designed to interrupt
huge voltages and currents without damage.
As soon as contacts within a circuit breaker are moved apart from one another, an electrical
arc forms.
This arc needs to be extinguished as quickly as possible to prevent damage to the breaker
or unsafe conditions for workers.
Extinguishing the arc is accomplished by a material called a dielectric that doesn’t
conduct electricity.
For lower voltages, the circuit breakers can be located in a sealed container under vacuum
to avoid electricity conducting in the air between the contacts.
For higher voltage, breakers are often submerged in tanks filled with non-conductive oil or
dense dielectric gas.
These breakers give grid operators more control about how and when current gets interrupted.
Not every fault is the same and sometimes operators even know about a disturbance ahead
of time and can trigger breakers early to prevent cascading failures.
Many faults are temporary like lightning strikes or swaying tree branches.
A special kind of circuit breaker called a recloser can interrupt current for a short
period of time and re-energize the line to test if the fault has cleared.
Re-closers usually trip and reclose a few times, depending on their programming, before
deciding that a fault is permanent and locking out.
If electricity demand on the grid gets so high that it can’t be met by the utility,
substations may also be used to shed load.
Rolling blackouts are used to lower the total electrical demand to avoid bigger failures
on the grid.
One of the most important parts of the power grid is that different segments flow at different
voltages.
Voltage is a measure of electrical potential, somewhat equivalent to the pressure of a fluid
in a pipe.
At large power plants, electricity is produced at a somewhat low voltage of around 10-30
kilovolts or kV.
From there, the voltage is increased much higher using transformers so that it can travel
along transmission lines.
Using a higher voltage reduces the losses along the way, making them more efficient
but also much more dangerous.
This is why overhead transmission lines are so tall - to keep them out of the way of trees
and human activities.
But, when transmission lines reach the populated areas which they serve, it’s not feasible
to keep them so high in the air.
So, prior to distribution, the voltage of the grid needs to be brought back down, again
using transformers located within a substation.
A transformer is an extremely simple device that relies on the alternating current of
the grid to function.
It consists of two adjacent coils of wire.
As the voltage in one coil changes, it creates a magnetic field.
This field couples with the other coil, inducing a voltage.
The incredible part of a transformer has to do with the number of loops in each coil.
The induced voltage will be proportional to the ratio of loops.
For example, if the transmission side of a transformer has 1000 loops while the distribution
side has 100, the voltage on the distribution side will be 10 times less.
This simple but incredible fact makes it possible for us to step up or down voltage as necessary
to balance the safety and efficiency along each part of the power grid.
The simplicity of transformers is great in a lot of ways, but it also means that it can
be difficult to make fine adjustments to the power leaving the substation.
Because of this, many many substations include equipment for monitoring and controlling the
power on the grid.
Instrument transformers are small transformers used to measure the voltage or current on
the grid or provide power to system monitoring devices.
Depending on varying transmission and distribution losses, the voltage on the grid can swing
outside an acceptable range.
Regulators are devices with multiple taps that can make small adjustments - up or down
- to the distribution voltage on feeder lines leaving the substation toward customers.
If you look closely you can sometimes see the regulator dial indicating the tap position.
All that different equipment requires lots of maintenance.
The final and most important role of a substation is that it be safe for electricians and linemen
to inspect, repair, and replace equipment.
Substations are usually the only locations where extra-high voltage power lines get close
to the ground, so safety is absolutely critical.
The buswork running along the substation is protected from short-circuit by large insulators
to avoid arcs to ground.
Even the connections into each piece of equipment are done through a device called a bushing
which maintains a safe distance between energized lines and the grounded metal housings.
Some substations have large concrete walls to serve as fire barriers between equipment.
All substations are built with a grid of grounding rods and conductors buried below the surface.
In the event of a fault, the substation needs to be able to sink lots of current into the
ground to trip the breakers as quickly as possible.
This grounding grid also makes sure that the entire substation and all its equipment are
kept at the same voltage level, called an equipotential, so that touching any piece
of equipment doesn’t create a flow of electricity through a person.
Finally, substations are surrounded by large fences and warning signs to make absolutely
sure that any wayward citizens know to stay out.
In many ways, the grid is a one-size-fits-all system - a gigantic machine to which we all
connect spinning in perfect synchrony across, in some cases, an entire continent.
On the other hand, our electricity needs, including when we need it, how much we need,
and how reliably it should be delivered vary widely.
Power requirements are vastly different between a sensitive research facility and a suburban
residential neighborhood, between a military base and country club golf course, and between
a steel mill and a bowling alley.
Likewise, every electrical substation is customized to meet the needs of the infrastructure it
links together.
As the grid gets smarter, as demand patterns change, and as we (hopefully!) continue to
replace fossil fuel generation with sources of renewable energy to curb global warming,
managing our electrical infrastructure will only get more challenging.
So, substations will continue to play a critical role in controlling and protecting the power
grid.
Just like electricity on the grid, internet traffic goes through several steps along the
way.
As I sat in an airport writing this video, I was definitely wondering if one of those
steps might be a hacker or organization recording my traffic.
Unfortunately, people have come up with lots of ways to intercept web traffic and use that
information nefariously, which is why I use NordVPN.
Some web traffic is already encrypted, but I don’t want to keep track of whatever protocol

There’s no limit on bandwidth, and it works on all my devices.
I don’t leave my house unlocked when I’m away, even though I know the likelihood of

It’s just not worth the risk.
If your privacy and security online is important to you, they’re offering an awesome discount

metadata.title: Electrical Substation Layout Configurations | Radial, Tapped, LILO & Interconnected
metadata.author: Kognito Key
metadata.shortDescription:
Not every substation is built the same way, and the design choice can mean the difference between a brief outage and a total blackout.

This video covers electrical substation layout configurations. A substation adjusts and transfers high voltage electricity from power generation plants to local consumption networks. We look at the radial layout and the tapped arrangement, both of which feature a single feed source and remain vulnerable to complete power outages during equipment failures. We then cover the LILO (Line In Line Out) architecture, which routes extended distribution lines directly through newly established facilities for enhanced security, and the interconnected substation, the highest standard of safety and dependability, which links multiple alternative pathways to prevent total system blackouts.

In this video, you’ll learn:

What a substation is, and the role it plays in the power grid
How the radial layout works, and why it’s vulnerable to total outages
How the tapped arrangement compares to the radial layout
How the LILO architecture improves reliability at a higher cost
How interconnected substations prevent total system blackouts
Why interconnected networks form what’s known as the electric grid

Great for electrical engineering students studying power systems and power distribution.

Which substation layout is most common where you live? Tell me in the comments. If this helped, subscribe for more power systems concepts explained clearly, and watch next video to keep learning.
