metadata.title: Substation Design | 30–60–90–IFC | Keentel Engineering
metadata.author: Keentel Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
How does a substation electrical design progress from an early concept to a sealed, construction-ready package?

In this video, Keentel Engineering explains the 30%, 60%, 90% and Issued for Construction milestones used in professional substation design.

Each milestone has a specific purpose. The 30% package confirms the concept, the 60% package coordinates the engineering disciplines, the 90% package verifies the completed design, and the IFC package provides the sealed documents used for construction.

You will learn:

• What is included in 30%, 60%, 90% and IFC packages
• How interconnection requirements affect substation design
• When equipment ratings and fault duties are confirmed
• Why multidisciplinary coordination is critical at 60%
• How grounding, foundations and cable routes are coordinated
• The difference between a 90% package and an IFC package
• When long-lead equipment should be released for procurement
• What a licensed professional engineer’s seal represents
• How controlled revisions are handled after IFC
• How the design becomes the final as-built record

Read the complete substation electrical design guide:
https://keentelengineering.com/substation-electrical-design-process

Explore Keentel’s substation design services:
https://keentelengineering.com/service/substation-design

Chapters:

0:00 Introduction
0:43 Why Substations Are Designed in Milestones
1:30 The 30% Package: Concept and Preliminary Design
2:15 The 60% Package: Detailed Design and Coordination
3:01 The 90% Package: Checked and Review-Ready
3:51 Issued for Construction: The Final IFC Package
4:41 Deliverable Maturity at a Glance
5:50 The Licensed Professional Engineer’s Seal
6:39 The Standards Framework Behind Each Milestone
7:58 Keentel Engineering’s Substation Design Services
9:04 Case Studies: Five Milestone Progressions
10:27 Frequently Asked Questions
15:03 Conclusion

Subscribe for practical guidance on substation design, protection and control, power-system studies, grid interconnection and electrical engineering.

#SubstationDesign #SubstationEngineering #ElectricalEngineering #GridInterconnection #KeentelEngineering

segments.text: Welcome to Keintel Engineering.
Substations are not drawn in a single
pass. A safe, constructable, code
compliant substation emerges through a
disciplined sequence of design
milestones, 30%, 60%, 90%, and issued
for construction in which the design
matures from concept to a sealed build
ready package. In this video, we walk
through what each milestone delivers,
what is deliberately left unfinished at
each stage, how multiddiscipline
coordination prevents field change
costs, and how the licensed engineers
seal fits into the sequence. We also
cover the standards framework behind
each milestone, five real world case
studies, and 18 frequently asked
questions across two FAQ sections. A
substation is a tightly coupled system
of electrical, civil, structural, and
protection and control elements in a
confined footprint. No engineer designs
all of it correctly in one attempt. The
milestone model makes the design
reviewable at defined levels of
completeness, so problems surface while
they are still lines on a drawing, not
steel in the yard. The input that shapes
every milestone is the interconnection.
The system impact study establishes
point of interconnection requirements.
fault duties and metering and protection
needs. Preliminary 30% values are
explicitly meant to be validated once
the fault model is finalized. A project
that treats interconnection as an
afterthought routinely finds at 60% that
equipment selected at 30% is now
underrated. The purpose of the 30%
package is to confirm the station
concept is viable while changes are
still cheap. The key tasks at 30% are a
preliminary electrical load and capacity
basis, voltage selection and major
equipment sizing, a preliminary fault
duty basis flagged for system impact
study validation, an initial single line
diagram, and the design criteria
document, the single source of truth for
every subsequent milestone. What is
deliberately not finished at 30% matters
equally. Schematic and wiring diagrams,
detailed grounding grid calculations,
foundation design, and final equipment
specifications are intentionally
immature. Committing to that detail
before the fault model is confirmed
wastess hours. The 60% phase will erase.
The 60% package is the primary
coordination milestone, detailed enough
for a credible class 2 construction cost
estimate. The key tasks at 60% are
finalizing major equipment
specifications against validated fault
duties, developing the protection and
control scheme, detailed cable sizing
and routing, preliminary grounding grid
and lightning protection studies, and a
multiddiscipline clash review
increasingly conducted against a
coordinated 3D model. This is where
projects are won or lost. The most
common avoidable rework is a grounding
grid and a foundation or duct bank
layout designed in isolation, then
colliding in the field. Running the
clash review at 60% makes that conflict
a red line on a drawing, not a field
change order during construction. The
90% package is fully checked and
essentially ready for final issue. The
distinction from 60% is completeness and
verification, not new scope. 90% has
three dimensions. Technical adequacy
calculations support the ratings shown
and protection settings, grounding
results, clearances and equipment
selections are verified against the
design criteria. Drafting standard
compliance, borders, title blocks,
drawing numbers, symbols, and cross
references are correct and consistent.
Editorial quality, errors, omissions,
and inconsistencies between sheets are
resolved, and each calculation carries
its checklist. 90% is a verification
gate, not a design gate. If new
engineering is appearing at 90%, the 60%
package was not complete. Issued for
construction, IFC is the comprehensive
sealed package a contractor builds from.
Nothing appears at IFC that has not
already been seen and reviewed. The IFC
set contains a complete finalized sealed
construction drawing set, foundation and
grounding plans and final protection and
control schematics, conduit and cable
routing details and bill of materials,
final specifications and procurement
documentation and all 90% review
comments dispositioned and incorporated.
IFC
is a status not an endpoint. Field
conditions, vendor certified dimensions,
and requests for information generate
revisions after issue. Each tracked,
re-checked, and reissued as controlled
revisions. After construction, the
design becomes the asbuilt record set.
Every major deliverable follows a
maturity arc from concept to sealed
across the four milestones. The power
one line starts as a concept at 30%
becomes detailed at 60% and is finalized
and sealed at FFC. The protection
oneline and protection and control
package follows the same arc. The
general arrangement moves from
preliminary layout to detailed to
sealed. Grounding and lightning
protection begin with a design basis
referencing ILE E80 and ILE E 998 at 30%
become a preliminary study at 60% and
reach a final sealed calculation at FC.
Cable and conduit schedules progress
from routing concept to detailed sizing
to final sealed schedules. Major
equipment specifications move from an
equipment list at 30% to near final
specification at 60% to issued for
procurement at IFC. The bill of
materials develops at 60% and is
finalized at IFC. The construction cost
estimate is preliminary at 30% and class
2 capable at 60%. The engineer's seal on
a substation drawing carries three
implications. Responsible charge. The
ceiling engineer exercised direct
control and personal supervision of the
work. The seal is not a rubber stamp.
Jurisdiction. The ceiling engineer must
hold a current license in the state
where the project is located. Regardless
of where the engineering firm is based.
Accountability. The seal ties the work
to a named licensed individual who is
professionally and legally accountable
under that state's engineering practice
act. Sealing generally occurs at final
issue IFC and sometimes a subsequent
100% interim packages at 30% and 60% are
typically marked preliminary or not for
construction and are not sealed because
they are explicitly subject to change.
11 ILE E standards and several codes
govern substation design across the
milestone sequence for grounding and
personnel safety, ILE E80 for grounding
grid design, ILE E1 for resistivity

connections for protection automation
and control IE C37.2 2 for device

videos.full_text: Welcome to Keintel Engineering. Substations are not drawn in a single pass. A safe, constructable, code compliant substation emerges through a disciplined sequence of design milestones, 30%, 60%, 90%, and issued for construction in which the design matures from concept to a sealed build ready package. In this video, we walk through what each milestone delivers, what is deliberately left unfinished at each stage, how multiddiscipline coordination prevents field change costs, and how the licensed engineers seal fits into the sequence. We also cover the standards framework behind each milestone, five real world case studies, and 18 frequently asked questions across two FAQ sections. A substation is a tightly coupled system of electrical, civil, structural, and protection and control elements in a confined footprint. No engineer designs all of it correctly in one attempt. The milestone model makes the design reviewable at defined levels of completeness, so problems surface while they are still lines on a drawing, not steel in the yard. The input that shapes every milestone is the interconnection. The system impact study establishes point of interconnection requirements. fault duties and metering and protection needs. Preliminary 30% values are explicitly meant to be validated once the fault model is finalized. A project that treats interconnection as an afterthought routinely finds at 60% that equipment selected at 30% is now underrated. The purpose of the 30% package is to confirm the station concept is viable while changes are still cheap. The key tasks at 30% are a preliminary electrical load and capacity basis, voltage selection and major equipment sizing, a preliminary fault duty basis flagged for system impact study validation, an initial single line diagram, and the design criteria document, the single source of truth for every subsequent milestone. What is deliberately not finished at 30% matters equally. Schematic and wiring diagrams, detailed grounding grid calculations, foundation design, and final equipment specifications are intentionally immature. metadata.title: Phinergy and Rosendin Unlock New Grid Capacity for Data Centers
metadata.author: IVY Press Room
metadata.shortDescription:
Hello, I’m an AI digital avatar of Josh Weiss, President of 10 to 1 Public Relations. Not the real Josh Weiss. Here’s a Q&A Recap of a press release distributed on Nov. 2, 2026 by Phinergy titled Phinergy and Rosendin Unlock New Grid Capacity for Data Centers. For more information, you can also visit the website one, zero, letters T, O, the number one, letter P as in Public, R as in Relations, dot com forward slash ivypressroom forward slash phinergy.

How can data centers connect to the power grid faster when utilities can't deliver full capacity?
Phinergy's aluminum-air generator helps data centers jump ahead of the interconnection queue by acting as a grid-flexibility resource that reduces peak demand on the grid. According to a white paper released by Phinergy and Rosendin Electric, if data centers reduce grid demand for just 1 percent of annual operating hours, existing U.S. electricity systems could integrate up to 70 gigawatts of new data center capacity without a single grid upgrade.

How does clean backup power technology address increasing state restrictions on diesel generators at data centers?
More than 45 states now have moratoriums or restrictions affecting new data center development, largely driven by concerns over diesel generator emissions, noise and strain on local grids. Phinergy's aluminum-air generator delivers clean, quiet, community-friendly backup power as a direct replacement for diesel generators, and Rosendin Electric has validated the AAG as a solution that meets stringent planning and local conditions for development.

What alternatives to diesel generators are available for data center backup power?
A white paper released by Phinergy and Rosendin Electric compares the aluminum-air generator directly against diesel generators and lithium-ion battery systems as backup power options for data centers. The AAG offers a zero-emission profile, multi-day runtime, compact footprint and the ability to integrate into existing data center architectures, and unlike diesel generators, Phinergy's AAG operates cleanly and quietly, making it compatible with increasingly strict state and local environmental requirements.

How can data center operators reduce environmental impact without sacrificing uptime or reliability?
Phinergy's aluminum-air generator is designed to deliver clean backup power while maintaining the reliability that data center operators require for AI inference and cloud workloads. Rosendin Electric Senior Vice President Bill Mazzetti confirmed that data center clients are asking for power solutions that reduce environmental impact without sacrificing uptime, and the AAG delivers on both, providing clean, quiet and resilient on-premises power.

What impact will rising AI workloads have on U.S. grid infrastructure and data center power demand?
U.S. data center electricity consumption could reach 380 to 790 terawatt-hours by 2030, representing 9 to 17 percent of total U.S. electricity consumption, according to EPRI's Powering Intelligence 2026 report cited by Phinergy. The surge in AI workloads is driving data center demand into direct conflict with grid capacity constraints, requiring new approaches to power flexibility, and Phinergy and Rosendin Electric released a white paper outlining how aluminum-air generation can serve as a strategic flexibility tool for the AI era.

Which technologies are transforming backup power systems for high-density AI data centers?
Aluminum-air generation is emerging as a transformative alternative to traditional diesel generators and battery systems for AI-era data centers. Phinergy's aluminum-air generator functions as a grid-flexibility resource while simultaneously providing clean emergency backup power, a dual capability not available from conventional diesel systems, and Phinergy recently completed a module milestone validation through the Net Zero Innovation Hub for Data Centers, moving the technology closer to full scalability for hyperscale operators.

What features matter most when selecting a backup power solution for a data center in a power-constrained market?
According to a white paper by Phinergy and Rosendin Electric, the most critical features for backup power in power-constrained markets include zero-emission performance, multi-day runtime, a compact footprint and the ability to function as a grid-flexibility resource.

This video explains how the power auction system works, why wholesale prices near some clusters have spiked as much as 267%, and who actually ends up paying for the grid upgrades. Try it for 7 days. No card needed. https://techdamentals.com/?ref=yt https://techdamentals.com/newsletter?ref=yt

segments.text: A powergrid called PJM, which covers
Virginia and 12 other states, saw its
wholesale electricity price jump 11
times in 2 years.
That is not because the power plants
themselves got more expensive to run.
Here is why. Data centers built for
artificial intelligence are plugging
into the grid faster than new power
plants or wires can be built.
Before we get into it, if you like this
video, please give it a like and
subscribe to the channel.
It would tremendously help a small
channel like mine keep producing quality
videos and more of them.
Electricity is priced in layers before
it ever reaches your house.
First, someone has to generate it at a
power plant. Second, someone has to move
it over long-distance wires called
transmission.
Third, someone moves it from a
neighborhood substation to your house
called distribution.
Most of the eastern half of the country
runs its power plants through an auction
system.
The biggest one is a system called PJM,
covering 13 states including Virginia.
Virginia has the largest cluster of data
centers in the world. Once a year, PJM
runs an auction where power plant owners
bid to promise electricity for the
hottest day of the year.
That auction price is called a capacity
price and it gets passed into everyone's
bill.
In the 2024 to 2025 auction, that price
per megawatt day.
One year later, for 2026 to 2027, it hit
the maximum allowed under federal rules.
Data centers built for artificial
intelligence need enormous amounts of
electricity and they need it now.
New power plants and transmission lines
take years of approval and construction
before they can help. When a huge new
customer arrives faster than new power
plants, the auction price spikes for
everyone in the region.
The data center itself is an old idea,
not a new one.
The first purpose-built computer room is
usually traced to a government computer
called ENIAC, which went live in 1946.
By 1963, companies and government
agencies were building dedicated cooled
rooms just to house mainframe computers.
When cloud computing arrived in the
2000s, companies stopped keeping servers
in their own office closets and rented
space in shared facilities instead.
None of that early history had anything
to do with artificial intelligence.
Every time you check a bank balance,
stream a show, or save a photo, a data
center is doing the work.
Most existing data center capacity still
runs ordinary cloud storage and business
software, not artificial intelligence.
AI servers are a new and very
power-hungry tenant moving into a
building type that was already large and
already growing.
An AI server rack can use far more
electricity than the ordinary servers
that run email or web pages.
Global data center electricity demand is
set to jump about 26 to 27% in 2026 to
roughly 565 terawatt hours.
That growth is concentrated enough in
certain places that it does not spread
out evenly across the country.
Building a new power plant or a major
transmission line used to be fast, and
it has gotten much slower.
A US Department of Energy research lab
found that power projects finished
between 2000 and 2007 took under 2 years
to connect.
Projects completed between 2018 and 2023
took a median of 5 years, and only 19%
of all requests from that period had
been built by late 2023.
A new power plant or transmission line
now takes a median of 5 years to connect
to the grid.
A data center, by contrast, can often be
built and wired for power in just 1 to 2
years.
A new power plant moves at the speed of
years of permits and construction.
A new data center moves at the speed of
months of construction and a grid
connection request.
That mismatch is a big reason prices
spike in specific places instead of
rising smoothly everywhere.
When a new data center asks a utility to
connect, the utility often has to spend
money on new substations, transformers,
or lines.
Historically, those costs were spread
across every rate payer in the utility's
territory.

metadata.title: Powering the AI Boom: Co-locating Batteries with Data Centers
metadata.author: FlexGen
metadata.shortDescription:
How can hyperscale and AI data centers connect to the grid faster while protecting power quality? FlexGen explains how data center co-location with battery energy storage can smooth volatile loads, accelerate interconnection, and de-risk projects.

Co-location began on the generation side of the meter, pairing batteries with wind and solar to firm up intermittent renewable output. Today, it is becoming just as critical on the load side of the meter, especially for hyperscale data centers operating at hundreds of megawatts with rapid, AI-driven transient loads. 

Modern AI training workloads can create massive step loads, with demand spiking from zero to full power and back again in milliseconds. Those fast transients can outpace traditional grid infrastructure, creating challenges for utilities, developers, and mission-critical facilities that require pristine power quality. 

In this video, FlexGen explores how battery energy storage systems can act as a shock absorber between the data center and the grid. By placing storage behind a single point of interconnection, co-location can help:

• Smooth volatile data center power demand
• Improve power quality for sensitive server loads
• Reduce the impact of AI-driven step loads
• Accelerate or de-risk utility interconnection approvals
• Support grid caps and site operating limits
• Enable islanding during grid outages
• Keep critical data center operations online
• Coordinate generation, load, and storage in real time

FlexGen’s HybridOS™ serves as the digital brain of the site, orchestrating batteries, generation, and load so data centers can operate reliably within grid limits. Whether managing a utility-imposed cap, bridging capacity gaps, islanding during an outage, or resynchronizing with the grid, HybridOS enables the fast-response control modern data centers require.

Co-location is no longer just a renewable generation strategy. For AI infrastructure, hyperscale data centers, and critical power facilities, it is becoming a practical architecture for faster grid connection, cleaner power profiles, and more resilient operations.

Learn how FlexGen can de-risk your next energy storage or data center power project.

voltage volatility is highest and where

data center.

the foundations of conventional power
system design.

storage that has a single point of

bringing their own power capacity on
site, developers can bypass or

traditional grid expansion.

colocation allows you to leverage
existing capacity today, transforming a
delayed project into a connected site.

shock absorber, smoothing out power
fluctuations and ensuring the draw from
the grid is smooth and predictable.
This has become critical for data
centers.
Unlike a standard industrial warehouse,
data centers house highly sensitive
servers that require pristine power
quality and leave little margin for
fluctuations in voltage or frequency.

power demands that spike from zero to
100% and back again in milliseconds.
These violent transients outpace the
physical limits of traditional grid
infrastructure. Conventional power
plants rely on the mechanical inertia of
massive spinning turbines, heavy
equipment that simply cannot ramp up or
down quickly enough to match these rapid
swings in power demand. And this can
lead to severe equipment damage and
system instability.

facility, but also threatens the
mechanics of the local grid. This is why
utilities are often reluctant to approve
massive volatile loads without first
undertaking time-consuming studies and
expensive long-term grid upgrades.

point of interconnection, you introduce
an instantaneous response to the site's
power profile. The system can ramp up or
down in a fraction of a second.
By doing this, it absorbs the wild
swings in power demand that are unique
to data centers.
From the grid's perspective, when you
colocate your data center with
batteries, your facility no longer looks
like a volatile, high-impact burden.
Instead, it looks like a smaller,
stabilized load that fits within the
grid's current limits.
This load smoothing effectively de-risks
the project, potentially allowing you to
secure interconnection approvals years
earlier by proving you won't stress the
local network.
Managing two distinct asset classes at
one site creates a level of complexity
that basic controllers simply can't
handle effectively. Without intelligent
orchestration, your asset and your
battery can actually end up competing
for the same limited inverter capacity.
FlexGen's Hybrid OS serves as the site's
digital brain, providing the precise,
real-time coordination needed to
navigate complex operational hurdles.
For example, if the utility dictates you
cannot exceed a 50 MW limit on a
particularly hot day, Hybrid OS
intelligently throttles on-site
generation while using the battery to
bridge the gap.
This ensures the data center stays at
100% capacity without ever violating the
grid's cap. And during a total grid
failure, the system can island the site
to keep the servers running
independently.
When the grid returns, Hybrid OS will
manage the delicate resynchronization
process, matching the utility's
frequency perfectly to prevent any dips
in power quality that would otherwise
trigger costly outages.
Ultimately, Colocation serves as the
critical release valve, minimizing the
impact of curtailment on both sides of
the meter. It enables generators to
maximize their yield while providing the
fast response, full capacity power that

Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are becoming an increasingly important part of modern data center infrastructure. But adding a BESS to a data center campus is more than simply connecting a battery to the electrical system.

In this video, we explore how BESS integration impacts data center power quality, harmonics, voltage stability, grid strength, resonance, protection, ride-through performance, and overall electrical system behavior.

The key engineering insight is simple: the battery stores the energy, but the inverter determines what the grid actually sees.

For data center owners, developers, utilities, EPC contractors and electrical engineers, understanding these issues early in the design process can help prevent costly power-quality problems, interconnection delays and commissioning issues.

metadata.title: Why AI Data Centers Are Overwhelming the Grid (It’s Not Just Generation)
metadata.author: The Clean Energy Edge Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
AI data centers are being announced and built at a pace the U.S. electric grid was never designed for — and the biggest constraint isn’t generation. It’s substations and grid infrastructure.

In this episode of The Clean Energy Edge Podcast, Russ Bates is joined by Ben Watkins, P.E., Vice President at ARM Group, to break down what’s really happening behind the scenes as AI-driven load reshapes the power system.

This conversation goes beyond headlines to explain why AI data centers are fundamentally different from traditional data centers, how extreme load volatility stresses substations and transmission systems, and why grid upgrades are becoming the pacing item for development across the U.S.

🔍 What this episode covers:

The key differences between traditional vs. AI data centers

Why AI training workloads create massive, near-instantaneous load swings

How substations actually work — and why they’re a critical bottleneck

Why upgrading one substation can trigger cascading grid impacts

New vs. existing substation upgrades and siting challenges

Supply-chain and equipment lead-time constraints (transformers, breakers, insulators)

Why engineering decisions are increasingly driven by timeline, not optimization

The role of batteries and fast-ramping generation in managing AI load

Why early engineering coordination is essential for successful projects

What developers, utilities, municipalities, and communities should understand before approving AI data centers

Ben works at the intersection of substation engineering, grid infrastructure, and large-scale project execution, supporting complex energy and industrial projects across the U.S.

🔗 About ARM Group

ARM Group provides multidisciplinary engineering, environmental, and project support services for complex energy, infrastructure, and industrial projects nationwide.

🌐 Website: https://www.armgroup.net/ 

📧 Email: info@armgroup.net

metadata.title: 219. Spiky AI Loads Are Forcing a Rethink of Data Center Power
metadata.author: The POWER Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
The way artificial intelligence (AI) data centers draw power may be a harder problem for utilities than how much they draw. Training clusters can swing load by large amounts in milliseconds, and many facilities drop offline when the grid is stressed, which can make a grid problem worse.

In this episode of The POWER Podcast, POWER Executive Editor Aaron Larson talks with Brad Witter, senior vice president of Industrial Digital at Generac, about what fundamentally changes with AI loads and how the power architecture around them is evolving. Topics include:

• Why AI training loads are spikier than those of traditional data centers, and why that matters for both grid operators and on-site generation.
• What utilities are asking of hyperscalers, including bringing their own generation and limiting load swings.
• How battery energy storage and grid-forming inverters can act as a buffer between data centers and the grid.
• Why validating these systems depends on utility-scale simulation, since no one can build a half-gigawatt proof of concept.
• How Generac is approaching integrated power solutions, and where AI itself can help solve the problems it creates.

Witter also shares what he thinks will separate the data centers that get their power strategy right from those that don’t.

For more on the conversation, read the companion article at: https://www.powermag.com/spiky-ai-loads-are-forcing-a-rethink-of-data-center-power.

videos.full_text: Hi everyone. This is Aaron Larson, executive editor of Power Magazine, and you're listening to the Power Podcast. On today's episode, I'm joined by Brad Ritter, who is senior vice president of Industrial Digital with Generac. So Brad, thank you for joining me. Please tell a little bit about yourself and and your background. >> Sure. Thanks, Aaron. So I joined Generac through an acquisition about four years ago, and I focus on industrial technology kind of from pre-sales to post-sales and everything in between for our global solutions, especially as we align with this expansion we're seeing in the data center market. >> People hear about AI data centers and and they tend to think about the scale and the the massive power demand that they require, but from your perspective, what fundamentally [clears throat] changes compared to, you know, traditional hyperscale locations or or colocation when when you look at the load for AI data centers? >> Yeah, I think it comes in in two or three different categories, and I think most people can understand that just the density of the load of these new AI-centered hyperscale locations is unprecedented. You know, I think the the latest data center, you know, that's being proposed in Utah is equal to the entire state's load. So just the magnitude and impact of that amount of load going over our grid, and we've heard, you know, for decades that our grid's eventually going to be in trouble. This is really pushing the edge of what the grid is capable of delivering from a load and capacity perspective, but it isn't just the magnitude, it's the activity that AI, you know, puts into the grid from a power perspective. So AI training data centers have very, very spiky loads. So when you take potentially the largest load on a grid from a distribution feeder perspective and you say it's going to swing up down 50% you know at an millisecond level you know as it does its thing that's a very very tricky thing for the grid to to handle. Grids like really stable you know not fluctuating kind of load patterns so that they can prepare they can predict and they can uh uh deliver and the spikiness is every bit as much of a problem as the magnitude is. The third thing is when grids see intermittent issues when they're struggling typically these data centers are very very sensitive to power quality so when the grid starts struggling a lot of times they will automatically go offline which actually creates a really bad situation for the utility making a bad problem even worse. So it's grid fault response so those are kind of the three things the magnitude the spikiness and then the fault intolerance of some of these load centers you know when when the grid does struggle. >> You did talk about the spikiness. What specifically do AI loads do different from from those traditional data centers? >> Yeah it is it's the training of the models that they go through which where they're where they're uh processing really really large amounts of data so when these GPUs are all clustered together working on the same workload so let's say a thousand of GPUs sitting together working on one model when that step is done and they move on to the next step or there's an interruption they all interrupt at once right so I think that the uniqueness here is if in a traditional data center you might have thousands of nodes of compute all interacting and working somewhat independently right so one would spin up one would spin down and so the load factor of a normal data center would much be much flatter right because they all kind of balance each other up when they go up and down whereas these clustered units all work together so when one goes up they all go up and so that's what really is is generating that that spikiness. >> With that in mind, are you seeing any like early warning signs for example that that traditional data center power architectures are being pushed beyond maybe their original design or assumptions? >> Yeah, and that comes in a couple flavors as well. I mean, obviously we'll talk about the utility impact of this because it's extremely challenging to the utility, but from a hyperscaler, you know, behind the meter sense on the load side, it's also a big challenge because anytime we do off-grid power or bridge power solutions where people bring their own power, which in certain cases they have to or whether it be in the case of a utility backup solution like diesel generators, all of that power generation source is spinning and it does not like that spikiness. In fact, you know, turbines can actually be damaged when you go up and down that much and can crack things and break things when when that has that spikiness of load. So trying to flatten that load is both in the interest of the onsite generation and backup capacity and capability as well as what's sitting, you know, from a front of the meter, you know, utility facing as well. So it's a problem for everybody that creates power. Spikiness is like the the one thing you don't want to get in terms of predictability and and uh generation perspectives. >> And I'd like to talk about kind of the push and pull that goes on between utilities and AI developers because developers, of course, are racing to deploy capacity as fast as they can while the utilities have to figure out a way to connect these unusually large loads. So where do those different priorities come into conflict that that you've seen? >> Well, I think you hit the nail on the head, which is, you know, the developers want to go faster and the utilities want to go slower, right? They cannot turn on a dime and add an extra 50% of capacity, you know, into an already struggling infrastructure from a from a capacity perspective. So so that does put them at odds. So there're a lot of different things happening, FERC's getting involved. There are a lot of new paths to market that folks are looking for and and I think you will see more and more that these hyperscalers in the agreements that they ink with utilities to go faster, they will take on a bigger portion of the investment required, you know, into the market. But what from a practical perspective what we're seeing is a lot of utilities are requiring hyperscalers to bring their own generation, right? So they have to augment their generation capability with onsite capabilities such as turbines or fuel cells, etc. Any type of thing to kind of offset that in the interim while the you know, while the utility catches up. The other thing is they have to behave differently when they do connect to the grid. So if you look at the grid's ultimate capacity, you want to be able to limit the impact of that new load on there from that spikiness component. So a lot of the utilities are requiring certain things from these large load centers to come online and behaviors that in the past have been impossible for them to achieve at at any kind of scale that would limit the spikiness, it would limit what they did during a grid fault to make it better for the grid. So the grid's in a bit of a uh they can kind of say what they need from these large loads as they come online. So it's put them in a position where they can help mitigate some of the challenges that they have with this and and build kind of a common interest amongst themselves to how we can go fast. But it is certainly there [clears throat] is lots and lots of time being dedicated in the industry right now on how to bridge that gap, you know, to get where we we ultimately go with with a larger you know, grid source uh available. >> Would you say that the utilities and grid operators are kind of in the driver's seat and they can uh specify what behaviors and designs are necessary before they connect a a AI data center? >> I >> mean I I think by nature yes, in general. You know, but there's also other things that that would compel them to want to go faster for community benefits and you know revenue and and different things. So I would say I I would cautiously say yes, they're in the driver's seat from the perspective of getting the how we're going to get this load connected and what the criteria is, which is a good place for them to be, right? And and so I think it's a good balance of power with with the customer demand, driving speed, but then being able to kind of mandate how that speed is is going to be managed. So I I think it's a good balance as we figure out what what we these compromises are looking like. >> Sure. And you you mentioned the speed and that's kind of a buzzword we hear a lot nowadays about speed to power, how fast can we get these gas turbines online or engines online or other sources of power online. So the idea that it would be worthwhile and beneficial for them to invest in their own power plant infrastructure, you know, with turbine infrastructure etc. based on natural gas, that that would be unprecedented before that it would be cost effective from a total value to the hyperscaler that they would invest in their own power plant as a bridge to when the utility can do that. And, know, the the hyperscalers are going as fast as they can to to get this capacity put in place. >> And if the traditional backup power can only serve part of the solution, what does uh more modern power architecture look like for AI data centers? >> Yeah, it's a good question cuz, you know, first of all, say what what is amazing when you get into this density of power in in a single facility. When you start thinking about the numbers, if if you look at even a 200 megawatt location, you you could be looking at hundreds of generators on that particular site to serve that backup need. And then when you think about the diesel fuel capacity and all this stuff, it is massive infrastructure people are putting in place. They need to be able to have that backup power, but they need to be able to integrate with the grid differently. And really, what we are seeing and what a lot of the utility requirements are kind of creating is this need for a buffer. And that really comes in the form of energy storage. We're kind of on the third leg of this stool of challenge. And it also can provide a smoothing capability to help on the backup power side of things, you know, when they're they're off-grid as well. So we see a lot of that coming. I I think it could come from two different sources as well, the UPS providers. You know, their UPS infrastructure is huge in the data center and that's always there and and really kind of protects power with batteries at the edge, you know, kind of in the rack where the GPUs are located. However, they don't really help with any kind of load smoothing or grid stability kind of issues. And so I think you'll see UPS providers are intending to push their capabilities closer out to the meter while battery energy storage can kind of stand alone at that front line as an opportunity to to be that bigger buffer. You could call it a facility UPS infrastructure. So I think those are the two solutions you'll see UPS is creeping up closer to the meter and supporting some of those those use cases as well as battery energy storage being almost a necessity for some of the utility requirements that we're seeing as kind of table stakes for getting that error connect agreement secured. >> I actually had the opportunity to visit operational data center out in DC during our data center power exchange event and it is amazing to see the backup power that they have on site. So it's it is quite amazing to see. >> Yeah, absolutely. >> So we also hear about grid forming inverters. What are they and and why could they matter in AI infrastructure? >> Well, if the batteries are the buffer, you know, the inverters are the delivery of that buffer. So there there are there are new inverter technologies that are basically, I'd say, high-speed inverters. So what they can do is connected in parallel to the loads. I mean, that's exactly what we're talking about. You remember when you had to download the drivers and try to get them to work on the specific operating system and then get everything at the BIOS level. That is exactly the complication that happens. You're just dealing with multi-million dollar pieces of equipment and trying then to get them all tweaked and tuned uh to work together. That is the type of work. And so the more integrated that package is out of the box, the better it's going to be for the the overall solution for sure. >> Of course, there's a paradox that 's going on with AI because AI is all of these issues with power, but at the same time, it can be very helpful in solving a lot of the power problems and challenges that we're facing. So, I'd like to get your perspective and Generac's perspective on what you're using AI for to perhaps improve equipment life cycles and and other systems. >> Yeah. So, I mean, there's a lot going on in the industry right now. I think it starts with just engineering, you know, efficiency on the user level side. So, we obviously use a lot of AI at the user level or the employee level. That that's pretty obvious. I think then other areas are system modeling and even looking at machine learning to look at predictive failure algorithms and how can we run our, you know, plants more efficiently? How can we increase our quality systems with things like vision systems that, you know, with AI enabled that our manufacturing facilities? So, we're looking at all of that as a way to build better product and then very quickly learn from the data that we get from the field to improve that. So, that that continuous development loop just to build better products. But then on the market side, you know, I think I just was meeting with someone this morning who was talking about a research project that was showing how large language models can really be used to to speed up all of this solution and simulation capability that's required to really kind of prove how these things are all going to work together. So, I think then on the system implementation and customer-facing side, that modeling is going to provide a lot of capability and horsepower that would, you know, traditionally have been very brute forced in terms of, you know, proving whether things can work and and modeling that. And I think just even in the power system alone, I think predictive load forecasting and all of this has been going on in years at the utility level, but I think with this complexity and this this interaction with the grid that a lot of these large load centers are having to have, you'll more of this AI capability from a forecasting perspective really play into their distribution management and load management strategies at the facility. So it's kind of, you know, encapsulating all of that and I think we're we're seeing this, but it's it's an ironic circular loop where AI is creating the very problem that AI is going to help solve, which is an interesting interesting perspective of things. But but we we definitely see that that there's a there's an equality there that's in the circular loop of this thing. >> So when you look, you know, let's say five years ahead, what do you think will distinguish the AI data centers that got their power strategy right from those that maybe didn't? >> This is going to seem like not a very intellectual statement, but first of all that they got online and that they've been able to to activate, right? Because I think when you look at the the time frame of some of these things, I think one of the biggest challenges is to work out an agreement with the utility that ultimately you know becomes beneficial to both parties and is actually actionable and deliverable so that they deliver the power systems that they need to operate their facilities. So I think, you know, the biggest challenge in all this is this are very very complicated power systems that have to happen you know very very quickly and we're testing out a lot of new technologies and capabilities that that haven't fully been proven you know in that marketplace. So I think the ones that get it right are the ones that work and I know that sounds kind of elementary, but I think that's one of those things. And then I think in the cases of where they have to build bridging power solutions where they have to build something now, those that figure out how that will ultimately transition into supporting their site when it does get connected to the utility, they those will see the maximum benefit from the investment, right? So they don't have to rip stuff out and they don't have to replace it, but that just becomes a seamless transition to win that power capability from the utilities available. So I think to some extent it's, you know, when the the tree that produces the great the good fruits going to be the one that got it right from a macro perspective. >> Well, it's going to be fun to see because you know you think back five years ago, I don't think I even knew what AI was yet at that point and today I can't imagine living without it. So it's it's just a crazy world that we're living in. >> So It is. It's going as fast I mean obviously in our lifetime we haven't seen anything that's moved this fast before and I think it is accelerating every day is not showing any signs of of slowing down and I think a lot of people talk about is this a bubble? You know in all bubbles I've ever seen you still end up having a step function in terms of growth even if it backs off in outer years we're still at an unprecedented level of investment over the next you know decade in terms of building out this capacity and you know the big interesting thing I I look at is in five years what will the AI models and power requirements be because I think the the transformation comes when someone figures out how to deliver AI at 1/100th of the power cost. Then we have an interesting capacity perspective in terms of well if all the sudden the new models require a lot less power that that's a transformation that I think is where it'll be interesting to see where that goes because we're still at the infancy of this capability. It's still very much a brute force technology right now that power is is is powering but it'll be interesting to see as the models become and the technology become more efficient how that allows us to scale as well. >> Well, it's been a really interesting conversation and I appreciate your time Brad again for listeners. I've been speaking with Brad Witter who is senior vice president of Industrial Digital with Generac. Do you have any last words to leave the audience with? >> Not really. I appreciate you having me on the show always excited to talk about this as we're in an unprecedented level of change and it's going to be interesting right over the next couple of years for sure. Just thanks for having me. >> All right. Thank you Brad.

metadata.title: Why Tech Companies Are Quietly Cancelling AI Data Centers
metadata.author: Economy Media
metadata.shortDescription:
Why Tech Companies Are Quietly Cancelling AI Data Centers

Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, tech companies have invested hundreds of billions of dollars in AI infrastructure, especially data centers and GPUs. However, many projects are now being delayed or canceled due to electrical grid limitations, rising energy costs, and shortages of key electrical components. 

Experts also believe Nvidia has overestimated future demand for AI chips, encouraging companies like Google, OpenAI, and Oracle to buy excessive amounts of GPUs. 

Although Nvidia achieved record profits, its growing inventory suggests possible oversupply and supply chain concerns. If demand continues slowing, many planned AI data centers may never become operational.

metadata.title: How Tiny Data Centers Could Solve AI’s Power Crunch
metadata.author: Latitude Media
metadata.shortDescription:
We’ve been sold a very specific story about AI data centers: bigger is always better. But is that true?

There’s no question that we need a lot more computation to push the limits of large language models. But there’s a new debate emerging around how it should get built. 

Over the last year, distributed computing has gained attention as a possible solution to the challenges facing data centers. They’re being framed as a way to avoid costly grid upgrades, reduce local opposition, use empty office buildings, and even give homeowners a financial stake in AI.

It’s turning into a distributed energy story. Companies like Span, Sunrun, Arcadia, and Generate Capital are exploring residential and commercial compute nodes paired with solar and batteries. Others, like Perimeter, are turning old office buildings into data centers.

So far, the market is very small. But what would it take to scale these models? And are there hidden impacts on the grid that we need to consider?

This week, Jim Kapsis, CEO of the Ad Hoc Group, joins us to explore the concept. He recently wrote about distributed data centers for The Gist newsletter. 

Plus, we talk about the fallout from Jensen Huang’s departure from NVIDIA, and explore some storylines in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections.

And so I think that's one. There's placing them at substations where there is headroom. So utility owned substations. I think Eprey has done some studies there and is is piling something at one or more substations. So that's interesting. There's the actual like the commercial buildings themselves. I'm a little less optimistic there's many opportunities inside buildings because it turns out retrofitting a building to make it work for like a data center that like can actually handle Yeah and if you don't own the building like who's doing it? >> you fire codes and weight of the servers >> cooling like fiber all these things that you need it seems really hard. Not there might be some edge cases where it where it works, but I think really hard. And I think if you can find maybe in suburban, exurban parks like buildings that have parking lots and they have large interconnects and have headroom, you can stick a modular data center, like a prefab data center, right? Like there are companies like Armada or Flexnode and others that are like in that market, um Crusoe, etc. And those can get, right, deployed. And I'm I'm kind of interested in going you mentioned EV charging. You know, we are seeing a good amount of money going into despite where we are in EVs at this exact moment in this country, although, you know, as one friend of mine just said, the Iran war might have been the the best thing for climate that Trump ever did. But the you know, if we if we start moving in the right direction on EVs, we we are building a good amount of level three charges in this country. But the utilization rates aren't particularly good. I mean, I think on average it's like 15% in the most used areas it's like 30%. I mean, that's a lot of opportunity. Those are really big interconnects and there's a lot of capacity there. And so I've been talking to folks in that space and they're just been looking at it. But where it's going to get really interesting is where I think there's a big potential opportunity, the way that those were set up is that with regulators and utilities is that there are special EV rates that those facilities are on. And the way that those rates were written, you can't actually add something like a major additional load and still be on the EV rate. So either they're going to have to make changes to the rate structure, which the good news about that is that will be out in the public, it'll be transparent, it'll be a conversation, it may take a little while. Or, I was talking to my team about this having looked into it, it may be possible to switch to opt out of the EV tariff, just go onto a normal CNI tariff and colocate a data center and now you're no longer on the special tariff, you're on your normal tariff, but you don't care because you're using so much power, you're getting so much revenue that everyone's ending up better off in the end. So I think that's an interesting I'm really interested about that space that we'll see how it evolves, but there's going to be some regulatory work that has to happen potentially, but there seems like there is, you know, I think there are, you know, many gigawatts available capacity that it only growing as we build out more and more L3 chargers and those L3 chargers are getting bigger, right? That's not like 250 kilowatt hours in Europe. I think now they're deploying thousand kilowatt chargers. So we're going to see bigger chargers with larger capacity, which might be good opportunity for co-location and more utilization, >> What do you guys think about the residential model, you know, led by Span and Sunrun? It's the home battery provides backup, grid services, and also keeps the GPUs online. So it seems like, you know, you have multiple use cases that could come into conflict. What do you think about the actual use of GPUs as part of a solar and battery system and is it a model that will actually tie enough to compute together? Anybody have strong opinions on it? >> I think that there is a a certain percentage of the residential population that will buy in, but I still think that the vast majority of homeowners are skeptical and just want their energy bills to be simple and be left alone. And so I don't think it's for everyone. I don't. Like and I would be like to be proven wrong on that, but I think my my gut is that the vast majority of people will not buy into that, but I think the ones that that do is is substantial, maybe like 10 percent, you know? And that's a substantial amount and you could do something with it. I question whether the interoperability of the grid is strong enough to make that work at the distribution level and what additional um you know, as likes to say, these idiots out there didn't know how hard it was to build a power plant. They didn't know what they were doing at the hyperscale level. I question whether people know what they're doing at the aggregate distribution level. >> I think that's exactly right. I think so [laughter] I mean >> Oh yeah. >> my I think >> So much so much agreement. It's disgusting. >> I know. I mean so my client's the largest deployer of distributed data centers in the country and called available infrastructure and the bigger challenge for me as a project finance guy is that, you know, what you find is for the 5 megawatt data centers and up you can get 3 to 5 year offtakes really easily. So there's a ton of banks, others who want to buy that compute. Um, when you start going towards the 250 kilowatt data centers, so we're rolling out 5,000 data centers at Crown Castle Towers right now for instance across the country. Um, those data centers get their contracts from smart cities players. So think LG and IBM who like control traffic lights or are providing services to Waymo or other things, right? But those are not ubiquitous. So those have very high returns because they're selling their tokens merchant. But you know, for folks who want long-term contracts, you have to wait for those smart city folks to win the local contract for controlling traffic lights or whatever it is before you get your long-term contract, right? And so part of the problem with residential is that you can certainly do it and it's a lot of money. You know, it's like $150,000 to put this thing in your garage or outside. Um, but you're getting merchant tokens, right? So it's not a long-term fixed price uh offtake. And so like part of the challenge I think we're going to have with these distributed data centers is the CTOs who are buying these this compute have not gotten comfortable with data centers below five megawatts yet. >> Full disclosure, we work with Span uh and my my sense of the residential market, at least in their experience is that uh new construction is a lot easier and being able to sell you know across multiple homes all at once >> yeah. >> New cul-de-sacs. Uh and also it's just part of that it's part of the community, it's part of the kind of the deal. And I think what's interesting at least with what they're putting forward and and there are some other players that have not announced that they're doing this too by the way that I think is coming soon. Um they're going to provide free power to customers. And so like you're never going to have to pay your power bill ever again. Now again, the big data center level we know the hyperscalers have offered a lot of money to communities and they're like we don't want it. But I don't know. I think this is an opportunity uh in particularly in new construction. But in the short run for retrofit they're mostly going to CNI locations like telecommunications deployments which is kind of kind of what you said. >> Okay, let's wrap up with some post election analysis. I think by now everyone is really sick of the phrase blue tsunami. Maybe we should be talking about I don't know, the green undertow, something like that. >> No, Stephen. >> We saw >> [laughter] >> Oh my. >> We saw a couple of big shifts on the state level. You know, people are waking up to the importance of local electricity regulation. Um we saw PUCs move in a clean energy friendly direction in certain states. New crop of governors were elected with a more expansive view on leveraging DERs and influencing utility regulation. has said he's working with many of those incoming governors. So I'm just curious from your like now that we've had some time to digest the election any storylines emerging for you as ones to watch? Um Jim, what are the most consequential ones for you right now? >> I mean certainly I mean everyone's eyes seem to be on on you know on Texas which you guys have talked about before and I think Governor you know so elect is still putting her team together Um, and they're being [clears throat] pretty tight-lipped from what I understand, uh, in terms of what their intentions are. Um, so I think there's a little bit of wait and see. There there's some indications that uh, Jigar, I'm curious your perspective and Carolyn, given where you are, that, um, it may not be as sort of as negative on the data center front as may, uh, have, you know, been talked about during here during the election. I think that to me is the big question. In some of these moderate states or not even moderate states that well, until a few weeks ago we thought of as not moderate at all, uh, where you have governors that are going to have to govern to the middle, it's true that people don't like data centers, but it's also true that unions and trades and others like to build things and and understand the economic development benefits of of building data centers. So to me it's can you change the the the the compact? What's the we talked about this earlier. What's the new way forward and can the governors in some of these states like Texas, because it's such an important one, can can they say this is we're going to do it differently and here's how we're going to do it, but then keep moving forward, you know, with certain amount of development? Because as Carolyn mentioned too earlier, if the alternative is the big campuses go overseas and all we're doing is distributed like I'm all I'm for distributed. We that's that's been the subject of the episode, but there's some limitations on what we can do, right, on the distributed side. So we still I think want to build those bigger data centers, but we just need to build them in a different way and take a deep breath and figure out what is going to be socially acceptable. So I think that, you know, Texas is interesting. Um, I'm actually maybe the most interested in places that where you've got the trifectas on the Democratic side. >> I think six states? >> yeah, like of the Wisconsin or a Michigan like how where do they actually go? Like how anti whatever, utilities, anti data centers, um, pro clean energy, which again, I would like not to see all those things kind of framed in that way. >> Yeah. >> Um, I think that's a big question for me. >> And also, can they get beyond 100% clean energy mandates, right? How creative will they get on the clean energy side rather than going back to um >> Yeah, but I also think you know, affordability is so important everywhere that everyone's going to have to look at it in in that context. I think the Arizona election, by the way, the last commission like undid their energy efficiency resource standard, right? Just killed all efficiency funding in Arizona. I would like to think that this new commission's going to go in a slightly different direction. Um, so my eyes are on that on Arizona in that case as well. what do you think? >> So I think that when you think about where the election went, a lot of the voters who voted for the 457 new state legislators around the country um were Steve Bannon and Tucker Carlson followers. And so I think that when you think about how broad this coalition is, it's not really a clean energy coalition. It's more of a god damn it, we kept telling you to focus on cost of living, now freaking do it, right? And that's why I think utilities are in the crosshairs cuz they have not proposed anything that will get rates to inflation or lower, and so it will be imposed on them. I think a lot of it's going to be grid utilization, a lot of it's going to be demand flexibility, load flexibility, a lot of the things that we've talked about. I think on the data center side, almost every one of these governors ran on a moratorium. So there's almost nothing they can do except to provide some sort of safe harbor number, but like it is impossible for Governor-elect Acton in Ohio to come out when there's like I think it was 40 out of 41 county ballot initiatives basically are banning data centers above 25 megawatts, right? And so like there's no way that she can now say, psych, like here's another gigawatt data center, right? And so I just think that there's a level of understanding that everyone needs. Like I just think most people have not sat down I think with the election results and realized that we're in a whole new world, right? This is not modify your previous position slightly for this moment. It's you know, you have to show in visible ways that you care deeply about the affordability crisis that we sit in today. And that's not solar wind, that's not this and that. That's just people like they don't care about AI versus China. Nobody cares about AI versus China, especially after all of like Black October and the AI the Anthropic S1. Like let them all burn to the ground. No one cares. >> Well, judging from the debate over the permitting bill, I don't think progressive environmentalists have have internalized that new world. All right, Caroline, you've had, you know, a week and a half, almost two weeks to really think about the election. You run policy for a major corporation. What have you what do you what questions do you still have? What have you figured out? >> I don't know that I have any more questions and that have been that have already been articulated. I think that where I am focused is actually less on the policies and the regulations and more on what are the commercial structures that solve the political moment, right? And so I think that we as an industry have a tendency to go shop and lobby and defend our own book, whether your book is renewables or your book is thermal or your book is storage or whatever it is. And you can have a few trade groups that present a bridge against, you know, renewable general or clean general, left general versus, you know, thermal on the left or thermal on the other side and stuff. And I I don't think that's going to work anymore. Um so what I'm focused on and what my team is focused on right now and is being informed by the policy team is like, what are the integrated commercial solutions that are going to work? How do you look at upgrades in the natural gas space, but, you know, combine that with virtual power at the residential space? How do you how do you make it easier to solve all governor's problems at once as opposed to going and, you know, arguing your piece of the political pie? And I think the companies that go and argue their piece of the political pie, and I will say that is 99% of all companies in this space, whether you are a supplier, uh you know, third party or utility, we all just sort of go and argue our book are um I think if we do that, it's going to be very unproductive and we'll end up with some very aggressive and potentially populist limiting um legislation. And what we what I don't want to see is the energy community be tone deaf, not present innovative commercial opportunities, and we end up getting very short-term fixes that look politically um astute, but don't fix the market in the long run, right? And I think that's a big risk overall. And so where I'm focused mentally and where I sort of focus and focus the growth team and focus everyone over here is like, no, let's let's be the company that innovates on the commercial offering and integrate something that that speaks to all parts of the problem here. And if, you know, if we can do that as an industry, I think uh we could get some really great long-term change. If we can't, we're going to be fighting each other and we're going to get some pretty short-term aggressive um and potentially even regressive uh shifts in the market. >> Absolutely. Urgent moment of creative thinking. >> I think we're going to have to close it out there. Caroline Gohlin is the chief growth and policy officer of NRG. Thank you. Good to see you. >> Thank you, Stephen. >> Jigar Shah is the co-managing partner of Multiplier. Great to see you, my friend. >> Of course. >> And Jim Kapsis is the founder and CEO of The Ad Hoc Group. Great to see you, Jim. Thanks for joining us. >> Good to be here. Always fun to be with you guys. >> That's it for the show. Open Circuit is produced by Latitude Media. The show is edited by me, Sean Marquand, and Anne Bailey. You can find all of our episodes on Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcast. And you can get transcripts at latitudemedia.com. Check out all of our coverage there and sign up for our newsletter. And of course, you can get all of our episodes on Latitude Media's YouTube channel. So if you like the show, make sure you hit subscribe. Thanks so much for being here. I'm Stephen Lacey. We'll catch you next week.

metadata.title: Biggest Challenges in India’s Battery Storage Market Explained | BESS Podcast
metadata.author: SAUR ENERGY
metadata.shortDescription:
In this podcast, the Saur Energy team — Prasanna Singh (Group Editor) and Manish Kumar (Deputy Editor) — discuss the key challenges facing the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) market in India.

As India rapidly expands renewable energy, battery storage is becoming critical for grid stability, peak power management and energy transition. However, the Indian BESS market still faces multiple hurdles in deployment, policy, cost and ecosystem development.

Watch the full podcast to understand the future of energy storage in India.

Topics covered in this episode

00:00 Introduction
01:10 What is Battery Energy Storage (BESS)?
03:20 Why India needs energy storage
06:00 Key challenges in BESS deployment
10:30 Policy & regulatory barriers
14:10 Cost and manufacturing challenges
18:30 Future of BESS market in India

metadata.title: Lockton Energy And Power Podcast | Scaling Success: Expanding A BESS Business
metadata.author: Lockton Europe
metadata.shortDescription:
What does it take to successfully scale a battery energy storage system (BESS) business in today's rapidly evolving energy market?

In this episode of the Lockton Energy & Power Podcast, Rufus Camm, Lockton Global Energy Account Director, sits down with Andrew Willis, Founder and CEO of Kona Energy, to explore the opportunities and challenges shaping the future of energy storage.

Whether you're a developer, investor, insurer or energy professional, this conversation offers valuable insights into the factors driving growth in the global energy storage market.

Lockton Companies LLP is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority, firm reference number 523069.

metadata.title: Fluence and the BESS Boom | The Future of Battery Storage Logistics
metadata.author: Project Cargo Professionals
metadata.shortDescription:
Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) have become one of the fastest-growing sectors in project cargo – but with larger, heavier equipment and increasingly complex deliveries, logistics providers face a whole new set of challenges.

Recorded live at Breakbulk Europe 2026, Markus Gemmel, Logistics & Operations Manager EMEA at Fluence, explains why BESS has become such a major opportunity for project logistics and what it takes to deliver these critical energy storage systems around the world. 

Fluence, one of the world's leading battery energy storage companies, is helping utilities and renewable energy developers deploy grid-scale storage projects across Europe, the Americas and Australia. Markus shares an insider's view of the logistics behind this rapidly expanding market, from breakbulk shipping and heavy transport through to remote project site delivery. 

In this Project Cargo Professionals interview:
• Why battery storage units are getting larger and heavier
• Design features driving the shift from containers to breakbulk shipping
• Competing with the wind industry for vessel space
• Delivering oversized battery systems to remote greenfield sites
• The challenges of transporting lithium-ion batteries safely
• Local manufacturing and European supply chains
• The growing shortage of specialist trailers and ADR-qualified drivers
• What logistics companies need to know to win BESS business

Whether you work in project cargo, heavy lift, renewables or energy logistics, this conversation offers valuable insight into one of the industry's fastest-growing cargo sectors—and why battery storage is becoming a defining opportunity for specialist logistics providers.

🎙️ Recorded live at Breakbulk Europe 2026 in Rotterdam, Netherlands.
👉 Connect with Markus on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/markus-gemmel-12b35a12/

Hosted by Luke King and produced by Prospect Communications, a specialist PR consultancy for the project cargo sector. For all business enquires relating to the podcast, email Luke@prospectcomms.co.uk and visit https://www.projectcargopros.com/ 

About Our Sponsor: UTC Overseas 
UTC Overseas is a global project logistics and freight forwarding specialist, providing tailored end-to-end solutions for complex cargo movements. With 43 offices across 22 countries and a trusted worldwide partner network, UTC delivers ocean, air, rail, inland transport and turnkey project logistics for customers around the globe. 
👉 Visit https://utcoverseas.com

metadata.title: 01 What is BESS and Why Poland
metadata.author: Jerzy Kuzminski
metadata.shortDescription:
The first episode of the English edition of Best in BESS — a podcast for international investors and developers exploring the Polish battery energy storage market.

Poland has one of the largest BESS pipelines in Europe. But navigating the local specifics — four DSOs, TSO requirements, evolving regulations, and administrative delays — requires experience. This podcast gives you the real picture.

🔋 In this episode:
00:00 Intro — what this podcast is about 
04:10 Why Poland? Pipeline, subsidies, and first projects going live 
07:29 What is BESS — the basics and why we need energy storage 
11:31 Cell manufacturers vs system integrators — a critical distinction 
13:00 Business models: stand-alone, C&I, and hybrid projects 
15:50 What's inside a battery container — components and hidden costs 
24:14 Development process overview 
27:13 The real challenges: administrative delays and investor overoptimism

📌 Who is this for? International investors, developers, EPC contractors, and energy professionals considering BESS projects in Poland.

🎙️ Host: Jerzy Kuźmiński
www.linkedin.com/in/kuzminski-jerzy

💼 Looking to enter the Polish BESS market? 
contact@greenedge-solutions.com
www.greenegde-solutions.com

🔔 Subscribe and turn on notifications for new episodes!

metadata.title: From EVs to BESS: Why capital is flowing to batteries – with Laurent Segalen and Stefan Mueller
metadata.author: The smarter E
metadata.shortDescription:
Recorded at two major European energy events – the SolarPower Summit in Brussels and the Battery Business & Development Forum in Frankfurt – this week’s episode explores why batteries have become one of the fastest-growing and most strategically important technologies driving the global energy transition.

We’re joined by two leading industry voices, **Laurent Segalen**, clean energy investor and host of the *Redefining Energy* podcast, and **Stefan Mueller**, Chief Operating Officer and co-founder of ENERPARC, to unpack how battery innovation is reshaping electric mobility, renewable energy markets, charging infrastructure, and the future of the electricity grid.

In the first conversation, Laurent explains why electrification is entering a new phase of acceleration. Falling battery prices, rapidly improving EV technology, and the economics of electricity versus fossil fuels are transforming the outlook for transport – from passenger vehicles to commercial fleets and heavy-duty trucks.

The discussion explores why electric trucks are becoming increasingly attractive for logistics operators, with lower operating costs, reduced maintenance requirements, and improving charging solutions strengthening the business case. Laurent also explains why stationary battery storage will be essential for supporting high-power EV charging, creating flexibility across the electricity system, and enabling higher shares of renewable energy.

In the second half of the episode, Stefan shares insights from the rapidly expanding European battery energy storage system (BESS) market, where grid-scale batteries, solar-plus-storage projects, and behind-the-meter solutions are opening new opportunities for utilities, investors, and energy-intensive businesses.

A major focus of the conversation is how the economics of battery projects are evolving – from merchant energy trading and balancing markets to peak shaving, energy-cost optimization, and helping companies access more reliable renewable power.

Stefan also explains what investors and financial institutions need to see for large-scale BESS projects to become bankable, and why clear regulation, grid access, and digital optimization will be key to unlocking the next wave of growth.

The episode also explores:
- Why battery costs are falling faster than many expected
- How EVs and BESS are changing the economics of energy
- Why electric trucks could scale faster than previous forecasts suggested
- The future role of hydrogen versus electrification in transport
- How AI and software will manage increasingly complex energy systems
- And why batteries could help us make far better use of existing electricity infrastructure

---
🔔 **Subscribe for more conversations on solar, storage, eMobility, and Europe’s energy transition**

https://www.linkedin.com/company/the-smarter-e/posts/?feedView=all

✉️ podcast@thesmartere.com
