But of course, you need to balance the whole system and that's to balance the system, you just have two way uh which are which are called space and time. Space are more interconnector, bigger grids, and time is batteries. And the great thing is what we've seen here is that the battery technology is now good, stabilized, understood, bankable, and these are the discussion we have had here. >> And when we're talking about e-mobility in particular, of course one of the major impacts of the conflict in the Middle East, the recent blockade of oil and gas supplies as well as on oil and on petrol fuels, diesel, kerosene, what kind of impact do you anticipate for the transportation sector? >> Well, it started to happen for EVs, and now it's going to happen for vans and trucks. And I think that the story of the electrification of transportation is the big story of the next 10 years. Because yes, people talk about data centers. Yes, people talk about heat pumps, you know, cooling, heating, but the main driver of electricity growth is going to be the electrification of transport. And now we reach a point in certain places, sector, but it's just getting bigger and bigger where you've got price parity, you've got fantastic product. And of course, it's a very very strong competition because the Chinese are ahead, and you'll have two type of Western companies, the one who adapt and the one who will go into oblivion because they did not turn the corner fast enough. >> But when we're talking about EVs or trucks and vans, like you say, these can tend to be relatively long investment cycles, can't they? That people might replace their car every 10 years or so, or if you're turning a fleet around, it could be a very lengthy process. Do you think this will be a slow process or a quick one? >> So, yeah, I understand that it takes 20 years to rotate a a car passenger fleet. I think for trucks can be faster, probably something like 10 years. Look, there's a lot of emotional connection of someone with his car, but when it comes to trucks, it's it's pure economics. So, the price of diesel is going to become higher. And if you look at the the economics of truck, it's not just the cost of the of of fuel, it's the cost of maintenance. And the cost of maintenance is very it's it's sometimes is bigger than the cost of the fuel. And the great thing with electric truck is that the the the the maintenance costs are are much lower. The big challenge we're going to have now is about charging. It's going to be charging depot, it's going to be fast charging, but there's a lot of progress being made right now. And the interesting thing is I'll just give you two stats. Um in China 2025 versus 2024, the amount of power sold through EV charging is up 45%. So that's going very very fast. If I look at Norway who was the first to electrify its fleet because now 100% of every new new car is electric, the main EV charging networks in 2025 for the first time made money. So it takes about 2-3 years for the charging infrastructure to start being a very profitable investment. And now of course it's going to accelerate. And it's true that there's you know it's always the chicken and egg, you know, do I need the the EVs to get the charging infrastructure or is it charging infrastructure to get EVs? But but now the the the the financial signals which are given to to investors is that now EV charging is a profitable um option within 18 months of uh you know ramping up the curve. So the I mean I'm extremely positive. It's going to happen. You can put whatever regulation you want, you know, to push it, to slow it. Just the technology is there and the economics are there. >> And when we're talking about trucks, why why do you think this kind of long haul or short haul haul or trucking logistics is particularly important in terms of the energy transition? >> Well, because if you look at um the oil consumption the 100 million barrel per day that we have where it's not very clear how much is stuck in almost and you know by the time this goes out nobody knows but roughly 50% of oil is for land transportation which is going to be 2/3 EV 1/3 truck then you've got 10% which is aviation then 10% that's maritime and 30% which is chemical if you look chemical oil is very hard to displace marine jet fuel I don't know but now you have 50% technically of the oil consumption which is at play and it's happening now. So this is you want to reduce emission you want to reduce CO2 you want to reduce you know climate change you want to enhance energy security electrification of transport with the economic sticks all boxes. >> And it will also be a big driver of demand for the renewable energy industry. And when we're looking at the charging of trucks of these big fleets and these charging depots as you say you know then we're talking about megawatt scale charging how big of a challenge is that? >> No it's not really a challenge because and that's the beauty of batteries you can put batteries everywhere you will have the batteries inside the truck but you will have the batteries at the EV charging level you will have the batteries at the distribution level at the transmission level batteries are fantastic you will have batteries you know 100 megawatts at the you know at the the level and then you will have, you know, tens of megawatts at the distribution levels and then inside the EV charging the station you're going to have two, three, four megawatts and which means that we can create all those buffers and people say always going to be redundant but that's how you make a strong system. So the people say oh every time we're going to charge our cars is going to rub the grid or just for city deliveries or or stupid or both. No, they have no idea what they're talking about. We will with batteries make sure that we can charge those those trucks and it's going to be okay. >> And the major reason for having the storage at these truck depots or layover sites where they may be charging is because then you don't you can get around the grid operator. You don't need that additional grid connection for this huge off-take from the truck. >> Exactly and and the truck will need to charge fast and then there's there's no truck for 10 minutes and then the new truck needs to charge fast again. I I know there's a lot of proponents of battery swapping but at the end of the day the less the less you move those parts in and out and the easier it's going to be. So I believe that a good organization of batteries from big to medium to small and as at the digital layer is just getting better and better and better will allow us to you know to charge those truck fast and without any trauma for the for for the for the system. >> And as an investor from the investor side is that where you see smart money going? Is there investor appetite for these battery systems, these charging systems for the electrification of of haulage? >> So what we're seeing is um the the great scale big batteries has really taken off phenomenally the past 3-4 years. So, investors starts to be very comfortable in 500 MW batteries and it seemed the bigger the better. But then, I have personally concentrated on behind the meter batteries and there's a lot of opportunities from 2 MW down to half a MW down to even 100 kW to replace diesel generators. So, the the beauty of the battery is that prismatic 314 amp hour CATL LFP cell and it's it's the LEGO. So, you know, you you you can put 200 of them and you get a small battery or you can put a thousand of them and you're going to get a medium-size battery or you can put, you know, tens Well, not tens of the you know, several thousand of them and you're going to get a bigger battery. It is the prismatic LFP cell. The first time I saw it was at uh the smarter E in Munich a few years ago and I said, "This is it. This is how we build an industry. It's so perfect. It's so scalable." Plus, because it's the same product, the price are going down and there's there's a better understanding. So, the moment I saw that battery, I said, "Okay, we have the tool now." >> Yeah, as soon as I I saw her passing by and I will love her till I die. I've heard that saying before, maybe that was your prismatic cell moment at the smarter E. But what about like hydrogen and alternative fuels? That was often being advanced for for trucking in particular, long haul. Any chance left? >> Well, I mean, some people may try. What I saw is that uh Cummins who was uh one of the biggest proponent just uh did a $500 million uh write-off their all hydrogen system. And those guys are they are the you know they are selling uh diesel trucks. I've seen um the CEO of Air Products who was the one of the most bullish uh proponent of hydrogen being fired by his board after losing 3 billion. So, if you want to lose money go to hydrogen. You're pretty sure you're going to burn it. >> But then how did we get this momentum behind hydrogen, particularly talking about um transportation? That was that was really pushed very hard. Green hydrogen for transportation. How did it build so much momentum? >> Well, it's very simple. Um the biggest energy lobbying group uh in Europe is Hydrogen Europe. They have a budget of 70 million euro per year to advertise whatever crap they want financed by the fossil fuel industry. So, yeah, you can create a hype with a nice PR budget, but the economics don't make any sense. You make a 2-minute calculation, you're going to realize that your green hydrogen is equivalent to a barrel of oil at $500. So, fine. $500. Right now the price is uh you know around the $100 per barrel used to be 60 a few months ago. So, the only question I always ask who's paying the difference between 100 and 500? Is it going to be the government, the taxpayer, the green premium, you name it? But everybody likes the idea, nobody wants to pay for it. So, yeah, whatever. >> Okay, well, turning back to the electrification of transport. >> I prefer. >> [laughter] >> Well, do do you really feel that it's it's one of the most exciting developments in in kind of the energy transition uh right at the moment on the back of this second energy crisis? >> Yeah, I Look, for me there are three very, very powerful dynamics. As I said, the first one is on is around grid management, which means digital space and time. The lot of development also in long-term transmission. And you know, and and just better grid management. So, that's what that's one. The second thing is going to be all the data centers because they're coming. There is a huge amount of money being put in the US, but it's coming here. Now, the question I always have is did we see that type of bubble before when 25 years ago they told us that the internet would consume half of the power in the world within a decade, which of course never happened? And I look at the a light bulb I just bought, a very, you know, very very bright light bulb, and it says 100 W. But in fact, if you look at the details, it says, "No, it's 8 W equivalent to the former 100 W." >> Yeah. >> So, the lighting we had a times 12 uh gain in energy efficiency, and maybe in chips we're going to have the same type of energy efficiency, and people are going to realize that those gigawatt data centers, you know, but you but but you but you never know. >> Mhm. >> So, data centers, yes, very exciting, but just in the US with the supply chain issue of getting your transformers, of you know, uh getting your turbines, only half of the data center announced this year are just being built right now. So, it's going to come, but I don't think it's going to be as big or as transformational as people think it will be. And of course, the last point is the whole eating heating, cooling, and people always say, "Yeah, but you know, high high temperature." It's okay, fine. Forget about high temperature. Low temperature, anything be below 200 C, we can electrify that and we will. >> Okay, which is particularly space heating and kind of some low temperature industrial processes. >> like food industry, hospitals. Yeah. We can cut half of our industrial gas consumption if we concentrate on simple existing technologies, which is low grade heat. If people want to do R&D on high grade heat, good for them. But I'm interested in what's investable. >> Sure, and what's possible today. And high grade heat, perhaps the smelting, can be left for our green hydrogen friends. >> Look, whatever they want. I don't care. I'm not touching it. >> [laughter] >> Laurent here at the Solar Power Summit 2026. Thank you very much for joining this Battery Podcast. >> My pleasure. >> [music] [music] >> Well, here at the Battery Business and Development Forum in Frankfurt, large scale batteries are very much in focus and it's really one of the hottest topics in the renewable energy sector more widely here in Germany, in Europe, but also globally to some some extent. And to discuss these developments, some of the challenges and the great opportunity, I'm joined by Stefan Müller, who is the Chief Operating Officer and co-founder at Enerparc. Thank you for joining this Battery Podcast. >> Also, thanks a lot to be here. >> Now, Stefan, what are your expectations for for batteries here in Germany? It really is um a huge amount of buzz about this segment of the industry. >> Yeah, but I think the good thing is there is something behind the bus. It's not only the bus word, it's really a lot of things are happening. The good thing on on the whole battery market is that it's quite fragmented and I think it's a good sign. So, you have really small batteries, 1 MW hour for own consumption, then you have behind the meter, you combine whatever car or even truck charging with battery systems which are then in the market. You have co-located, you have retrofit, you have standalone. And I think this wide variation gives us, I would say, a nice flowers of of the whole market. So, and I think this is this is at the moment it's not only buses, it's really something is happening there. >> So, there's lots of various opportunities for developers like that. >> It is. >> And what are your expectations in terms of volume? You know, we've heard about this huge pipeline that's kind of applied for awaiting for permission to connect to the grid. Can you talk about megawatts or gigawatts of capacity? >> I think we will we are in the same situation where we've been always with PV in the last few years. So, we always underestimate the market dynamics. For sure, there there we need to be a bit more conservative and also the banks need to be conservative, but on on the other hand, I see a lot of installations going on. As I mentioned before, fragmented market from C&I market to residential. We have also the batteries in the car. I mean, we have also a few speakers here in the round. They are 100 GW hours standing on the street and are not in use. So, and I think there are a lot of new opportunities coming up. But for us, the most important part is the very traditional way. We have a PV plant and we do retrofit with, I would say, green or gray energy batteries in the range of 5 to 10 MW hours. And this is, I would say, a very solid number. A lot of retrofit will happen, but in total, I I we will see, I think much, much more gigawatt hours connected in the next 12 to 24 months than we see on the paper right now. I'm pretty sure. And I speak about more gigawatts. >> Okay. And the opportunity, the needs that these batteries are fulfilling. We've heard about these very low capture rates. I think Germany last year was something like over 500 hours of negative prices in the power markets. That's really this volatility is really what's driving batteries. >> Correct. And this is the interesting part, no? So, on the other hand, you can be full merchant and and be active on on this. But on the other hand, you cannot do also peak shaving behind the meter. So, I think there are a lot of revenue streams which are interesting for a simple battery. And this is not only the the inertia stuff. This can be also secondary, primary. This can be peak shaving. This can be only green energy so that you balance the PPAs and can offer a base load PPA. I think this is what we haven't done before. And this is also super interesting. >> Okay. And that would be working with a big energy off-taker to be able to provide them with >> Correct. >> 24/7 clean power. >> Correct. Because very simple. I mean, we just signed also 65 gigawatt hours in 1 year of delivery for for a large steel many many many manufacturer. And in generally, they they don't like this up and down which we have. So, if we can balance this a little bit and we combine probably wind and solar and the big peaks or the big down times, we cover them with a with a smaller battery. This would be perfect. And then automatically, we are much more interested to work with these off-takers. So, I think to balance this with batteries, perfect. >> Well, there's a lot of discussion here in Frankfurt about the the revenue stack. So, so you've mentioned a number of different revenue streams. What is the appetite from investors and from lenders in terms of merchant revenue, right? That's that's the kind of arbitrage trading, buying high, uh low, selling high. Yeah. Um how much merchant risk can you take on as a developer? >> No, yeah. I think um at the moment this is probably a bit of a bit of misunderstanding. People see only the battery as one asset and you pump in energy and you take it out. But the reality is different. There is energy trader in the market and if he sees there is negative prices or positive or whatever, they try to make money with it. So you sell and buy, a bit like with in the normal stock exchange in Frankfurt. And finally, you have to deliver the energy sooner or later. And this is what you do then with the battery. So if you ask a trader how often he trades per day, he says probably 25 times per day. And if you ask him how often he use the battery, he said, "I don't know." So and this shows a bit there is a is a is a financial market and then there is a real energy market behind it. And both things are coming together now and I think this is super interesting right now. >> But you have to have the battery there to be able to deliver when >> Sure. If not, then for sure then you make a lot of loss. >> Okay. >> So I we call it we call it asset-backed trading, yeah. Um and this is then full on the on the merchant market. What happens if we have too many or even more batteries in the market in two, three, four, five years? For sure this has an impact and probably the peaks, negative peaks or even the high positive peaks will be much shorter, not so long anymore because there are batteries in the back who immediately can switch on and switch off. So the question is for how long merchant can work and this is the crystal ball. >> Yeah, well when you look at the at the market dynamics and how they are evolving, we've seen we've seen elsewhere, like in Australia is a great example where there was this crazy volatility in the market, but then the big batteries came in and they really addressed a lot of that volatility very effectively. >> so the best example, I mean we see Australia and the market is to be honest, we are also in Australia it's quite boring right now. But I think this is the way how it should work. Yeah, if there is volatility, this is what energy traders like. But if the volatility is gone, then they do something else. And I think Australia is a good example. You see also California as a good example. The duck curve, you shift things. This is more physical. And from the energy trading perspective, yeah, it's then not so interesting anymore. But I think this is the way how the market works. And I think it's good. >> And while there is volatility, there is an opportunity. How long that volatility lasts here in Germany? >> And this is the big question if you want to finance this project. No, and this is here the big elephant in the room. A lot of banks are here. I think partly official and partly unofficial to understand what are the market dynamics. And I think it's it's for sure it's not so easy. But the good thing is there is already a track record. So I think just now there is a presentation of of Entrix who are presenting the results of 2025, the revenue streams. And this is important for the for the financing. To get I would say a bit more clarity and to mitigate the risk in getting more information about what happened in the market in 25. And I think this gives them a good progress for 2026 and 27. For how long it last? This is the big question. >> Well, you mentioned Entrix and and there are a lot of young companies that are moving into this space because there is this dynamic market and and a lot of opportunity. What really excites you in terms of the young companies that are coming in and delivering these innovations to this emerging battery market? >> I think the world has changed dramatically. If we would have had a talk here whatever 2 years ago, complete different market scenario right now. AI is is everywhere. It's not also not only a buzzword anymore. And I think the the the whole programming activities, the data analyzing is very important. One single truth. So if you have a big data lake, how you get the right information out of it to make the right decision. And I think there are I would say traditional startups like Sonnen and Fenecon even more mobility house but even they they are big. Um, and there are a lot of new players in the market who probably can overtake these guys left and right. Uh, and everything is related more to to making a good forecast to making to deliver the right information for making a decision. So for example, we work with a handful of these partners in the market and they whatever one company has battery A other company has battery B and then we get the information on the dashboard and this gives us the right information to say should we sell now or should we wait for half an hour or even a day. And all these players in the market they are super interesting right now. >> Okay, so it's about distilling this complexity and and enabling traders like Enphase to make a decision to make a call. >> is. >> Okay. >> And I think there are even more and I've seen another players in the market with very new startups who try to analyze what we can do behind the meter. There is is I would say a bit of freedom where the DSO are happy about it. So for example, peak shaving, yeah. It's it's good for everyone. It's distresses the the grid on one hand. So it's good for the DSO and for the for the for the off-taker it is interesting they can save money. And I think there is a lot of playground behind and then just mentioned truck charging and you automatically if you want to make a truck charging system then you need really a 1 megawatt power and this means you need a battery behind it and you can use this battery when there is no charging. So and this is interesting and this is everything behind the meter. And I think there are also a lot of new startups who try to to analyze the everything what happens behind the meter and try to optimize this. And this is where where we are where we can distress the grid and this is interesting. And I've seen also here a few players who try to to to to bundle this. We call it pooling. That means a normal grid grid connection point when a PV plant is connected is utilized only by 25% or something, yeah? Um and in wind it is it's around probably a bit more than 30%. So, the the the German grid is quite bored, yeah? Um in 80% of the time. So, we we need to find a way how we can increase the utilization of each grid connection point and this can be even with data center off-takers, I don't know, a good mixture so that we can we do not have to to to to enhance the grid in the way how how it's how we expect it so that we that we can use the existing grid to put more energy into it. And this automatically means that the dynamic grid fees will go down, yeah? Because if you have the same grid and you utilize it more, then the cost will go down. And I think this is the main driver now. >> Yeah, and so the batteries can deliver a lot of efficiency to the system and we don't need to run quite so many poles and wires and use the poles and wires we have more effectively. But, how are these the grid operators then seeing batteries as an opportunity? Is it kind of friend or foe? There's a lot of discussion here about the challenges in getting a grid connection and negotiating an agreement with a distribution system operator. >> Yeah, I think in summary we can say if you have like in Germany 866 DSOs, it cannot be efficient. Point. So, that's it. >> Done. >> But, it's good and bad, yeah? And the bad thing is that we have 866 different formats, different PDF formats. One want to have even fax, other one email. So, I think this is the biggest challenge for us. But, on the other hand, existing player on the market like EnBW, we have around 400 sites in Germany. So, that means we are in touch with around 300 DSO quite often. So, and here we we can we are in direct contact with the DSO and they are very small DSOs. And if you have already an existing plant and to enhance it with I don't know, green battery or grey battery into the existing plan, then I think it works. And this is what they understand, you know, so because everyone knows utilization rate of one grid connection points is definitely to know, and battery can help to increase this. >> Well, we've also heard some kind of nightmare stories of where the grid connection agreement can change kind of while you're already developing your battery project. Do stories like that surprise you? >> mean it's there. I mean, we had here probably had it the the one guy of the grid agency. Uh he made a nice speech and he tried to explain this because he want to find a solution, but then somebody called, "Don't let him out." Uh and and this is this is really the issue right now. It's a lot of politics on one hand. Um unfortunately, it is politics, and then on the other hand, you have the grid agency in Germany. He tried to find a solution. But I mean, the the the other elephant in the room with FCA, so flexible connection agreement, but if you ask these 500 people who signed it already, probably you will not see a single hand, yeah? Because everyone, and this is the other side of the coin, every uh DSO or TSO development with the with their own FCA, and this is a disaster. This doesn't really work. And this is what we also in the market don't understand. I mean, in the UK, uh I think you have three DSOs, I don't know, whatever. So, and there is an FCA in the market. And in even in the Netherlands from TenneT, who is one of our TSO, there is one FCA in the market, which is fair, yeah? So, they really can take it and bring it to Germany. I don't know why they don't do it. It's really it's an issue. It's really a big issue. >> But are you confident that that this kind of issue will be overcome over time? We heard about learnings from trying to sign an FCA and working with grid operators in partnership. >> Yeah, I think this is a bit a bit the German style. You always try to make it perfect and and let a lot of things in in in into this contract, and then the contract get larger and larger and more complicated. And I always say the same sentence and probably you heard it. A project is only a project if you find a bank who finance it. So, and if the bank doesn't understand this FCA because it's too complicated and there are too many variables inside, then you don't get a financing. That's it. That's the the simple rule. And this is what politicians very often underestimate. >> Well, there was also a lot of discussion about grid fees that you have to pay the the system operator to connect to charge and discharge potentially. We've seen that that double taxation issue in Germany resolved, but how big a threat uh are grid fees to kind of project viability? >> Yeah. I mean, I always say we can accept everything. But it must be uh predictable. Yeah? So, if we see the about cost in social, it's the one time payment. It's one number and it's fixed and you paid in advance, boom, fine. If the system is running 5 years, 10 years, 20 years, it doesn't matter what you paid in the beginning. But if you have a flexible pre-payment, yeah, um then I think it's an issue and if this has no cap, then again the bank can come in and say, "Hey, come on. We we we are the lender. Uh we cannot predict and forecast the amount of flexible amount which you pay into the as as a grid fee into it." And then they don't finance it. Very simple. So, predictable is the key. >> We need certainty. >> Sure. >> Okay. >> And again, it's we the banks, no? So, and this is the most important part. And we hope that this really understands the grid agency. And this is the I think they are on the way to get it because there's also a group of banks who are talking to each other in one association and they speak to the grid agency and they speak to the politicians as a only as an enabler. They are not lobbyist or whatever. They only say, "If you do this, then we do not finance." That's it. >> Well, and it's a powerful voice to have at the table. >> is. >> And it's good to see it behind battery energy storage here at the BBD F Stefan Müller, uh the COO of Enerpark. Thank you very much for joining the smarterE >> Thanks a lot. >> And thank you for watching here today in Frankfurt. This podcast is a Climate Copy production. Nicole Schäfer is our producer and graphic designer. Ina Gößen, Wolfgang Weicht, and Peggy Häuser-Ziele from Solar Promotion support on coordination and marketing. And Matthew Denney is our editor. Be sure to follow, like, and subscribe on YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or wherever you found us. Get in touch with feedback, comments, or suggestions at podcast@thesmartere.com. And we're now less than 2 weeks away from The smarter E 2026 at Messe München. We'll be recording a special series of the podcast at the event, so keep an eye out for the pod crew. I'm Jonathan Gifford, and thanks for joining me on another episode of The smarter E podcast.

metadata.title: West Texas Land is Perfect for Data Centers, Says LandBridge Founder
metadata.author: Cool Vector
metadata.shortDescription:
David Capobianco's company, LandBridge, owns 270,000 surface acres in West Texas, and he's pleased to explain why the land's profitability has tripled in three years. The reason has to do with data centers. 

LandBridge is a publicly traded affiliate of Five Point Energy, of which Capobianco is CEO. The company's share price is being carefully watched by investors looking for evidence of a new paradigm in land ownership. Acreage once used primarily for ranching or energy extraction in the Permian Basin is now seen as ideal for data centers. 

In an wide-ranging interview with Cool Vector, Capobianco details the attractive features of his "powered land" in the Delaware sub-basin, spanning West Texas and New Mexico: it sits on top of the lowest-cost natural gas in North America, it has plentiful produced and brackish water for cooling, it is proximate to good fiber connectivity and carbon sequestration resources, and it is governed by an exceptionally friendly Texas regulatory regime. 

What's more, the Delaware land is far away from any population center, removing community apprehension as a barrier to development. 

LandBridge's surface acreage is "open for business," says Capobianco, meaning any potential digital infrastructure partner can expect rapid support in the development of data centers, including proprietary water infrastructure developed by LandBridge, which processes some 4 million barrels of water daily across the Permian. Cooling capabilities have become more and more critical as new technology, such as Nvidia's Blackwell chips, runs hotter and hotter. 

Capobianco describes the opportunity for renewable energy in the Permian as important but not sufficient on its own. Because hyperscalers are locked in an "existential" battle for data center development, the more consistent energy provided by bountiful West Texas natural gas is in high demand. He says the only renewable energy capable of fully powering a data center is nuclear. 

He also details the business plan of LandBridge, which makes money from land leases as well as power margins and some mineral rights. Capobianco predicts well-suited land in the Permian and elsewhere will "re-rate" now that investors recognize a net new source of revenue in the form of digital infrastructure. 

Says Capobianco: "The need is great, the race is on."

metadata.title: The Grid Can't Keep Up — So Data Centers Are Building Their Own Power!
metadata.author: The Clean Energy Edge Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Data centers need massive amounts of electricity. But what happens when the power grid can't keep up?

With AI and cloud computing driving electricity demand higher, data-center developers are facing a growing challenge: getting enough reliable power when they need it.

And there's another controversy. Should homeowners and businesses have to pay higher electricity bills to support these massive facilities?

Some states are introducing restrictions, special electricity rates, and policies encouraging data centers to supply more of their own power.

Meanwhile, developers are exploring alternatives to waiting years for utilities to deliver the electricity they need.

In this episode of the Clean Energy Edge Podcast, Russ explores:

- Why data centers are increasingly considering their own power generation.
- How states and utilities are responding to growing electricity demand.
- Why solar and battery storage could play a major role in powering these facilities.
- How new approaches to building utility-scale solar, including the Maverick system, could help accelerate deployment while reducing field labor and making better use of available land.

Natural gas, solar, battery storage, and other technologies all have roles to play. The challenge is developing reliable, cost-effective solutions that can be built fast enough.

Data centers aren't just changing how much electricity America needs. They're changing how we're going to produce and deliver it.

For more information about the Maverick solar system and how NXTGEN can help evaluate large-scale solar opportunities, contact info@nxtgencleanenergy.com.

segments.text: There's a lot of controversy surrounding
data centers right now, and one of the
biggest concerns is that they're driving
up electricity costs for the rest of us.
Think about this. You've got companies
investing billions of dollars in massive
data centers that can consume as much
electricity as a small city. And
somebody has to pay for the new power
plants, the transmission lines, the
substations, and other infrastructure
needed to support them. So, here's a
question. Should homeowners and
businesses be paying higher electric
bills to help support these massive
facilities?
And here's another problem that's
challenging how these data centers are
being developed. The electric grid, it
simply can't keep up with how quickly
they want to build.
And that's leading to something pretty
interesting. Instead of waiting years
for utilities to deliver the electricity
they need, some data center developers
are looking at bringing their own power.
And in some places, state governments
are starting to push them in that
direction. Let's get into it.
Look at what's happening around the
country. In New York, Governor Kathy
Hochul announced a one-year moratorium
on permits for new hyperscale data
centers in July 2026, along with a
proposal to have data centers generate
their own electricity or pay more to use
the grid. Here in Ohio, regulators have
approved special electricity rates
requiring large data centers to make
long-term financial commitments. That's
helping to protect existing customers
from paying for infrastructure they may
never fully use. And other states and
communities are considering restrictions
as concerns grow over electricity cost,
water usage, and grid capacity. The
message is pretty clear. If you're going
to build a massive data center, you need
a plan to power it, and the rest of us
shouldn't be picking up that tab.
But regulation is only part of the
story. The other issue is time. We've
talked in previous episodes about how
long it can take to connect new power
projects to the electric grid. Now,
imagine you're developing a
multi-billion dollar data center. You've
got the land, you've got customers,
you've got financing, and then the
utility tells you it could be years
before it can deliver the amount of
electricity you need.
What do you do?
Well, you can wait. You can look for
another location.
Or you can start exploring ways to
generate some or all of that electricity
yourself. And that's exactly the
direction some developers are moving.
We're talking about dedicated natural
gas generation, solar, battery storage,
and combinations of different
technologies. Sometimes that generation
is located directly on the data center
property. Other times, it might be
developed nearby and connected through
dedicated infrastructure. And in many
cases, the facility may still maintain a
connection to the utility grid. That's
an important distinction. Bringing your
own power doesn't necessarily mean
disconnecting from the grid. It means
having greater control over where your
electricity comes from and when it
becomes available.
So, what does it actually take to power
one of these facilities?
Well, let's say you're developing a data
center that needs several hundred
megawatts of electricity. That's a
serious amount of power, and this is
where I think solar and battery storage
have a tremendous opportunity.
Large-scale solar can generate
substantial amounts of electricity,
while battery storage allows you to
store some of that energy and use it
when it's needed most.
Together, they can reduce how much
electricity a data center needs to
purchase from the grid. It can help
manage peak demand and provide greater
flexibility. And unlike natural gas
generation, solar projects aren't
waiting years for gas turbines to become
available.
That doesn't mean solar and batteries
alone will necessarily power massive
data center around the clock. You still
need to evaluate the facility's
electricity demand, the storage
requirements, and whether additional
generation or a grid connection is
required. But here's what I think is
important. Instead of waiting for the
utility to provide all that electricity,
data center developers have an
opportunity to take greater control of
their power supply. And solar and
battery storage, that's a major part of
the solution.
And this brings me to something else I
think the industry needs to consider.
If data centers are going to start
developing more of their own generation,
how quickly can we actually build it?
Because there's not much benefit in
bringing your own power if it takes just
as long to develop and construct as
waiting for the utility.
This is where I think we need to start
looking at different approaches to
building large-scale solar.
At NextGen, we're working with a system
called Maverick. It's a
factory-assembled solar array designed
to dramatically reduce the amount of
field labor required to build large
solar projects.
Rather than assembling thousands of
individual components in the field, much
of that work is completed before the
system ever arrives on site. The result
is faster deployment, less field labor,
and the ability to generate more
electricity from a given amount of land
compared with traditional solar designs.
And think about why that matters for
data center developers. Land, it can be
expensive. Construction schedules are
critical, and the sooner you can bring
generation online, the sooner you can
start using that electricity.
Because if speed is the problem, we
should be looking at solutions that can
actually help us build faster.
So, here's where I think this is
heading. Data centers aren't going away.
AI, cloud computing, and the growing
demand for digital infrastructure are
going to continue driving the need for
electricity.
But the days of assuming the utility
will simply deliver hundreds of
megawatts whenever a developer needs it,
that's coming to an end. States are
becoming more concerned about protecting
existing electricity customers.
Utilities are struggling to keep up with
requests for new capacity. And
developers are starting to recognize
that having a reliable power strategy is
just as important as having the land and
financing. That's going to create some
tremendous opportunities for companies
that can develop and build generation
faster, more efficiently, and at a
competitive cost.
And maybe that's the bigger story here.
Data centers aren't just changing how
much electricity America needs, they're
changing how we're going to produce and
deliver it.
Think about it. We'll catch you next
time.

metadata.title: Energy Insights: A Conversation between ERCOT and PJM leaders
metadata.author: ERCOTISO
metadata.shortDescription: The 2025 ERCOT Innovation Summit opening panel was a candid conversation between ERCOT President and CEO Pablo Vegas and PJM President and CEO Manu Asthana about the rapid load growth the country is experiencing and what the future state of the grid looks like. Moderated by ERCOT SVP and COOO Woody Rickerson.

metadata.title: Powered Land Explained: The Race for Energy Infrastructure
metadata.author: Schneider Electric
metadata.shortDescription:
On this episode of the Renewable Roundup, Russell Reading speaks with Kenny Schoolcraft of Zeigo Network about “Powered Land” — land that comes bundled with grid access or interconnection privilege. Kenny explains what Powered Land means, why it’s suddenly in high demand, and how it shortens development timelines and reduces execution risk for data centers, renewables and investors.



They discuss how market differences (ERCOT, PJM, MISO, CAISO, etc.) shape the value of powered land, why transmission and interconnection queues are the current bottleneck, and how hyperscalers and corporates are adapting their strategies to secure quick, reliable power.

metadata.title: Why PJM is looking at the Texas grid
metadata.author: Texas Energy & Power
metadata.shortDescription:
ERCOT made a choice years ago that most of the country is now reconsidering. Texas runs an energy-only market with no capacity payments, connects generation through connect-and-manage, sorts out delivery in dispatch, and pushes interconnection risk onto developers. That design is a big part of why Texas has added generation faster than any other U.S. grid.


PJM, the operator for much of the eastern U.S., is now weighing whether to move in that direction. A white paper from the operator describes a shift from managing surplus to managing scarcity as data center demand outruns new supply. The paper lays out three pathways: long-term bilateral contracts, differential reliability standards for new loads, or an ERCOT-style tilt toward an energy and ancillary services market with a smaller role for capacity. The scale is large in both regions. ERCOT is now considering roughly 445 gigawatts of large-load interconnection requests against an 85-gigawatt system, while in PJM, one Dominion territory alone projects 70 gigawatts of new demand against a 24-gigawatt peak.


On this episode of the Energy Capital Podcast, Joshua Rhodes talks with Josephus Allmond, Virginia’s chief energy officer, about what separates the two grids and what PJM can take from the Texas model. Allmond points to ERCOT’s interconnection speed as the clearest lesson, given PJM’s projected 700 days from queue to agreement before construction even starts.


He also points to the state line, where borrowed fixes hit a wall. Virginia’s State Corporation Commission requires large customers to pay a generation charge for 14 years, even when a data center builds its own power. A load that sources its own generation, Allmond says, ends up “paying their own way and then turning around and paying Dominion.” The conversation works through:


* ERCOT versus PJM structure, energy-only and connect-and-manage against PJM’s capacity market and consensus-driven stakeholder process, and why one moves faster.


* PJM’s three pathways, and how the energy-market tilt is the one Allmond reads as closest to ERCOT.


* The large-load tools, controllable load resources, and behind-the-meter generation in Texas, and the Virginia charge that makes the same moves uneconomic.


* Interconnection speed, ERCOT’s developer-risk model against PJM’s roughly 700-day queue.


What PJM borrows from ERCOT, and what it refuses to give up, will shape how fast the East Coast grid can serve the load now lining up.
